content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 1: Short title, commencement and application

Q: Who is liable for punishment under the Indian criminal code for offences committed outside India?
A: Any person liable under Indian law to be tried for an offence committed beyond India will be dealt with as if the act was committed within India. The law also applies to any citizen of India outside the country, any person on an Indian-registered ship or aircraft, and anyone committing an offence targeting an Indian computer resource from outside India. [Source: Section 1, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, commencement and application

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 1: Short title, commencement and application

Q: What does Section 1 of BNS 2023 cover regarding jurisdiction?
A: Section 1 of BNS 2023 establishes the title, commencement date, and jurisdictional application of the Act. It states that every person in India is subject to this code, and extends its reach to Indian citizens globally, people on Indian-registered ships or aircraft, and individuals abroad targeting Indian computer resources. [Source: Section 1, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, commencement and application

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 1: Short title, commencement and application

Q: If an Indian citizen commits a murder outside the borders of India, can they be tried in India?
A: Yes. If an Indian citizen commits a murder in any place outside and beyond India, they can be tried and convicted of murder in any place in India where they may be found. [Source: Section 1, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, commencement and application

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 1: Short title, commencement and application

Q: What conditions must be met for a foreigner outside India to be prosecuted under Indian criminal law?
A: A person in a place outside and beyond India can be prosecuted under Indian law if they commit an offence that targets a computer resource located in India. [Source: Section 1, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, commencement and application

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 1: Short title, commencement and application

Q: Are there any groups or laws explicitly exempted from the application of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
A: Yes, nothing in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita affects the provisions of any Act punishing mutiny and desertion of officers, soldiers, sailors, or airmen in the service of the Government of India, nor does it affect any special or local law. [Source: Section 1, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, commencement and application

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 1: Short title, commencement and application

Q: When an act committed outside India is deemed an offence under this code, how is it treated legally?
A: The act committed outside India is treated in the exact same manner as if such act had been committed within India, making the person liable to be dealt with according to the provisions of this code. [Source: Section 1, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Short title, commencement and application

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: How are definitions treated under the Indian criminal code?
A: The definitions section provides specific meanings for various terms used throughout the Act to ensure consistent interpretation. These definitions apply unless the context requires otherwise. [Source: Section 2, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What is Section 2 of BNS 2023 about?
A: Section 2 of BNS 2023 contains the definitions of key terms used throughout the Sanhita. It establishes the legal meaning of specific words to ensure uniform understanding across all subsequent provisions. [Source: Section 2, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: If a term is defined in the definitions section but used in a different context later in the law, how should it be interpreted?
A: The terms defined in this section carry their specified meanings throughout the Act unless a contrary intention appears from the specific context in which they are used later. [Source: Section 2, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What is the primary requirement for a term's definition to apply to a specific provision?
A: The definition applies universally across the Act, provided that the context of the specific provision does not indicate a contrary intention. [Source: Section 2, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: Is there any limitation to the application of the definitions provided in this section?
A: Yes, the definitions apply generally, but they are limited by any contrary intention that may appear from the context of a specific provision where the term is used. [Source: Section 2, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 2: Definitions

Q: What is the legal effect of a word being defined in this section?
A: The legal consequence is that the defined word must be interpreted strictly according to its provided meaning everywhere it appears in the Act, overriding general dictionary definitions, unless context dictates otherwise. [Source: Section 2, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Definitions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 3: General explanations

Q: How does Indian criminal law interpret offences committed jointly by multiple people with a shared intention?
A: When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of those persons is held liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone. [Source: Section 3, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: General explanations

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 3: General explanations

Q: What does Section 3 of BNS 2023 establish regarding criminal liability and joint acts?
A: Section 3 of BNS 2023 provides general explanations for interpreting the code. It establishes that every penal provision is subject to general exceptions, that words referring to acts extend to illegal omissions, and that individuals acting with a common intention or intentionally cooperating in a criminal act are equally liable. [Source: Section 3, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: General explanations

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 3: General explanations

Q: If two jailors take turns guarding a prisoner and both intentionally omit to give him food, causing his death from starvation, what is their liability?
A: Both jailors are guilty of murder because they knowingly cooperated in causing the prisoner's death by illegally omitting to furnish him with food during their respective times of attendance. [Source: Section 3, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: General explanations

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 3: General explanations

Q: Under what condition is an individual liable for a criminal act committed by multiple people requiring specific criminal knowledge?
A: Whenever an act is criminal only because it is done with a specific criminal knowledge or intention, each person who joins in the act is liable only if they joined with that specific knowledge or intention. [Source: Section 3, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: General explanations

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 3: General explanations

Q: Do definitions of offences explicitly state that children under seven cannot commit them?
A: No, the definitions of offences do not expressly state this. However, they must be understood subject to the general exception that nothing is an offence if done by a child under seven years of age. [Source: Section 3, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: General explanations

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 3: General explanations

Q: What is the legal consequence if an offence is committed partly by an act and partly by an illegal omission?
A: The law treats causing an effect partly by an act and partly by an omission as the exact same offence as if it were caused entirely by an act or entirely by an omission. [Source: Section 3, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: General explanations

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 4: Punishments

Q: What types of punishments can be awarded to offenders under Indian criminal law?
A: Offenders can be punished with death, imprisonment for life, rigorous or simple imprisonment, forfeiture of property, fine, and community service. [Source: Section 4, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishments

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 4: Punishments

Q: What does Section 4 of BNS 2023 list?
A: Section 4 of BNS 2023 lists the various punishments to which offenders are liable under the Sanhita. These include death, life imprisonment, two types of imprisonment (rigorous and simple), forfeiture of property, fine, and community service. [Source: Section 4, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishments

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 4: Punishments

Q: If an offender is sentenced to imprisonment, what form must the labor take if it is rigorous?
A: If an offender is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment, the imprisonment must involve hard labour. [Source: Section 4, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishments

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 4: Punishments

Q: What are the two specific descriptions of imprisonment recognized as punishments?
A: The two descriptions of imprisonment recognized are rigorous imprisonment, which involves hard labour, and simple imprisonment. [Source: Section 4, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishments

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 4: Punishments

Q: Are there any alternative forms of punishment besides imprisonment and death listed in this section?
A: Yes, the section also lists forfeiture of property, fine, and community service as valid punishments. [Source: Section 4, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishments

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 4: Punishments

Q: What is the consequence for an offender regarding their assets under the prescribed punishments?
A: One of the possible consequences for an offender is the forfeiture of their property or the imposition of a monetary fine. [Source: Section 4, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishments

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 5: Commutation of sentence

Q: Who has the authority to change or commute a criminal sentence under Indian law?
A: The appropriate Government, which is either the Central Government or the State Government depending on the offence, has the authority to commute any punishment to another punishment without the offender's consent. [Source: Section 5, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commutation of sentence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 5: Commutation of sentence

Q: What does Section 5 of BNS 2023 state about commuting a sentence?
A: Section 5 of BNS 2023 explains that the appropriate Government can commute any sentence to any other punishment under the Sanhita without needing the consent of the offender, in accordance with the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. [Source: Section 5, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commutation of sentence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 5: Commutation of sentence

Q: If a person is sentenced to death for an offence against a law relating to the executive power of the Union, who decides whether to commute the sentence?
A: In cases involving a sentence of death or an offence related to the executive power of the Union, the Central Government acts as the appropriate Government and decides on the commutation. [Source: Section 5, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commutation of sentence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 5: Commutation of sentence

Q: What condition must be met regarding the offender's agreement when a government decides to commute their sentence?
A: The government may commute the punishment without requiring the consent of the offender. [Source: Section 5, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commutation of sentence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 5: Commutation of sentence

Q: Is the State Government able to commute sentences for all types of offences?
A: No, the State Government is only the appropriate Government for offences against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends. [Source: Section 5, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commutation of sentence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 5: Commutation of sentence

Q: What is the legal consequence of the government exercising its power under this section?
A: The original punishment prescribed to the offender is legally substituted with any other punishment under the code, as determined by the appropriate Government. [Source: Section 5, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Commutation of sentence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 6: Fractions of terms of punishment

Q: How are fractions of terms of punishment calculated under Indian criminal law?
A: When calculating fractions of terms of punishment, imprisonment for life is reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years. [Source: Section 6, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fractions of terms of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 6: Fractions of terms of punishment

Q: What is Section 6 of BNS 2023 about?
A: Section 6 of BNS 2023 deals with calculating fractions of terms of punishment. It explicitly states that for the purpose of calculating fractions, life imprisonment is considered equivalent to a twenty-year imprisonment term. [Source: Section 6, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fractions of terms of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 6: Fractions of terms of punishment

Q: If a court needs to impose a punishment that is exactly one-half of a life imprisonment sentence, how many years would that be?
A: It would be ten years, because the law requires imprisonment for life to be reckoned as equivalent to imprisonment for twenty years when calculating fractions. [Source: Section 6, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fractions of terms of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 6: Fractions of terms of punishment

Q: When does the rule treating life imprisonment as twenty years apply?
A: This rule applies specifically and only when there is a need for calculating fractions of terms of punishment. [Source: Section 6, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fractions of terms of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 6: Fractions of terms of punishment

Q: Does treating life imprisonment as twenty years mean a life sentence automatically ends after twenty years?
A: No, the twenty-year equivalence is an exception created solely for the mathematical purpose of calculating fractions of terms of punishment, not for determining the actual duration of a life sentence. [Source: Section 6, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fractions of terms of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 6: Fractions of terms of punishment

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section for judges calculating partial sentences?
A: The consequence is that judges have a fixed mathematical baseline of twenty years to use whenever they are legally required to calculate a fractional portion of a life sentence. [Source: Section 6, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fractions of terms of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 7: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

Q: Can a court decide the type of imprisonment if the law allows for either rigorous or simple?
A: Yes, when an offender is punishable with imprisonment that may be of either description, the sentencing Court has the authority to direct whether the imprisonment shall be wholly rigorous, wholly simple, or partly rigorous and partly simple. [Source: Section 7, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 7: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

Q: What power does Section 7 of BNS 2023 grant to a sentencing court?
A: Section 7 of BNS 2023 gives the Court the discretion to decide the nature of imprisonment when the law allows for either description. The Court can order the sentence to be entirely rigorous, entirely simple, or a mixture of both. [Source: Section 7, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 7: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

Q: If a person is sentenced to two years in prison for an offence that allows either type of imprisonment, can the judge order one year of hard labor and one year without?
A: Yes, the judge is fully competent to direct in the sentence that any part of the imprisonment shall be rigorous and the rest shall be simple. [Source: Section 7, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 7: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

Q: What is the legal condition required for a judge to split a sentence into partly rigorous and partly simple?
A: The condition is that the offender must be convicted of an offence that is explicitly punishable with imprisonment which may be of either description. [Source: Section 7, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 7: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

Q: Is the court forced to choose only one type of imprisonment for the entire duration of the sentence?
A: No, the court is not limited to a single type; it has the explicit option to decree that any part of the imprisonment shall be rigorous and the rest simple. [Source: Section 7, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 7: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

Q: What is the consequence of this section for the execution of a prison sentence?
A: The consequence is that the prison authorities must execute the sentence exactly as directed by the court, applying rigorous conditions for the specified period and simple conditions for the remainder, or applying one type for the whole term if so ordered. [Source: Section 7, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sentence may be (in certain cases of imprisonment) wholly or partly rigorous or simple

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 8: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

Q: What happens if a convicted person fails to pay the fine ordered by the court?
A: If an offender defaults on payment of a fine, the Court can direct that the offender suffer imprisonment for a certain term. This default imprisonment is in addition to any other imprisonment the offender is already sentenced to or liable for. [Source: Section 8, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 8: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

Q: Can you explain Section 8 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 8 of BNS 2023 outlines the rules regarding fines and default imprisonment. It states that unlimited fines cannot be excessive, sets maximum default imprisonment terms (up to one-fourth of the maximum offence term), and details proportional release upon partial payment of the fine. [Source: Section 8, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 8: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

Q: If a person is sentenced to a fine of one thousand rupees and four months' imprisonment in default, what happens if they pay seven hundred and fifty rupees after serving one month?
A: If seven hundred and fifty rupees are paid or levied at or before the expiration of the first month, the person will be immediately discharged as soon as the first month has expired, because the time served is proportional to the unpaid part of the fine. [Source: Section 8, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 8: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

Q: What is the maximum imprisonment term a court can impose in default of payment if the offence is punishable with both imprisonment and fine?
A: The term of imprisonment in default of payment shall not exceed one-fourth of the maximum fixed term of imprisonment for that specific offence. [Source: Section 8, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 8: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

Q: Are there limits on default imprisonment if the original offence is punishable only with a fine or community service?
A: Yes, in such cases, the default imprisonment must be simple, and it cannot exceed two months for fines up to five thousand rupees, four months for fines up to ten thousand rupees, and one year in any other case. [Source: Section 8, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 8: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

Q: If an offender dies before fully paying a fine, does the debt disappear?
A: No, the death of the offender does not discharge any property which would, after his death, be legally liable for his debts from the liability to pay the fine. [Source: Section 8, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Amount of fine, liability in default of payment of fine, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 9: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

Q: How is a person punished if their single criminal act is composed of multiple smaller actions that are also offences?
A: If an offence is made up of parts that are themselves offences, the offender shall not be punished with the punishment of more than one of such offences, unless the law expressly provides otherwise. [Source: Section 9, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 9: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

Q: What rule does Section 9 of BNS 2023 lay down for cumulative offences?
A: Section 9 of BNS 2023 establishes limits on punishment when an offence comprises several distinct offences, or falls under multiple definitions. It mandates that the offender cannot receive a more severe punishment than the Court could award for any one of those individual offences. [Source: Section 9, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 9: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

Q: If a man gives another person fifty strokes with a stick, can he be imprisoned for fifty separate instances of causing hurt?
A: No, he is liable to only one punishment for the whole beating, not a separate punishment for every single blow, even though each blow voluntarily caused hurt. [Source: Section 9, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 9: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

Q: Under what condition does the rule against multiple punishments apply when combined acts create a different offence?
A: The rule applies when several acts, where one or more would independently constitute an offence, combine to constitute a different offence. In this case, the punishment cannot exceed what the Court could award for any one of the offences. [Source: Section 9, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 9: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

Q: Is there an exception to the rule treating continuous physical blows against one person as a single offence?
A: Yes, if a third party interferes during the beating and the offender intentionally strikes that third party, the blow given to the third party is not part of the original act, and the offender is liable to a separate punishment for that distinct blow. [Source: Section 9, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 9: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

Q: What is the practical outcome for sentencing when an act falls under multiple separate legal definitions of an offence?
A: The outcome is that the Court is restricted from awarding a cumulative sentence; it cannot punish the offender more severely than the maximum punishment allowed for any single one of those defined offences. [Source: Section 9, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of punishment of offence made up of several offences

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 10: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

Q: How is a person punished if the court is certain they committed a crime but unsure exactly which specific crime from a list of possibilities?
A: If a judgment states that an offender is guilty of one of several specified offences, but it is doubtful which one, the offender must be punished for the offence that carries the lowest punishment among them. [Source: Section 10, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 10: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

Q: What does Section 10 of BNS 2023 say about doubtful judgments?
A: Section 10 of BNS 2023 dictates that when a judgment finds a person guilty of one out of several possible offences without certainty of which one, the court must apply the penalty for the offence with the lowest provided punishment, unless all carry the same punishment. [Source: Section 10, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 10: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

Q: If a judge determines a defendant is guilty of either simple theft or aggravated theft, but evidence doesn't clarify which, how should the judge sentence them?
A: The judge is required to punish the defendant for simple theft, assuming it carries the lowest punishment, because the law mandates applying the lowest penalty when there is doubt between specified offences. [Source: Section 10, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 10: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

Q: What is the primary condition required for this rule of applying the lowest punishment to take effect?
A: The primary condition is that the judgment must explicitly specify that the person is guilty of one of several offences, while simultaneously stating that it is doubtful exactly which of those specific offences they are guilty of. [Source: Section 10, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 10: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

Q: Is the court required to pick the lowest punishment if all the doubtful offences carry the exact same penalty?
A: No, the rule to pick the lowest punishment only applies if the same punishment is not provided for all the offences in question. [Source: Section 10, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 10: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

Q: What is the consequence of this provision for a defendant facing ambiguous charges?
A: The consequence is that the defendant receives the benefit of the doubt regarding severity, ensuring they cannot be subjected to a harsher sentence unless their guilt for that specific, harsher offence is proven beyond doubt. [Source: Section 10, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of person guilty of one of several offences, judgment stating that it is doubtful

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 11: Solitary confinement

Q: When can a court order solitary confinement for a convicted person?
A: A court can order solitary confinement when a person is convicted of an offence for which the Court has the power to sentence them to rigorous imprisonment. [Source: Section 11, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 11: Solitary confinement

Q: What does Section 11 of BNS 2023 outline?
A: Section 11 of BNS 2023 outlines the conditions and limits for solitary confinement. It allows courts to order solitary confinement for offenders facing rigorous imprisonment, subject to a maximum of three months overall, scaled according to the total sentence length. [Source: Section 11, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 11: Solitary confinement

Q: If an offender is sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for eight months, what is the maximum duration of solitary confinement the judge can order?
A: The maximum duration the judge can order is a time not exceeding two months, because the total term of imprisonment exceeds six months but does not exceed one year. [Source: Section 11, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 11: Solitary confinement

Q: What is the prerequisite condition for a court to even have the option of ordering solitary confinement?
A: The prerequisite condition is that the person must be convicted of an offence for which the Court under this Sanhita has the power to sentence them to rigorous imprisonment. [Source: Section 11, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 11: Solitary confinement

Q: Are there limits to how much solitary confinement can be ordered based on the total sentence length?
A: Yes, it cannot exceed one month for sentences up to six months, two months for sentences up to one year, and three months for sentences exceeding one year. [Source: Section 11, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 11: Solitary confinement

Q: What is the absolute maximum consequence in terms of solitary confinement time regardless of the sentence length?
A: The absolute maximum consequence is that solitary confinement cannot exceed three months in the whole, regardless of how long the total imprisonment sentence is. [Source: Section 11, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Solitary confinement

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 12: Limit of solitary confinement

Q: How must a sentence of solitary confinement be executed practically?
A: Solitary confinement must be executed in periods not exceeding fourteen days at a time, with intervals between those periods that are at least as long as the periods of confinement themselves. [Source: Section 12, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 12: Limit of solitary confinement

Q: Can you explain Section 12 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 12 of BNS 2023 imposes strict limits on the execution of solitary confinement to prevent continuous isolation. It mandates a maximum of fourteen days at a time with equal intervals between, and restricts it to seven days per month for sentences exceeding three months. [Source: Section 12, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 12: Limit of solitary confinement

Q: If a prisoner is serving a six-month sentence with solitary confinement ordered, can they be kept in isolation for fourteen consecutive days in the second month?
A: No, because when the total imprisonment awarded exceeds three months, solitary confinement cannot exceed seven days in any one month of the whole imprisonment. [Source: Section 12, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 12: Limit of solitary confinement

Q: What is the required condition for the duration of intervals between periods of solitary confinement?
A: The intervals between the periods of solitary confinement must be of not less duration than the periods of solitary confinement themselves. [Source: Section 12, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 12: Limit of solitary confinement

Q: Does the limit of solitary confinement change if the overall imprisonment sentence is longer than three months?
A: Yes, if the imprisonment awarded exceeds three months, an additional limitation applies: solitary confinement shall not exceed seven days in any one month of the whole imprisonment awarded. [Source: Section 12, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 12: Limit of solitary confinement

Q: What is the consequence of this rule for prison authorities?
A: Prison authorities must carefully schedule the solitary confinement to ensure it is broken up by mandatory intervals and never exceeds the strict 14-day or 7-day-per-month limits, depending on the total sentence length. [Source: Section 12, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Limit of solitary confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 13: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

Q: How are repeat offenders treated if they commit serious crimes multiple times under specific chapters of the law?
A: If a person previously convicted of an offence under Chapter X or Chapter XVII punishable by three years or more commits another offence under those chapters with a similar potential sentence, they face an enhanced punishment. [Source: Section 13, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 13: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

Q: What does Section 13 of BNS 2023 say?
A: Section 13 of BNS 2023 details enhanced punishment for repeat offenders. It states that someone previously convicted of an offence under Chapter X or XVII (punishable by 3+ years) who commits another such offence is subject to life imprisonment or up to ten years' imprisonment. [Source: Section 13, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 13: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

Q: If a man is convicted in India of a Chapter X offence punishable by four years, serves his time, and then commits a Chapter XVII offence punishable by five years, what sentence does he face for the second offence?
A: Because of his previous conviction, he is subject to enhanced punishment for the subsequent offence, meaning he can face imprisonment for life, or imprisonment of either description for a term extending to ten years. [Source: Section 13, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 13: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

Q: What conditions must be met regarding the previous conviction for this enhanced punishment to apply?
A: The previous conviction must be by a Court in India for an offence punishable under Chapter X or Chapter XVII of the Sanhita, and the offence must be punishable with imprisonment for a term of three years or upwards. [Source: Section 13, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 13: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

Q: Is this enhanced punishment applicable to repeat offences across all chapters of the Sanhita?
A: No, this specific enhancement explicitly applies only to offences punishable under Chapter X or Chapter XVII of the Sanhita. [Source: Section 13, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 13: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

Q: What is the legal consequence for a repeat offender under this section?
A: The consequence is that the maximum possible penalty for their subsequent offence is severely escalated to imprisonment for life, or imprisonment up to ten years, regardless of the original penalty for that second offence. [Source: Section 13, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enhanced punishment for certain offences after previous conviction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 14: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

Q: Is a person guilty of a crime if they act because they genuinely believe the law requires them to do so due to a factual misunderstanding?
A: No, an act is not an offence if it is done by a person who, by reason of a mistake of fact and not a mistake of law, in good faith believes himself to be bound by law to do it. [Source: Section 14, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 14: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

Q: What is Section 14 of BNS 2023 about?
A: Section 14 of BNS 2023 provides a general exception for acts done by a person bound by law or by a mistake of fact. It protects individuals from criminal liability if they are legally obligated to act, or if they act in good faith under a factual mistake believing they are legally obligated. [Source: Section 14, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 14: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

Q: If a court officer is ordered to arrest Y, but after due enquiry mistakenly believes Z is Y and arrests Z, has the officer committed a crime?
A: No, the officer has committed no offence because he arrested Z under a good faith mistake of fact, believing himself bound by law to execute the court's order. [Source: Section 14, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 14: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

Q: What two key conditions are required for a mistake to excuse an otherwise criminal act under this section?
A: The mistake must be a mistake of fact, not a mistake of law, and the person must have acted in good faith believing themselves to be bound by law. [Source: Section 14, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 14: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

Q: Does this protection apply if a person misunderstood the law itself rather than the facts of the situation?
A: No, the section explicitly states that the belief must be by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law. A mistake of law does not provide this protection. [Source: Section 14, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 14: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

Q: What is the consequence of this section for a soldier acting under the lawful orders of a superior officer to fire on a mob?
A: The consequence is that the soldier has committed no offence, as they are acting as a person who is bound by law to do the act in conformity with lawful commands. [Source: Section 14, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 15: Act of Judge when acting judicially

Q: Can a judge be held criminally liable for actions taken in their official judicial capacity?
A: No, nothing is an offence which is done by a Judge when acting judicially in the exercise of any power given to them by law. [Source: Section 15, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of Judge when acting judicially

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 15: Act of Judge when acting judicially

Q: Can you explain Section 15 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 15 of BNS 2023 provides absolute judicial immunity from criminal prosecution. It establishes that any act done by a Judge while acting judicially, in the exercise of their legal powers or powers they believe in good faith they possess, is not an offence. [Source: Section 15, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of Judge when acting judicially

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 15: Act of Judge when acting judicially

Q: If a judge orders the imprisonment of a person, but it is later found the judge technically lacked the jurisdiction for that specific order, is the judge criminally liable?
A: No, as long as the judge acted judicially and in good faith believed they were exercising a power given to them by law, their act is not an offence. [Source: Section 15, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of Judge when acting judicially

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 15: Act of Judge when acting judicially

Q: What is the primary condition for a judge to claim this immunity?
A: The primary condition is that the Judge must be acting judicially in the exercise of a power given by law, or a power they believe in good faith is given to them by law. [Source: Section 15, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of Judge when acting judicially

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 15: Act of Judge when acting judicially

Q: Does a judge have immunity for acts done outside their judicial role?
A: This exception implies that the immunity only covers acts done when acting judicially; acts outside their judicial capacity are not protected by this section. [Source: Section 15, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of Judge when acting judicially

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 15: Act of Judge when acting judicially

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section for the legal system?
A: The consequence is that Judges are protected from criminal liability for their rulings and judicial actions, allowing them to perform their duties and exercise their powers independently without fear of personal prosecution. [Source: Section 15, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of Judge when acting judicially

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 16: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

Q: Is someone criminally liable if they perform an act strictly following a court order?
A: No, an act done in pursuance of, or warranted by, a judgment or order of a Court is not an offence, provided the act is done while the judgment or order remains in force. [Source: Section 16, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 16: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

Q: What is Section 16 of BNS 2023 about?
A: Section 16 of BNS 2023 provides immunity for acts done pursuant to a judgment or order of a Court. It protects individuals executing court orders from criminal liability, even if the Court ultimately lacked jurisdiction, as long as they acted in good faith believing the jurisdiction existed. [Source: Section 16, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 16: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

Q: If an executioner carries out a death sentence based on a court's warrant, but it's later discovered the court had no legal jurisdiction to issue that warrant, is the executioner guilty of murder?
A: No, the executioner commits no offence, provided they acted in good faith believing that the Court had the proper jurisdiction to pass the judgment or order. [Source: Section 16, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 16: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

Q: What is a necessary condition regarding the court order itself for this protection to apply?
A: A necessary condition is that the act must be done whilst such judgment or order remains in force. [Source: Section 16, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 16: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

Q: Does this protection disappear if it is proven the court had absolutely no jurisdiction to issue the order?
A: The protection still applies notwithstanding that the Court may have had no jurisdiction, with the explicit exception that the person executing the order must have believed in good faith that the jurisdiction existed. [Source: Section 16, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 16: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

Q: What is the practical consequence of this section for law enforcement officials executing warrants?
A: The consequence is that officials are legally protected from criminal prosecution when executing active court orders, allowing them to perform their duties without having to independently verify the court's underlying legal jurisdiction. [Source: Section 16, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done pursuant to judgment or order of Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 17: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

Q: Is an act considered a crime if the person doing it is legally justified or mistakenly believes they are legally justified?
A: No, an act is not an offence if it is done by a person who is justified by law, or who, due to a mistake of fact and not a mistake of law, in good faith believes themselves to be justified by law in doing it. [Source: Section 17, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 17: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

Q: Can you explain Section 17 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 17 of BNS 2023 provides a defense for acts done by individuals who are justified by law or who act under a good faith mistake of fact believing they are justified. This protects people who intervene in situations reasonably appearing to require legal intervention, even if they are factually mistaken. [Source: Section 17, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 17: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

Q: If a man sees what looks like a murder in progress and tackles the apparent attacker to bring them to the police, but it turns out the tackled person was actually defending themselves, has the man committed assault?
A: No, he has committed no offence because he acted under a mistake of fact in good faith, believing himself justified by the law that allows citizens to apprehend murderers in the act. [Source: Section 17, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 17: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

Q: What kind of mistake must a person make for this section to provide a valid legal defense?
A: The mistake must be a mistake of fact made in good faith; the defense explicitly requires that it not be by reason of a mistake of law. [Source: Section 17, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 17: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

Q: Does this section protect someone who commits a crime because they misunderstood what the law actually allows?
A: No, the section explicitly excludes protection for a mistake of law. The belief of justification must stem from a factual misunderstanding of the situation, not a misunderstanding of the law itself. [Source: Section 17, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 17: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

Q: What is the consequence of this rule for citizens witnessing apparent crimes?
A: The consequence is that citizens are legally empowered and protected from criminal liability if they intervene in good faith to stop what reasonably appears to be a serious crime, even if their factual assessment of the situation turns out to be wrong. [Source: Section 17, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 18: Accident in doing a lawful act

Q: Is someone criminally responsible if they cause harm purely by accident while doing something entirely legal?
A: No, an act is not an offence if it is done by accident or misfortune, without any criminal intention or knowledge, provided it occurred while doing a lawful act in a lawful manner, by lawful means, and with proper care. [Source: Section 18, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accident in doing a lawful act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 18: Accident in doing a lawful act

Q: What does Section 18 of BNS 2023 cover?
A: Section 18 of BNS 2023 establishes the defense of accident in doing a lawful act. It states that accidental harm is not an offence if the action was inherently lawful, performed using lawful means, lacking criminal intent, and executed with proper care and caution. [Source: Section 18, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accident in doing a lawful act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 18: Accident in doing a lawful act

Q: If a man is legally chopping wood with an axe and the axe head suddenly flies off and kills a bystander despite the man taking proper care, is he guilty of a crime?
A: No, if there was no want of proper caution on his part, his act is excusable as an accident or misfortune and is not an offence. [Source: Section 18, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accident in doing a lawful act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 18: Accident in doing a lawful act

Q: What standard of care is required for an accidental harm to be legally excused under this section?
A: The lawful act must be done with proper care and caution for the accidental harm to be excused. [Source: Section 18, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accident in doing a lawful act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 18: Accident in doing a lawful act

Q: Is the defense of accident available if the underlying activity itself was illegal?
A: No, the defense is expressly limited; it only applies when the accident happens in the doing of a lawful act in a lawful manner by lawful means. [Source: Section 18, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accident in doing a lawful act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 18: Accident in doing a lawful act

Q: What is the legal consequence when all conditions of this section are met in a case of accidental harm?
A: The consequence is full exoneration; the act is deemed entirely excusable and does not constitute any criminal offence. [Source: Section 18, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Accident in doing a lawful act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 19: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

Q: Is an action a crime if it was done knowing it might cause harm, but purely to prevent a much worse disaster?
A: No, an act is not an offence if done without criminal intention, but rather in good faith to prevent or avoid other harm to person or property, even if the doer knew the act was likely to cause some harm. [Source: Section 19, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 19: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

Q: What principle does Section 19 of BNS 2023 establish?
A: Section 19 of BNS 2023 establishes the defense of necessity. It protects individuals who knowingly cause a lesser harm if they act without criminal intent and in good faith to prevent a greater, imminent harm to people or property. [Source: Section 19, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 19: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

Q: If a ship captain must deliberately steer into a small boat with two people to avoid a collision with a large boat carrying thirty people, is he guilty of a crime if he sinks the small boat?
A: No, if he alters course without intention to run down the small boat and in good faith to avoid danger to the larger boat's passengers, he is not guilty, provided the danger avoided was serious enough to excuse the risk. [Source: Section 19, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 19: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

Q: What factual question must be resolved to justify causing harm to prevent other harm?
A: It must be determined as a question of fact whether the harm to be prevented was of such a nature and so imminent as to justify or excuse the risk of doing the harmful act. [Source: Section 19, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 19: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

Q: Does this defense apply if the person had a hidden, malicious intention to cause the lesser harm while pretending to prevent the greater harm?
A: No, a crucial limitation is that the act must be done without any criminal intention to cause harm, and purely in good faith for the purpose of avoiding the other harm. [Source: Section 19, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 19: Act likely to cause harm, but done without criminal intent, and to prevent other harm

Q: What is the legal consequence for someone who pulls down a neighbor's house to stop a massive fire from spreading to the rest of the town?
A: The consequence is that the person is not guilty of any offence regarding the destruction of the house, provided the harm prevented was imminent and severe enough to excuse the act. [Source: Section 19, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 20: Act of a child under seven years of age

Q: Can a very young child be held criminally responsible for their actions under Indian law?
A: No, nothing is an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age. [Source: Section 20, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child under seven years of age

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 20: Act of a child under seven years of age

Q: What does Section 20 of BNS 2023 state about young children?
A: Section 20 of BNS 2023 states a rule of absolute legal immunity based on age, explicitly declaring that no act done by a child under seven years of age is considered an offence. [Source: Section 20, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child under seven years of age

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 20: Act of a child under seven years of age

Q: If a six-year-old child picks up a loaded gun and accidentally shoots someone, can the child be charged with manslaughter?
A: No, the child cannot be charged with any offence because the law explicitly dictates that acts done by a child under seven years of age are not offences. [Source: Section 20, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child under seven years of age

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 20: Act of a child under seven years of age

Q: What is the sole condition required to invoke the protection of this section?
A: The sole condition is that the child committing the act must be under seven years of age. [Source: Section 20, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child under seven years of age

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 20: Act of a child under seven years of age

Q: Are there any exceptions to this rule where a six-year-old might still be prosecuted for a particularly heinous crime?
A: No, there are no exceptions stated in this section; the immunity for a child under seven is absolute regardless of the nature of the act. [Source: Section 20, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child under seven years of age

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 20: Act of a child under seven years of age

Q: What is the legal consequence of an act committed by a toddler that would otherwise be a crime?
A: The consequence is that the legal system completely absolves the toddler of any criminal liability, treating the act as a non-offence. [Source: Section 20, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child under seven years of age

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 21: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

Q: Can a child between the ages of seven and twelve be held criminally responsible for an act?
A: A child above seven and under twelve is not guilty of an offence if they have not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of their conduct on that specific occasion. [Source: Section 21, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 21: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

Q: Can you explain Section 21 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 21 of BNS 2023 provides conditional immunity for children aged between seven and twelve years. It states that an act by such a child is not an offence if the child lacked the mature understanding necessary to comprehend the nature and consequences of what they were doing at the time. [Source: Section 21, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 21: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

Q: If an eleven-year-old child sets fire to a building as a prank, without understanding that it could destroy property or hurt people, can they be convicted of arson?
A: No, if it is proven that the child had not attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of setting the fire, they commit no offence. [Source: Section 21, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 21: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

Q: What factual determination must a court make to grant immunity to a ten-year-old child?
A: The court must determine whether the child had attained sufficient maturity of understanding to judge the nature and consequences of their specific conduct on that occasion. [Source: Section 21, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 21: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

Q: Does this section automatically excuse all criminal acts committed by any child under twelve?
A: No, it does not provide automatic immunity for children above seven. The immunity is conditional and depends entirely on the child lacking sufficient maturity of understanding. A mature child in this age bracket can still be held liable. [Source: Section 21, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 21: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

Q: What is the consequence for a mature eleven-year-old who fully understands that stealing is wrong and commits a theft?
A: Because the child possesses sufficient maturity to judge the nature and consequences of their conduct, they do not qualify for the protection under this section and can be held criminally liable for the theft. [Source: Section 21, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a child above seven and under twelve years of age of immature understanding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 22: Act of a person of unsound mind

Q: Is a person legally culpable if they commit a crime while suffering from a severe mental illness?
A: No, an act is not an offence if done by a person who, at the time of doing it, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that what they are doing is wrong or contrary to law, by reason of unsoundness of mind. [Source: Section 22, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 22: Act of a person of unsound mind

Q: What does Section 22 of BNS 2023 establish?
A: Section 22 of BNS 2023 establishes the legal defense of insanity. It excuses a person from criminal liability if, at the exact time the act was committed, unsoundness of mind made them incapable of understanding the nature of their act or recognizing that it was wrong or illegal. [Source: Section 22, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 22: Act of a person of unsound mind

Q: If a man suffering from severe delusions attacks a stranger, genuinely believing the stranger is a demon about to kill him, is he guilty of assault?
A: No, if his delusions constitute an unsoundness of mind that rendered him incapable of knowing that his act was wrong or contrary to law at the time he did it, he commits no offence. [Source: Section 22, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 22: Act of a person of unsound mind

Q: What is the critical timing requirement for proving unsoundness of mind under this section?
A: The critical requirement is that the incapacity must exist exactly at the time of doing the act. Past or subsequent mental illness is not sufficient to trigger this specific defense. [Source: Section 22, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 22: Act of a person of unsound mind

Q: If a person with a known mental illness fully understands that they are stealing a car and knows it is illegal, can they use this defense?
A: No, because despite having a mental illness, if they are still capable of knowing the nature of the act and that it is wrong or contrary to law at the time they do it, the defense does not apply. [Source: Section 22, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 22: Act of a person of unsound mind

Q: What is the legal consequence for an individual whose actions meet the criteria described in this section?
A: The consequence is that the individual is completely exempted from criminal liability for the act, as the law deems them incapable of forming the necessary criminal intent. [Source: Section 22, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 23: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

Q: Can severe intoxication serve as a defense against a criminal charge?
A: Yes, but only if the person was so intoxicated they couldn't know the nature of their act or that it was wrong, and crucially, the intoxicating substance must have been administered to them without their knowledge or against their will. [Source: Section 23, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 23: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

Q: What rule does Section 23 of BNS 2023 lay down regarding intoxication?
A: Section 23 of BNS 2023 establishes involuntary intoxication as a defense. It states that an act is not an offence if the person was incapacitated by intoxication, provided the intoxicant was given to them without their consent or knowledge. [Source: Section 23, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 23: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

Q: If someone secretly slips a powerful hallucinogen into a man's drink, and the man subsequently damages a storefront while completely unable to understand what he is doing, is he guilty of vandalism?
A: No, he commits no offence because he was incapable of knowing the nature of his act due to intoxication that was caused by something administered to him without his knowledge. [Source: Section 23, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 23: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

Q: What specific condition must be met regarding how the intoxication occurred for this defense to be valid?
A: The thing which intoxicated the person must have been administered to them without their knowledge or against their will. [Source: Section 23, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 23: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

Q: Does this defense apply to a person who gets blackout drunk voluntarily at a bar and commits a crime?
A: No, the defense explicitly requires that the intoxication be caused against the person's will or without their knowledge. Voluntary intoxication provides no protection under this section. [Source: Section 23, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 23: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

Q: What is the consequence of proving involuntary intoxication under this section?
A: The legal consequence is that the involuntarily intoxicated person is treated similarly to a person of unsound mind and is exonerated from criminal liability for acts committed while in that incapacitated state. [Source: Section 23, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act of a person incapable of judgment by reason of intoxication caused against his will

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 24: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

Q: How does the law handle crimes requiring specific knowledge when the offender was voluntarily drunk?
A: If an offence requires particular knowledge or intent, a voluntarily intoxicated person is liable to be dealt with as if they had the exact same knowledge they would have had if they had been completely sober. [Source: Section 24, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 24: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

Q: What does Section 24 of BNS 2023 establish regarding intent and intoxication?
A: Section 24 of BNS 2023 establishes a presumption of knowledge for voluntarily intoxicated offenders. It states that if a crime requires specific knowledge or intent, an intoxicated person is legally presumed to have the knowledge of a sober person, unless the intoxication was involuntary. [Source: Section 24, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 24: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

Q: If a man gets heavily drunk at a party of his own free will, then takes another guest's expensive watch, claiming later he was too drunk to know it wasn't his, can he be charged with theft?
A: Yes, because his intoxication was voluntary, the law will deal with him as if he had the same knowledge he would have had if sober, which includes knowing the watch belonged to someone else. [Source: Section 24, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 24: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

Q: Under what condition does the presumption of sober knowledge not apply to an intoxicated person?
A: The presumption does not apply if the thing which intoxicated the person was administered to them without their knowledge or against their will. [Source: Section 24, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 24: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

Q: Does this section automatically supply both the required intent and the required knowledge to a voluntarily intoxicated person?
A: The text explicitly states the person shall be dealt with as if he had the same knowledge as he would have had if sober, but it does not expressly state the same presumption applies to intent, leaving a slight distinction between imputed knowledge and imputed intent. [Source: Section 24, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 24: Offence requiring a particular intent or knowledge committed by one who is intoxicated

Q: What is the consequence of this section for a person trying to use voluntary intoxication as a defense against a charge like possessing stolen goods?
A: The consequence is that the defense will fail; the court will impute the knowledge that the goods were stolen to the offender just as if they were sober, stripping away the intoxication defense. [Source: Section 24, BNS 2023]
