Q: Is the abettor always punished the same as the main offender for every single crime in the code?
A: No, they receive the same punishment only if no express provision is made by the Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment. If the law explicitly assigns a different penalty for abetting a particular crime, that specific provision overrides this general rule. [Source: Section 49, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 49: Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment

Q: What is the consequence of this law for people who orchestrate crimes but let others do the dirty work?
A: The consequence is that the mastermind or facilitator cannot use their physical absence from the crime scene to escape full liability; they will face the same severe prison sentence or fine as the person who actually pulled the trigger or stole the money. [Source: Section 49, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of abetment if act abetted is committed in consequence and where no express provision is made for its punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 50: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

Q: What happens if you encourage someone to commit a crime with one specific intention, but they carry it out with a completely different intention in mind?
A: You will be punished with the punishment provided for the offence that would have been committed if the act had been done with your original intention, regardless of the different intention the actual perpetrator had. [Source: Section 50, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 50: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

Q: Can you explain Section 50 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 50 of BNS 2023 clarifies liability when the abettor and the perpetrator have different mindsets. It states that an abettor is punished based on their own intention or knowledge in instigating the act, not based on the differing intent of the person who actually commits it. [Source: Section 50, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 50: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

Q: If you hand a friend a weapon intending for them to merely threaten and scare someone, but your friend uses it with the intent to murder and succeeds, how are you judged as the abettor?
A: You would be punished for abetting the offence you intended (e.g., criminal intimidation or causing hurt), because you are punished based on the offence that would have been committed if the act had been done with your original intention, not the murderer's intention. [Source: Section 50, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 50: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

Q: What must differ between the abettor and the perpetrator for this specific section to determine the abettor's punishment?
A: The person abetted must do the act with a different intention or knowledge from that of the abettor. [Source: Section 50, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 50: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

Q: Can an abettor be held liable for a far more severe crime if the person they hired decides to go rogue and commit a worse crime with a more malicious intent?
A: No, the abettor is protected from the rogue intent of the perpetrator. They are punished with the punishment provided for the offence matching their own intention or knowledge and with no other. [Source: Section 50, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 50: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

Q: What is the consequence of this rule for the legal assessment of accomplices?
A: The consequence is that courts must independently evaluate the mens rea (guilty mind) of the abettor separate from the principal offender, ensuring accomplices are punished precisely for what they intended to happen, not for the independent psychological choices of the actual criminal. [Source: Section 50, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment of abetment if person abetted does act with different intention from that of abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 51: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

Q: If you encourage someone to commit a crime, but they commit a different crime instead, can you be held responsible for what they actually did?
A: Yes, you are liable for the different act as if you directly abetted it, provided the act done was a probable consequence of your abetment and was committed under its influence. [Source: Section 51, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 51: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

Q: What is the rule under Section 51 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 51 of BNS 2023 states that an abettor is liable when the person they abetted commits a different act than the one intended, provided the new act was a probable consequence of the original instigation or conspiracy. [Source: Section 51, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 51: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

Q: If a man instigates his friend to burn down a rival's house, and while burning it, the friend decides on his own to also steal some jewelry from inside, is the instigator guilty of abetting the theft?
A: No, the instigator is guilty of abetting the arson, but not the theft, because the theft was a distinct act and not a probable consequence of the burning. [Source: Section 51, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 51: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

Q: What conditions make an abettor liable for a different act than the one they initially encouraged?
A: The different act must be a probable consequence of the abetment, and it must have been committed under the influence of the instigation or in pursuance of the conspiracy. [Source: Section 51, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 51: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

Q: Does this mean an abettor is always responsible for every single thing the perpetrator does, no matter how unpredictable?
A: No, the abettor's liability is strictly limited by the proviso that the different act must be a probable consequence of the abetment. They are not liable for entirely unrelated or unforeseeable distinct acts. [Source: Section 51, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 51: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

Q: What is the consequence of this rule for people who provide weapons for a robbery?
A: The consequence is that if the robbers use those weapons to murder someone during the robbery, the person who merely provided the weapons can be held liable for the murder, as it is a probable consequence of an armed robbery. [Source: Section 51, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor when one act abetted and different act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 52: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

Q: Can an abettor be punished twice if the person they helped commits both the planned crime and an additional, related crime?
A: Yes, if the additional act constitutes a distinct offence from the abetted act, and both are committed, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences. [Source: Section 52, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 52: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

Q: What does Section 52 of BNS 2023 establish?
A: Section 52 of BNS 2023 establishes cumulative punishment for abettors. If an abettor is liable for a different act under Section 51, and that act is committed alongside the originally abetted act, the abettor can be punished separately for both distinct offences. [Source: Section 52, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 52: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

Q: If someone encourages a protestor to resist arrest by the police, and the protestor not only resists but also punches and severely injures the officer, what crimes is the instigator liable for?
A: The instigator is liable for both abetting the resistance of arrest and abetting the grievous hurt, assuming they knew that causing such hurt was a likely consequence of resisting the arrest. [Source: Section 52, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 52: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

Q: What determines if an abettor faces cumulative punishment rather than just a single punishment?
A: The different act committed must be in addition to the original act abetted, and it must constitute a distinct offence in the eyes of the law. [Source: Section 52, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 52: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

Q: Is the abettor automatically punished for the additional distinct offence even if they had no idea it might happen?
A: No, their liability for the additional offence depends on the rules of Section 51, meaning the additional act must have been a probable consequence of their abetment that they reasonably could have anticipated. [Source: Section 52, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 52: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

Q: What is the consequence of this section for individuals who incite riots?
A: The consequence is that inciters can be held cumulatively liable for a multitude of distinct offences committed during the riot (like property damage, assault, and arson), leading to significantly stacked prison sentences. [Source: Section 52, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 53: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

Q: If you hire someone to beat a person up, but they end up accidentally killing the victim during the beating, can you be charged with murder?
A: Yes, if you abetted the act with the intent to cause one effect (hurt), but it causes a different effect (death), you are liable for the different effect if you knew the act abetted was likely to cause it. [Source: Section 53, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 53: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

Q: How does Section 53 of BNS 2023 address unintended consequences?
A: Section 53 of BNS 2023 states that an abettor is liable for the actual effect caused by the abetted act, even if they intended a different effect, provided the abettor knew that the act was likely to cause the effect that actually occurred. [Source: Section 53, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 53: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

Q: A man instigates his friend to severely beat a rival with an iron rod, intending only to cause grievous hurt. The friend does so, but the rival dies from the injuries. What is the instigator's liability?
A: If the instigator knew that beating someone with an iron rod was likely to cause death, he is liable to be punished with the punishment provided for murder, even though he only intended grievous hurt. [Source: Section 53, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 53: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

Q: What key piece of knowledge must the abettor possess to be held liable for an unintended effect?
A: The abettor must have known that the act they abetted was likely to cause that different, unintended effect. [Source: Section 53, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 53: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

Q: What if the resulting effect was a complete, unforeseeable freak accident that the abettor did not know was likely?
A: If the abettor did not know that the act abetted was likely to cause that specific different effect, they would not be held liable for it under this section. [Source: Section 53, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 53: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

Q: What is the legal consequence of this rule for someone who abets violent crimes?
A: The consequence is that the abettor bears the risk of the violence escalating. They cannot hide behind a claim of limited intent if the severe outcome was a known and likely result of the violent act they instigated. [Source: Section 53, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of abettor for an effect caused by act abetted different from that intended by abettor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 54: Abettor present when offence is committed

Q: What happens to your legal status if you plan a crime and then physically show up at the scene while it is being committed?
A: If you would be punishable as an abettor while absent, but you are actually present when the offence is committed, the law deems that you have committed the offence yourself. [Source: Section 54, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor present when offence is committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 54: Abettor present when offence is committed

Q: What is the rule of presence outlined in Section 54 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 54 of BNS 2023 legally elevates an abettor to a principal offender. It states that whenever a person who would be liable as an abettor is physically present during the commission of the offence, they are deemed to have committed the act directly. [Source: Section 54, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor present when offence is committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 54: Abettor present when offence is committed

Q: If a woman provides the lockpicks for a burglary and helps plan it, and then stands inside the house watching her partner use the picks to steal a safe, is she just an abettor?
A: No, because she was present when the offence was committed, she shall be deemed to have committed the burglary herself, legally making her a primary offender rather than merely an abettor. [Source: Section 54, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor present when offence is committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 54: Abettor present when offence is committed

Q: What are the two requirements to elevate someone's status under this section?
A: The person must be someone who would be liable to be punished as an abettor if they were absent, and they must be present when the act or offence is actually committed. [Source: Section 54, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor present when offence is committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 54: Abettor present when offence is committed

Q: Does simply being present at a crime scene automatically make you a primary offender under this section?
A: No, you must also be someone who would otherwise be liable as an abettor (meaning you instigated, conspired, or aided). Mere innocent presence without any prior abetment does not trigger this section. [Source: Section 54, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor present when offence is committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 54: Abettor present when offence is committed

Q: What is the consequence of this deeming provision for the prosecution of accomplices?
A: The consequence is that prosecutors do not need to prove an accomplice directly committed the physical elements of the crime if they can prove prior abetment and physical presence; the law automatically treats them as if they committed the act. [Source: Section 54, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abettor present when offence is committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 55: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: How severely can you be punished if you try to hire a hitman to murder someone, but the hitman never actually attempts the murder?
A: If you abet an offence punishable with death or life imprisonment, and the offence is not committed, you can be punished with up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 55, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 55: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: What does Section 55 of BNS 2023 establish regarding uncommitted severe crimes?
A: Section 55 of BNS 2023 sets the punishment for abetting crimes punishable by death or life imprisonment when the crime is ultimately not committed. It provides a base penalty of up to seven years, which increases to up to fourteen years if any hurt is caused during the abetment. [Source: Section 55, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 55: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: A man instigates his brother to murder their uncle. The brother attacks the uncle but only manages to injure him before fleeing. The uncle survives. What is the instigator's liability?
A: Because the abetted offence (murder) was not committed, but an act was done that caused hurt in consequence of the abetment, the instigator is liable to imprisonment for up to fourteen years and a fine. [Source: Section 55, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 55: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: What specific severity of the intended crime triggers the application of this section?
A: The offence that was abetted must be an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life. [Source: Section 55, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 55: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: Does this seven-year penalty apply if the law has a specific, different punishment explicitly written for abetting that exact crime?
A: No, this punishment only applies if no express provision is made under the Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment. If a specific provision exists, it overrides this general rule. [Source: Section 55, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 55: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: What is the legal consequence of this section for failed assassination plots?
A: The consequence is that the conspirators face very serious jail time (up to 7 or 14 years depending on whether hurt was caused), ensuring that highly dangerous plots are severely punished even if the primary goal completely fails. [Source: Section 55, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 56: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: If you encourage someone to commit a crime that carries a prison sentence, but they back out, can you still be punished?
A: Yes, if you abet an offence punishable with imprisonment and it is not committed, you can be punished with up to one-fourth of the longest prison term provided for that offence. [Source: Section 56, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 56: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: What is Section 56 of BNS 2023 about?
A: Section 56 of BNS 2023 penalizes unsuccessful abetment. If a person abets an offence punishable with imprisonment but the crime isn't carried out, the abettor faces up to one-fourth of the maximum sentence, or one-half if the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant bound to prevent it. [Source: Section 56, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 56: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: A man tries to bribe a witness to give false evidence, but the witness refuses and tells the truth instead. Has the man committed a crime?
A: Yes, the man has committed the offence of abetment. Even though the witness did not give false evidence, the instigator is punishable under this section for the unsuccessful attempt. [Source: Section 56, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 56: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: What determines the maximum punishment an abettor can receive if the intended crime is not committed?
A: The base punishment extends to one-fourth of the longest term provided for the abetted offence, but it increases to one-half if either the abettor or the person abetted is a public servant whose duty is to prevent that offence. [Source: Section 56, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 56: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: Does this one-fourth penalty rule apply to every single crime that isn't successfully committed?
A: No, it only applies if no express provision is made under the Sanhita for the punishment of such abetment. If a specific law dictates a different penalty for a failed abetment, that specific law applies instead. [Source: Section 56, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 56: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: What is the consequence of this section for police officers who encourage citizens to commit crimes?
A: The consequence is severely enhanced liability. If a police officer abets a robbery, even if the robbery never happens, the officer faces up to one-half of the maximum sentence for robbery due to their duty to prevent it. [Source: Section 56, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 57: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

Q: Is the punishment more severe if you encourage a large crowd of people to commit a crime, rather than just one person?
A: Yes, whoever abets the commission of an offence by the public generally, or by any group exceeding ten persons, faces up to seven years of imprisonment and a fine. [Source: Section 57, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 57: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

Q: What does Section 57 of BNS 2023 address?
A: Section 57 of BNS 2023 addresses mass instigation. It prescribes a specific, severe penalty (up to seven years in prison) for anyone who abets the general public or a group of more than ten people to commit an offence. [Source: Section 57, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 57: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

Q: If a person puts up posters across a city urging a specific religious sect of thousands of members to attack a rival sect's procession, what offence have they committed?
A: By instigating a group of more than ten persons to commit a violent offence, the person has committed the offence of mass abetment defined in this section, regardless of whether the attack actually happens. [Source: Section 57, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 57: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

Q: What is the minimum threshold of people that must be targeted for this specific section on mass abetment to apply?
A: The abetment must be directed at the public generally, or at any number or class of persons exceeding ten in number. [Source: Section 57, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 57: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

Q: Does this section apply if you only abet exactly ten people?
A: No, the text specifies "exceeding ten". If you abet exactly ten people, or fewer, this specific section with its seven-year penalty does not apply, though general abetment laws still would. [Source: Section 57, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 57: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

Q: What is the consequence of this law for individuals who use social media to incite mass riots?
A: The consequence is that they can be swiftly prosecuted and face up to seven years in prison for the act of mass incitement alone, acting as a strong deterrent against weaponizing large crowds or the general public. [Source: Section 57, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetting commission of offence by public or by more than ten persons

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 58: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: Can you be punished for knowing about a plot to commit a major crime like murder, and actively hiding that information?
A: Yes, if you voluntarily conceal a design to commit an offence punishable by death or life imprisonment to facilitate the crime, or give false information about it, you can be imprisoned for up to seven years if the crime occurs. [Source: Section 58, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 58: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: What is the purpose of Section 58 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 58 of BNS 2023 criminalizes the active concealment of severe criminal plots. It punishes anyone who, intending to facilitate a crime punishable by death or life imprisonment, hides the plan (including using encryption) or spreads false information about it. [Source: Section 58, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 58: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: A man knows robbers plan to hit a bank on the east side of town. To help them, he calls the police and falsely reports that the robbery will happen on the west side. What is his liability?
A: The man is punishable under this section for making a false representation respecting the design of the dacoity with the intent to facilitate it, thereby misleading the authorities. [Source: Section 58, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 58: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: What specific intent must the person concealing the plot have to be found guilty under this section?
A: The person must act intending to facilitate, or knowing it to be likely that they will thereby facilitate, the commission of the offence. Mere passive knowledge without the intent to facilitate is not covered here. [Source: Section 58, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 58: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: What is the punishment if the person conceals the plot, but the police foil the crime and it never happens?
A: If the offence is not committed, the punishment is reduced to imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, along with a fine. [Source: Section 58, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 58: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

Q: What is the consequence of this section for accomplices who use encrypted messaging apps to hide terrorist plots?
A: The consequence is that the explicit mention of "use of encryption or any other information hiding tool" legally strips away digital anonymity; using these tools to conceal a deadly plot is a direct, punishable act of facilitation. [Source: Section 58, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 59: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

Q: What happens if a police officer knows about a planned robbery they are supposed to prevent, but they intentionally keep quiet about it to let it happen?
A: The officer commits a serious crime. A public servant who voluntarily conceals a criminal design they are duty-bound to prevent, intending to facilitate the crime, faces severely enhanced punishments depending on the severity of the planned crime. [Source: Section 59, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 59: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

Q: How does Section 59 of BNS 2023 deal with corrupt public servants?
A: Section 59 of BNS 2023 penalizes public servants who conceal criminal plots they have a duty to prevent. If they hide the design or give false information to facilitate the crime, they face up to half the maximum sentence if the crime occurs, or ten years if it's a life/death offence. [Source: Section 59, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 59: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

Q: An officer learns a gang plans to rob a jewelry store. He wants a cut of the money, so he deliberately omits this information from his reports. Is he guilty of a crime?
A: Yes, he has by an illegal omission concealed the existence of the design to commit robbery, intending to facilitate it. He is liable to severe punishment under this section for failing his legal duty. [Source: Section 59, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 59: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

Q: What specific relationship must the public servant have with the planned offence for this section to apply?
A: It must be an offence which it is their duty as a public servant to prevent. Not every public servant is duty-bound to prevent every crime. [Source: Section 59, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 59: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

Q: What is the maximum penalty for the public servant if the planned crime was punishable by death, but the crime never actually took place?
A: If the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment, the public servant can be punished with up to ten years in prison, regardless of whether the offence was ultimately committed or not. [Source: Section 59, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 59: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

Q: What is the consequence of this rule for law enforcement accountability?
A: The consequence is that officers cannot claim passive ignorance or mere negligence when they turn a blind eye to crimes; intentional silence or the use of encryption to hide plots makes them heavily liable as criminal facilitators. [Source: Section 59, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant concealing design to commit offence which it is his duty to prevent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 60: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: Is it a crime to help hide a plot for a lesser crime, like a standard theft or fraud, that only carries a prison sentence?
A: Yes, if you intend to facilitate a crime punishable with imprisonment, and you voluntarily conceal the plot or lie about it to help the criminals succeed, you can be punished. [Source: Section 60, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 60: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: What is the rule under Section 60 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 60 of BNS 2023 deals with concealing plots for offences punishable by standard imprisonment. It penalizes anyone who hides the design of such an offence to facilitate it, imposing up to one-fourth of the maximum sentence if the crime occurs, or one-eighth if it does not. [Source: Section 60, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 60: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: A security guard learns his friends plan to shoplift from the store he guards. To help them, he lies to the store manager about which aisles the security cameras are covering. What is his liability if they are caught before stealing anything?
A: Because he made a false representation to facilitate the offence, and the offence was not committed, he is liable to imprisonment extending to one-eighth of the longest term provided for that theft. [Source: Section 60, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 60: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: What actions constitute concealment under this section?
A: Concealment involves voluntarily hiding the existence of the design by any act or illegal omission, or making any representation which the person knows to be false respecting such design. [Source: Section 60, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 60: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: Can someone be punished under this section if they accidentally forgot to mention the plot, without any intention of helping the criminals?
A: No, the law explicitly requires that the person act intending to facilitate, or knowing it to be likely that they will thereby facilitate, the commission of the offence. Accidental omission is not sufficient. [Source: Section 60, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 60: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

Q: What is the consequence of this tiered punishment system for concealment?
A: The consequence is that the law proportionately ties the punishment of the facilitator to both the severity of the planned crime and whether the plan actually succeeded, ensuring fairness while still deterring the shielding of criminal conspiracies. [Source: Section 60, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing design to commit offence punishable with imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 61: Criminal conspiracy

Q: What is it called when two or more people agree to break the law together?
A: It is designated a criminal conspiracy when two or more persons agree with a common object to do an illegal act, or to do a legal act by illegal means. [Source: Section 61, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal conspiracy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 61: Criminal conspiracy

Q: How does Section 61 of BNS 2023 define a conspiracy?
A: Section 61 of BNS 2023 defines criminal conspiracy as an agreement between two or more people to commit an illegal act, or to use illegal means for a legal act. It also dictates that the punishment matches that of abetment for severe crimes, and specifies up to six months imprisonment for lesser conspiracies. [Source: Section 61, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal conspiracy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 61: Criminal conspiracy

Q: Two businessmen agree to artificially inflate stock prices using illegal insider trading methods, though the goal of making money is legal. Are they guilty of criminal conspiracy?
A: Yes, because they agreed with a common object to do an act which is not illegal by illegal means, their agreement constitutes a criminal conspiracy. [Source: Section 61, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal conspiracy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 61: Criminal conspiracy

Q: What is required to turn a mere agreement into a punishable conspiracy if the agreement is NOT to commit an actual offence, but just to use illegal means?
A: If the agreement is not to commit an offence, it only amounts to a criminal conspiracy if some act besides the agreement is done by one or more parties in pursuance thereof. [Source: Section 61, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal conspiracy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 61: Criminal conspiracy

Q: Can you be charged with conspiracy if the illegal act you agreed to do was just a minor stepping stone to your main, legal goal?
A: Yes, the law explicitly states it is immaterial whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of such agreement, or is merely incidental to that object. The agreement itself is still a crime. [Source: Section 61, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal conspiracy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 61: Criminal conspiracy

Q: What is the consequence of this definition for organized crime rings?
A: The consequence is that law enforcement can prosecute the leaders and planners of a criminal syndicate simply for making the agreement to commit severe crimes, even if they haven't personally carried out the underlying offences yet. [Source: Section 61, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal conspiracy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 62: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

Q: Can you be sent to jail if you try to commit a crime but fail?
A: Yes, whoever attempts to commit an offence and does an act towards its commission is punishable. If there's no specific punishment for the attempt, they face up to one-half of the maximum sentence provided for the actual offence. [Source: Section 62, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 62: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

Q: What is the general rule for attempts under Section 62 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 62 of BNS 2023 provides a general penalty for attempting crimes. If a person attempts an offence and takes an active step towards it, but fails, and no other law specifies the penalty for that attempt, they are punished with up to half the maximum term of the intended offence. [Source: Section 62, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 62: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

Q: A pickpocket reaches into a man's coat intending to steal his wallet, but the pocket is completely empty. Can the pickpocket be convicted of anything?
A: Yes, the pickpocket is guilty of an attempt to commit theft under this section because he did an act towards the commission of the offence, even though the theft was factually impossible due to the empty pocket. [Source: Section 62, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 62: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

Q: What are the two distinct elements required to be convicted of an attempt under this general section?
A: The person must attempt to commit an offence (or cause it to be committed), and in doing so, they must actually do any act towards the commission of the offence. [Source: Section 62, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 62: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

Q: Does this "half-sentence" rule apply to someone attempting murder?
A: Only if there is no express provision made by the Sanhita for the punishment of such attempt. Since attempted murder usually has its own specific section and punishment, this general half-sentence rule would not apply there. [Source: Section 62, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 62: Punishment for attempting to commit offences punishable with imprisonment for life or other imprisonment

Q: What is the consequence of this broad section for law enforcement?
A: The consequence is that it provides a universal safety net; police and prosecutors do not have to wait for criminals to successfully complete a dangerous crime before arresting them, as the mere active attempt is always criminalized. [Source: Section 62, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 63: Rape

Q: What specific physical acts constitute the crime of rape under Indian law?
A: Under clause (a), rape includes penetration of the penis to any extent into the vagina, mouth, urethra, or anus. Under clause (b), it includes inserting any object or body part into the vagina, urethra, or anus. Clauses (c) and (d) further include manipulating the body to cause penetration, or applying the mouth to the vagina, anus, or urethra, when done without valid consent. [Source: Section 63, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 63: Rape

Q: How does Section 63 of BNS 2023 define rape?
A: Section 63 of BNS 2023 provides a comprehensive definition of rape. It details the physical acts of non-consensual penetration (penile, object, or oral) and enumerates the seven circumstances that render consent invalid, such as coercion, deception, intoxication, or the victim being a minor. [Source: Section 63, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 63: Rape

Q: A man forces his way into a woman's home and, under threat of stabbing her, inserts a foreign object into her body against her will. Is this legally considered rape?
A: Yes, inserting any object into the vagina, urethra, or anus under the threat of hurt (which vitiates consent) clearly falls under the definition of rape in this section. [Source: Section 63, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 63: Rape

Q: How does the law define the quality of consent required to avoid a rape charge?
A: Consent means an unequivocal voluntary agreement where the woman, by words, gestures, or communication, expresses willingness to participate in the specific sexual act. [Source: Section 63, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 63: Rape

Q: Can a husband be charged with rape for non-consensual sexual intercourse with his own wife?
A: According to Exception 2 of this section, sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife is not rape, provided the wife is not under eighteen years of age. [Source: Section 63, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 63: Rape

Q: What is the legal consequence of a woman freezing in fear and not fighting back during an assault?
A: The legal consequence is that her lack of resistance cannot be used to prove she agreed to the act; the law explicitly provides that a woman who does not physically resist shall not by reason only of that fact be regarded as consenting. [Source: Section 63, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 64: Punishment for rape

Q: What is the minimum jail sentence a person can receive for committing a standard rape?
A: A person who commits rape shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years, and which may extend to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 64, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 64: Punishment for rape

Q: What does Section 64 of BNS 2023 outline regarding sentencing?
A: Section 64 of BNS 2023 outlines the severe punishments for rape. It sets a baseline minimum of 10 years for general rape, and mandates harsher sentences (minimum 10 years to remainder-of-life imprisonment) for aggravated rape committed by police, public servants, relatives, or those in authority. [Source: Section 64, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 64: Punishment for rape

Q: If a police officer takes a woman into his custody at the station house and commits rape against her there, what is his specific liability?
A: He is guilty of aggravated rape under sub-section (2) because he is a police officer committing the act in the premises of a station house on a woman in custody, making him liable for rigorous imprisonment of at least ten years up to the remainder of his natural life. [Source: Section 64, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 64: Punishment for rape

Q: What definition does the law provide to clarify the meaning of a life sentence for aggravated forms of rape under this section?
A: For aggravated rape under sub-section (2), imprisonment for life is explicitly defined to mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life. [Source: Section 64, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 64: Punishment for rape

Q: Do standard prison terms apply if a man rapes a woman knowing she is pregnant or suffering from a severe disability?
A: No, these acts are considered exceptions to the standard punishment and fall under aggravated rape in sub-section (2), which carries a harsher maximum penalty extending to imprisonment for the remainder of his natural life. [Source: Section 64, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 64: Punishment for rape

Q: What is the consequence of this section for individuals in positions of trust, like teachers or guardians?
A: The consequence is that they are held to a much stricter legal standard; abusing their authority to commit rape triggers the aggravated punishment clauses, reflecting the law's severe condemnation of exploiting power imbalances. [Source: Section 64, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 65: Punishment for rape in certain cases

Q: Is the punishment for rape different if the victim is a very young child?
A: Yes, raping a woman under sixteen carries a minimum of twenty years imprisonment. If the victim is under twelve years of age, the minimum is twenty years, extending to the remainder of natural life, and it can also be punished with death. [Source: Section 65, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 65: Punishment for rape in certain cases

Q: What specific scenarios does Section 65 of BNS 2023 address?
A: Section 65 of BNS 2023 provides the most severe punishments for the rape of minors. It mandates a minimum twenty-year sentence for raping a victim under sixteen, and allows for the death penalty if the victim is under twelve. [Source: Section 65, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 65: Punishment for rape in certain cases

Q: A man is convicted of raping an eleven-year-old girl. Besides life imprisonment, what other ultimate penalty might the judge impose?
A: Because the victim is under twelve years of age, the judge has the statutory authority under this section to sentence the perpetrator to death. [Source: Section 65, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 65: Punishment for rape in certain cases

Q: What specific financial obligation does this section place on the convicted offender?
A: The offender must pay a fine that is just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses and rehabilitation of the victim, and this fine must be paid directly to the victim. [Source: Section 65, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 65: Punishment for rape in certain cases

Q: Can a judge decide to sentence someone to only ten years in prison for raping a fourteen-year-old if they show remorse?
A: No, the law removes judicial discretion for lenient sentencing in these cases; it mandates rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall *not be less* than twenty years for a victim under sixteen. [Source: Section 65, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 65: Punishment for rape in certain cases

Q: What is the overarching consequence of this section regarding the state's stance on child sexual abuse?
A: The consequence is that the state classifies the rape of young minors among the most heinous crimes imaginable, elevating it to a capital offence and prioritizing the direct financial restitution of the victim's medical and rehabilitative needs. [Source: Section 65, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for rape in certain cases

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 66: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

Q: What is the punishment if a woman dies or is left in a vegetative state as a result of a rape?
A: The perpetrator shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a minimum of twenty years, extending up to the remainder of their natural life, or with the death penalty. [Source: Section 66, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 66: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

Q: What does Section 66 of BNS 2023 specify regarding extreme outcomes of rape?
A: Section 66 of BNS 2023 specifies the punishment for cases where an injury inflicted during the commission of a rape causes the death of the victim or leaves her in a persistent vegetative state. The penalty is a minimum of twenty years in prison, up to a natural life sentence or the death penalty. [Source: Section 66, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 66: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

Q: During a sexual assault, the attacker chokes the victim so severely that her brain is deprived of oxygen, leaving her in a permanent, unresponsive coma. What specific penalty does he face under this section?
A: Because he inflicted an injury during the rape that caused the woman to be in a persistent vegetative state, he faces rigorous imprisonment for at least twenty years, natural life imprisonment, or death. [Source: Section 66, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 66: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

Q: What specific legal standard defines the maximum non-lethal prison sentence under this section?
A: The maximum non-lethal sentence is imprisonment for life, which the section explicitly defines as imprisonment for the remainder of that person's natural life. [Source: Section 66, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 66: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

Q: Can the perpetrator escape the death penalty or life sentence if they didn't explicitly intend to kill the victim, but merely injured her during the rape and she died accidentally?
A: No, the statute does not require an explicit intent to kill. It only requires that in the course of the rape, the offender inflicts an injury which causes the death or vegetative state, making them strictly liable for the fatal outcome of their violence. [Source: Section 66, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 66: Punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of victim

Q: What is the consequence of this law for perpetrators who try to silence their victims through extreme physical violence?
A: The consequence is that elevating the violence to lethal or near-lethal levels (like causing a vegetative state) automatically exposes the perpetrator to the highest possible penalties in the justice system, including execution. [Source: Section 66, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 67: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

Q: Can a man be punished for forcing his wife to have sex with him if they are currently separated?
A: Yes, if a husband has sexual intercourse with his wife without her consent while they are living separately, he can be imprisoned for two to seven years and fined. [Source: Section 67, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 67: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

Q: What does Section 67 of BNS 2023 criminalize?
A: Section 67 of BNS 2023 criminalizes non-consensual sexual intercourse by a husband upon his wife when they are living separately (either under a legal decree or otherwise). It carries a punishment of two to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 67, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 67: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

Q: A couple has been informally living in separate houses for six months due to marital issues. One night, the husband visits and forces himself on her. Can he be charged under this specific section?
A: Yes, because they are living separately (whether under a decree of separation or otherwise) and the act was without her consent, he is liable to imprisonment of two to seven years under this section. [Source: Section 67, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 67: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

Q: Does this law only apply if the couple has a formal, court-ordered divorce or separation decree?
A: No, the law explicitly applies whether they are separated under a decree of separation or otherwise, covering informal, de facto separations as well. [Source: Section 67, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 67: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

Q: Are the acts constituting "sexual intercourse" under this section different from the general definition of rape?
A: No, the explanation clarifies that "sexual intercourse" in this section means any of the exact same physical acts mentioned in clauses (a) to (d) of the general rape definition in Section 63. [Source: Section 67, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 67: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation

Q: What is the legal consequence of this section regarding the marital rape exception?
A: The consequence is that while standard marital rape is an exception under Section 63, the law removes that marital immunity the moment the spouses begin living separately, protecting the bodily autonomy of estranged wives. [Source: Section 67, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 68: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

Q: Is it a crime for a boss or a jail warden to use their power to convince a subordinate or inmate to sleep with them, even if no physical force is used?
A: Yes, if a person in authority abuses their position to induce or seduce a woman under their charge into sexual intercourse, it is punishable by five to ten years in prison, even if it doesn't strictly amount to rape. [Source: Section 68, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 68: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

Q: What is the focus of Section 68 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 68 of BNS 2023 focuses on the abuse of power for sexual exploitation. It penalizes public servants, managers of institutions, and persons in fiduciary relationships who use their authority to induce or seduce women under their charge into sexual intercourse. [Source: Section 68, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 68: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

Q: A hospital manager uses his administrative power to heavily pressure a junior nurse into a sexual relationship by constantly hinting she will be fired if she refuses. Is this punishable under this section?
A: Yes, because he is on the management of a hospital and abused that position of authority to induce a woman in the premises to have sexual intercourse, he is liable to rigorous imprisonment for five to ten years. [Source: Section 68, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 68: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

Q: What specific types of relationships are covered under this abuse of authority statute?
A: The statute covers persons in a position of authority or fiduciary relationship, public servants, superintendents/managers of jails, custody places, or women's/children's institutions, and hospital management or staff. [Source: Section 68, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 68: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

Q: Can the perpetrator defend themselves by claiming the woman eventually agreed, so it wasn't technically rape?
A: No, this section explicitly covers situations where the sexual intercourse does "not amounting to the offence of rape." The crime is the abuse of authority to induce the act, making the technical presence of coerced "agreement" irrelevant to guilt under this section. [Source: Section 68, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 68: Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

Q: What is the consequence of this law for power dynamics in professional and institutional settings?
A: The consequence is that it legally recognizes that true consent is impossible when one party holds significant structural power over the other's livelihood or freedom, strictly criminalizing the exploitation of that power imbalance. [Source: Section 68, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 69: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

Q: Can a man be sent to prison for tricking a woman into sleeping with him by faking his identity or making a fake promise to marry her?
A: Yes, having sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means—such as hiding your identity or making a promise to marry without any intention of keeping it—can be punished with up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 69, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 69: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

Q: How does Section 69 of BNS 2023 address sexual deception?
A: Section 69 of BNS 2023 criminalizes sexual intercourse obtained through deceitful means or a false promise of marriage. If a man has sex with a woman by making a marriage promise he never intended to fulfill, or by using deceit like suppressing his identity, he faces up to ten years imprisonment. [Source: Section 69, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 69: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

Q: A man creates a fake profile online, lies about his name and religion, and promises a woman a lucrative job promotion at his non-existent company to convince her to sleep with him. What crime has he committed?
A: He has committed the offence of sexual intercourse by deceitful means, as the law explicitly defines deceitful means to include inducement by false promise of employment or promotion, and marrying by suppressing identity. [Source: Section 69, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 69: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

Q: What must be proven regarding a "promise to marry" for it to be considered criminal deceit under this section?
A: It must be proven that the man made the promise to marry the woman without any intention of fulfilling the same at the time the promise was made, merely using it as a ploy for sexual access. [Source: Section 69, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 69: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

Q: Is it a crime under this section if a man genuinely intends to marry a woman, they have consensual sex, but later they break up due to incompatible personalities?
A: No, because the section requires that the promise to marry be made without any intention of fulfilling the same. A genuine promise that later falls apart due to normal relationship breakdowns is not considered deceitful means. [Source: Section 69, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 69: Sexual intercourse by employing deceitful means, etc

Q: What is the consequence of this statute for men who use manipulative lies to obtain consent?
A: The consequence is that consent obtained through fundamental, identity-altering fraud or completely hollow promises of marriage is legally invalidated, making the sexual act a heavily punishable offence, even if it doesn't meet the traditional physical force criteria for rape. [Source: Section 69, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 70: Gang rape

Q: How severely are groups of people punished if they participate in a rape together?
A: When a woman is raped by a group or by people acting with common intention, each person faces a minimum of twenty years to natural life in prison. If the victim is under eighteen, the punishment is natural life or the death penalty. [Source: Section 70, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Gang rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 70: Gang rape

Q: What are the penalties for gang rape established in Section 70 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 70 of BNS 2023 sets extreme penalties for gang rape. For an adult victim, the punishment is a minimum of twenty years to life (natural life). For a victim under eighteen, the punishment is mandatory natural life imprisonment or the death penalty. [Source: Section 70, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Gang rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 70: Gang rape

Q: Three men plan to assault a seventeen-year-old girl. One holds her down while the other two commit the rape. What is the legal fate of the man who only held her down?
A: Because they acted in furtherance of a common intention, each of those persons (including the one holding her) shall be deemed to have committed the offence of rape and, due to her age, faces mandatory natural life imprisonment or death. [Source: Section 70, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Gang rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 70: Gang rape

Q: How does this law ensure that all participants in a gang rape are held equally responsible?
A: The law states that where a group acts in furtherance of a common intention, each of those persons shall be deemed to have committed the offence of rape, stripping away any defense of "I was just watching" or "I didn't actually penetrate." [Source: Section 70, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Gang rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 70: Gang rape

Q: Are there any lenient sentencing options for a participant who was pressured by the group into joining the gang rape of a minor?
A: No, the law allows no leniency or exceptions; if the victim is under eighteen, the statute mandates punishment of imprisonment for life (meaning the remainder of natural life) or with death for each participant. [Source: Section 70, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Gang rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 70: Gang rape

Q: What is the consequence of the financial provisions within the gang rape section?
A: The consequence is that the perpetrators are legally forced to bear the financial burden of the atrocity; any fines imposed must be just and reasonable to cover the victim's medical expenses and rehabilitation, and must be paid directly to her. [Source: Section 70, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Gang rape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 71: Punishment for repeat offenders

Q: What happens to a person who is convicted of rape more than once?
A: A repeat offender who has been previously convicted of rape or related extreme sexual offences, and is convicted again, shall be punished with natural life imprisonment or the death penalty. [Source: Section 71, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for repeat offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 71: Punishment for repeat offenders

Q: What does Section 71 of BNS 2023 mandate for recidivists?
A: Section 71 of BNS 2023 mandates severe enhanced penalties for repeat offenders of specific sexual crimes (Sections 64, 65, 66, or 70). A subsequent conviction under any of these sections requires a sentence of imprisonment for the remainder of natural life, or death. [Source: Section 71, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for repeat offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 71: Punishment for repeat offenders

Q: A man who served ten years for a rape conviction in his twenties is released and later convicted of participating in a gang rape. What is his mandatory minimum sentence now?
A: Because he has a previous conviction under Section 64 and is subsequently convicted under Section 70, he is a repeat offender and must be punished with imprisonment for the remainder of his natural life, or with death. [Source: Section 71, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for repeat offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 71: Punishment for repeat offenders

Q: What specific prior convictions trigger the application of this repeat offender statute?
A: The previous conviction must be for an offence punishable under section 64 (Rape), section 65 (Rape of a minor), section 66 (Causing death/vegetative state), or section 70 (Gang rape). [Source: Section 71, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for repeat offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 71: Punishment for repeat offenders

Q: Does this section apply if the person's first conviction was for sexual harassment under Section 75, and their second conviction is for rape under Section 64?
A: No, the first conviction must specifically be under Sections 64, 65, 66, or 70. A prior conviction for a lesser sexual offence like harassment does not trigger the mandatory life/death penalty of this specific section. [Source: Section 71, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for repeat offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 71: Punishment for repeat offenders

Q: What is the overarching consequence of this law for the criminal justice system's handling of serial rapists?
A: The consequence is a "two strikes" policy for severe sexual violence; the state permanently removes repeat offenders from society either by execution or by ensuring they die in prison, completely eliminating the possibility of a third offence. [Source: Section 71, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for repeat offenders

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 72: Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc

Q: Is it legal for a newspaper to publish the name or a photograph of a rape victim?
A: No, printing or publishing the name or any matter that makes known the identity of a victim of rape or related sexual offences is a crime punishable by up to two years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 72, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 72: Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc

Q: What prohibition is established by Section 72 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 72 of BNS 2023 strictly prohibits the disclosure of the identity of victims of specific sexual offences. Anyone who prints or publishes their name or identifying details faces up to two years of imprisonment, with only narrow, authorized exceptions allowed. [Source: Section 72, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 72: Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc

Q: A journalist writes an article about a sexual assault case and, while leaving out the victim's name, includes her exact workplace, job title, and neighborhood, making it easy for locals to identify her. Has the journalist broken the law?
A: Yes, the journalist has published "matter which may make known the identity" of the victim, which is an offence punishable under this section even if the actual name was withheld. [Source: Section 72, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 72: Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc

Q: Under what circumstances can the police authorize the publication of a victim's identity?
A: The officer-in-charge of the police station or the investigating officer can authorize publication in writing if they are acting in good faith for the purposes of the investigation (e.g., to track down kidnappers). [Source: Section 72, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disclosure of identity of victim of certain offences, etc

Q: If the victim of a sexual assault is deceased, can their family authorize the media to publish the victim's name to raise awareness?
A: Yes, if the victim is dead, the next of kin can authorize the publication in writing, but this authorization can only be given to the chairman or secretary of a recognized welfare institution or organization, not directly to general media. [Source: Section 72, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the consequence of this strict privacy law for the media and the public?
A: The consequence is that the law legally shields victims of sexual violence from social stigma and media harassment, ensuring that fear of public exposure does not deter them from reporting the crimes to the police. [Source: Section 72, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 73: Printing or publishing any matter relating to Court proceedings without permission

A: Section 73 of BNS 2023 restricts the reporting of court proceedings for sexual offences. It criminalizes the publication of any matter related to such trials without the Court's prior permission, aiming to protect the privacy of the proceedings, punishable by up to two years in prison. [Source: Section 73, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 73: Printing or publishing any matter relating to Court proceedings without permission
