Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 74: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

Q: What is the punishment for physically assaulting or grabbing a woman to intentionally disrespect or violate her modesty?
A: Assaulting or using criminal force against a woman with the intent to outrage her modesty, or knowing it is likely to do so, is punishable by one to five years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 74, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 74: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

Q: How does Section 74 of BNS 2023 address non-penetrative sexual violence?
A: Section 74 of BNS 2023 criminalizes assault or the use of criminal force against a woman with the specific intent (or knowledge of likelihood) to outrage her modesty. It sets a mandatory minimum sentence of one year, extending up to five years. [Source: Section 74, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 74: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

Q: A man purposefully gropes a woman on a crowded bus and then tries to run away. What specific crime has he committed under this section?
A: He has used criminal force against the woman, intending to outrage (or knowing it was likely to outrage) her modesty, making him liable for imprisonment of one to five years. [Source: Section 74, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 74: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

Q: What is the key mental element (mens rea) required to convict someone under this section, aside from the physical assault?
A: The prosecution must prove the offender acted intending to outrage her modesty, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty. [Source: Section 74, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 74: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

Q: Can a person be punished under this section if they accidentally bumped into a woman and knocked her over, without any sexual or insulting intent?
A: No, accidental force lacks the required intent or knowledge of likelihood to outrage her modesty. This section specifically targets intentional, modesty-outraging assaults. [Source: Section 74, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 74: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her modesty

Q: What is the consequence of having a mandatory minimum sentence for this offence?
A: The consequence is that judges cannot let offenders off with merely a fine or a few days in jail; a conviction guarantees at least one year of imprisonment, reflecting the seriousness with which the law views the violation of a woman's bodily autonomy and dignity. [Source: Section 74, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 75: Sexual harassment

Q: What specific behaviors legally count as sexual harassment, and can you go to jail for them?
A: Sexual harassment includes unwelcome physical contact, demanding sexual favors, forcing a woman to look at pornography, or making sexually colored remarks. Yes, physical/demand/pornography offences carry up to three years in jail, while remarks carry up to one year. [Source: Section 75, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual harassment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 75: Sexual harassment

Q: How does Section 75 of BNS 2023 define and punish sexual harassment?
A: Section 75 of BNS 2023 defines sexual harassment through four specific acts: unwelcome physical advances, demanding sexual favors, showing pornography against her will, and making sexually colored remarks. It prescribes up to three years imprisonment for the first three acts, and up to one year for the remarks. [Source: Section 75, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual harassment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 75: Sexual harassment

Q: A male boss constantly makes explicit, unwanted comments about a female employee's body and sex life, though he never touches her. Is this a crime?
A: Yes, making sexually coloured remarks constitutes the offence of sexual harassment under clause (iv), and he can be punished with up to one year in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 75, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual harassment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 75: Sexual harassment

Q: What are the three acts of sexual harassment that carry the harsher maximum penalty of three years?
A: The acts are: (i) physical contact and advances involving unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures, (ii) a demand or request for sexual favours, and (iii) showing pornography against the will of a woman. [Source: Section 75, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual harassment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 75: Sexual harassment

Q: Does this law criminalize consensual flirting or mutually acceptable sexual banter between coworkers?
A: No, the law specifically uses the words "unwelcome" for physical advances and "against the will" for pornography. Remarks must be sexually colored and, in the context of harassment, implicitly unwelcome to constitute an offence. [Source: Section 75, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual harassment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 75: Sexual harassment

Q: What is the legal consequence of separating "sexually coloured remarks" from the other harassment clauses?
A: The consequence is a tiered sentencing structure; the law acknowledges that while verbal harassment is a crime (punishable up to 1 year), physical advances, extortion of favors, and forcing pornography are significantly more severe violations requiring harsher maximum penalties (up to 3 years). [Source: Section 75, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sexual harassment

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 76: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe

Q: What is the punishment for physically attacking a woman to forcefully undress her?
A: Assaulting or using criminal force against a woman with the intent to disrobe her or compel her to be naked is punishable by three to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 76, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 76: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe

Q: What specific offence is addressed in Section 76 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 76 of BNS 2023 addresses the offence of using assault or criminal force against a woman with the specific intention of disrobing her or compelling her to be naked. It carries a mandatory minimum sentence of three years, extending to seven years. [Source: Section 76, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 76: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe

A: Because he assaulted the woman with the intention of disrobing her, he is liable to imprisonment of three to seven years under this section. [Source: Section 76, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 76: Assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe

A: The prosecution must prove that the accused assaulted or used criminal force against the woman, and that they did so with the specific intention of disrobing her or compelling her to be naked. [Source: Section 76, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 77: Voyeurism

Q: Is it illegal to secretly film a woman while she is getting dressed in her own bedroom?
A: Yes, secretly watching or capturing images of a woman engaging in a private act where she expects privacy constitutes voyeurism. The punishment is one to three years in prison for a first offence, and three to seven years for subsequent convictions. [Source: Section 77, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voyeurism

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 77: Voyeurism

Q: How does Section 77 of BNS 2023 define the crime of voyeurism?
A: Section 77 of BNS 2023 defines voyeurism as watching or capturing/disseminating images of a woman engaging in a private act where she reasonably expects privacy. It prescribes tiered punishments: 1-3 years for a first conviction, and 3-7 years for repeat offences. [Source: Section 77, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voyeurism

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 77: Voyeurism

Q: A woman consents to her boyfriend taking intimate photos of her, but they break up and he posts the photos online without her permission. Is this covered under the voyeurism law?
A: Yes, Explanation 2 of this section clearly states that if she consented to the capture of the images but not to their dissemination, disseminating them to third persons is considered an offence under this section. [Source: Section 77, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voyeurism

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 77: Voyeurism

Q: How does the law define a "private act" for the purposes of a voyeurism charge?
A: A "private act" includes acts where genitals, posterior, or breasts are exposed or covered only in underwear, using a lavatory, or doing a sexual act not ordinarily done in public, in a place reasonably expected to provide privacy. [Source: Section 77, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voyeurism

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 77: Voyeurism

Q: Is it voyeurism if a security camera in a public bank lobby captures a woman adjusting her clothing?
A: No, because a public bank lobby is not a place where she would "usually have the expectation of not being observed", so adjusting clothing there does not meet the strict legal criteria of a "private act" under this section. [Source: Section 77, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voyeurism

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 77: Voyeurism

Q: What is the consequence of this law for "revenge porn"?
A: The consequence is that "revenge porn" is directly criminalized; the law recognizes that initial consent to capturing an image does not grant blanket consent to share it, making malicious dissemination a punishable act of voyeurism. [Source: Section 77, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 78: Stalking

Q: What are the legal consequences of repeatedly following a woman or tracking her online activity against her wishes?
A: Repeatedly following or contacting a woman despite clear disinterest, or monitoring her electronic communications, constitutes stalking. It is punishable by up to three years in prison for a first offence, and up to five years for repeat offences. [Source: Section 78, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stalking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 78: Stalking

Q: What behaviors constitute stalking under Section 78 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 78 of BNS 2023 defines stalking as repeatedly following or contacting a woman who has indicated disinterest, or monitoring her internet/electronic communication. It prescribes up to three years imprisonment for the first conviction and up to five years for subsequent ones. [Source: Section 78, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stalking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 78: Stalking

Q: A man constantly replies to a woman's public social media posts, emails her every day, and uses software to track when she is online, even after she told him to leave her alone. Is he stalking her?
A: Yes, by monitoring her internet use and attempting to contact her repeatedly despite a clear indication of disinterest, he has committed the offence of stalking under this section. [Source: Section 78, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stalking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 78: Stalking

Q: What is a crucial prerequisite regarding the victim's reaction before physical following or contacting can legally be classified as stalking?
A: The repeated following or contacting must occur "despite a clear indication of disinterest by such woman". [Source: Section 78, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stalking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 78: Stalking

Q: Can a licensed private investigator or police officer be charged with stalking if they follow a female suspect to gather evidence of a crime?
A: No, the conduct does not amount to stalking if it was pursued for preventing or detecting crime by someone entrusted with that responsibility by the State, or if the conduct was reasonable and justified in the particular circumstances. [Source: Section 78, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stalking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 78: Stalking

Q: What is the legal consequence of including the monitoring of electronic communication in the stalking definition?
A: The consequence is that the law modernizes the protection of women, recognizing that severe harassment can happen entirely online (cyberstalking) without the perpetrator ever being in the physical presence of the victim. [Source: Section 78, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stalking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 79: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

Q: Can you be arrested simply for saying something highly insulting and inappropriate to a woman in public?
A: Yes, uttering words, making sounds or gestures, or exhibiting objects intending to insult a woman's modesty, or intruding on her privacy, is a crime punishable by up to three years of simple imprisonment and a fine. [Source: Section 79, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 79: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

Q: How does Section 79 of BNS 2023 protect a woman's modesty from verbal or visual insults?
A: Section 79 of BNS 2023 penalizes anyone who, intending to insult a woman's modesty, uses words, sounds, gestures, or exhibits objects meant to be seen or heard by her, or intrudes upon her privacy. The penalty is up to three years of simple imprisonment. [Source: Section 79, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 79: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

Q: A man stands outside a woman's window and makes explicit, lewd gestures, ensuring she can see him from inside her home. What offence is this?
A: He has made a gesture intending to insult the modesty of the woman, intending that such gesture shall be seen by her, which makes him punishable under this section for up to three years in prison. [Source: Section 79, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 79: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

Q: What must be the perpetrator's specific intention when they utter the words or make the gestures?
A: They must act "intending to insult the modesty of any woman" and intending that the word/sound be heard or the gesture/object be seen by that specific woman. [Source: Section 79, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 79: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

Q: If two men are loudly telling inappropriate jokes to each other in a park, and a woman overhears them by accident and feels insulted, are the men guilty under this section?
A: Likely no, because the law requires that they speak the words *intending* to insult the modesty of *that* woman, and *intending* that the words be heard by *her*. Accidental overhearing lacks this specific, targeted intent. [Source: Section 79, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 79: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

Q: What is the consequence of this section for street harassment, commonly known as "eve-teasing"?
A: The consequence is that it provides a specific legal mechanism to prosecute street harassers; catcalling, lewd sounds, and flashing objects are explicitly criminalized as attacks on modesty, even if no physical assault occurs. [Source: Section 79, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Word, gesture or act intended to insult modesty of a woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 80: Dowry death

Q: What is the legal outcome if a woman dies under suspicious circumstances shortly after her wedding, and her husband's family had been demanding money from her?
A: If a woman dies unnaturally within seven years of marriage, and it's shown she faced cruelty or harassment over dowry demands shortly before her death, it is legally deemed a "dowry death," punishable by seven years to life in prison. [Source: Section 80, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 80: Dowry death

Q: What is the legal definition of a "dowry death" under Section 80 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 80 of BNS 2023 defines "dowry death" as the death of a woman caused by burns, bodily injury, or unnatural circumstances within seven years of marriage, where it is shown she was subjected to dowry-related cruelty soon before her death. [Source: Section 80, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 80: Dowry death

Q: A woman who has been married for four years is found dead from poisoning. An investigation reveals her in-laws severely harassed her the week prior because her family couldn't pay them a demanded sum of cash. Who is legally responsible for the death?
A: Under this section, because the unnatural death occurred within seven years of marriage and followed dowry-related harassment, it is called a "dowry death," and the husband or relative who harassed her shall be deemed to have caused her death. [Source: Section 80, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 80: Dowry death

Q: What are the three strict chronological conditions required to classify a fatality as a "dowry death"?
A: The death must occur within seven years of her marriage, it must occur otherwise than under normal circumstances (burns/injuries/unnatural), and the cruelty or harassment must be shown to have happened "soon before her death". [Source: Section 80, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 80: Dowry death

Q: Can this section be used to prosecute a husband if his wife dies of an unexpected but entirely natural heart attack five years into their marriage, even if he did demand dowry?
A: No, the section requires that the death be caused by burns, bodily injury, or occur "otherwise than under normal circumstances." A death from a natural medical cause does not fit the criteria for a dowry death charge. [Source: Section 80, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 80: Dowry death

Q: What is the legal consequence of the phrase "shall be deemed to have caused her death"?
A: The consequence is a legal presumption of guilt; if the prosecution proves the unnatural death within seven years and the preceding dowry harassment, the law automatically deems the harassers as the killers, shifting the burden to them to prove otherwise, facing 7 years to life. [Source: Section 80, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dowry death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 81: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

Q: What happens if a man tricks a woman into believing they are legally married so she will sleep with him?
A: A man who deceitfully makes a woman believe she is lawfully married to him, causing her to cohabit or have sexual intercourse with him under that false belief, can be imprisoned for up to ten years. [Source: Section 81, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 81: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

Q: What crime is defined in Section 81 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 81 of BNS 2023 defines the crime of deceitfully inducing a belief of lawful marriage. It penalizes a man who tricks an unmarried woman into believing she is legally married to him to secure cohabitation or sexual intercourse, with a maximum penalty of ten years imprisonment. [Source: Section 81, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 81: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

Q: A married man stages a fake wedding ceremony with a priest actor to convince his new girlfriend they are legally married so she will move in with him. What law has he broken?
A: He has broken the law against cohabitation caused by deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage, as he used deceit to make a woman not lawfully married to him believe she was, securing cohabitation. [Source: Section 81, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 81: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

Q: What are the two distinct outcomes of the deceit that can trigger a conviction under this section?
A: The deceit must cause the woman to either cohabit with him OR have sexual intercourse with him, while believing she is lawfully married to him. [Source: Section 81, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 81: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

Q: Can a man be convicted under this section if both parties knew the marriage ceremony was legally invalid but decided to live together anyway as partners?
A: No, the law requires that the man causes the woman to believe she is lawfully married "by deceit". If there is no deceit and she knows the truth, the cohabitation is not criminal under this specific section. [Source: Section 81, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 81: Cohabitation caused by man deceitfully inducing belief of lawful marriage

Q: What is the legal consequence of this section regarding fraudulent marriages?
A: The consequence is that the law recognizes the profound psychological and social damage of a fake marriage, treating the sexual access gained through such profound fraud as a severe crime comparable to rape. [Source: Section 81, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 82: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

Q: Is bigamy illegal in India?
A: Yes, marrying someone else while you already have a living husband or wife (in cases where such second marriage is void) is a crime punishable by up to seven years in prison. Hiding the first marriage from the second spouse raises the penalty to ten years. [Source: Section 82, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 82: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

Q: How does Section 82 of BNS 2023 address bigamy?
A: Section 82 of BNS 2023 criminalizes marrying again during the lifetime of a spouse. Bigamy is punishable by up to seven years in prison. If the offender conceals the existence of the first marriage from the new spouse, the punishment can extend to ten years. [Source: Section 82, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 82: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

Q: A woman, without getting a divorce, marries a new man and lies to him, saying she has never been married before. What specific penalty does she face?
A: Because she committed bigamy while having concealed the fact of the former marriage from the person with whom the subsequent marriage was contracted, she is liable under sub-section (2) to imprisonment for up to ten years. [Source: Section 82, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 82: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

Q: Under what specific circumstances does a second marriage NOT constitute criminal bigamy under this section?
A: It is not bigamy if the first marriage was declared void by a competent Court, or if the first spouse has been continually absent and unheard of as alive for seven years, provided the person informs the new spouse of these facts before marrying. [Source: Section 82, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 82: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

Q: A man's wife went missing in a shipwreck and hasn't been heard from in eight years. If he marries again, is he committing bigamy?
A: No, under the exception, if the spouse has been continually absent for the space of seven years and not heard of as alive, the subsequent marriage is not a crime, provided he informs his new bride of the situation. [Source: Section 82, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 82: Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

Q: What is the legal consequence of sub-section (2) regarding the victim of the second marriage?
A: The consequence is that the law provides enhanced protection and retribution for the innocent second spouse who was defrauded, treating the deceit involved in hiding the first marriage as an aggravating factor that increases the maximum sentence. [Source: Section 82, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 83: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage

Q: What is the penalty for faking a marriage ceremony?
A: Anyone who goes through a marriage ceremony dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention, knowing it does not result in a lawful marriage, can be punished with up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 83, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 83: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage

Q: What does Section 83 of BNS 2023 penalize regarding marriage ceremonies?
A: Section 83 of BNS 2023 penalizes the act of fraudulently going through a marriage ceremony. If a person dishonestly participates in a marriage ritual knowing it holds no legal validity, they face up to seven years of imprisonment. [Source: Section 83, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 83: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage

Q: To appease his conservative parents, a man pays a woman to act as his bride in a fake temple wedding, with both knowing the ceremony isn't legally binding but intending to defraud his parents into giving them wedding gifts. Has he committed a crime?
A: Yes, he went through the ceremony of being married dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention, knowing he is not thereby lawfully married, making him liable for up to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 83, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 83: Marriage ceremony fraudulently gone through without lawful marriage

A: It must be proven that they went through the ceremony "dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention", and with the specific knowledge that they were "not thereby lawfully married". [Source: Section 83, BNS 2023]

content:

A: No, because while they know they aren't lawfully married, they are acting for entertainment, not going through the ceremony "dishonestly or with a fraudulent intention" as required by the law. [Source: Section 83, BNS 2023]

content:

A: The consequence is that the state protects the institution of marriage by criminalizing the mockery or fraudulent use of its rituals, ensuring that fake weddings cannot be legally used as tools for extortion, deceit, or social fraud. [Source: Section 83, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 84: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

Q: Is it a crime to run away with someone else's wife for an illicit affair?
A: Yes, enticing, taking away, or concealing a married woman with the intent to have an illicit sexual relationship with her is a crime punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 84, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 84: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

Q: What conduct is criminalized under Section 84 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 84 of BNS 2023 criminalizes enticing, taking away, concealing, or detaining a married woman. If a person does this knowing she is married, with the intent that she may have illicit intercourse with anyone, they face up to two years in prison. [Source: Section 84, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 84: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

Q: A man convinces his married neighbor to leave her husband and hides her in his apartment so they can carry on a secret affair. What law has he broken?
A: He has broken the law against enticing or taking away a married woman, as he concealed her knowing she is a wife, with the intent that she may have illicit intercourse with him. [Source: Section 84, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 84: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

Q: Does this law only apply if the man intends to have intercourse with the married woman himself?
A: No, the law states the intent must be that she may have illicit intercourse "with any person," meaning he is guilty even if he is kidnapping/enticing her to facilitate an affair for someone else. [Source: Section 84, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 84: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

Q: If a woman runs away from an abusive husband and a friend hides her to protect her from violence, is the friend guilty under this section?
A: No, because the friend is concealing her for protection, not with the required criminal intent that she may have "illicit intercourse with any person." [Source: Section 84, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 84: Enticing or taking away or detaining with criminal intent a married woman

Q: What is the historical and legal consequence of this statute regarding the concept of marriage?
A: The consequence is that the law historically treats a married woman's marital residence and fidelity as something legally protected against third-party interference, penalizing those who actively disrupt a marriage for illicit sexual purposes. [Source: Section 84, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 85: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

Q: What is the legal penalty for domestic violence or cruelty inflicted by a husband or in-laws?
A: If a husband or his relatives subject a woman to cruelty, they can be punished with up to three years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 85, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 85: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

Q: What does Section 85 of BNS 2023 address?
A: Section 85 of BNS 2023 addresses domestic cruelty. It states that whoever, being the husband or a relative of the husband, subjects a woman to cruelty, shall be punished with imprisonment extending to three years and a fine. [Source: Section 85, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 85: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

Q: A woman's mother-in-law verbally abuses her daily, denies her food, and locks her in a room. Can the mother-in-law be arrested?
A: Yes, because she is a relative of the husband and is subjecting the woman to cruelty, she is liable for punishment up to three years in prison under this section. [Source: Section 85, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 85: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

Q: Who are the specific categories of perpetrators that can be charged under this specific domestic cruelty section?
A: The section strictly applies only to perpetrators who are "the husband or the relative of the husband of a woman". [Source: Section 85, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 85: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

Q: Can this specific section be used to charge a woman's boss if he subjects her to cruelty at work?
A: No, this section explicitly only applies to "the husband or the relative of the husband". Cruelty by a boss would fall under different criminal statutes, like harassment or assault. [Source: Section 85, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 85: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

Q: What is the consequence of having a dedicated section for cruelty by a husband or in-laws?
A: The consequence is that the law formally recognizes and creates specific legal recourse for the unique, systemic abuse women often face within their marital homes from their spouses or extended marital families. [Source: Section 85, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Husband or relative of husband of a woman subjecting her to cruelty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 86: Cruelty defined

Q: What specific acts are legally considered "cruelty" against a wife by her husband or in-laws?
A: Cruelty includes willful conduct likely to drive a woman to suicide or cause grave injury to her life, limb, or mental/physical health. It also includes harassing her to coerce unlawful demands for property (like dowry). [Source: Section 86, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cruelty defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 86: Cruelty defined

Q: How does Section 86 of BNS 2023 define "cruelty" for the purposes of domestic violence laws?
A: Section 86 of BNS 2023 defines cruelty as willful conduct likely to cause a woman to commit suicide or suffer grave physical or mental injury. It also defines cruelty as harassment aimed at coercing her or her family to meet unlawful property demands, or punishing them for failing to do so. [Source: Section 86, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cruelty defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 86: Cruelty defined

Q: A husband constantly belittles his wife, isolates her from her friends, and tells her daily that she is worthless, causing her to develop severe clinical depression. Does this psychological abuse legally count as "cruelty"?
A: Yes, because his willful conduct is of such a nature as is likely to cause grave injury or danger to the mental health of the woman, it satisfies the legal definition of cruelty under clause (a). [Source: Section 86, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cruelty defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 86: Cruelty defined

Q: What are the two distinct categories of "cruelty" provided in this definition?
A: The first category is willful conduct causing physical/mental danger or suicidal ideation. The second category is harassment specifically linked to unlawful property demands (dowry harassment). [Source: Section 86, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cruelty defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 86: Cruelty defined

Q: If a husband and wife have normal, everyday arguments about household chores that momentarily upset the wife, is that criminal "cruelty"?
A: No, normal marital friction is not covered. The law specifies "wilful conduct which is of such a nature as is likely to drive the woman to commit suicide or to cause grave injury or danger," requiring a high threshold of severity. [Source: Section 86, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cruelty defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 86: Cruelty defined

Q: What is the consequence of explicitly including mental health in this definition?
A: The consequence is that the law empowers courts to prosecute domestic abusers for severe psychological and emotional violence, recognizing that domestic cruelty is not limited solely to visible physical beatings. [Source: Section 86, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cruelty defined

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 87: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

Q: What is the punishment for kidnapping a woman to force her to marry someone against her will?
A: Kidnapping or abducting a woman to compel her into marriage, or to force her into illicit intercourse, is punishable by up to ten years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 87, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 87: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

Q: What offences are covered under Section 87 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 87 of BNS 2023 covers kidnapping, abducting, or inducing a woman to compel her into marriage or illicit intercourse. Using criminal intimidation, abuse of authority, or compulsion to achieve these ends is punishable by up to ten years imprisonment. [Source: Section 87, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 87: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

Q: A powerful local politician threatens to destroy a young woman's family business unless she goes with him to a remote estate, intending to force her to sleep with him. What crime is this?
A: Because he used criminal intimidation to induce the woman to go from any place with the intent that she be forced into illicit intercourse, he is punishable by up to ten years in prison under this section. [Source: Section 87, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 87: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

Q: Besides physical kidnapping, what other methods of coercion are explicitly criminalized under this section if used to force illicit intercourse?
A: The section explicitly criminalizes the use of "criminal intimidation", "abuse of authority", or "any other method of compulsion" to induce a woman to go from any place for illicit intercourse. [Source: Section 87, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 87: Kidnapping, abducting or inducing woman to compel her marriage, etc

Q: Does this law apply if a woman voluntarily elopes with her boyfriend to get married because her parents disapprove?
A: No, the law targets kidnapping or abduction with the intent that she be compelled to marry "against her will". If the woman is a consenting adult acting of her own free will, no crime is committed under this section. [Source: Section 87, BNS 2023]

content:

Q: What is the legal consequence of this section for cases of "forced marriage"?
A: The consequence is that forced marriages are inherently criminalized at the abduction/coercion stage; the state can aggressively prosecute the perpetrators for the kidnapping and intimidation itself before the forced wedding even takes place. [Source: Section 87, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 88: Causing miscarriage

Q: Is it illegal to cause a pregnant woman to have a miscarriage?
A: Yes, voluntarily causing a miscarriage is punishable by up to three years in prison, or up to seven years if the woman is "quick with child" (advanced pregnancy). However, it is legal if done in good faith to save the woman's life. [Source: Section 88, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 88: Causing miscarriage

Q: How does Section 88 of BNS 2023 regulate miscarriages/abortions outside the framework of medical termination laws?
A: Section 88 of BNS 2023 criminalizes voluntarily causing a miscarriage unless done in good faith to save the mother's life. The penalty is up to three years, increasing to up to seven years if the fetus is developed ("quick with child"). [Source: Section 88, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 88: Causing miscarriage

Q: A pregnant woman takes illicit herbal remedies specifically to induce a miscarriage on herself, without consulting a doctor or facing a life-threatening medical emergency. Has she committed a crime?
A: Yes, the Explanation explicitly states that "a woman who causes herself to miscarry, is within the meaning of this section," making her liable for up to three or seven years depending on the stage of pregnancy. [Source: Section 88, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 88: Causing miscarriage

Q: What is the only statutory defense provided in this section for causing a miscarriage?
A: The only defense provided within this specific section is if the miscarriage is caused "in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman." [Source: Section 88, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 88: Causing miscarriage

Q: What legally distinguishes a three-year penalty from a seven-year penalty under this section?
A: The distinction relies on whether the woman is "quick with child" (meaning she can feel fetal movement, usually denoting a later stage of pregnancy). If she is, the penalty increases to a maximum of seven years. [Source: Section 88, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 88: Causing miscarriage

Q: What is the consequence of the Explanation clause regarding the pregnant woman herself?
A: The consequence is that the law treats self-induced, non-medical abortions (outside the legal framework of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act) as a criminal offence committed by the pregnant woman against her own fetus. [Source: Section 88, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 89: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

Q: What is the punishment for forcing a woman to have an abortion or causing her to miscarry against her will?
A: Causing a miscarriage without the pregnant woman's consent is an extremely severe crime, punishable by life imprisonment or up to ten years in prison, regardless of the stage of pregnancy. [Source: Section 89, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 89: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

Q: What is the penalty under Section 89 of BNS 2023 for non-consensual miscarriage?
A: Section 89 of BNS 2023 elevates the crime of causing a miscarriage to a much higher severity if done without the woman's consent. It abolishes the "quick with child" distinction for this scenario, prescribing a maximum penalty of life imprisonment or up to ten years. [Source: Section 89, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 89: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

Q: An abusive husband sneaks abortifacient drugs into his pregnant wife's food because he doesn't want the child, causing her to lose the pregnancy. What is his specific liability?
A: Because he committed the offence of causing a miscarriage without the consent of the woman, he is liable to imprisonment for life or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 89, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 89: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

Q: Does the stage of pregnancy matter if the miscarriage is forced upon the woman without her consent?
A: No, this section explicitly states that the punishment applies "whether the woman is quick with child or not", making the lack of consent the primary aggravating factor. [Source: Section 89, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 89: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

Q: Can a doctor forcibly perform an abortion on a conscious, capable woman who refuses the procedure, even if the doctor believes her life is in danger?
A: Generally no. While Section 88 has a life-saving exception, Section 89 severely punishes acting "without the consent of the woman." Medical ethics and law require consent from capable patients, prioritizing bodily autonomy. [Source: Section 89, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 89: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

Q: What is the legal consequence of the severe penalty difference between Section 88 (consensual/self-induced) and Section 89 (non-consensual)?
A: The consequence is that the state recognizes forced miscarriage as a profound violation of both fetal life and maternal bodily autonomy, treating the circumvention of the mother's consent as an atrocity warranting life imprisonment. [Source: Section 89, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing miscarriage without woman’s consent

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 90: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

Q: What happens if someone tries to cause an illegal miscarriage, but the pregnant woman dies as a result of the procedure?
A: If a person acts with intent to cause a miscarriage and causes the woman's death, they face up to ten years in prison. If they did this without the woman's consent, the punishment increases to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 90, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 90: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

Q: How does Section 90 of BNS 2023 treat maternal death during an illegal abortion?
A: Section 90 of BNS 2023 dictates that causing a pregnant woman's death while attempting to cause a miscarriage is punishable by up to ten years. If the act was done without her consent, the penalty is life imprisonment. [Source: Section 90, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 90: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

Q: A back-alley practitioner performs a dangerous, consensual, illegal abortion. The procedure goes wrong, and the woman dies. The practitioner claims they never meant to kill her. Are they guilty of causing her death under this section?
A: Yes, they are guilty and face up to ten years in prison. The Explanation clearly states it is not essential to this offence that the offender should know the act is likely to cause death. [Source: Section 90, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 90: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

Q: What are the two distinct sentencing tiers for causing maternal death during a miscarriage attempt?
A: The standard tier is up to ten years imprisonment. However, if the act intended to cause the miscarriage was done "without the consent of the woman," the tier elevates to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 90, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 90: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

Q: Can the offender use the defense that the woman's death was entirely accidental and unforeseeable during the abortion attempt?
A: No, the statute imposes strict liability for the resulting death. As long as the intent to cause the miscarriage was present, the lack of knowledge that the act was deadly is not a valid defense against this charge. [Source: Section 90, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 90: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

Q: What is the consequence of this strict liability rule for illegal abortion providers?
A: The consequence is that illegal abortion providers act at their own absolute peril regarding the mother's life; any fatal complication automatically results in severe homicide-level charges, regardless of their medical intent or lack of malice toward the mother. [Source: Section 90, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Death caused by act done with intent to cause miscarriage

Q: What is the punishment for intentionally injuring a fetus so that it is born dead or dies shortly after birth?
A: Doing an act before a child's birth with the intent to prevent it from being born alive, or to cause it to die after birth, is punishable by up to ten years in prison and a fine, unless done in good faith to save the mother's life. [Source: Section 91, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 91: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

Q: What specific pre-birth violence is addressed in Section 91 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 91 of BNS 2023 penalizes acts done before a child's birth with the specific intention of either preventing the child from being born alive (feticide) or causing it to die after birth (infanticide). The punishment is up to ten years imprisonment. [Source: Section 91, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 91: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

Q: A man repeatedly strikes a pregnant woman in the abdomen, explicitly stating he wants to ensure the baby doesn't survive delivery. The baby is born alive but dies a week later from the internal injuries sustained in the womb. Is the man guilty under this specific section?
A: Yes, he did an act before birth with the intention of causing the child to die after its birth, and the child did die as a result, making him liable for up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 91, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 91: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

Q: What is the only statutory defense for an act that prevents a child from being born alive?
A: The only defense is if the act is "caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the mother." [Source: Section 91, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 91: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

Q: Does this section apply if a doctor performs a legal, routine abortion early in the pregnancy?
A: No, standard legal abortions do not fall under this section. This section specifically targets malicious acts intended to kill a child near birth or cause it to die shortly after, treating it as akin to a near-homicide of a developing child. [Source: Section 91, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 91: Act done with intent to prevent child being born alive or to cause to die after birth

Q: What is the consequence of this section bridging the gap between fetal life and independent life?
A: The consequence is that perpetrators cannot escape murder-like charges simply because the fatal injury was inflicted *before* the child was legally considered a full person; if the pre-birth injury intentionally causes death during or after birth, severe penalties apply. [Source: Section 91, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 92: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

Q: If someone tries to murder a pregnant woman, but she survives and her unborn child dies instead, what is the crime?
A: If a person does an act that would amount to culpable homicide if the woman died, but instead it causes the death of her "quick" (developed) unborn child, they can be punished with up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 92, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 92: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

Q: How does Section 92 of BNS 2023 handle the accidental killing of a fetus during an assault on the mother?
A: Section 92 of BNS 2023 applies when an offender commits an act against a pregnant woman that would constitute culpable homicide if she died. If she survives but her "quick unborn child" dies as a result, the offender is punished with up to ten years imprisonment. [Source: Section 92, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 92: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

Q: A robber shoots a pregnant woman in the chest, intending to kill her. She survives through emergency surgery, but the bullet strikes and kills the advanced fetus. What is the robber liable for regarding the fetus?
A: As per the Illustration, because he did an act likely to cause the death of the woman (which would be culpable homicide), and thereby caused the death of the quick unborn child, he is guilty of an offence under Section 92. [Source: Section 92, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 92: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

Q: What legal requirement regarding the state of the pregnancy is necessary to invoke this specific section?
A: The law requires that the unborn child must be a "quick unborn child" (meaning the mother can feel its movements, indicating an advanced stage of pregnancy). [Source: Section 92, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 92: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

Q: If a person accidentally hits a pregnant woman with their car due to mild negligence, and she loses the baby, does Section 92 apply?
A: No, because Section 92 specifically requires that the act be done under circumstances where "if he thereby caused death he would be guilty of culpable homicide." Mild negligence does not amount to culpable homicide. [Source: Section 92, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 92: Causing death of quick unborn child by act amounting to culpable homicide

Q: What is the consequence of this section regarding the legal concept of transferred malice?
A: The consequence is that the law effectively transfers the murderous intent from the mother to the advanced fetus; the perpetrator is held criminally liable for a severe fetal homicide even though their primary target was the mother. [Source: Section 92, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 93: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

Q: What is the penalty for a parent abandoning a young child in a public place to get rid of them?
A: A parent or caretaker who exposes or leaves a child under twelve years of age in any place with the intention of wholly abandoning them can be punished with up to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 93, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 93: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

Q: What offence does Section 93 of BNS 2023 criminalize regarding child welfare?
A: Section 93 of BNS 2023 criminalizes the exposure and abandonment of a child under twelve by their parent or caretaker. Leaving a child in any place with the intent to wholly abandon them carries a penalty of up to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 93, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 93: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

Q: A desperate mother leaves her three-year-old toddler alone at a busy railway station with a note, intending never to return. What crime has she committed?
A: She has committed the offence of exposure and abandonment of a child, as she is the mother of a child under twelve and left the child with the intention of wholly abandoning them. [Source: Section 93, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 93: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

Q: What specific age limit applies to the child for this section to be applicable?
A: The child must be under the age of twelve years. [Source: Section 93, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 93: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

Q: What happens if a parent abandons a child in a forest and the child dies of exposure or starvation? Are they only charged under this section?
A: No, the Explanation clarifies that this section does not prevent the offender from being tried for murder or culpable homicide if the child actually dies as a consequence of the exposure. [Source: Section 93, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 93: Exposure and abandonment of child under twelve years of age, by parent or person having

Q: What is the overarching consequence of this law for parental responsibility?
A: The consequence is that the law enforces a strict duty of care; parents cannot unilaterally terminate their obligations by simply discarding young children, making abandonment a severe criminal act independent of whether the child actually gets physically hurt. [Source: Section 93, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 94: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

Q: Is it a crime to secretly bury a baby that was born dead to hide the fact that a birth occurred?
A: Yes, secretly burying or disposing of the dead body of a child (whether it died before, during, or after birth) to intentionally conceal the birth is a crime punishable by up to two years in prison. [Source: Section 94, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 94: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

Q: What does Section 94 of BNS 2023 prohibit regarding deceased infants?
A: Section 94 of BNS 2023 prohibits the concealment of a birth through the secret disposal of a dead body. Anyone who secretly buries or disposes of an infant's corpse to hide the fact of its birth faces up to two years imprisonment. [Source: Section 94, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 94: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

Q: An unmarried woman gives birth to a stillborn baby. Fearful of social stigma, she wraps the body and secretly buries it in the woods at night without telling anyone. Is this illegal?
A: Yes, by secretly burying the dead body of the child to intentionally conceal the birth, she has committed an offence punishable by up to two years in prison under this section. [Source: Section 94, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 94: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

Q: Does it matter for this specific charge whether the baby was murdered or naturally stillborn?
A: No, the law applies whether such child died "before or after or during its birth." The crime is the act of secret disposal to conceal the birth, independent of the cause of death. [Source: Section 94, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 94: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

Q: If a family holds a small, private, but lawful funeral for a stillborn baby on their own property, are they guilty of concealing a birth?
A: No, because a lawful, recorded funeral lacks the element of "secretly burying" to "intentionally conceal or endeavour to conceal the birth." The law targets clandestine disposals meant to hide the pregnancy/birth from society or authorities. [Source: Section 94, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 94: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

Q: What is the consequence of this law regarding public health and criminal investigations?
A: The consequence is that the state mandates transparency regarding all human births and deaths; criminalizing secret disposals prevents individuals from easily covering up infanticides, illegal abortions, or maternal deaths under the guise of unrecorded stillbirths. [Source: Section 94, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealment of birth by secret disposal of dead body

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 95: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

Q: What happens to a gang leader who uses young children to pickpocket or sell drugs for him?
A: Anyone who hires or employs a child to commit a crime faces a minimum of three years and up to ten years in prison. If the child actually commits the crime, the adult is also punished for that specific crime as if they committed it themselves. [Source: Section 95, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 95: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

Q: What is the penalty under Section 95 of BNS 2023 for using children in criminal activities?
A: Section 95 of BNS 2023 severely penalizes hiring or engaging a child to commit an offence, setting a minimum sentence of three years up to ten years. If the offence is carried out, the adult is additionally punished as if they personally committed the underlying crime. [Source: Section 95, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 95: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

Q: A smuggler pays a 10-year-old boy to carry illegal weapons across a state border. The boy is caught. What is the smuggler's liability under this section?
A: The smuggler is liable for 3 to 10 years for employing the child, AND because the offence of weapon smuggling was committed, the smuggler is also punished with the penalty for weapon smuggling as if he had carried the weapons himself. [Source: Section 95, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 95: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

Q: Does this section apply to using children in the production of illegal adult media?
A: Yes, the Explanation explicitly states that hiring, employing, engaging, or using a child for sexual exploitation or pornography is covered within the meaning of this section. [Source: Section 95, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 95: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

Q: If a parent genuinely didn't know their child was committing crimes, but benefited financially from the stolen goods, can they be charged under this section?
A: Not under Section 95, as it requires active "hiring, employing or engaging" the child to commit an offence. Passive receipt of stolen goods or mere negligence is handled under different legal sections. [Source: Section 95, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 95: Hiring, employing or engaging a child to commit an offence

Q: What is the consequence of this section for organized crime syndicates that exploit juvenile justice laws?
A: The consequence is that it closes a major loophole; crime bosses can no longer shield themselves by using minors (who face lenient juvenile penalties) as foot soldiers, because the bosses will now face severe, compounded adult penalties for the children's actions. [Source: Section 95, BNS 2023]
