content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 96: Procuration of child

Q: What is the crime of "procuration of child" under BNS 2023?
A: Procuration of a child involves inducing a child to go anywhere or do any act with the intention or knowledge that the child will likely be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse. It is punishable by up to ten years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 96, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procuration of child

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 96: Procuration of child

Q: How does Section 96 of BNS 2023 penalize the procuration of minors?
A: Section 96 of BNS 2023 penalizes anyone who induces a child to move locations or perform acts, intending or knowing it is likely that the child will be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse with another person, carrying a penalty of up to ten years imprisonment. [Source: Section 96, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procuration of child

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 96: Procuration of child

Q: A neighbor offers to give a teenage girl a ride to the mall, knowing fully well that he is actually taking her to a house where adult men intend to sexually exploit her. Is he guilty of a crime even if he doesn't touch her himself?
A: Yes, by inducing the child to go to another place knowing it is likely she will be forced or seduced to illicit intercourse with another person, he is guilty of procuration of a child and faces up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 96, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procuration of child

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 96: Procuration of child

Q: What specific intent or knowledge must be proven against the person who induces the child?
A: It must be proven that they acted with the intent that the child be forced/seduced to illicit intercourse, or with the knowledge that it was "likely" such a thing would happen. [Source: Section 96, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procuration of child

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 96: Procuration of child

Q: If a taxi driver drives a runaway teen to a hotel, completely unaware that she plans to meet older men there for illicit intercourse, is the driver guilty under this section?
A: No, because the driver lacks the requisite criminal "intent" or "knowledge that it is likely" that the child will be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse. Mere transportation without criminal knowledge does not constitute procuration. [Source: Section 96, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procuration of child

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 96: Procuration of child

Q: What is the consequence of this section for human trafficking networks?
A: The consequence is that it criminalizes the "recruiters" or "facilitators" within trafficking rings; people who merely convince or lure children into dangerous situations are punished severely even if they are not the end-stage abusers. [Source: Section 96, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Procuration of child

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 97: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

Q: What is the penalty for kidnapping a young child specifically to steal the jewelry they are wearing?
A: Kidnapping or abducting a child under ten years old with the intention of dishonestly taking movable property from their person is punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 97, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 97: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

Q: What specific form of kidnapping is addressed in Section 97 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 97 of BNS 2023 addresses kidnapping or abducting a child under ten years of age with the specific intent to dishonestly take movable property (like jewelry or clothing) from the child's person. It carries a penalty of up to seven years imprisonment. [Source: Section 97, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 97: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

Q: A thief snatches a five-year-old child from a park, takes the child behind a building to strip them of an expensive gold necklace, and then leaves the child there. What is the appropriate charge?
A: The appropriate charge is kidnapping or abducting a child under ten years of age with the intent to steal from its person, punishable by up to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 97, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 97: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

Q: What is the age threshold for the victim in this specific kidnapping/theft section?
A: The child must be "under the age of ten years". [Source: Section 97, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 97: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

Q: If a kidnapper takes a 15-year-old teenager to steal their smartphone, can they be charged under Section 97?
A: No, because Section 97 strictly applies only to children "under the age of ten years." The kidnapping and theft of the teenager would be prosecuted under general kidnapping and robbery/theft sections instead. [Source: Section 97, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 97: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

Q: What is the consequence of having a dedicated section for this specific crime?
A: The consequence is that the law acknowledges the unique vulnerability of very young children who are often targeted purely for the valuables placed on them by their parents, ensuring a severe kidnapping penalty applies even if no ransom is demanded. [Source: Section 97, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting child under ten years of age with intent to steal from its person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 98: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: What is the punishment for selling a child into the sex trade?
A: Selling, hiring out, or disposing of a child with the intent or knowledge that they will be used for prostitution or illicit intercourse is punishable by up to ten years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 98, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 98: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: What does Section 98 of BNS 2023 criminalize regarding the trafficking of children?
A: Section 98 of BNS 2023 criminalizes selling, letting to hire, or disposing of a child intending or knowing they will be used for prostitution, illicit intercourse, or any unlawful/immoral purpose. It is punishable by up to ten years imprisonment. [Source: Section 98, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 98: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: A desperate parent "gives" their teenage daughter to a brothel owner in exchange for money. What is the parent's liability?
A: The parent is liable to imprisonment for up to ten years for selling or disposing of the child with the intent or knowledge that she would be used for the purpose of prostitution. [Source: Section 98, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 98: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: Under Explanation 1, what presumption does the court make if a female under eighteen is sold to a brothel manager?
A: The court legally presumes, until the contrary is proved, that the person disposing of her did so with the specific intent that she would be used for the purpose of prostitution. [Source: Section 98, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 98: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: How does Explanation 2 define "illicit intercourse" in the context of this section?
A: It defines "illicit intercourse" as sexual intercourse between persons not united by marriage or by any recognized union/tie that constitutes a quasi-marital relation under their personal law or custom. [Source: Section 98, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 98: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: What is the legal consequence of Explanation 1 for prosecutors fighting child trafficking?
A: The consequence is that it shifts the burden of proof; prosecutors do not need to independently prove the seller's intent if the buyer is a known brothel manager, making it much easier to secure convictions against those who sell children into the sex trade. [Source: Section 98, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 99: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: What is the penalty for buying or obtaining a child for prostitution?
A: Buying, hiring, or obtaining possession of a child with the intent or knowledge that they will be used for prostitution or illicit intercourse is a severe crime punishable by a minimum of seven years, extending up to fourteen years in prison. [Source: Section 99, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 99: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: How does Section 99 of BNS 2023 penalize the "buyers" in child trafficking?
A: Section 99 of BNS 2023 targets the demand side of child trafficking, penalizing anyone who buys, hires, or obtains a child for prostitution or immoral purposes. It mandates a strict minimum sentence of seven years, up to a maximum of fourteen years. [Source: Section 99, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 99: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: A man pays a criminal syndicate to obtain a 14-year-old child for him to exploit sexually. What is the specific minimum punishment he faces under this section?
A: Because he bought or obtained possession of the child for illicit intercourse, he faces a mandatory minimum sentence of "not less than seven years" which may extend to fourteen years in prison. [Source: Section 99, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 99: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: What is the key difference in sentencing structure between the "seller" (Section 98) and the "buyer" (Section 99) of a child?
A: While the seller faces "up to ten years", the buyer faces a much harsher penalty with a strict mandatory minimum of seven years, extending up to fourteen years. [Source: Section 98, BNS 2023; Section 99, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 99: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: If a wealthy individual "buys" an abused child from a trafficker strictly to rescue them and hand them over to child protective services, are they guilty under this section?
A: No, because the section requires obtaining the child "with intent that such child shall... be employed or used for the purpose of prostitution or illicit intercourse... or for any unlawful and immoral purpose." Rescuing lacks this criminal intent. [Source: Section 99, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 99: Buying child for purposes of prostitution, etc

Q: What is the legal consequence of imposing a harsh mandatory minimum sentence specifically for the "buyers"?
A: The consequence is that the state aggressively targets the financial demand that drives child trafficking; by ensuring that buyers face guaranteed, lengthy prison time (minimum 7 years), it aims to destroy the economic market for child exploitation. [Source: Section 99, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 100: Culpable homicide

Q: What makes an act "culpable homicide" under BNS 2023?
A: Culpable homicide is causing death by doing an act with the intention of causing death, or the intention of causing a bodily injury likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death. [Source: Section 100, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 100: Culpable homicide

Q: How does Section 100 of BNS 2023 define culpable homicide?
A: Section 100 of BNS 2023 defines culpable homicide as causing death through an act done with the intention of causing death, the intention of causing bodily injury likely to cause death, or the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death. [Source: Section 100, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 100: Culpable homicide

Q: A man knows his neighbor is hiding behind a bush. He intentionally tricks his friend into shooting into that bush by saying there is a deer there. The friend shoots and kills the neighbor. Who is guilty of culpable homicide?
A: The man who tricked his friend is guilty of culpable homicide because he induced the act intending or knowing it was likely to cause the neighbor's death. The friend who fired may be guilty of no offence as he lacked intent/knowledge. [Source: Section 100, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 100: Culpable homicide

Q: Under Explanation 1, what happens if an attacker injures someone who is already sick, causing them to die sooner than they would have?
A: The attacker "shall be deemed to have caused his death," meaning the pre-existing disease or infirmity does not excuse the attacker from culpable homicide if the injury accelerated the death. [Source: Section 100, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 100: Culpable homicide

Q: Can an attacker claim they are not guilty of homicide because the victim could have survived if they had received better medical treatment?
A: No, Explanation 2 states that the person who causes the fatal bodily injury is deemed to have caused the death, even if resorting to proper remedies and skillful treatment might have prevented the death. [Source: Section 100, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 100: Culpable homicide

Q: What is the consequence of Explanation 3 regarding the death of a child during childbirth?
A: The consequence is that while killing a fetus in the womb is not homicide, it *can* amount to culpable homicide if any part of the child has been brought forth (partially born), even if the child hasn't breathed or been completely born yet. [Source: Section 100, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 101: Murder

Q: What distinguishes murder from culpable homicide in Indian law?
A: Murder is an aggravated form of culpable homicide where the intent to cause death is clear, the bodily injury intended is known to be fatal or is objectively sufficient to cause death, or the act is imminently dangerous without excuse. [Source: Section 101, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 101: Murder

Q: How does Section 101 of BNS 2023 classify when culpable homicide amounts to murder?
A: Section 101 of BNS 2023 establishes four clauses making culpable homicide murder: specific intent to kill, intent to cause known fatal injury, inflicting injury sufficient in ordinary course to cause death, or acting with imminent danger without excuse. It also lists five Exceptions where the crime reverts to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. [Source: Section 101, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 101: Murder

Q: A man knows his neighbor has a weakened spleen. He punches the neighbor in the spleen intending to cause injury, and the neighbor dies. Is this murder?
A: Yes, under clause (b), because the act causing death was done with the intention of causing such bodily injury as the offender knew was likely to cause the death of that specific person. [Source: Section 101, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 101: Murder

Q: What are the specific conditions required under Exception 1 for "grave and sudden provocation" to reduce murder to culpable homicide?
A: Under Exception 1, the offender must be deprived of self-control by grave/sudden provocation and kill the provoker. However, the provocation cannot be sought by the offender, given by a public servant obeying the law, or given in lawful private defense. [Source: Section 101, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 101: Murder

Q: If two men get into a sudden, unplanned fistfight in the heat of passion, and one kills the other without acting cruelly or taking undue advantage, is it murder?
A: No, under Exception 4, culpable homicide is not murder if committed without premeditation in a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, provided the offender didn't take undue advantage. [Source: Section 101, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 101: Murder

Q: What is the legal consequence of Exception 5 regarding consent?
A: The consequence is that if an adult victim (above 18) voluntarily consents to suffer death or take the risk of death, the killer's offence is reduced from murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. [Source: Section 101, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 102: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

Q: What happens if a person intends to kill someone, but accidentally kills an innocent bystander instead?
A: If a person intends or knows they are likely to cause death, and accidentally kills someone they didn't intend to, the law treats the crime exactly as if they had killed their intended target (the doctrine of transferred malice). [Source: Section 102, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 102: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

Q: How does Section 102 of BNS 2023 address the accidental killing of an unintended victim?
A: Section 102 of BNS 2023 dictates that if a person commits culpable homicide by killing someone whose death they neither intended nor foresaw, the crime is still of the exact same description as if they had killed their intended target. [Source: Section 102, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 102: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

Q: An assassin shoots at a politician but misses, accidentally killing a child in the crowd. What is the assassin guilty of regarding the child?
A: The assassin is guilty of the murder of the child, because under this section, the culpable homicide committed is of the same description as if he had caused the death of the politician he intended to kill. [Source: Section 102, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 102: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

Q: Does the offender need to have any malice or ill-will towards the actual victim for this section to apply?
A: No, the section explicitly applies when the offender causes the death of a person "whose death he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause." [Source: Section 102, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 102: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

Q: Can an offender claim their crime should be downgraded to manslaughter because they didn't mean to hit the person who actually died?
A: No, this section prevents that defense. The legal severity of the crime transfers entirely from the intended victim to the actual victim. [Source: Section 102, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 102: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

Q: What is the consequence of this statute for public safety?
A: The consequence is that it ensures criminals cannot escape full murder charges when their deadly actions indiscriminately harm innocent bystanders, cementing the legal principle that deadly intent, once acted upon, carries full liability regardless of who the bullet strikes. [Source: Section 102, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 103: Punishment for murder

Q: What are the legal punishments for committing murder in India?
A: The standard punishment for murder is death or life imprisonment, plus a fine. If the murder is committed by a mob of five or more people based on identity (like caste, race, or sex), every member faces death or life imprisonment and a fine. [Source: Section 103, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 103: Punishment for murder

Q: What sentencing guidelines are provided in Section 103 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 103 of BNS 2023 mandates that murder be punished with death or life imprisonment. Sub-section (2) specifically addresses mob lynching/hate crimes, stipulating that if a group of five or more commits murder based on race, caste, sex, etc., each member receives death or life imprisonment. [Source: Section 103, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 103: Punishment for murder

Q: A mob of six people attacks and kills a man solely because of his religious beliefs. What specific legal provision applies to their sentencing?
A: Under sub-section (2), because a group of five or more persons acting in concert committed murder on the ground of personal belief/community, each member of the group shall be punished with death or life imprisonment. [Source: Section 103, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 103: Punishment for murder

Q: What are the two specific criteria required to trigger the specialized punishment under sub-section (2)?
A: It requires a group of "five or more persons acting in concert," and the murder must be committed on the ground of "race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground." [Source: Section 103, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 103: Punishment for murder

Q: If three people conspire and kill someone because of their language, do they fall under the specialized mob lynching provision of sub-section (2)?
A: No, because sub-section (2) explicitly requires a group of "five or more persons". However, they would still face death or life imprisonment under the general murder provision in sub-section (1). [Source: Section 103, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 103: Punishment for murder

Q: What is the socio-legal consequence of adding sub-section (2) to the murder statute?
A: The consequence is that the law now formally recognizes and specifically codifies "mob lynching" and hate crimes as distinct, aggravated forms of murder, ensuring collective accountability for identity-based violence. [Source: Section 103, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 104: Punishment for murder by life-convict

Q: What happens if an inmate who is already serving a life sentence commits a murder in prison?
A: An individual who commits murder while already under a sentence of life imprisonment will be punished with death or with a life sentence that strictly means the remainder of their natural life. [Source: Section 104, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder by life-convict

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 104: Punishment for murder by life-convict

Q: How does Section 104 of BNS 2023 penalize murder committed by a life-convict?
A: Section 104 of BNS 2023 states that whoever, being under a sentence of life imprisonment, commits murder shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for the remainder of their natural life. [Source: Section 104, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder by life-convict

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 104: Punishment for murder by life-convict

Q: A prisoner serving life for a previous crime murders a prison guard. What sentencing options does the judge have?
A: The judge must sentence the prisoner to death, or to life imprisonment which, according to this section, shall strictly mean the remainder of that person's natural life, removing the possibility of standard parole or remission. [Source: Section 104, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder by life-convict

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 104: Punishment for murder by life-convict

Q: What specific clarification does this section make regarding the definition of "imprisonment for life" for repeat murderers?
A: It explicitly clarifies that in this specific scenario, imprisonment for life "shall mean the remainder of that person’s natural life." [Source: Section 104, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder by life-convict

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 104: Punishment for murder by life-convict

Q: Does this severe sentencing rule apply if a prisoner serving a 10-year sentence (not life) commits murder?
A: No, this specific section only applies to whoever is "under sentence of imprisonment for life." A prisoner serving a shorter term would be charged under the standard murder provisions of Section 103. [Source: Section 104, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder by life-convict

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 104: Punishment for murder by life-convict

Q: What is the consequence of this section for the penal system?
A: The consequence is that it provides a supreme deterrent against prison violence by lifers; since a standard life sentence might otherwise allow for eventual release, this ensures repeat killers are either executed or permanently locked away until death. [Source: Section 104, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for murder by life-convict

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 105: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

Q: What is the punishment for killing someone without it qualifying legally as murder (e.g., manslaughter)?
A: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder is punishable by up to life imprisonment or 5 to 10 years if done with intent to kill/injure. If done only with the knowledge it might cause death (without intent), it is punishable by up to 10 years. [Source: Section 105, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 105: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

Q: How does Section 105 of BNS 2023 structure the punishment for culpable homicide?
A: Section 105 of BNS 2023 provides a two-tiered punishment system. If the act was done with the intent to cause death or fatal injury, the penalty is life imprisonment or 5-10 years. If done only with the knowledge of likely death but no intent, the penalty is up to 10 years. [Source: Section 105, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 105: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

Q: A man, severely provoked by a sudden insult, grabs a heavy stick and strikes another man, intending to cause a fatal head injury, and the man dies. It is ruled culpable homicide (not murder) due to provocation. What is the penalty tier?
A: Because the act was done with the intention of causing death or fatal bodily injury (even though provoked), he falls under the first tier and shall be punished with life imprisonment, or 5 to 10 years in prison. [Source: Section 105, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 105: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

Q: What mental state distinguishes the lighter sentencing tier (up to 10 years) from the heavier tier (life or 5-10 years) in this section?
A: The heavier tier applies if there is "intention" to cause death or fatal injury. The lighter tier applies if the act is done with mere "knowledge that it is likely to cause death, but without any intention to cause death". [Source: Section 105, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 105: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

Q: Is there a mandatory minimum sentence for culpable homicide where intent to kill is proven?
A: Yes, if the act is done with intent to cause death or fatal injury, and the judge opts for a term instead of life, the term "shall not be less than five years". [Source: Section 105, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 105: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

Q: What is the legal consequence of separating intention from knowledge in sentencing for homicide?
A: The consequence is that judges can proportionately punish offenders based on their level of malice; deliberate, intentional acts (even if mitigated by provocation) receive harsher minimums than reckless acts where the offender knew death was possible but didn't desire it. [Source: Section 105, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 106: Causing death by negligence

Q: What is the penalty for accidentally killing someone through a rash or negligent act (like medical negligence)?
A: Under BNS 2023, causing death by negligence is generally punishable by up to five years in prison. However, if the act is done by a registered medical practitioner while performing a medical procedure, the maximum punishment is reduced to two years. [Source: Section 106, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death by negligence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 106: Causing death by negligence

Q: How does Section 106 of BNS 2023 penalize causing death by negligence?
A: Section 106 of BNS 2023 establishes penalties for causing death by rash/negligent acts not amounting to homicide. Sub-section (1) imposes up to 5 years for general negligence, but only up to 2 years for registered medical practitioners. Sub-section (2) imposes up to 10 years for hit-and-run drivers who escape without reporting the incident. [Source: Section 106, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death by negligence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 106: Causing death by negligence

Q: A doctor makes a fatal error during surgery due to negligence. Separately, a construction worker negligently drops a brick, killing a pedestrian. Do they face the same maximum sentence?
A: No. Under sub-section (1), the construction worker faces up to five years in prison for general negligence, while the registered medical practitioner faces a reduced maximum of up to two years for negligence during a medical procedure. [Source: Section 106, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death by negligence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 106: Causing death by negligence

Q: What are the two distinct actions a negligent driver must take to avoid the severe "hit-and-run" penalty under sub-section (2)?
A: To avoid the elevated 10-year penalty under sub-section (2), the driver must not escape, and they must report the incident to a police officer or a Magistrate soon after it occurs. [Source: Section 106, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death by negligence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 106: Causing death by negligence

Q: Does the reduced 2-year penalty for doctors apply to any person claiming to be a healer?
A: No, the Explanation specifies that it only applies to a "registered medical practitioner," meaning someone with recognized medical qualifications whose name is entered in the National or State Medical Register. [Source: Section 106, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death by negligence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 106: Causing death by negligence

Q: What is the legal consequence of sub-section (2) for road accidents?
A: The consequence is that the law strongly disincentivizes "hit-and-run" incidents; drivers who cause fatal accidents but flee to evade responsibility face double the standard negligence penalty (up to 10 years instead of 5). [Source: Section 106, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing death by negligence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 107: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

Q: What is the punishment for convincing or helping a child or mentally ill person to commit suicide?
A: Abetting the suicide of a child, a person of unsound mind, a delirious person, or an intoxicated person is a severe crime punishable by death, life imprisonment, or up to ten years in prison, plus a fine. [Source: Section 107, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 107: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

Q: How does Section 107 of BNS 2023 protect vulnerable populations from suicidal instigation?
A: Section 107 of BNS 2023 severely punishes anyone who abets the suicide of highly vulnerable individuals—specifically children, persons of unsound mind, delirious persons, or intoxicated persons. The penalty is death, life imprisonment, or up to 10 years imprisonment. [Source: Section 107, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 107: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

Q: A cruel caregiver continually taunts a severely mentally disabled patient, ultimately handing them poison and encouraging them to take it. The patient dies by suicide. What is the caregiver's liability?
A: Because the victim was a person of unsound mind, the caregiver is guilty of abetment of suicide under this specific section and can be punished with death or life imprisonment. [Source: Section 107, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 107: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

Q: What four specific categories of vulnerable victims trigger this aggravated abetment section?
A: The four categories are: any child, any person of unsound mind, any delirious person, and any person in a state of intoxication. [Source: Section 107, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 107: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

Q: Does this section apply if a person abets the suicide of a healthy, sober 30-year-old adult?
A: No, abetting the suicide of a healthy, sober adult falls under the general abetment of suicide law (Section 108), not this aggravated section, which is strictly reserved for those lacking mental capacity or maturity. [Source: Section 107, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 107: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

Q: What is the underlying legal rationale for punishing this crime with the death penalty or life imprisonment?
A: The consequence reflects the law's view that causing the death of someone incapable of making a rational choice to die (due to youth or mental impairment) by manipulating them into suicide is morally and legally equivalent to outright murder. [Source: Section 107, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide of child or person of unsound mind

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 108: Abetment of suicide

Q: What is the penalty for driving someone to commit suicide or helping them do it?
A: If any person commits suicide, whoever abets (instigates, encourages, or assists) the commission of that suicide is punishable by up to ten years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 108, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 108: Abetment of suicide

Q: How does Section 108 of BNS 2023 penalize the abetment of suicide?
A: Section 108 of BNS 2023 establishes that if any person commits suicide, anyone who abets the suicide shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine. [Source: Section 108, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 108: Abetment of suicide

Q: An employer relentlessly harasses and illegally extorts an employee for months, driving the employee into such deep despair that they leave a suicide note blaming the employer and take their own life. Is the employer liable?
A: Yes, if the harassment and extortion are proven to have instigated or driven the employee to the act, the employer can be charged with abetment of suicide and face up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 108, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 108: Abetment of suicide

Q: What must actually occur for a person to be convicted under this specific section?
A: The victim must actually commit suicide. The section explicitly begins with the condition, "If any person commits suicide..." [Source: Section 108, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 108: Abetment of suicide

Q: Is the punishment the same if the person who commits suicide is a 12-year-old child?
A: No, if the victim is a child, the crime falls under the much stricter Section 107 (Abetment of suicide of child), which carries the death penalty or life imprisonment, rather than the general 10-year limit of Section 108. [Source: Section 108, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 108: Abetment of suicide

Q: What is the legal consequence of this section regarding psychological abuse?
A: The consequence is that severe psychological abuse, bullying, or harassment that directly causes a person to take their own life is criminalized, ensuring abusers can be held criminally responsible for a death even if they never laid a hand on the victim. [Source: Section 108, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abetment of suicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 109: Attempt to murder

Q: What is the penalty for attempting to murder someone?
A: Attempting to commit murder is generally punishable by up to 10 years in prison. However, if the victim is actually hurt during the attempt, the penalty can extend to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 109, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 109: Attempt to murder

Q: How does Section 109 of BNS 2023 handle the crime of attempted murder?
A: Section 109 of BNS 2023 penalizes acts done with murderous intent. Sub-section (1) provides up to 10 years imprisonment for the attempt, escalating to life imprisonment if hurt is caused. Sub-section (2) mandates death or remainder-of-life imprisonment if the offender is already a life-convict and causes hurt. [Source: Section 109, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 109: Attempt to murder

Q: A person intends to poison their boss. They buy poison and mix it into the boss's food, but before the boss eats it, the police discover it. What is the offender guilty of?
A: Under Illustration (d), by purchasing the poison, mixing it, and placing it where it would be served, the offender has moved beyond mere preparation and committed the offence of attempt to murder. [Source: Section 109, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 109: Attempt to murder

Q: What differentiates the two distinct sentencing tiers within sub-section (1)?
A: The primary tier provides up to 10 years for a mere attempt. The escalated tier (up to life imprisonment) applies specifically "if hurt is caused to any person by such act". [Source: Section 109, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 109: Attempt to murder

Q: If a man buys a gun intending to kill his rival but just keeps it in his closet, has he committed attempted murder?
A: No. As per Illustration (c), merely buying and loading a gun constitutes preparation. He has "not yet committed the offence" of attempted murder until he takes a direct step toward the act, such as firing the gun at the victim. [Source: Section 109, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 109: Attempt to murder

Q: What is the legal consequence of sub-section (2) for violent prison inmates?
A: The consequence is an absolute zero-tolerance policy for life-convicts; if an inmate already serving life attempts to murder a guard or fellow inmate and causes any hurt, they face a mandatory escalation to the death penalty or a strict natural-life sentence. [Source: Section 109, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to murder

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 110: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

Q: What is the punishment for trying to kill someone under circumstances that wouldn't amount to full murder (like during a sudden, provoked fight)?
A: Attempting to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder is punishable by up to three years in prison. If the victim is actually hurt during the attempt, the penalty increases to up to seven years. [Source: Section 110, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 110: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

Q: What does Section 110 of BNS 2023 criminalize?
A: Section 110 of BNS 2023 criminalizes the attempt to commit culpable homicide not amounting to murder. It prescribes a base penalty of up to 3 years imprisonment, which escalates to up to 7 years if the victim suffers hurt during the attempt. [Source: Section 110, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 110: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

Q: A man, severely provoked by a sudden insult, pulls out a gun and shoots at the insulter. He misses completely. What is the appropriate charge?
A: Under the Illustration, because he fired on grave and sudden provocation (which would reduce the crime from murder to culpable homicide if death occurred), he is guilty of attempt to commit culpable homicide and faces up to three years in prison. [Source: Section 110, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 110: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

Q: What specific factor causes the maximum penalty under this section to more than double from 3 years to 7 years?
A: The penalty escalates to up to seven years "if hurt is caused to any person by such act." [Source: Section 110, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 110: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

Q: How does this section differ from Attempt to Murder (Section 109)?
A: This section strictly applies when the offender acts under circumstances that legally mitigate the crime (like grave provocation or sudden fight) such that, if death had occurred, it would only be culpable homicide, not murder. Section 109 lacks these mitigating circumstances. [Source: Section 110, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 110: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

Q: What is the legal consequence of creating a separate attempt charge for mitigated homicide?
A: The consequence is proportional justice; the law recognizes that someone who tries to kill in the heat of a sudden, provoked passion is less legally culpable than a cold-blooded attempted murderer, and caps their maximum sentence much lower (7 years vs. life). [Source: Section 110, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit culpable homicide

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 111: Organised crime

Q: How does Indian law define and punish "organised crime"?
A: Organised crime involves a group indulging in continuing unlawful activities (like kidnapping, extortion, or cyber-crimes) using violence or unlawful means for material benefit. Punishments range from five years to life, or death if a murder is involved, accompanied by heavy minimum fines. [Source: Section 111, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 111: Organised crime

Q: What constitutes organised crime according to Section 111 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 111 of BNS 2023 defines organised crime as any continuing unlawful activity committed by a syndicate using coercion or violence for material gain. It establishes severe penalties: death or life imprisonment under sub-section (2)(a) if death results, and minimum five-year sentences under sub-sections (3) and (4) for abetting or mere membership in the syndicate. [Source: Section 111, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 111: Organised crime

Q: A mafia boss orders his gang to run an extortion racket. They have three previous charge-sheets against them. During an extortion attempt, they kill a business owner. What is the minimum fine the boss faces under the organized crime statute?
A: Because the offence resulted in death, under sub-section (2)(a), the boss shall be punished with death or life imprisonment, and shall be liable to a fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees. [Source: Section 111, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 111: Organised crime

Q: What specific legal history must exist for a gang's actions to qualify as a "continuing unlawful activity" under Explanation (ii)?
A: Under Explanation (ii), the activity must involve a cognizable offence punishable by three years or more, and more than one charge-sheet must have been filed against the syndicate before a competent Court within the preceding ten years, with the Court having taken cognizance. [Source: Section 111, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 111: Organised crime

Q: Can the wife of a gang member be prosecuted under this section solely for hiding her husband from the police?
A: No, the proviso to sub-section (5) explicitly states that the punishment for harbouring or concealing an offender does not apply in cases where the harbour or concealment is by the spouse of the offender. [Source: Section 111, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 111: Organised crime

Q: What is the consequence of sub-section (7) for people who hold assets for mafia members?
A: The consequence is that it attacks the financial infrastructure of gangs; anyone holding movable or immovable property on behalf of a syndicate member that they cannot satisfactorily account for faces three to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 111, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 112: Petty organised crime

Q: How does the law handle organized gangs that commit smaller crimes like pickpocketing or cheating?
A: Committing acts like theft, snatching, cheating, or unauthorized ticket selling as a member of a group or gang is considered "petty organised crime," punishable by one to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 112, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Petty organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 112: Petty organised crime

Q: What does Section 112 of BNS 2023 categorize as petty organised crime?
A: Section 112 of BNS 2023 categorizes crimes like trick theft, snatching, cheating, unauthorized betting, and selling exam papers committed by a group or gang as petty organised crime. Sub-section (2) prescribes a punishment of one to seven years imprisonment. [Source: Section 112, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Petty organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 112: Petty organised crime

Q: A group of three individuals coordinate to skim credit cards at ATMs across the city. What specialized charge applies to their coordinated activity?
A: Because they are a group committing theft through card skimming, they are committing petty organised crime under sub-section (1), punishable by one to seven years in prison under sub-section (2). [Source: Section 112, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Petty organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 112: Petty organised crime

Q: Does a person need to commit the physical act jointly with the gang to be charged under this section?
A: No, sub-section (1) specifies that whoever commits these acts "either singly or jointly," as long as they are "a member of a group or gang," is said to commit petty organised crime. [Source: Section 112, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Petty organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 112: Petty organised crime

Q: Does this section require the formal filing of previous charge-sheets over ten years, like the main "Organised Crime" section?
A: No, Section 112 does not include the complex "continuing unlawful activity" prerequisite of Section 111; it simply requires the act to be committed by a member of a group or gang. [Source: Section 112, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Petty organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 112: Petty organised crime

Q: What is the legal consequence of creating a specific "petty" organized crime category?
A: The consequence is that it provides law enforcement a specialized tool to dismantle low-level, high-volume criminal networks (like coordinated pickpocketing rings or exam-cheating mafias) without having to meet the extremely high evidentiary bar of the major organized crime statute. [Source: Section 112, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Petty organised crime

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 113: Terrorist act

Q: What acts legally qualify as terrorism under Indian criminal law?
A: A terrorist act involves using bombs, weapons, hazardous substances, or criminal force with the intent to threaten India's unity, security, or economy, or to strike terror in people. It also includes kidnapping to compel a government, or counterfeiting currency to destabilize the economy. [Source: Section 113, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Terrorist act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 113: Terrorist act

Q: How does Section 113 of BNS 2023 define and punish a terrorist act?
A: Section 113 of BNS 2023 comprehensively defines terrorist acts (including bombings, assassinations, and economic sabotage via counterfeiting) intended to threaten India's security or strike terror. Sub-section (2) mandates death or life imprisonment if death occurs, and 5 years to life for other terrorist acts. [Source: Section 113, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Terrorist act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 113: Terrorist act

Q: A militant group smuggles millions in high-quality counterfeit Indian currency into the country with the express intent of destroying the monetary stability of India. Is this terrorism?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1)(a)(iv), damaging the monetary stability of India by way of production, smuggling, or circulation of counterfeit Indian currency with the intent to threaten economic security constitutes a terrorist act. [Source: Section 113, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Terrorist act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 113: Terrorist act

Q: What specific intent must accompany the violent acts for them to be classified as terrorism under sub-section (1)?
A: The acts must be done with the intent "to threaten or likely to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty, security, or economic security of India" or "to strike terror or likely to strike terror in the people." [Source: Section 113, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Terrorist act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 113: Terrorist act

Q: Can a wife be sent to prison under sub-section (6) for hiding her husband in their house after he commits a terrorist bombing?
A: No, the proviso to sub-section (6) explicitly states that the punishment for voluntarily harbouring or concealing a terrorist does not apply if the harbour or concealment is by the spouse of the offender. [Source: Section 113, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Terrorist act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 113: Terrorist act

Q: What is the consequence of the Explanation at the end of Section 113 regarding overlapping laws?
A: The consequence is that it creates a specific procedural safeguard; to prevent arbitrary application of anti-terror laws, an officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police must explicitly decide whether to register the case under BNS Section 113 or under the specialized Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967. [Source: Section 113, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Terrorist act

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 114: Hurt

Q: What is the basic legal definition of causing "hurt" to someone?
A: Causing "hurt" simply means causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity to any person. [Source: Section 114, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 114: Hurt

Q: How does Section 114 of BNS 2023 define the concept of hurt?
A: Section 114 of BNS 2023 defines hurt concisely: whoever causes bodily pain, disease, or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt. [Source: Section 114, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 114: Hurt

Q: A prankster intentionally infects a coworker's coffee with a severe stomach virus, causing the coworker to be violently ill for a week, though there is no permanent damage or physical bruising. Has the prankster caused hurt?
A: Yes, by causing a "disease" or "infirmity" to the person, the prankster has met the definition of causing hurt under this section. [Source: Section 114, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 114: Hurt

Q: What three specific physical outcomes are listed as constituting "hurt"?
A: The three outcomes are bodily pain, disease, or infirmity. [Source: Section 114, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 114: Hurt

Q: Does the law require that the victim's skin be broken or bones fractured for it to be considered "hurt"?
A: No, the definition only requires causing "bodily pain." Therefore, a hard slap or a punch that only causes pain without leaving a visible mark still qualifies as hurt. [Source: Section 114, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 114: Hurt

Q: What is the legal consequence of this broad definition of hurt?
A: The consequence is that criminal law protects individuals not just from severe traumatic injuries, but from any non-consensual infliction of pain or sickness, providing a foundational baseline for prosecuting all levels of physical assault. [Source: Section 114, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 115: Voluntarily causing hurt

Q: What is the punishment for intentionally hurting someone (e.g., getting into a minor physical altercation)?
A: Intentionally causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity to someone is punishable by up to one year in prison, or a fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both. [Source: Section 115, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 115: Voluntarily causing hurt

Q: How does Section 115 of BNS 2023 penalize voluntarily causing hurt?
A: Section 115 of BNS 2023 defines voluntarily causing hurt as acting with the intent or knowledge of causing bodily pain, disease, or infirmity. Sub-section (2) prescribes a penalty of up to one year imprisonment or a fine up to ten thousand rupees for this offence. [Source: Section 115, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 115: Voluntarily causing hurt

Q: Two neighbors argue, and one intentionally throws a rock that hits the other's leg, causing temporary pain and bruising. What is the maximum jail time for this offence?
A: Because he acted with the intention of causing hurt, he has voluntarily caused hurt under sub-section (1), and under sub-section (2), he can be punished with imprisonment extending up to one year. [Source: Section 115, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 115: Voluntarily causing hurt

Q: Under sub-section (1), what two mental states can qualify an act as "voluntarily" causing hurt?
A: The act must be done with the "intention" of causing hurt, or with the "knowledge" that he is likely thereby to cause hurt. [Source: Section 115, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 115: Voluntarily causing hurt

Q: Is the punishment under Section 115 applicable to every single instance of voluntarily causing hurt?
A: No, sub-section (2) explicitly states "except in the case provided for by sub-section (1) of section 122," meaning that hurt caused under sudden provocation (covered by Section 122) has a different legal standard and penalty. [Source: Section 115, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 115: Voluntarily causing hurt

Q: What is the consequence of distinguishing between mere "hurt" and "voluntarily causing hurt"?
A: The consequence is that accidental bumps or clumsiness that cause pain are not criminalized; the law only punishes the infliction of pain when accompanied by explicit malicious intent or reckless knowledge. [Source: Section 115, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 116: Grievous hurt

Q: What specific types of injuries are classified as "grievous hurt" in Indian law?
A: Grievous hurt includes emasculation, permanent loss of sight/hearing, destruction or permanent impairment of any member/joint, permanent disfiguration of the head/face, bone/tooth fractures, or any hurt endangering life or causing severe pain/inability to follow ordinary pursuits for 15 days. [Source: Section 116, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 116: Grievous hurt

Q: How does Section 116 of BNS 2023 categorize grievous hurt?
A: Section 116 of BNS 2023 exhaustively lists eight specific kinds of hurt designated as "grievous": emasculation, permanent privation of sight or hearing, privation/impairment of any member/joint, permanent head/face disfiguration, fracture/dislocation of a bone/tooth, and severe hurt causing 15 days of severe pain or incapacitation. [Source: Section 116, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 116: Grievous hurt

Q: During a bar fight, a man punches another in the mouth, completely knocking out two of his front teeth. Does this qualify as grievous hurt?
A: Yes, under clause (Seventh), the fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth is specifically designated as grievous hurt. [Source: Section 116, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 116: Grievous hurt

Q: What is the specific time threshold required under clause (Eighth) for a non-permanent injury to still be considered "grievous"?
A: Under clause (Eighth), the hurt must cause the sufferer to be in severe bodily pain, or unable to follow his ordinary pursuits, for the space of fifteen days. [Source: Section 116, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 116: Grievous hurt

Q: If a person is punched and gets a bruised rib that hurts but allows them to continue working normally for two weeks, is it grievous hurt?
A: No, unless the bone is actually fractured or dislocated, or the injury endangers life, or it incapacitates them/causes severe pain for a full fifteen days, it remains simple hurt, not grievous hurt. [Source: Section 116, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 116: Grievous hurt

Q: What is the legal consequence of codifying this specific list of injuries?
A: The consequence is that it removes judicial ambiguity in defining severe bodily harm; prosecutors can easily elevate a standard assault charge to an aggravated "grievous hurt" charge simply by proving the injury matches one of these eight explicit statutory definitions. [Source: Section 116, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 117: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

Q: What is the penalty for intentionally causing someone a severe, permanent injury (grievous hurt)?
A: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt is generally punishable by up to seven years in prison. If the injury puts the victim in a permanent vegetative state or permanent disability, the minimum sentence is ten years, up to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 117, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 117: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

Q: How does Section 117 of BNS 2023 punish voluntarily causing grievous hurt?
A: Section 117 of BNS 2023 establishes penalties for intentionally or knowingly causing grievous hurt. Sub-section (2) provides up to 7 years imprisonment. Sub-section (3) escalates this to 10 years to life if permanent disability or vegetative state occurs. Sub-section (4) provides up to 7 years for mob attacks based on identity. [Source: Section 117, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 117: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

Q: An attacker intends to break a victim's arm with a bat, but instead strikes their head, putting them in a permanent vegetative state. What penalty does the attacker face?
A: Because the attacker intended to cause grievous hurt (broken bone) and actually caused grievous hurt resulting in a persistent vegetative state, under sub-section (3), they shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a minimum of ten years, which may extend to life. [Source: Section 117, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 117: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

Q: What legal clarification does the Explanation provide about intending one type of grievous hurt but causing another?
A: The Explanation states that if a person intends or knows they are likely to cause one kind of grievous hurt, but actually causes a different kind of grievous hurt, they are still legally said to have "voluntarily caused grievous hurt." [Source: Section 117, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 117: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

Q: Can a mob of four people be charged under the specific hate-crime provision of sub-section (4)?
A: No, sub-section (4) explicitly requires "a group of five or more persons acting in concert" to trigger that specific liability for causing grievous hurt based on identity. [Source: Section 117, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 117: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

Q: What is the consequence of adding sub-section (3) regarding vegetative states?
A: The consequence is that it treats injuries that completely destroy a person's quality of life (permanent disability or vegetative state) as near-equivalents to murder, imposing a strict minimum sentence of ten years up to natural-life imprisonment. [Source: Section 117, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 118: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

Q: What happens if an assault is committed using a deadly weapon, poison, or fire?
A: Using dangerous weapons, explosives, poison, fire, or animals to voluntarily cause hurt elevates the penalty to up to three years. If these dangerous means are used to cause *grievous* hurt, the penalty escalates to a minimum of one year, up to ten years or life imprisonment. [Source: Section 118, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 118: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

Q: How does Section 118 of BNS 2023 penalize assaults involving dangerous instruments?
A: Section 118 of BNS 2023 aggregates penalties for using lethal weapons, fire, poison, explosives, or animals to cause harm. Sub-section (1) provides up to 3 years for causing simple hurt this way, while sub-section (2) provides 1 to 10 years, or life imprisonment, for causing grievous hurt via these means. [Source: Section 118, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 118: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

Q: A man gets angry and purposefully sics his trained attack dog on a mail carrier, causing severe, permanent disfiguration to the carrier's face (grievous hurt). Under what specific provision is he charged?
A: He is charged under sub-section (2) for voluntarily causing grievous hurt "by means of any animal" (a method defined in sub-section 1), and faces life imprisonment or a term from one to ten years. [Source: Section 118, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 118: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

Q: List at least four of the "dangerous means" explicitly categorized in sub-section (1).
A: The categorized means include: instruments for shooting/stabbing/cutting, fire/heated substances, poison/corrosive substances, explosive substances, deleterious inhalants/substances, and animals. [Source: Section 118, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 118: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

Q: Do these elevated penalties apply if the dangerous weapon is used strictly under grave and sudden provocation?
A: No, both sub-sections explicitly state "except in the case provided for by section 122," which handles hurt/grievous hurt caused on grave and sudden provocation under a different sentencing framework. [Source: Section 118, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 118: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

Q: What is the legal consequence of this section regarding the method of assault?
A: The consequence is that the law heavily penalizes the *method* of violence independent of the *result*; even if a knife or acid attack only results in minor simple hurt, the use of such deadly means automatically triples the maximum sentence (from 1 year to 3 years) compared to an unarmed assault. [Source: Section 118, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt by dangerous weapons or means

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 119: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

Q: What is the punishment for beating someone to extort money or force them to commit a crime?
A: Causing hurt to extort property or force an illegal act is punishable by up to ten years in prison. If the perpetrator causes *grievous* hurt for these purposes, the penalty increases to life imprisonment or up to ten years. [Source: Section 119, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 119: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

Q: How does Section 119 of BNS 2023 deal with extortionary violence?
A: Section 119 of BNS 2023 criminalizes causing bodily harm to extort property or constrain someone to do an illegal act. Sub-section (1) punishes simple hurt for this purpose with up to 10 years. Sub-section (2) punishes grievous hurt for this purpose with life imprisonment or up to 10 years. [Source: Section 119, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 119: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

Q: A gang captures a bank manager and breaks his legs (grievous hurt) to force him to hand over the vault codes (extorting property/constraining an illegal act). What penalty do they face?
A: Under sub-section (2), because they voluntarily caused grievous hurt for the purpose of extortion or constraining an illegal act, they shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 119, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 119: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

Q: Under sub-section (1), what are the two primary ulterior motives that elevate the crime of causing hurt to a 10-year offence?
A: The two motives are: 1) extorting any property or valuable security, and 2) constraining the sufferer (or interested person) to do anything illegal or which may facilitate an offence. [Source: Section 119, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 119: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

Q: If an attacker hurts someone just because they are angry, without trying to take property or force an illegal act, does this 10-year penalty apply?
A: No, standard assault without the specific motive of extortion or constraining an illegal act falls under standard hurt (Section 115) which only carries up to one year in prison, not ten. [Source: Section 119, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 119: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

Q: What is the legal consequence of coupling the intent to extort with the act of causing hurt?
A: The consequence is a massive escalation in penalty; a basic punch that usually carries 1 year in prison jumps to 10 years if that punch was thrown to force the victim to hand over their wallet or commit a crime, recognizing extortionate violence as a severe threat to public order. [Source: Section 119, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort property, or to constrain to an illegal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 120: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

Q: What is the penalty for police brutality, specifically torturing a suspect to extract a confession?
A: Voluntarily causing hurt to extort a confession, gather information about an offence, or compel the return of property is punishable by up to seven years in prison. If grievous hurt is caused, the penalty increases to up to ten years. [Source: Section 120, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 120: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

Q: How does Section 120 of BNS 2023 address custodial torture and vigilante justice?
A: Section 120 of BNS 2023 criminalizes causing hurt (up to 7 years) or grievous hurt (up to 10 years) for the purpose of extorting a confession, extracting information about an offence, or compelling the restoration of property. It directly targets police misconduct and coercive debt collection. [Source: Section 120, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 120: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

Q: A police officer arrests a theft suspect and severely beats him, fracturing his ribs (grievous hurt), to force him to reveal where the stolen goods are hidden. What is the officer's liability?
A: Under sub-section (2) and corresponding Illustration (b), the officer voluntarily caused grievous hurt to extort information leading to the detection of an offence/restoration of property, and is punishable by up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 120, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 120: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

Q: Besides extorting a confession, what other specific purpose related to property triggers this section if someone uses violence?
A: Causing hurt for the purpose of "constraining the sufferer... to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand" triggers this section. [Source: Section 120, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 120: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

Q: Does this section only apply to public servants like police officers or revenue agents?
A: No, while the Illustrations focus on police and revenue officers, the statute begins with "Whoever," meaning it applies equally to private citizens (like a landlord violently torturing a tenant to collect rent). [Source: Section 120, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 120: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to extort confession, or to compel restoration of

Q: What is the systemic consequence of Section 120 on law enforcement practices?
A: The consequence is that it explicitly criminalizes the "third degree"; any police officer who resorts to physical violence or torture to solve cases or recover stolen goods faces severe felony charges, reinforcing the absolute prohibition against custodial torture. [Source: Section 120, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 121: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

Q: What is the penalty for attacking a public servant, like a police officer or tax collector, while they are working?
