A: Causing hurt to a public servant to deter them from their duty is punishable by up to five years in prison. If the attacker causes grievous hurt, the penalty increases to a minimum of one year and up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 121, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 121: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

Q: How does Section 121 of BNS 2023 protect public servants from violence?
A: Section 121 of BNS 2023 provides enhanced penalties for assaulting public servants. Sub-section (1) punishes causing simple hurt to deter a public servant with up to 5 years imprisonment. Sub-section (2) punishes causing grievous hurt with 1 to 10 years imprisonment. [Source: Section 121, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 121: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

Q: A building inspector arrives to shut down an illegal construction site. The owner punches the inspector, causing a black eye (simple hurt), to force him to leave. What is the owner's liability?
A: Under sub-section (1), because the owner voluntarily caused hurt to deter a public servant from discharging his duty, he is punishable by imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years. [Source: Section 121, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 121: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

Q: What specific intent or context must accompany the hurt to trigger the enhanced penalties of this section rather than standard assault laws?
A: The hurt must be caused to a public servant while they are discharging their duty, or with the intent to prevent/deter them from discharging their duty, or in consequence of something they did in the lawful discharge of their duty. [Source: Section 121, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 121: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

Q: If a police officer is off-duty in civilian clothes and gets into a bar fight over a personal dispute, does the attacker face these enhanced penalties?
A: No, this section specifically requires the violence to be related to the public servant "discharging his duty as such public servant" or in consequence of their official actions. A purely personal dispute falls under standard assault laws. [Source: Section 121, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 121: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

Q: What is the systemic consequence of making an assault on a public servant a specialized offence with higher penalties?
A: The consequence is that it heavily deters citizens from using violence to obstruct government operations, ensuring that state machinery (like law enforcement, revenue collection, and regulation) can function without constant physical threats to its personnel. [Source: Section 121, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt to deter public servant from his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 122: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

Q: What happens if a person assaults someone because they were severely and suddenly provoked?
A: If a person causes hurt on grave and sudden provocation, the maximum penalty drops significantly to just one month in prison. If they cause grievous hurt under the same provocation, the maximum penalty drops to five years. [Source: Section 122, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 122: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

Q: How does Section 122 of BNS 2023 mitigate the punishment for assault?
A: Section 122 of BNS 2023 mitigates penalties for hurt caused under grave and sudden provocation. Sub-section (1) caps the penalty for simple hurt at 1 month imprisonment. Sub-section (2) caps the penalty for grievous hurt at 5 years. [Source: Section 122, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 122: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

Q: A man walks into his house and catches his business partner stealing from his safe. In a sudden rage, he punches the partner, breaking his jaw (grievous hurt). What is his maximum legal exposure?
A: Because he voluntarily caused grievous hurt on grave and sudden provocation, under sub-section (2), his maximum punishment is mitigated to five years imprisonment, rather than the standard seven years for grievous hurt. [Source: Section 122, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 122: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

Q: What critical condition must be met regarding the victim's identity for the attacker to claim the provocation defense under this section?
A: The attacker must neither intend nor know himself to be likely to cause hurt "to any person other than the person who gave the provocation." [Source: Section 122, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 122: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

Q: Can an attacker claim provocation if they deliberately went looking for a fight and goaded the victim into insulting them?
A: No, the Explanation states this section is subject to the proviso of Exception 1 of Section 101, which explicitly disqualifies provocation if it was sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse to cause harm. [Source: Section 122, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 122: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

Q: What is the legal consequence of reducing the penalty for provoked assault to a maximum of one month?
A: The consequence is that the law acknowledges human frailty and loss of self-control; while vigilante violence is still illegal, a brief lapse in judgment caused by severe, unexpected provocation is punished far less harshly than premeditated malice. [Source: Section 122, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing hurt or grievous hurt on provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 123: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

Q: What is the punishment for drugging or poisoning someone to commit another crime (like slipping someone a date-rape drug or slipping a guard a sleeping pill)?
A: Administering poison or any stupefying, intoxicating, or unwholesome drug to cause hurt, or to facilitate another crime, is punishable by up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 123, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 123: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

Q: How does Section 123 of BNS 2023 penalize the use of drugs or poison in criminal acts?
A: Section 123 of BNS 2023 criminalizes the administration of poison or stupefying/intoxicating drugs with the intent to cause hurt, or with the intent to commit or facilitate an offence. It prescribes a punishment of up to 10 years imprisonment. [Source: Section 123, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 123: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

Q: A thief slips a strong sleeping pill into a security guard's coffee to knock him out so the thief can rob a jewelry store. What specific physical assault charge applies?
A: The thief is guilty under this section because they administered a stupefying/unwholesome drug with the intent to facilitate the commission of an offence (robbery), and faces up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 123, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 123: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

Q: Besides intending to cause "hurt," what other specific intent is listed that makes drugging someone a 10-year offence?
A: Administering the drug with the intent "to commit or to facilitate the commission of an offence" also triggers the 10-year penalty. [Source: Section 123, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 123: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

Q: Does this section apply if a bartender accidentally serves a drink with spoiled milk that makes a customer violently ill?
A: No, the offence requires the *intent* to cause hurt, the *intent* to commit/facilitate an offence, or the *knowledge* that it is likely to cause hurt. An honest accident lacks this mens rea. [Source: Section 123, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 123: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

Q: What is the consequence of broadly including "stupefying" and "intoxicating" drugs alongside "poison" in this section?
A: The consequence is that date-rape scenarios (using roofies/alcohol) and premeditated incapacitation for theft are treated with the exact same severe gravity (up to 10 years) as attempting to slowly poison someone's organs. [Source: Section 123, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing hurt by means of poison, etc., with intent to commit an offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 124: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

Q: How does Indian law punish acid attacks?
A: Causing damage, burns, or disfigurement by throwing acid is punishable by a minimum of ten years up to life imprisonment, along with a fine that must be paid directly to the victim for medical expenses. Merely attempting an acid attack carries a 5 to 7 year sentence. [Source: Section 124, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 124: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

Q: What are the penalties under Section 124 of BNS 2023 for acid attacks?
A: Section 124 of BNS 2023 imposes a strict penalty of 10 years to life imprisonment for causing damage or deformity by throwing or administering acid (sub-section 1). Sub-section (2) punishes attempted acid attacks with 5 to 7 years imprisonment. Fines must cover the victim's medical expenses. [Source: Section 124, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 124: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

Q: An attacker throws acid at a woman but completely misses, splashing it on a brick wall instead. What penalty does the attacker face?
A: Under sub-section (2), because the attacker attempted to throw acid with the intention of causing damage/deformity, they shall be punished with imprisonment for a term between five and seven years, even though no physical injury occurred. [Source: Section 124, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 124: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

Q: What specific directives does sub-section (1) give regarding the financial fine imposed on the attacker?
A: The two provisos state that the fine shall be "just and reasonable to meet the medical expenses of the treatment of the victim" and that the fine "shall be paid to the victim." [Source: Section 124, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 124: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

Q: If an attacker throws a strong, burning alkaline substance (like concentrated lye) instead of a traditional acidic liquid, does this section still apply?
A: Yes, Explanation 1 explicitly expands the definition of "acid" to include "any substance which has acidic or corrosive character or burning nature" capable of causing scarring, disfigurement, or disability. [Source: Section 124, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 124: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

Q: What is the legal consequence of Explanation 2 regarding the severity of the damage?
A: The consequence is that the defense cannot argue for a lesser sentence by claiming the victim's scars can eventually be fixed by plastic surgery; the damage/deformity "shall not be required to be irreversible" for the 10-year-to-life sentence to apply. [Source: Section 124, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 125: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

Q: What is the punishment for reckless behavior that puts people in danger, like firing a gun into the air or dropping heavy items off a balcony?
A: Doing a rash or negligent act that endangers human life is punishable by up to three months in prison. If the act actually causes simple hurt, it goes up to six months; if it causes grievous hurt, it goes up to three years. [Source: Section 125, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 125: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

Q: How does Section 125 of BNS 2023 grade the punishment for reckless endangerment?
A: Section 125 of BNS 2023 creates a three-tier system for rash/negligent acts endangering life. The base act carries up to 3 months imprisonment. Under clause (a), if simple hurt results, the penalty is up to 6 months. Under clause (b), if grievous hurt results, it is up to 3 years. [Source: Section 125, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 125: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

Q: A negligent forklift driver speeds through a warehouse and knocks over a heavy pallet onto a coworker, breaking the coworker's leg (grievous hurt). What is the maximum prison sentence for the driver?
A: Because his negligent act endangered life and ultimately caused grievous hurt, under clause (b), he shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years. [Source: Section 125, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 125: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

Q: What mental state is required to secure a conviction under this general endangerment statute?
A: The act must be done "rashly" or "negligently" to the extent that it endangers human life or the personal safety of others. Intent to harm is not required. [Source: Section 125, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 125: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

Q: Does a person face the 3-year penalty if their reckless act kills someone?
A: No, if the rash or negligent act causes *death*, it is no longer covered by this section; it escalates to Section 106 (Causing death by negligence), which carries a standard penalty of up to five years. [Source: Section 125, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 125: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

Q: What is the legal consequence of establishing a base penalty for endangerment even when no one gets hurt?
A: The consequence is that law enforcement can intervene and prosecute objectively dangerous behavior (like severe reckless driving or mishandling explosives) *before* a tragedy occurs, preventing harm rather than just reacting to it. [Source: Section 125, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering life or personal safety of others

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 126: Wrongful restraint

Q: What does the law mean by "wrongful restraint"?
A: Wrongful restraint occurs when someone intentionally obstructs another person from proceeding in a direction they have a legal right to go. It is punishable by up to one month in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 126, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 126: Wrongful restraint

Q: How does Section 126 of BNS 2023 define and punish wrongful restraint?
A: Section 126 of BNS 2023 defines wrongful restraint as voluntarily obstructing a person from proceeding in a direction they have a right to proceed. Sub-section (2) prescribes a penalty of up to 1 month simple imprisonment or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 126, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 126: Wrongful restraint

Q: A shopkeeper stands in the middle of a public sidewalk and physically blocks his rival from walking past his store, though the rival can easily walk the other way. Has the shopkeeper committed a crime?
A: Yes, under the Illustration for Section 126, because the rival has a right to pass along the public path and the shopkeeper voluntarily obstructs him without a good faith belief in a lawful right to do so, he is guilty of wrongful restraint. [Source: Section 126, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 126: Wrongful restraint

Q: What is the core condition regarding the victim's movement that makes the obstruction "wrongful"?
A: The obstruction must prevent the person "from proceeding in any direction in which that person has a right to proceed." [Source: Section 126, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 126: Wrongful restraint

Q: A landowner legitimately believes a shortcut across his field is private property, so he puts up a fence to stop hikers. It turns out to be a public easement. Is he guilty of wrongful restraint?
A: No, the Exception states that obstructing a private way over land/water which a person in good faith believes they have a lawful right to obstruct is not an offence under this section. [Source: Section 126, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 126: Wrongful restraint

Q: What is the legal consequence of differentiating restraint from confinement?
A: The consequence is that merely blocking someone's path in one direction (restraint) is treated as a very minor misdemeanor (1 month maximum), whereas totally trapping someone (confinement) is treated as a much more serious offence. [Source: Section 126, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 127: Wrongful confinement

Q: What is the penalty for locking someone in a room or preventing them from leaving a specific area against their will?
A: Wrongfully confining someone within certain limits is punishable by up to one year in prison. The penalty increases significantly based on the duration of the confinement (e.g., 3+ days is up to 3 years, 10+ days is up to 5 years) or if done for extortion. [Source: Section 127, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 127: Wrongful confinement

Q: How does Section 127 of BNS 2023 define and grade the punishment for wrongful confinement?
A: Section 127 of BNS 2023 defines wrongful confinement as restraining a person to prevent them from proceeding beyond circumscribing limits. Penalties scale up: up to 1 year for basic confinement, up to 3 years for 3+ days, up to 5 years for 10+ days, and up to 3 years extra for secretive/extortionate confinement. [Source: Section 127, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 127: Wrongful confinement

Q: A man locks his employee in a windowless basement for two weeks (14 days) to prevent him from quitting. What is the maximum sentence the employer faces for the confinement duration?
A: Because he wrongfully confined the person for ten days or more, under sub-section (4), he is punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to five years, plus a mandatory minimum fine. [Source: Section 127, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 127: Wrongful confinement

Q: What distinguishes "wrongful confinement" (Section 127) from mere "wrongful restraint" (Section 126)?
A: Restraint only blocks a person from going in a specific direction, while confinement completely prevents the person "from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits" (i.e., trapping them). [Source: Section 127, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 127: Wrongful confinement

Q: What is the penalty under sub-section (5) if a kidnapper continues to hold a victim even after knowing a court has issued a writ for their release?
A: The kidnapper faces up to two years imprisonment *in addition* to any other term of imprisonment they are liable for under the chapter. [Source: Section 127, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 127: Wrongful confinement

Q: What is the consequence of the escalating time-based penalties in sub-sections (3) and (4)?
A: The consequence is that the law incentivizes the swift release of captives; kidnappers face exponentially harsher maximum sentences the longer they hold someone against their will, escalating from 1 year to 5 years based purely on duration. [Source: Section 127, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongful confinement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 128: Force

Q: In legal terms, what exactly constitutes using "force" against another person?
A: Using force means causing motion, changing the motion, or stopping the motion of a person (or a substance that touches them/their clothes) using bodily power, by disposing of a substance, or by inducing an animal to move. [Source: Section 128, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 128: Force

Q: How does Section 128 of BNS 2023 legally define the use of "force"?
A: Section 128 of BNS 2023 defines force as causing, changing, or ceasing motion to another person, or to a substance that contacts them/their clothes. It specifies three ways to cause this motion: by bodily power, by disposing a substance, or by inducing an animal. [Source: Section 128, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 128: Force

Q: A prankster ties a tripwire across a doorway. A victim walks through, hits the wire, and falls down. Has the prankster used "force" under this definition even without touching the victim?
A: Yes, under clause (b), the prankster disposed a substance (the wire) in a manner that caused a change/cessation of motion to the victim without any further act on his part, fulfilling the legal definition of using force. [Source: Section 128, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 128: Force

Q: What are the three exclusive ways listed in the proviso by which the motion/change of motion must be caused to qualify as "force"?
A: The three ways are: (a) by his own bodily power; (b) by disposing any substance so motion takes place without further action; and (c) by inducing any animal to move/change/cease motion. [Source: Section 128, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 128: Force

Q: If a person shouts "Boo!" and another person gets scared and jumps backward, has the shouter used "force" under this section?
A: No, because the motion was not caused by bodily power acting upon them, the disposing of a substance, or the inducing of an animal. It was a purely psychological reaction to sound, which doesn't fit the physical definition of force here. [Source: Section 128, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 128: Force

Q: What is the legal consequence of including "substances" and "animals" in the definition of force?
A: The consequence is that the law eliminates loopholes for indirect physical assault; setting a trap, pouring boiling water, or siccing a dog on someone are legally treated as the exact same direct use of "force" as punching them with a fist. [Source: Section 128, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 129: Criminal force

Q: When does the use of physical force become illegal "criminal force"?
A: Force becomes "criminal force" when it is used intentionally, without the person's consent, either to commit an offence, or with the intent/knowledge that it will cause injury, fear, or annoyance to that person. [Source: Section 129, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 129: Criminal force

Q: What are the parameters of "criminal force" under Section 129 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 129 of BNS 2023 stipulates that force is criminal when used intentionally and without consent to commit an offence, or when intended/known to be likely to cause injury, fear, or annoyance to the victim. [Source: Section 129, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 129: Criminal force

Q: A man is bathing in a river. As a cruel joke, another man pours boiling water into the river upstream, knowing it will scald the bather. Is this criminal force?
A: Yes, under Illustration (g), by pouring the boiling water he intentionally causes motion in a substance that contacts the bather. Since he did this without consent, knowing it would cause injury/annoyance, he has used criminal force. [Source: Section 129, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 129: Criminal force

Q: What three specific negative outcomes to the victim must the offender intend (or know are likely) to convert simple force into "criminal force"?
A: The offender must intend or know it is likely that the force will cause "injury, fear or annoyance" to the person. [Source: Section 129, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 129: Criminal force

Q: A doctor forcibly restrains an unconscious, thrashing patient during an emergency surgery to save their life. Is this criminal force?
A: No, because while it is intentional force without explicit active consent, it is not done to commit an offence, nor is it done intending to cause injury, fear, or annoyance (it is done to heal/save). [Source: Section 129, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 129: Criminal force

Q: What is the consequence of including the word "annoyance" in the definition of criminal force?
A: The consequence is that non-injurious physical harassment—like intentionally pushing past someone in the street, aggressively splashing water on them, or forcibly pulling up a veil—is fully criminalized even if it doesn't cause physical pain. [Source: Section 129, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal force

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 130: Assault

Q: What does the crime of "assault" actually mean under Indian law?
A: In Indian law, "assault" is not the act of hitting someone (that is criminal force or hurt); assault is merely making a gesture or preparation that makes someone reasonably fear that you are about to use criminal force against them (like raising a fist). [Source: Section 130, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 130: Assault

Q: How does Section 130 of BNS 2023 define assault?
A: Section 130 of BNS 2023 defines assault as making any gesture or preparation intending/knowing it is likely to cause any person present to apprehend that criminal force is about to be used against them. [Source: Section 130, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 130: Assault

Q: During an argument, a man snarls "I'm going to beat you," and aggressively picks up a heavy stick. Even though he hasn't swung the stick yet, has he committed a crime?
A: Yes, under Illustration (c), taking up the stick is a gesture/preparation, and while the words alone aren't an assault, the gesture explained by the threatening words causes the apprehension of criminal force, making it an assault. [Source: Section 130, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 130: Assault

Q: What is the crucial psychological effect that the gesture/preparation must have on the victim to constitute assault?
A: It must cause the victim "to apprehend that he who makes that gesture or preparation is about to use criminal force to that person." [Source: Section 130, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 130: Assault

Q: If someone stands completely still with their hands in their pockets and yells, "I am going to punch you in the face!", is that assault?
A: No, the Explanation explicitly states that "Mere words do not amount to an assault." There must be a physical gesture or preparation accompanying the words to cause the apprehension of immediate force. [Source: Section 130, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 130: Assault

Q: What is the legal consequence of separating the definition of "assault" from "criminal force"?
A: The consequence is that the law criminalizes the *threat* of imminent violence independently of actual physical contact. It protects a person's right to be free from the fear and anticipation of being attacked, allowing police to arrest someone before a blow is actually struck. [Source: Section 130, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 131: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

Q: What is the basic penalty for assaulting or using criminal force against someone without a valid excuse?
A: The basic punishment for assault or using criminal force (when not done under grave and sudden provocation) is up to three months in prison, or a fine up to 1,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 131, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 131: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

Q: What is the general penalty for assault under Section 131 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 131 of BNS 2023 prescribes a punishment of up to 3 months imprisonment or a fine up to 1,000 rupees for assault or criminal force, provided it is not committed under grave and sudden provocation. [Source: Section 131, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 131: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

Q: A man gets annoyed at a slow walker on the sidewalk and violently shoves them out of the way. What is the maximum sentence he faces for this basic criminal force?
A: Because he used criminal force otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation, he shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months. [Source: Section 131, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 131: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

Q: Under Explanation 1, list two specific scenarios where an attacker cannot claim "grave and sudden provocation" as a defense to mitigate their assault.
A: Provocation cannot mitigate the offence if: 1) the provocation was sought/voluntarily provoked by the offender as an excuse, or 2) the provocation was given by a public servant acting in the lawful exercise of their powers. [Source: Section 131, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 131: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

Q: Can a person claim they were provoked into assaulting someone if that person was lawfully exercising their right of private defence?
A: No, Explanation 1 clause (c) explicitly states that provocation given by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence will not mitigate the punishment for an offence under this section. [Source: Section 131, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 131: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

Q: What is the legal consequence of Explanation 2 regarding the severity of provocation?
A: The consequence is that the law does not provide a rigid mathematical formula for what counts as "grave and sudden"; instead, whether the provocation was sufficient to mitigate the offence is explicitly left as a "question of fact" for the judge/jury to decide case-by-case. [Source: Section 131, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 132: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

Q: What is the penalty for using criminal force (like shoving) or threatening (assaulting) a public servant to stop them from doing their job?
A: Assaulting or using criminal force to deter a public servant from their duty is punishable by up to two years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 132, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 132: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

Q: How does Section 132 of BNS 2023 protect public servants from interference?
A: Section 132 of BNS 2023 penalizes assaulting or using criminal force against a public servant to deter them from their duty, or in consequence of their lawful actions, with imprisonment up to 2 years. [Source: Section 132, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 132: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

Q: A citizen aggressively raises a fist (assault) at a meter reader to scare him away from checking the electricity meter. Under what specific provision is this punished?
A: The citizen is punishable under Section 132 because they assaulted a public servant with intent to deter that person from discharging his duty, facing up to two years in prison. [Source: Section 132, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 132: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

Q: What distinguishes the offence in Section 132 from the similar offence in Section 121?
A: Section 121 specifically deals with voluntarily causing "hurt" (actual pain/injury) to a public servant and carries up to 5 years, while Section 132 deals with "assault or criminal force" (threats or non-injurious physical contact like shoving) and carries up to 2 years. [Source: Section 132, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 132: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

Q: If a police officer illegally breaks into a home without a warrant, and the homeowner shoves the officer out, does Section 132 apply?
A: No, this section only applies when the public servant is acting "in the execution of his duty" or "in the lawful discharge of his duty." An illegal, unconstitutional act is not a lawful discharge of duty. [Source: Section 132, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 132: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

Q: What is the legal consequence of separating assault on a public servant into its own section rather than treating it as basic assault?
A: The consequence is a significant sentence enhancement; while basic assault/criminal force (Section 131) carries a maximum of 3 months in prison, doing the exact same action to a public servant to deter them (Section 132) multiplies the maximum penalty eightfold to 2 years. [Source: Section 132, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force to deter public servant from discharge of his duty

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 133: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

Q: What is the penalty for assaulting someone specifically to publicly humiliate or dishonour them?
A: Assaulting or using criminal force with the specific intent to dishonour a person (and not under grave provocation) is punishable by up to two years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 133, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 133: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

Q: How does Section 133 of BNS 2023 address humiliating assaults?
A: Section 133 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 2 years imprisonment for anyone who assaults or uses criminal force against a person with the intent to dishonour them, provided it is not done under grave and sudden provocation. [Source: Section 133, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 133: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

Q: A bully publicly grabs a man and forcibly shaves his head and mustache in the town square to humiliate him. What specific assault charge applies?
A: Because the bully used criminal force intending thereby to dishonour that person, he shall be punished under this section with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years. [Source: Section 133, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 133: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

Q: What specific mental intent elevates a standard 3-month assault to a 2-year offence under this section?
A: The offender must act "intending thereby to dishonour that person." [Source: Section 133, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 133: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

Q: If the victim had just subjected the attacker to grave and sudden provocation, would this 2-year penalty for dishonouring them still apply?
A: No, the section explicitly states that the assault/criminal force must be "otherwise than on grave and sudden provocation given by that person" for this specific penalty to apply. [Source: Section 133, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 133: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

Q: What is the legal consequence of establishing a specific offence for "intent to dishonour"?
A: The consequence is that the law recognizes the severe psychological and social damage caused by humiliating physical acts (like blackening a face or parading someone naked), punishing the *dignitary* harm much more harshly (2 years) than the *physical* harm of a simple shove (3 months). [Source: Section 133, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force with intent to dishonour person, otherwise than on grave

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 134: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

Q: What is the punishment for mugging someone, specifically using force to try and steal something they are wearing or carrying?
A: Assaulting or using criminal force in an attempt to steal property that a person is wearing or carrying (like a purse snatching or chain snatching) is punishable by up to two years in prison. [Source: Section 134, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 134: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

Q: How does Section 134 of BNS 2023 penalize attempted muggings?
A: Section 134 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 2 years imprisonment for assaulting or using criminal force against a person in an attempt to commit theft of property they are wearing or carrying. [Source: Section 134, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 134: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

Q: A thief runs past a woman on the street and violently grabs her handbag, shoving her in the process, but fails to get the bag. What is the thief charged with?
A: Because the thief used criminal force in an attempt to commit theft of property the woman was carrying, they shall be punished under this section with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years. [Source: Section 134, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 134: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

Q: What specific condition must the targeted property meet for this section to apply during an attempted theft?
A: The property must be property "which that person is then wearing or carrying." [Source: Section 134, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 134: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

Q: Does this section apply if a thief violently pushes a homeowner out of the way to steal a television off a table?
A: No, the television is not property the homeowner is "then wearing or carrying," so while other assault or robbery charges would apply, this specific section targeting pickpockets and muggers would not. [Source: Section 134, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 134: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

Q: What is the consequence of linking assault specifically to the attempt to steal carried property?
A: The consequence is that street crimes like chain-snatching and purse-snatching are recognized as inherently violent acts against the person (punishable by up to 2 years), closing the gap between simple theft and full-blown robbery. [Source: Section 134, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to commit theft of property carried by a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 135: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

Q: What is the penalty for physically struggling with someone in an attempt to lock them up or confine them against their will?
A: Assaulting or using criminal force in an attempt to wrongfully confine someone is punishable by up to one year in prison, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 135, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 135: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

Q: How does Section 135 of BNS 2023 address attempted kidnapping or confinement?
A: Section 135 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 1 year imprisonment or a fine up to 5,000 rupees for assaulting or using criminal force in an attempt to wrongfully confine a person. [Source: Section 135, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 135: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

Q: A man tries to shove his girlfriend into a closet to lock her inside during an argument, but she fights him off and escapes. Under what section is his physical violence charged?
A: Because he used criminal force in attempting wrongfully to confine that person, he is punishable under this section with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year. [Source: Section 135, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 135: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

Q: What must be the specific goal of the assault or criminal force to trigger this section?
A: The assault or criminal force must be used "in attempting wrongfully to confine that person." [Source: Section 135, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 135: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

Q: If the offender successfully manages to lock the victim in the room, is Section 135 still the primary charge?
A: No, Section 135 applies to the *attempt* to wrongfully confine. If the confinement is successful, the primary charge escalates to actual wrongful confinement under Section 127, which carries its own set of penalties. [Source: Section 135, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 135: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

Q: What is the legal consequence of this section regarding the escalation of physical disputes?
A: The consequence is that standard assault (3 months) automatically quadruples in severity (to 1 year) if the state proves the *reason* for the assault was to trap or imprison the victim, taking the threat to personal liberty highly seriously. [Source: Section 135, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force in attempt to wrongfully confine a person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 136: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

Q: What is the penalty if someone is severely and suddenly provoked into assaulting someone?
A: Assault or criminal force committed under grave and sudden provocation is punishable by up to one month of simple imprisonment, or a fine up to 1,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 136, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 136: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

Q: How does Section 136 of BNS 2023 mitigate the penalty for provoked assault?
A: Section 136 of BNS 2023 reduces the punishment for assault or criminal force to a maximum of 1 month simple imprisonment or a 1,000 rupee fine if the act was committed on grave and sudden provocation given by the victim. [Source: Section 136, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 136: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

Q: A man catches his neighbor maliciously destroying his prized garden. In a sudden rage, he aggressively shoves the neighbor out of the yard. What is his maximum liability for the physical contact?
A: Because he used criminal force on grave and sudden provocation, he shall be punished under this section with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or a fine up to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 136, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 136: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

Q: Does this section apply if the attacker deliberately sought out the provocation as an excuse to assault the victim?
A: No, the Explanation states this section is subject to the same Explanation as Section 131, which explicitly disqualifies provocation that is sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender. [Source: Section 136, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 136: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

Q: Can a person claim provocation under this section if the provocation was given by a police officer lawfully executing an arrest warrant?
A: No, as per the incorporated Explanation from Section 131, provocation given by a public servant in the lawful exercise of their powers does not mitigate the offence. [Source: Section 136, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 136: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

Q: What is the legal consequence of reducing the penalty for provoked assault compared to unprovoked assault?
A: The consequence is that the law distinguishes between cold-blooded malice and a temporary, understandable (though still illegal) loss of self-control, reducing the maximum prison time from 3 months to 1 month for acts committed in the heat of passion. [Source: Section 136, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assault or criminal force on grave provocation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 137: Kidnapping

Q: What are the two legally defined types of kidnapping in Indian law?
A: Indian law recognizes two kinds of kidnapping: "kidnapping from India" (conveying someone outside the country without consent) and "kidnapping from lawful guardianship" (taking/enticing a minor or mentally unsound person away from their guardian without consent). [Source: Section 137, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 137: Kidnapping

Q: How does Section 137 of BNS 2023 define kidnapping?
A: Section 137 of BNS 2023 defines "kidnapping from India" (taking someone beyond national borders without consent) and "kidnapping from lawful guardianship" (taking a child or unsound person from their guardian without consent). Both are punished by up to 7 years imprisonment under sub-section (2). [Source: Section 137, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 137: Kidnapping

Q: A divorced father with no custody rights secretly takes his 6-year-old child from school and hides them at a friend's house without the mother's (the lawful guardian) permission. What crime is this?
A: Under clause (b), because he took a child out of the keeping of the lawful guardian without consent, he has committed kidnapping from lawful guardianship, punishable by up to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 137, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 137: Kidnapping

Q: What specific classes of victims are protected under clause (b) regarding kidnapping from lawful guardianship?
A: Clause (b) specifically protects "any child or any person of unsound mind." [Source: Section 137, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 137: Kidnapping

Q: Under the Exception, is a man guilty of kidnapping if he genuinely believes he is the father of an illegitimate child and takes custody of them, intending to raise them well?
A: No, the Exception protects a person who in good faith believes himself to be the father or entitled to lawful custody of an illegitimate child, provided the act is not committed for an immoral or unlawful purpose. [Source: Section 137, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 137: Kidnapping

Q: What is the legal consequence of creating the specific crime of "kidnapping from India" in clause (a)?
A: The consequence is that forcefully or deceitfully moving someone across an international border is treated as a distinct, severe sovereignty and human rights violation, carrying up to 7 years in prison, separate from the domestic custody issues of clause (b). [Source: Section 137, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 138: Abduction

Q: What is the difference between "kidnapping" and "abduction" in Indian criminal law?
A: While kidnapping specifically involves minors, persons of unsound mind, or taking someone out of India, "abduction" applies to anyone and occurs when a person is compelled by force, or induced by deceitful means, to go from any place. [Source: Section 138, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abduction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 138: Abduction

Q: How does Section 138 of BNS 2023 define abduction?
A: Section 138 of BNS 2023 defines abduction as compelling any person by force, or inducing them by any deceitful means, to go from any place. [Source: Section 138, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abduction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 138: Abduction

Q: A man tricks a woman into getting into his car by falsely claiming her husband has been in an accident and he is taking her to the hospital. Is this abduction?
A: Yes, because he induced the person to go from a place by deceitful means, he is said to "abduct" that person under Section 138. [Source: Section 138, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abduction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 138: Abduction

Q: What are the two specific methods listed in Section 138 that can be used to unlawfully move a person and constitute abduction?
A: The two methods are: compelling by "force," or inducing by "deceitful means." [Source: Section 138, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abduction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 138: Abduction

Q: If an adult woman voluntarily and knowingly agrees to run away with her lover without any force or deceit, has she been abducted?
A: No, because she was neither compelled by force nor induced by deceitful means; voluntary movement by a competent adult is not abduction. [Source: Section 138, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abduction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 138: Abduction

Q: What is the legal consequence of separating abduction from kidnapping?
A: The consequence is that the law recognizes two distinct evils: kidnapping focuses on violating *guardianship* rights (often involving minors who cannot consent), while abduction focuses on violating the *free will* of an individual (through force or fraud) regardless of their age. [Source: Section 138, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Abduction

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 139: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

Q: How severely does the law punish people who kidnap children or mutilate them to use them as beggars?
A: Kidnapping a child for begging carries a minimum of ten years up to life in prison. If the offender actually maims (mutilates) the child for begging, the penalty is a mandatory minimum of twenty years up to natural life in prison. [Source: Section 139, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 139: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

Q: What are the specific penalties under Section 139 of BNS 2023 for exploiting children for begging?
A: Section 139 of BNS 2023 imposes 10 years to life imprisonment for kidnapping a child for begging (sub-section 1), and a minimum of 20 years to natural life imprisonment for maiming a child for begging (sub-section 2). [Source: Section 139, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 139: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

Q: A criminal gang kidnaps a healthy 5-year-old child and intentionally blinds him so he can earn more money begging on the street. What is the gang's minimum sentence?
A: Because they maimed the child in order to employ him for begging, under sub-section (2), they shall be punishable with imprisonment which shall not be less than twenty years, and which may extend to natural life. [Source: Section 139, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 139: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

Q: Under sub-section (3), what legal presumption arises if a person who is not a child's lawful guardian is found using that child for begging?
A: It shall be legally presumed, unless proved otherwise, that the person kidnapped or obtained custody of the child specifically to use them for begging. [Source: Section 139, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 139: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

Q: Does the definition of "begging" only cover asking for money on the street, or does it include "performing" for money?
A: It includes performing; sub-section 4(i) explicitly defines begging to include soliciting alms under the pretence of singing, dancing, fortune telling, or performing tricks. [Source: Section 139, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 139: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

Q: What is the systemic consequence of the mandatory minimum sentences in this section?
A: The consequence is that the state treats child mutilation and child trafficking for forced begging as among the most heinous crimes in the penal code, ensuring that organized begging syndicates face near-permanent incarceration (20 years to natural life) if caught. [Source: Section 139, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 140: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

Q: What is the penalty for kidnapping someone for ransom or to murder them?
A: Kidnapping or abducting someone to murder them is punishable by up to life imprisonment. If the kidnapping is for ransom, or to compel a government/organization to act by threatening the victim's life, the penalty is death or life imprisonment. [Source: Section 140, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 140: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

Q: How does Section 140 of BNS 2023 grade aggravated forms of kidnapping and abduction?
A: Section 140 of BNS 2023 penalizes aggravated kidnapping/abduction: for murder (up to life imprisonment, sub-section 1); for ransom/coercion with death threats (death or life imprisonment, sub-section 2); for secret confinement (up to 7 years, sub-section 3); and for grievous hurt, slavery, or unnatural lust (up to 10 years, sub-section 4). [Source: Section 140, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 140: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

Q: Terrorists abduct a foreign ambassador and threaten to execute him unless the government releases several imprisoned gang members. What is the maximum penalty they face?
A: Under sub-section (2), because they abducted a person and threatened death to compel the Government to do an act, they are punishable with death, or imprisonment for life. [Source: Section 140, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 140: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

Q: What three specific illicit purposes elevate kidnapping to a 10-year offence under sub-section (4)?
A: The three purposes are: subjecting the person to 1) grievous hurt, 2) slavery, or 3) the unnatural lust of any person. [Source: Section 140, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 140: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

Q: Does sub-section (1) only apply if the kidnapper personally intends to pull the trigger and murder the victim?
A: No, it also applies if the person is kidnapped/abducted to "be so disposed of as to be put in danger of being murdered," meaning handing a victim over to a hostile party or leaving them in a deadly situation also qualifies. [Source: Section 140, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 140: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

Q: What is the legal consequence of including "to compel the Government... to do or abstain from doing any act" in sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that political hostage-taking and terrorism are explicitly classified alongside profit-driven ransom kidnapping as capital offences, allowing courts to sentence terrorists who take hostages to the death penalty. [Source: Section 140, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Kidnapping or abducting in order to murder or for ransom, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 141: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

Q: What is the penalty for importing a minor into India for illicit intercourse?
A: Importing a girl under 21 or a boy under 18 from a foreign country with the intent or knowledge that they will be forced or seduced into illicit intercourse is punishable by up to ten years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 141, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 141: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

Q: How does Section 141 of BNS 2023 penalize cross-border exploitation of minors?
A: Section 141 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 10 years imprisonment and a fine for importing a girl under 21 or a boy under 18 into India, with the intent or knowledge that they will be subjected to illicit intercourse. [Source: Section 141, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 141: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

Q: A trafficking ring smuggles a 19-year-old girl from Nepal into India to force her into sex work. Under what specific cross-border provision are they charged?
A: Because they imported a girl under the age of twenty-one years from a foreign country with the intent that she be forced into illicit intercourse, they are punishable under this section with imprisonment up to ten years. [Source: Section 141, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 141: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

Q: What are the specific age thresholds set in this section for victims imported from foreign countries?
A: The section protects "any girl under the age of twenty-one years" and "any boy under the age of eighteen years." [Source: Section 141, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 141: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

Q: If an offender imports a 22-year-old woman for forced illicit intercourse, does Section 141 apply?
A: No, this specific section only applies to the importation of girls under twenty-one and boys under eighteen; older victims would fall under general trafficking (Section 143) or slavery provisions. [Source: Section 141, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 141: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

Q: What is the legal consequence of targeting "importation" in this specific section?
A: The consequence is that prosecutors can charge human smugglers with a severe 10-year felony the moment the minor victim crosses the border into India, without having to wait for the actual sexual exploitation to occur, disrupting international sex trafficking rings early. [Source: Section 141, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Importation of girl or boy from foreign country

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 142: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

Q: If someone hides a kidnapping victim, what penalty do they face?
A: If a person knows someone has been kidnapped or abducted, and wrongfully conceals or confines them, they are punished exactly as if they had committed the kidnapping themselves, based on their own intent or purpose. [Source: Section 142, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 142: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

Q: How does Section 142 of BNS 2023 deal with accomplices who hide kidnapping victims?
A: Section 142 of BNS 2023 stipulates that anyone who knowingly conceals or confines a kidnapped/abducted person shall be punished in the same manner as if they had personally kidnapped or abducted the person for the same purpose. [Source: Section 142, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 142: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

Q: A criminal gang kidnaps a rich businessman for ransom and pays a local farmer to lock the businessman in his barn. The farmer knows the businessman is kidnapped. How is the farmer punished?
A: Because the farmer knowingly and wrongfully confined a kidnapped person for the purpose of ransom, under this section, he is punished as if he himself had kidnapped the person for ransom (which carries death or life imprisonment under Section 140). [Source: Section 142, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 142: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

Q: What specific knowledge must the person concealing the victim have for this section to apply?
A: The person must act "knowing that any person has been kidnapped or has been abducted." [Source: Section 142, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 142: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

Q: Does this section apply if a person unknowingly rents a room to kidnappers who keep a victim secretly confined inside?
A: No, the statute explicitly requires that the person acting must *know* that the person being concealed/confined has been kidnapped or abducted. Without that knowledge, this specific liability does not attach. [Source: Section 142, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 142: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

Q: What is the systemic consequence of punishing the concealer exactly the same as the original kidnapper?
A: The consequence is that it completely dismantles the "safehouse" network that kidnappers rely on; individuals cannot argue they were "just holding the person" to get a lighter sentence, as the law treats hiding a victim as legally equivalent to stealing them. [Source: Section 142, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wrongfully concealing or keeping in confinement, kidnapped or abducted person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 143: Trafficking of person

Q: How does Indian law define and punish human trafficking?
A: Trafficking involves recruiting, transporting, or receiving someone for exploitation (like slavery, sex work, or organ removal) using threats, force, fraud, or inducement. It carries a minimum of seven years in prison, up to life for multiple victims, children, or if police are involved. [Source: Section 143, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trafficking of person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 143: Trafficking of person

Q: What constitutes the offence of trafficking under Section 143 of BNS 2023, and what are the penalties?
A: Section 143 defines trafficking as recruiting/transporting/receiving persons for exploitation via force, fraud, abduction, or inducement. Basic trafficking is 7-10 years (sub-section 2). Trafficking children or multiple persons elevates the penalty to 10 years to life, or 14 years to life, respectively. [Source: Section 143, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trafficking of person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 143: Trafficking of person

Q: A factory owner uses a recruiter to deceive poor workers from another state with false promises of high wages, only to lock them in the factory and force them into unpaid servitude. Is the recruiter guilty of trafficking?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1), because the recruiter transported/received persons for the purpose of exploitation by "practising fraud, or deception," he commits the offence of trafficking and faces a minimum of seven years in prison. [Source: Section 143, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trafficking of person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 143: Trafficking of person

Q: According to Explanation 1, list four specific practices that fall under the definition of "exploitation."
A: Exploitation includes: physical exploitation, sexual exploitation, slavery/practices similar to slavery, servitude, beggary, or forced removal of organs. [Source: Section 143, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trafficking of person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 143: Trafficking of person

Q: If an adult victim initially signed a contract agreeing to travel and work for the trafficker, can the trafficker use that consent as a defense?
A: No, Explanation 2 explicitly states that "The consent of the victim is immaterial in determination of the offence of trafficking." [Source: Section 143, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trafficking of person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 143: Trafficking of person

Q: What is the legal consequence of sub-section (7) regarding public servants?
A: The consequence is that corruption in human trafficking is met with zero tolerance; if a police officer or public servant is involved in trafficking, they bypass all lighter sentencing tiers and face a mandatory minimum of natural life in prison. [Source: Section 143, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Trafficking of person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 144: Exploitation of a trafficked person

Q: What is the penalty for being a customer who buys sex from a trafficking victim?
A: Engaging a trafficked person for sexual exploitation is a crime. If the trafficked person is an adult, the penalty is 3 to 7 years in prison. If the victim is a trafficked child, the penalty is 5 to 10 years in prison. [Source: Section 144, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exploitation of a trafficked person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 144: Exploitation of a trafficked person

Q: How does Section 144 of BNS 2023 penalize the end-users of trafficking?
A: Section 144 criminalizes engaging a trafficked person for sexual exploitation. Sub-section (1) punishes exploiting a trafficked child with 5 to 10 years imprisonment. Sub-section (2) punishes exploiting a trafficked adult with 3 to 7 years imprisonment. Both require the offender to know or have reason to believe the person was trafficked. [Source: Section 144, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exploitation of a trafficked person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 144: Exploitation of a trafficked person

Q: A man visits an underground brothel and pays for sex, seeing clear signs that the woman is locked inside and controlled by a pimp (giving him reason to believe she is trafficked). What crime has he committed?
A: Because he engaged the person for sexual exploitation having reason to believe she was trafficked, under sub-section (2), he is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a minimum of three years, up to seven years. [Source: Section 144, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exploitation of a trafficked person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 144: Exploitation of a trafficked person

Q: What specific mental state must the prosecution prove the "customer" had regarding the victim's status to secure a conviction under this section?
A: The prosecution must prove the person acted "knowingly or having reason to believe" that the person/child had been trafficked. [Source: Section 144, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exploitation of a trafficked person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 144: Exploitation of a trafficked person

Q: Does this section penalize a business owner who knowingly hires a trafficked person for forced manual labor in a sweatshop?
A: No, this specific section only penalizes engaging the trafficked person "for sexual exploitation in any manner." Exploitation for labor would be prosecuted under the main trafficking statutes (Section 143) or slavery provisions. [Source: Section 144, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exploitation of a trafficked person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 144: Exploitation of a trafficked person

Q: What is the systemic consequence of explicitly criminalizing the "exploitation of a trafficked person"?
A: The consequence is that the law targets the economic demand side of human trafficking; "Johns" or customers who fuel the sex trafficking industry can no longer claim they didn't do the actual kidnapping, as buying sex from a known victim is now a severe felony carrying 3 to 10 years. [Source: Section 144, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exploitation of a trafficked person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 145: Habitual dealing in slaves

Q: What is the penalty for running a slave trade business?
A: Habitually buying, selling, importing, exporting, or trafficking in slaves is punishable by life imprisonment, or up to ten years in prison, along with a fine. [Source: Section 145, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Habitual dealing in slaves

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 145: Habitual dealing in slaves

Q: How does Section 145 of BNS 2023 deal with the slave trade?
A: Section 145 of BNS 2023 targets the systemic slave trade, stating that whoever habitually imports, exports, removes, buys, sells, traffics, or deals in slaves shall be punished with life imprisonment or up to 10 years imprisonment, plus a fine. [Source: Section 145, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Habitual dealing in slaves

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 145: Habitual dealing in slaves

Q: A cartel runs a continuous operation where they abduct migrants and sell them at auction to illegal mining camps as property. What specific slavery charge applies to the cartel leaders?
A: Because they "habitually" import, buy, sell, and deal in slaves as an ongoing enterprise, they are punishable under this section with imprisonment for life, or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 145, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Habitual dealing in slaves

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 145: Habitual dealing in slaves

Q: What specific word in this section distinguishes it from a one-off instance of buying or selling a person?
