A: The word "habitually" signifies that this section targets those who engage in the slave trade as a continuous practice or business. [Source: Section 145, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Habitual dealing in slaves

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 145: Habitual dealing in slaves

Q: If a person buys a slave just once, does Section 145 apply?
A: No, Section 145 requires the offender to act "habitually." A single transaction would be prosecuted under other sections dealing with slavery, trafficking (Section 143), or kidnapping. [Source: Section 145, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Habitual dealing in slaves

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 145: Habitual dealing in slaves

Q: What is the consequence of prescribing life imprisonment for habitual slave dealing?
A: The consequence is that it allows the state to permanently dismantle slave-trading networks by imposing maximum, life-long sentences on the brokers, auctioneers, and human smugglers who make slavery a sustained commercial enterprise. [Source: Section 145, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Habitual dealing in slaves

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 146: Unlawful compulsory labour

Q: What is the punishment for forcing someone to work against their will?
A: Unlawfully compelling any person to labor against their will is punishable by up to one year in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 146, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful compulsory labour

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 146: Unlawful compulsory labour

Q: How does Section 146 of BNS 2023 penalize forced labor?
A: Section 146 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment up to 1 year, or a fine, or both, for whoever unlawfully compels any person to labor against that person's will. [Source: Section 146, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful compulsory labour

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 146: Unlawful compulsory labour

Q: A landlord prevents a tenant from leaving the property and forces the tenant to clean the entire building to pay off a late rent debt, against the tenant's protests. What charge applies?
A: Because the landlord unlawfully compelled the person to labour against their will, the landlord is punishable under this section with imprisonment up to one year. [Source: Section 146, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful compulsory labour

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 146: Unlawful compulsory labour

Q: What specific condition regarding the victim's state of mind is required for this offence?
A: The labour must be compelled "against the will of that person." [Source: Section 146, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful compulsory labour

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 146: Unlawful compulsory labour

Q: Does this section apply if a judge sentences a convicted criminal to "rigorous imprisonment" which legally mandates hard labor in prison?
A: No, the section explicitly states the compulsion to labor must be done "unlawfully." Lawful compulsory labor ordered by a court is not an offence under this section. [Source: Section 146, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful compulsory labour

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 146: Unlawful compulsory labour

Q: What is the legal consequence of keeping "unlawful compulsory labour" as a separate, lesser charge from human trafficking?
A: The consequence is that it allows prosecutors to charge localized, non-systemic instances of forced labor (like forcing a debtor to work for a day) with a proportionate 1-year penalty, without needing to prove the complex elements of trafficking or slavery. [Source: Section 146, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful compulsory labour

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 147: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

Q: What is the highest penalty under Indian law for waging war against the Government?
A: Waging war, attempting to wage war, or abetting the waging of war against the Government of India is punishable by death or life imprisonment, and a fine. [Source: Section 147, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 147: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

Q: How does Section 147 of BNS 2023 address treasonous warfare?
A: Section 147 of BNS 2023 mandates the death penalty or life imprisonment for anyone who wages, attempts to wage, or abets the waging of war against the Government of India. [Source: Section 147, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 147: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

Q: A citizen joins an armed militant group taking over a border town and engaging in gunfights with the Indian Army to establish an independent state. What crime has he committed?
A: As per the Illustration, by joining an insurrection against the Government of India, he has committed the offence defined in this section and faces death or life imprisonment. [Source: Section 147, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 147: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

Q: What three distinct degrees of involvement in warfare against the State are all punished equally under this section?
A: The three degrees are: 1) actually waging war, 2) attempting to wage such war, and 3) abetting the waging of such war. [Source: Section 147, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 147: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

Q: Can someone be charged under this section for peacefully protesting against government policies?
A: No, peaceful protest does not constitute "waging war." Waging war implies an armed insurrection or violent use of force intended to overthrow or coerce the sovereign government. [Source: Section 147, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 147: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

Q: What is the systemic consequence of making the *attempt* to wage war punishable by death, just like the actual waging of war?
A: The consequence is that the law treats treasonous insurrection as so dangerous to the survival of the State that it does not wait for the rebellion to succeed or fully materialize; the mere attempt is treated as the ultimate crime. [Source: Section 147, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging, or attempting to wage war, or abetting waging of war, against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 148: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

Q: Is it a crime to secretly plan an armed rebellion against the Indian Government, even if no action is taken?
A: Yes, conspiring to wage war against the Government or overawe it using criminal force is punishable by life imprisonment or up to ten years in prison, even if no illegal act takes place to further the conspiracy. [Source: Section 148, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 148: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

Q: How does Section 148 of BNS 2023 punish conspiracies against the State?
A: Section 148 of BNS 2023 imposes life imprisonment or up to 10 years imprisonment for conspiring (within or outside India) to wage war against the Government, or conspiring to overawe the Central/State Government using criminal force. [Source: Section 148, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 148: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

Q: A group of citizens holds secret meetings where they agree to assassinate top political leaders and seize parliament by force, but police arrest them before they even buy weapons. What are they charged with?
A: Because they conspired to overawe the Central Government by means of criminal force, they are punishable under this section with life imprisonment or up to ten years, even though they took no further action. [Source: Section 148, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 148: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

Q: According to the Explanation, what standard requirement of general criminal conspiracy is explicitly waived in this section?
A: It waives the requirement of an overt act; it is "not necessary that any act or illegal omission shall take place in pursuance" of the conspiracy to constitute the offence under this section. [Source: Section 148, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 148: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

Q: If a group of foreign nationals plots an invasion of India while sitting in another country, does this Indian law apply to them?
A: Yes, the section explicitly covers whoever conspires "within or without and beyond India," granting extraterritorial jurisdiction over plots against the Indian State. [Source: Section 148, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 148: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

Q: What is the legal consequence of removing the requirement for an "overt act" in this specific conspiracy charge?
A: The consequence is that the State has maximum preemptive power; law enforcement can arrest and secure life sentences for treasonous conspirators the moment an agreement to rebel is reached, preventing any possibility of the plot advancing. [Source: Section 148, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Conspiracy to commit offences punishable by section 147

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 149: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

Q: What is the penalty for hoarding weapons or recruiting people to prepare for a rebellion against the Government?
A: Collecting men, arms, or ammunition to prepare to wage war against the Government of India is punishable by life imprisonment or up to ten years in prison, and a fine. [Source: Section 149, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 149: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

Q: How does Section 149 of BNS 2023 address the preparation phase of an insurrection?
A: Section 149 of BNS 2023 prescribes life imprisonment or up to 10 years imprisonment for anyone who collects men, arms, or ammunition, or otherwise prepares to wage war, with the intention of waging war against the Government of India. [Source: Section 149, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 149: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

Q: Intelligence agencies discover a wealthy sympathizer secretly stockpiling assault rifles and explosives in a warehouse to supply an upcoming separatist insurgency. What specific offence covers this stockpiling?
A: Because the sympathizer collected arms and ammunition with the intention of being prepared to wage war against the Government, they are punishable under this section with life imprisonment or up to ten years. [Source: Section 149, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 149: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

Q: What are the three specific forms of preparation explicitly listed in this section?
A: The section explicitly lists collecting 1) men, 2) arms, or 3) ammunition. [Source: Section 149, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 149: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

Q: If someone collects weapons purely for a large-scale smuggling operation with no political motive, are they charged under Section 149?
A: No, Section 149 specifically requires "the intention of either waging or being prepared to wage war against the Government of India." Without that treasonous intent, they would be charged under general arms trafficking laws, not this section. [Source: Section 149, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 149: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

Q: What is the legal consequence of separating "preparation" into its own distinct crime under Section 149?
A: The consequence is that while general criminal law rarely punishes mere preparation (only attempts), the extreme danger of insurrection means the State criminalizes the logistical setup of an insurgency (gathering fighters/guns) just as harshly as a full-blown conspiracy. [Source: Section 149, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Collecting arms, etc., with intention of waging war against Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 150: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

Q: What happens if a citizen knows about a plot to wage war against the government and actively hides it to help the rebels?
A: Concealing the existence of a design to wage war against the Government, with the intent or knowledge that hiding it will facilitate the war, is punishable by up to ten years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 150, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 150: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

Q: How does Section 150 of BNS 2023 penalize covering up an insurrection?
A: Section 150 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 10 years imprisonment on anyone who, by act or illegal omission, conceals a design to wage war against the Government, intending or knowing it is likely to facilitate the war. [Source: Section 150, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 150: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

Q: A local official learns that a militia is planning to attack a military base. To help the militia, the official deliberately deletes the intelligence reports from the police database. What is the official's crime?
A: By an act that concealed a design to wage war, intending to facilitate that war, the official is punishable under this section with imprisonment up to ten years. [Source: Section 150, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 150: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

Q: What are the two ways a person can effect the "concealment" required by this section?
A: Concealment can be done either "by any act" or "by any illegal omission" (failing to report it when legally obligated to do so). [Source: Section 150, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 150: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

Q: If a person accidentally loses a document that contained plans for a rebellion, meaning the plot remained concealed, are they guilty under this section?
A: No, the statute requires that the person concealed it "intending by such concealment to facilitate, or knowing it to be likely that such concealment will facilitate, the waging of such war." Accidents lack this treasonous intent. [Source: Section 150, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 150: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

Q: What is the consequence of holding individuals liable for an "illegal omission" regarding treasonous plots?
A: The consequence is that individuals who have a legal duty to report threats to the State (like police, magistrates, or even citizens under certain laws) can be imprisoned for 10 years simply for looking the other way and staying silent when they discover a rebellion forming. [Source: Section 150, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Concealing with intent to facilitate design to wage war

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 151: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

Q: What is the penalty for attacking or physically intimidating the President or a Governor to force a political decision?
A: Assaulting, wrongfully restraining, or overawing the President of India or a State Governor with criminal force to compel them to exercise (or refrain from exercising) their lawful powers is punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 151, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 151: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

Q: How does Section 151 of BNS 2023 protect the highest executive officers of the State?
A: Section 151 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 7 years imprisonment and a fine on anyone who assaults, restrains, or uses criminal force against the President of India or a State Governor with the intent to induce or compel them regarding the exercise of their lawful powers. [Source: Section 151, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 151: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

Q: Protesters barricade the Governor's car, wrongfully restraining him, and threaten violence unless he signs a controversial bill into law. What crime have they committed?
A: Because they wrongfully restrained the Governor with the intention of compelling him to exercise his lawful power, they are punishable under this section with imprisonment up to seven years. [Source: Section 151, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 151: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

Q: What specific intent must accompany the assault or criminal force for this severe 7-year penalty to apply instead of standard assault?
A: The intent must be "inducing or compelling the President of India, or Governor of any State, to exercise or refrain from exercising in any manner any of the lawful powers of such President or Governor." [Source: Section 151, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 151: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

Q: If a person assaults the Governor over a purely private, personal dispute regarding a real estate deal, does Section 151 apply?
A: No, Section 151 requires the intent to compel or restrain the exercise of the Governor's "lawful powers" (their official duties). A personal assault would be charged under standard assault statutes. [Source: Section 151, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 151: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

Q: What is the legal consequence of creating a specialized assault statute for the President and Governors?
A: The consequence is that physical intimidation aimed at coercing the heads of state is treated not just as a crime against the person, but as a severe political crime against the democratic process itself, elevating a 3-month assault charge to a 7-year felony. [Source: Section 151, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting President, Governor, etc., with intent to compel or restrain exercise of any lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 152: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

Q: What is the punishment for promoting secession or armed rebellion against India?
A: Exciting or attempting to excite secession, armed rebellion, subversive activities, or endangering the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India (by words, signs, or financial means) is punishable by life imprisonment or up to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 152, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 152: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

Q: How does Section 152 of BNS 2023 address acts against national integrity (the modern equivalent of sedition)?
A: Section 152 of BNS 2023 penalizes purposely or knowingly exciting secession, armed rebellion, subversive activities, or endangering India's sovereignty and unity using words, signs, or financial means, with life imprisonment or up to 7 years imprisonment. [Source: Section 152, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 152: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

Q: A radical leader uses social media to actively fundraise and recruit people to break a state away from India and form an independent country. What specific section covers this?
A: Because he used electronic communication and financial means to purposely excite secession and endanger the unity of India, he is punishable under Section 152 with life imprisonment or up to seven years. [Source: Section 152, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 152: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

Q: List three specific modes or methods explicitly mentioned in the section by which a person can commit this offence.
A: The offence can be committed by 1) spoken or written words, 2) signs/visible representation, 3) electronic communication, or 4) the use of financial means. [Source: Section 152, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 152: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

Q: Does this section criminalize a journalist writing a harsh article criticizing the government's economic policies and demanding the Prime Minister resign?
A: No, the Explanation specifically protects "Comments expressing disapprobation of the measures... of the Government with a view to obtain their alteration by lawful means," provided they do not excite secession, armed rebellion, or subversive activities. [Source: Section 152, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 152: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

Q: What is the systemic consequence of replacing the colonial "sedition" law with Section 152?
A: The consequence is a shift in focus; instead of punishing mere "disaffection" against the government (the old sedition standard), the law now specifically targets tangible threats to the nation itself—secession, armed rebellion, and subversive activities that endanger sovereignty. [Source: Section 152, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 153: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: Is it illegal in India to launch an armed attack against a foreign country that is at peace with India?
A: Yes, waging war, attempting to wage war, or abetting war against the Government of any foreign State that is at peace with India is punishable by life imprisonment or up to seven years in prison, plus a fine. [Source: Section 153, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 153: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: How does Section 153 of BNS 2023 protect India's foreign relations?
A: Section 153 of BNS 2023 makes it a crime, punishable by life imprisonment or up to 7 years imprisonment, to wage, attempt to wage, or abet the waging of war against the Government of any foreign State at peace with the Government of India. [Source: Section 153, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 153: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: A group of extremists in India plot and launch a cross-border artillery attack against a neighboring country with which India has a peace treaty, trying to start a war. What are they charged with under Indian law?
A: Because they waged or attempted to wage war against the Government of a foreign State at peace with India, they are punishable under this section with life imprisonment or up to seven years. [Source: Section 153, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 153: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: What specific relationship must exist between India and the foreign State for this section to apply?
A: The foreign State must be "at peace with the Government of India." [Source: Section 153, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 153: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: If a foreign country declares war on India, and an Indian citizen then joins a government-backed militia to fight against that foreign country, does Section 153 apply?
A: No, because the foreign State is no longer "at peace with the Government of India," acts of war against them would not fall under the prohibition of this section. [Source: Section 153, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 153: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: What is the consequence of India penalizing acts of war against foreign nations?
A: The consequence is that India prevents its territory from being used as a safe haven by mercenaries or non-state actors looking to destabilize allied or neutral nations, thereby protecting India from diplomatic crises and retaliatory strikes. [Source: Section 153, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Waging war against Government of any foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 154: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: What is the punishment for raiding or plundering a peaceful neighboring country from Indian soil?
A: Committing or preparing to commit depredation (raiding/plundering) on the territories of a foreign State at peace with India is punishable by up to seven years in prison, fine, and forfeiture of property. [Source: Section 154, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 154: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: How does Section 154 of BNS 2023 penalize cross-border raids?
A: Section 154 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 7 years imprisonment, plus fines and asset forfeiture, for committing or preparing to commit depredation on the territories of a foreign State at peace with India. [Source: Section 154, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 154: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: A criminal gang uses trucks in an Indian border village to launch a raid into a neighboring peaceful country, plundering a town's bank and fleeing back to India. What specific offence covers this?
A: Because they committed depredation on the territories of a foreign State at peace with India, they are punishable under Section 154 with up to seven years in prison and forfeiture of the stolen property and the trucks used. [Source: Section 154, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 154: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: Besides imprisonment and a fine, what specific financial penalty is mandated by this section regarding the tools and proceeds of the crime?
A: The section mandates the "forfeiture of any property used or intended to be used in committing such depredation, or acquired by such depredation." [Source: Section 154, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 154: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: Does this section apply if the raiding party solely targets Indian villages near the border?
A: No, this specific section only applies to depredation committed "on the territories of any foreign State." Domestic raids would be prosecuted under robbery, dacoity, or domestic terrorism laws. [Source: Section 154, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 154: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

Q: What is the legal consequence of including "makes preparations to commit" in this section?
A: The consequence is that Indian law enforcement can arrest the raiders and seize their vehicles and weapons before they cross the border to commit the plunder, preventing international incidents rather than just punishing them afterward. [Source: Section 154, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Committing depredation on territories of foreign State at peace with Government of India

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 155: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

Q: Is it a crime to buy or receive goods that you know were plundered from a foreign country during an illegal raid or war?
A: Yes, receiving property knowing it was taken during an illegal war or depredation against a peaceful foreign state (as defined in Sections 153 and 154) is punishable by up to seven years in prison and forfeiture of the property. [Source: Section 155, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 155: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

Q: How does Section 155 of BNS 2023 penalize the fencing of internationally plundered goods?
A: Section 155 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 7 years imprisonment, fine, and forfeiture of property on anyone who receives property knowing it was acquired via war against a peaceful foreign State (Section 153) or cross-border depredation (Section 154). [Source: Section 155, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 155: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

Q: A jeweler in India buys a large batch of gold bars at a heavy discount from a militia group, knowing the gold was looted from a bank in a neighboring peaceful country during an illegal raid. What is the jeweler charged with?
A: Because he received property knowing the same to have been taken in the commission of depredation (Section 154), he is punishable under Section 155 with imprisonment up to seven years, and the gold will be forfeited. [Source: Section 155, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 155: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

Q: What specific knowledge must the receiver possess for this section to apply?
A: The receiver must act "knowing the same to have been taken in the commission of any of the offences mentioned in sections 153 and 154" (illegal war or depredation against a peaceful state). [Source: Section 155, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 155: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

Q: If a person buys stolen jewelry, believing it was stolen from a house in their own Indian city, can they be charged under Section 155?
A: No, they would be charged with general receipt of stolen property (Section 317), not Section 155, because they lacked the knowledge that the property was taken during an international war or cross-border depredation. [Source: Section 155, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 155: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

Q: What is the legal consequence of this section regarding the profitability of cross-border raids?
A: The consequence is that by severely punishing the buyers and fencing networks within India, the State destroys the economic incentive for militias and gangs to launch illegal raids into neighboring countries, protecting regional stability. [Source: Section 155, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Receiving property taken by war or depredation mentioned in sections 153 and 154

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 156: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

Q: What is the penalty for a prison guard who deliberately lets a prisoner of war or State prisoner escape?
A: A public servant who has custody of a State prisoner or prisoner of war and voluntarily allows them to escape is punishable by life imprisonment or up to ten years in prison, plus a fine. [Source: Section 156, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 156: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

Q: How does Section 156 of BNS 2023 penalize corrupt officials regarding high-value prisoners?
A: Section 156 of BNS 2023 mandates life imprisonment or up to 10 years imprisonment, plus a fine, for any public servant who voluntarily allows a State prisoner or prisoner of war in their custody to escape. [Source: Section 156, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 156: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

Q: A military jailer accepts a massive bribe and leaves the cell door unlocked so a captured enemy general (a prisoner of war) can escape in the night. What is the jailer's specific crime?
A: Because he is a public servant who voluntarily allowed a prisoner of war in his custody to escape, he is punishable under this section with life imprisonment or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 156, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 156: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

Q: What specific classes of prisoners must the escaping individual belong to for this severe section to apply?
A: The escaped person must be either a "State prisoner" or a "prisoner of war." [Source: Section 156, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 156: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

Q: If a police officer takes a bribe to let a common thief escape from a local holding cell, does Section 156 apply?
A: No, Section 156 specifically applies only to the escape of a "State prisoner or prisoner of war." Letting a common criminal escape would fall under general dereliction of duty or corruption statutes (e.g., Section 261). [Source: Section 156, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 156: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

Q: What is the systemic consequence of imposing life imprisonment for this offence?
A: The consequence is that the State treats the deliberate release of its most dangerous political/military enemies by its own officials not just as corruption, but as tantamount to treason, imposing a near-maximum penalty to deter inside jobs. [Source: Section 156, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant voluntarily allowing prisoner of State or war to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 157: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

Q: What is the penalty if a guard's carelessness, rather than intent, leads to the escape of a State prisoner or prisoner of war?
A: A public servant whose negligence allows a State prisoner or prisoner of war to escape is punishable by simple imprisonment for up to three years, and a fine. [Source: Section 157, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 157: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

Q: How does Section 157 of BNS 2023 address dereliction of duty resulting in high-profile escapes?
A: Section 157 of BNS 2023 prescribes simple imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine for a public servant who negligently suffers a State prisoner or prisoner of war in their custody to escape. [Source: Section 157, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 157: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

Q: A guard falls asleep on duty after drinking, allowing a captured insurgent leader (a State prisoner) to pick the lock and escape. Is the guard guilty of a crime even though he didn't plan it?
A: Yes, because he negligently suffered a State prisoner to escape from confinement, he is punishable under this section with simple imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 157, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 157: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

Q: What mental state distinguishes the offence in Section 157 from the much harsher offence in Section 156?
A: Section 157 applies when the public servant acts "negligently" (carelessness), whereas Section 156 applies when the public servant acts "voluntarily" (intentional facilitation). [Source: Section 157, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 157: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

Q: Does this section permit a judge to sentence the negligent guard to rigorous (hard labor) imprisonment?
A: No, the statute explicitly limits the punishment to "simple imprisonment" for a term which may extend to three years, reflecting that the act was a careless mistake rather than malicious treason. [Source: Section 157, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 157: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

Q: What is the legal consequence of establishing strict criminal liability for negligence regarding these specific prisoners?
A: The consequence is that it places an extraordinarily high legal duty of care on guards holding prisoners of war/State; they cannot simply be fired for a mistake, but face up to 3 years in prison if their lack of diligence allows a national security threat to go free. [Source: Section 157, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant negligently suffering such prisoner to escape

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 158: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

Q: What is the penalty for a civilian who helps a prisoner of war escape or hides them from authorities?
A: Anyone who knowingly aids a State prisoner or prisoner of war to escape, rescues them, harbours them after escape, or resists their recapture is punishable by life imprisonment or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 158, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 158: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

Q: How does Section 158 of BNS 2023 penalize those who assist in the escape of State enemies?
A: Section 158 of BNS 2023 imposes life imprisonment or up to 10 years imprisonment, plus a fine, on anyone who knowingly aids, rescues, harbours, or resists the recapture of a State prisoner or prisoner of war. [Source: Section 158, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 158: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

Q: A farmer finds an escaped prisoner of war hiding in his barn. Knowing who the man is, the farmer gives him civilian clothes and hides him under hay when the military comes searching. What is the farmer's crime?
A: Because he knowingly harboured and concealed a prisoner of war who had escaped from lawful custody, he is punishable under Section 158 with life imprisonment or up to ten years. [Source: Section 158, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 158: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

Q: According to the Explanation, under what specific circumstance is a prisoner out on "parole" considered to have escaped from lawful custody?
A: A prisoner on parole is said to escape from lawful custody if he "goes beyond the limits within which he is allowed to be at large." [Source: Section 158, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 158: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

Q: If a person gives food to an injured stranger without knowing they are an escaped prisoner of war, are they guilty under Section 158?
A: No, the statute explicitly requires that the person "knowingly aids or assists" or harbours the prisoner. Without knowledge of the person's status, they lack the requisite intent for this severe offence. [Source: Section 158, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 158: Aiding escape of, rescuing or harbouring such prisoner

Q: What is the legal consequence of applying this law to anyone who "offers or attempts to offer any resistance to the recapture"?
A: The consequence is that anyone who physically interferes with law enforcement or military trying to re-arrest the escaped State prisoner faces the exact same maximum penalty (life imprisonment) as the people who orchestrated the escape in the first place. [Source: Section 158, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the punishment for trying to convince members of the armed forces to rebel against the government?
A: Abetting a mutiny or attempting to seduce an officer, soldier, sailor, or airman from their allegiance or duty to the Government of India is punishable by life imprisonment or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 159, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the penalty for inciting a military mutiny if the soldiers actually follow through and rebel?
A: If a person abets a mutiny in the Army, Navy, or Air Force, and the mutiny actually takes place as a result, the abettor is punishable by death, life imprisonment, or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 160, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the penalty for inciting a soldier to assault their commanding officer?
A: Abetting an assault by a soldier, sailor, or airman on their superior officer while the officer is executing their duties is punishable by up to three years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 161, BNS 2023]

A: Yes, the master of a merchant vessel can be fined up to 3,000 rupees if a deserter is concealed on board due to the master's negligence or lack of discipline, even if they were ignorant of the stowaway. [Source: Section 165, BNS 2023]
