Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 168: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

Q: How does Section 168 of BNS 2023 penalize military impersonation?
A: Section 168 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 3 months imprisonment, or a fine up to 2,000 rupees, for anyone who, not being a member of the armed forces, wears a garb or token resembling military use with the intent that they be believed to be a soldier, sailor, or airman. [Source: Section 168, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 168: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

Q: A con artist buys a realistic army uniform and wears it at a train station to solicit "donations for veterans" from unsuspecting passengers. What specific offence covers the wearing of the uniform?
A: Because he wore a garb resembling a soldier's with the intention that he be believed to be a soldier, he is punishable under Section 168 with up to three months in prison. [Source: Section 168, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 168: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

Q: What specific intent must accompany the wearing of the uniform for it to be a crime?
A: The person must wear the garb "with the intention that it may be believed that he is such a soldier, sailor or airman." [Source: Section 168, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 168: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

Q: Can an actor be arrested under this section for wearing a military uniform in a movie or stage play?
A: No, because the actor is performing and audiences know it is a play, the actor lacks the "intention that it may be believed that he is such a soldier," so the section does not apply. [Source: Section 168, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 168: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

Q: What is the legal consequence of criminalizing the mere wearing of the uniform with intent, even if no fraud is committed?
A: The consequence is that police can immediately arrest individuals impersonating military personnel to prevent them from accessing secure bases, obtaining classified information, or scamming civilians, without waiting for an actual act of fraud to occur. [Source: Section 168, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by soldier, sailor or airman

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 169: Candidate, electoral right defined

Q: In the context of election crimes, what exactly does "electoral right" mean?
A: An "electoral right" is defined as a person's right to stand as a candidate, not to stand, to withdraw from being a candidate, to vote, or to refrain from voting at an election. [Source: Section 169, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Candidate, electoral right defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 169: Candidate, electoral right defined

Q: How does Section 169 of BNS 2023 define key election terms?
A: Section 169 of BNS 2023 defines a "candidate" as a person nominated at any election, and an "electoral right" as the right to stand, not stand, withdraw as a candidate, vote, or refrain from voting. [Source: Section 169, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Candidate, electoral right defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 169: Candidate, electoral right defined

Q: A local leader is offered money not to file nomination papers for an upcoming election. If we need to determine if this violates an "electoral right," what defines that right?
A: Under Section 169 clause (b), the right "not to stand as" a candidate is explicitly defined as an electoral right, so interfering with it falls under election offences. [Source: Section 169, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Candidate, electoral right defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 169: Candidate, electoral right defined

Q: Under clause (a), at what precise point does a person legally become a "candidate" for the purposes of these offences?
A: A person becomes a candidate when they have "been nominated as a candidate at any election." [Source: Section 169, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Candidate, electoral right defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 169: Candidate, electoral right defined

Q: If a person simply expresses interest in running for office but has not filed any papers or been formally nominated, are they considered a "candidate" under this Chapter?
A: No, under clause (a), a "candidate" specifically means a person "who has been nominated," so mere aspirational politicians are not covered until official nomination. [Source: Section 169, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Candidate, electoral right defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 169: Candidate, electoral right defined

Q: What is the systemic consequence of defining "electoral right" to include the right *not* to do things (like withdrawing or refraining from voting)?
A: The consequence is that the law protects citizens and candidates from being bullied, bribed, or coerced into dropping out of a race or staying home on election day, ensuring elections are not manipulated by suppressing participation. [Source: Section 169, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Candidate, electoral right defined

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 170: Bribery

Q: Is it considered bribery if a politician pays someone to drop out of an election race?
A: Yes, giving any gratification to induce someone to exercise an electoral right (which includes withdrawing as a candidate) is the offence of bribery in elections. [Source: Section 170, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 170: Bribery

Q: How does Section 170 of BNS 2023 define election bribery?
A: Section 170 of BNS 2023 defines bribery as giving gratification to induce or reward someone for exercising an electoral right, or accepting gratification as a reward for exercising such a right. [Source: Section 170, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 170: Bribery

Q: A wealthy businessman gives a new car to a popular local candidate in exchange for that candidate withdrawing from the election so the businessman's preferred candidate will win. Has a crime been committed?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1), giving a gratification to induce a person to exercise an electoral right (withdrawing) constitutes the offence of bribery. [Source: Section 170, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 170: Bribery

Q: Under sub-section (3), if a person accepts a bribe to vote for Party A, but actually votes for Party B, is he still guilty of accepting a bribe?
A: Yes, the section states that a person who accepts a gratification as a motive for doing what he does not intend to do "shall be deemed to have accepted the gratification as a reward," so he is still guilty. [Source: Section 170, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 170: Bribery

Q: Is a politician guilty of bribery if they promise to build a new hospital in a town if the town's residents vote for them?
A: No, the proviso explicitly states that "a declaration of public policy or a promise of public action shall not be an offence under this section." [Source: Section 170, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 170: Bribery

Q: What is the legal consequence of sub-section (2) stating that a person who "offers or attempts to procure" gratification is deemed to give it?
A: The consequence is that an attempted bribe is treated legally as a completed bribe; prosecutors do not have to prove that money actually changed hands, only that the corrupt offer was made. [Source: Section 170, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 171: Undue influence at elections

Q: What constitutes "undue influence" during an election?
A: Undue influence at an election occurs when someone voluntarily interferes or attempts to interfere with the free exercise of any electoral right, such as by threatening a voter or candidate. [Source: Section 171, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Undue influence at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 171: Undue influence at elections

Q: How does Section 171 of BNS 2023 define the offence of undue influence at elections?
A: Section 171 of BNS 2023 defines undue influence as voluntarily interfering or attempting to interfere with the free exercise of any electoral right, explicitly including threatening a candidate/voter with injury or inducing fear of divine displeasure. [Source: Section 171, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Undue influence at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 171: Undue influence at elections

Q: A local religious leader tells his congregation that anyone who votes for Candidate X will be cursed by God and excommunicated. Is this an election offence?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2)(b), inducing a voter to believe they will become an object of "Divine displeasure or of spiritual censure" is deemed to interfere with the free exercise of an electoral right, constituting undue influence. [Source: Section 171, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Undue influence at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 171: Undue influence at elections

Q: What are the two specific methods of undue influence explicitly detailed in sub-section (2)?
A: The two methods are: (a) threatening injury of any kind, and (b) inducing belief of Divine displeasure or spiritual censure. [Source: Section 171, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Undue influence at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 171: Undue influence at elections

Q: A candidate gives a speech promising to pass a new law to lower taxes if elected. Opponents claim this is "undue influence" because it sways voters. Are the opponents correct?
A: No, under sub-section (3), "A declaration of public policy or a promise of public action... shall not be deemed to be interference" within the meaning of this section. [Source: Section 171, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Undue influence at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 171: Undue influence at elections

Q: What is the consequence of specifically criminalizing threats of "spiritual censure" in election law?
A: The consequence is that the law protects voters from religious coercion, preventing religious figures or institutions from weaponizing faith to manipulate democratic elections. [Source: Section 171, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Undue influence at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 172: Personation at elections

Q: What is the legal term for pretending to be someone else to steal their vote?
A: Applying for a voting paper in the name of another person (living, dead, or fictitious), or voting twice in one's own name, is the offence of "personation at an election." [Source: Section 172, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 172: Personation at elections

Q: How does Section 172 of BNS 2023 define personation at elections?
A: Section 172 of BNS 2023 states that applying for a ballot in another person's name, a fictitious name, or applying a second time in one's own name after already voting, constitutes the offence of personation at an election. [Source: Section 172, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 172: Personation at elections

Q: A man goes to a polling booth and votes. Later in the day, he puts on a hat and sunglasses, goes to a different booth in the same constituency, and tries to vote again under his own name. What is his crime?
A: Because he, having voted once, applied at the same election for a voting paper in his own name, he committed the offence of personation at an election. [Source: Section 172, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 172: Personation at elections

Q: What are the three types of identities a person might fraudulently assume that all fall under this section?
A: A person might assume the name of another person who is 1) living, 2) dead, or 3) a fictitious name. [Source: Section 172, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 172: Personation at elections

Q: If an elderly woman cannot travel to the polls, and legally authorizes her son to cast her ballot under a recognized proxy voting law, is the son guilty of personation?
A: No, the proviso explicitly states that nothing in the section applies to a person "authorised to vote as proxy for an elector under any law... in so far as he votes as a proxy." [Source: Section 172, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 172: Personation at elections

Q: What is the legal consequence of including "abets, procures or attempts to procure" in the definition of personation?
A: The consequence is that campaign managers or party workers who hire or organize fake voters can be charged with the exact same offence of personation as the individuals who actually cast the fraudulent ballots. [Source: Section 172, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation at elections

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 173: Punishment for bribery

Q: What is the punishment for offering or accepting a bribe during an election?
A: The offence of bribery at an election is punishable by up to one year in prison, or a fine, or both. However, if the bribery is done by "treating" (giving food or drink), it is punished only with a fine. [Source: Section 173, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 173: Punishment for bribery

Q: How does Section 173 of BNS 2023 penalize election bribery?
A: Section 173 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment up to 1 year, or a fine, or both for bribery, with a proviso that bribery by "treating" (food, drink, entertainment) is punishable by fine only. [Source: Section 173, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 173: Punishment for bribery

Q: A candidate hosts a massive free banquet with unlimited food and alcohol for a neighborhood, explicitly asking everyone who attends to vote for him. He is convicted of bribery. Can he be sent to prison?
A: No, because the gratification consisted of food and drink, this is classified as bribery by "treating," which the proviso states shall be punished with a fine only, not imprisonment. [Source: Section 173, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 173: Punishment for bribery

Q: According to the Explanation, what four specific items constitute the form of bribery known as "treating"?
A: The four items are food, drink, entertainment, or provision. [Source: Section 173, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 173: Punishment for bribery

Q: If a candidate hands out envelopes of cash to voters, does the "fine only" proviso apply?
A: No, cash does not fall under the definition of "treating" (food, drink, entertainment, provision). Therefore, cash bribery is punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 173, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 173: Punishment for bribery

Q: What is the legal consequence of separating "treating" from other forms of bribery regarding punishment?
A: The consequence is that the law recognizes a difference in severity between hard corruption (buying votes with cash) and traditional campaign hospitality (giving out food/entertainment), punishing the latter less harshly (fine only) to avoid criminalizing standard campaign events with jail time. [Source: Section 173, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for bribery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 174: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

Q: What is the penalty for voter intimidation or voting under a fake identity?
A: The offences of undue influence (like intimidation) or personation (fake voting) at an election are punishable by up to one year in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 174, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 174: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

Q: How does Section 174 of BNS 2023 penalize undue influence and personation?
A: Section 174 of BNS 2023 prescribes a uniform punishment of imprisonment up to 1 year, or a fine, or both, for whoever commits the offence of undue influence or personation at an election. [Source: Section 174, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 174: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

Q: A gang leader is caught threatening voters with violence if they approach the polling booth (undue influence), and another man is caught voting under a dead person's name (personation). Do they face different maximum prison sentences?
A: No, under Section 174, both undue influence and personation carry the exact same maximum penalty: imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 174, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 174: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

Q: What two distinct election offences does Section 174 combine into a single punishment provision?
A: It combines the offences of "undue influence" and "personation." [Source: Section 174, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 174: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

Q: Does Section 174 contain a "fine only" exception for minor forms of undue influence, similar to how Section 173 treats bribery by "treating"?
A: No, Section 174 has no proviso or exception; all forms of undue influence and personation are eligible for the full penalty of up to one year in prison. [Source: Section 174, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 174: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

Q: What is the legal consequence of prescribing up to one year in prison for personation?
A: The consequence is that voter fraud is treated as a serious criminal act, allowing the State to imprison individuals who attempt to subvert the democratic process by stealing the identities of living or dead citizens. [Source: Section 174, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for undue influence or personation at an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 175: False statement in connection with an election

Q: What is the penalty for publishing a vicious lie about a candidate's personal character to ruin their election chances?
A: Publishing a false statement of fact about a candidate's personal character or conduct, knowing it to be false and intending to affect the election result, is punishable by a fine. [Source: Section 175, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 175: False statement in connection with an election

Q: How does Section 175 of BNS 2023 address election-related defamation?
A: Section 175 of BNS 2023 imposes a fine on anyone who, with intent to affect an election result, publishes a false statement of fact (which they know/believe is false) regarding the personal character or conduct of a candidate. [Source: Section 175, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 175: False statement in connection with an election

Q: A newspaper editor, wanting Candidate A to lose, publishes a fabricated story claiming Candidate A was recently caught embezzling money from a charity, knowing the story is completely fake. What is the editor's punishment under this section?
A: Because the editor published a false statement of fact regarding the candidate's personal character with intent to affect the election result, the editor shall be punished with a fine under Section 175. [Source: Section 175, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 175: False statement in connection with an election

Q: What specific subject matter must the false statement relate to in order to trigger this offence?
A: The false statement must relate to the "personal character or conduct of any candidate." [Source: Section 175, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 175: False statement in connection with an election

Q: If a political rival publishes a false statement claiming that a candidate's *economic policy* will cost the town 10,000 jobs, does Section 175 apply?
A: No, the section specifically penalizes false statements in relation to the "personal character or conduct" of a candidate. False claims about public policy or political platforms do not fall under this section. [Source: Section 175, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 175: False statement in connection with an election

Q: What is the consequence of limiting the punishment for this offence to "fine" only, rather than imprisonment?
A: The consequence is that while the law seeks to deter malicious smear campaigns during elections, it avoids chilling political speech with the threat of jail time, balancing electoral integrity with freedom of expression. [Source: Section 175, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 176: Illegal payments in connection with an election

Q: What is the penalty for spending money to campaign for a candidate without their written permission?
A: Incurring or authorizing expenses to promote a candidate's election without their written authority is punishable by a fine of up to 10,000 rupees. [Source: Section 176, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal payments in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 176: Illegal payments in connection with an election

Q: How does Section 176 of BNS 2023 restrict independent campaign spending?
A: Section 176 of BNS 2023 imposes a fine up to 10,000 rupees on anyone who incurs or authorises expenses for public meetings, advertisements, or other promotional materials for a candidate without the candidate's general or special authority in writing. [Source: Section 176, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal payments in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 176: Illegal payments in connection with an election

Q: A wealthy supporter spends 5,000 rupees printing flyers to help Candidate Y win, but Candidate Y never gave written permission. What offence has the supporter committed?
A: Because the supporter incurred expenses for the purpose of promoting the election of the candidate without written authority, the supporter is punishable under Section 176 with a fine up to ten thousand rupees. [Source: Section 176, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal payments in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 176: Illegal payments in connection with an election

Q: What specific format must the candidate's authorization take to be valid under this section?
A: The authority must be "general or special authority in writing of a candidate." [Source: Section 176, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal payments in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 176: Illegal payments in connection with an election

Q: A volunteer buys a 5-rupee marker to make a sign for a candidate without asking. Five days later, the candidate gives them written approval for the purchase. Is the volunteer guilty?
A: No, the proviso states that if the unauthorized expenses do not exceed ten rupees, and the person obtains written approval from the candidate within ten days, they are deemed to have incurred the expenses with authority. [Source: Section 176, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal payments in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 176: Illegal payments in connection with an election

Q: What is the legal consequence of capping unauthorized election expenses and demanding written permission?
A: The consequence is that candidates retain strict legal control and accountability over the finances of their campaign, preventing shadow groups or rogue supporters from violating election spending limits on the candidate's behalf. [Source: Section 176, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal payments in connection with an election

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 177: Failure to keep election accounts

Q: What happens if a candidate or their agent fails to keep proper records of their election expenses?
A: Failing to keep legally required accounts of election expenses is punishable by a fine of up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 177, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure to keep election accounts

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 177: Failure to keep election accounts

Q: How does Section 177 of BNS 2023 punish the failure to maintain election accounting?
A: Section 177 of BNS 2023 prescribes a fine up to 5,000 rupees for anyone who is required by law to keep accounts of expenses incurred at or in connection with an election, but fails to do so. [Source: Section 177, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure to keep election accounts

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 177: Failure to keep election accounts

Q: A campaign manager ignores election commission rules requiring a ledger of all rally costs and keeps no records. What is the penalty under the BNS?
A: Because he was required by law to keep accounts of election expenses and failed to do so, he is punishable under Section 177 with a fine up to five thousand rupees. [Source: Section 177, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure to keep election accounts

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 177: Failure to keep election accounts

Q: Does this section independently define what election accounts must be kept?
A: No, it relies on external laws, applying only to those "being required by any law for the time being in force or any rule having the force of law to keep accounts." [Source: Section 177, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure to keep election accounts

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 177: Failure to keep election accounts

Q: If an ordinary voter spends 5 rupees on a bus ticket to go vote and doesn't keep a receipt, are they guilty under Section 177?
A: No, because an ordinary voter is not "required by any law... to keep accounts of expenses" related to their personal act of voting, this section does not apply to them. [Source: Section 177, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure to keep election accounts

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 177: Failure to keep election accounts

Q: What is the consequence of making the failure to keep election accounts a criminal offence?
A: The consequence is that it ensures financial transparency in democratic processes, giving authorities a legal mechanism to penalize candidates who try to hide illicit campaign funding by claiming they simply "lost the paperwork." [Source: Section 177, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure to keep election accounts

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 178: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: What is the punishment for manufacturing fake currency or government stamps?
A: Counterfeiting coins, government revenue stamps, currency notes, or bank-notes is punishable by life imprisonment, or imprisonment for up to ten years, and a fine. [Source: Section 178, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 178: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: How does Section 178 of BNS 2023 punish the production of counterfeit money and stamps?
A: Section 178 of BNS 2023 imposes life imprisonment, or up to 10 years imprisonment, and a fine, on anyone who counterfeits or knowingly performs any part of the process of counterfeiting coins, government revenue stamps, currency-notes, or bank-notes. [Source: Section 178, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 178: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: A criminal organization sets up a printing press and starts producing high-quality fake 500-rupee notes. What is the maximum sentence for the operators?
A: For counterfeiting currency-notes, they shall be punished under Section 178 with imprisonment for life, or up to ten years, and a fine. [Source: Section 178, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 178: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: Under Explanation (5), what physical alterations to an existing, genuine coin are legally considered "counterfeiting"?
A: Altering a genuine coin is considered "counterfeiting" if it involves "diminishing the weight or alteration of the composition, or alteration of the appearance of the coin." [Source: Section 178, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 178: Counterfeiting coin, Government stamps, currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: Under Explanation (3), if someone takes a genuine low-value stamp and alters it to look like a genuine high-value stamp, is that considered "counterfeiting" or just "altering"?
A: It is legally counterfeiting; a person commits the offence of "counterfeiting Government stamp" who counterfeits by causing a genuine stamp of one denomination to appear like a genuine stamp of a different denomination. [Source: Section 178, BNS 2023]

A: The consequence is that the State treats the production of fake currency as a severe attack on the nation's economic stability and sovereign integrity, punishing it with the highest severity alongside crimes like murder or treason. [Source: Section 178, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the penalty for intentionally using or trafficking fake money or stamps?
A: Importing, exporting, selling, buying, or intentionally using counterfeit coins, stamps, or currency notes as genuine is punishable by life imprisonment, or up to ten years in prison, and a fine. [Source: Section 179, BNS 2023]

[Source: Section 179, BNS 2023]

Q: Is it a crime simply to possess fake money if you plan to spend it?
A: Yes, possessing counterfeit currency or stamps, knowing they are fake and intending to use them as genuine, is punishable by up to seven years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 180, BNS 2023]

Q: How does Section 180 of BNS 2023 penalize the possession of counterfeit currency?
A: Section 180 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 7 years imprisonment, or a fine, or both, on anyone who possesses counterfeit coins, stamps, or currency/bank-notes, knowing they are counterfeit and intending to use them as genuine. [Source: Section 180, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Possession of forged or counterfeit coin, Government stamp, currency-notes or bank-

A: Because he possessed the counterfeit currency knowing it was fake and intending to use it as genuine, he is punishable under Section 180 with imprisonment up to seven years or a fine. [Source: Section 180, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the penalty for owning equipment used to make fake money?
A: Making, possessing, or selling machinery, dies, or materials intended for counterfeiting currency, coins, or government stamps is punishable by life imprisonment, or up to ten years in prison, and a fine. [Source: Section 181, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or possessing instruments or materials for forging or counterfeiting coin, Government stamp, currency-notes or bank-notes

A: Section 181 of BNS 2023 imposes life imprisonment, or up to 10 years imprisonment, and a fine, on anyone who makes, mends, buys, sells, or possesses machinery or materials knowing they are intended to be used for forging or counterfeiting coins, stamps, or currency-notes. [Source: Section 181, BNS 2023]

A: Because he made an instrument intended to be used for counterfeiting a currency-note, he is punishable under Section 181 with imprisonment for life, or up to ten years, and a fine. [Source: Section 181, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or possessing instruments or materials for forging or counterfeiting coin, Government stamp, currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 182: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: Is it a crime to make novelty or prop money that looks like real currency?
A: Yes, making, using, or delivering any document that resembles a currency note so closely that it is calculated to deceive is punishable by a fine of up to 300 rupees. [Source: Section 182, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 182: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: How does Section 182 of BNS 2023 regulate items resembling currency?
A: Section 182 of BNS 2023 prescribes a fine up to 300 rupees for making or using documents resembling currency-notes, and a fine up to 600 rupees if a person whose name is on the document refuses to disclose the maker's identity to police. [Source: Section 182, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 182: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: A toy company prints "play money" that looks so identical to real 100-rupee notes that children use them to trick local shopkeepers. What is the penalty for the company?
A: Because the company made a document so nearly resembling a currency-note as to be calculated to deceive, they are punishable under sub-section (1) with a fine up to three hundred rupees. [Source: Section 182, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 182: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: Under sub-section (2), what triggers the higher fine of up to six hundred rupees?
A: The 600-rupee fine is triggered if a person whose name appears on the offending document "refuses, without lawful excuse, to disclose to a police officer... the name and address of the person by whom it was printed or otherwise made." [Source: Section 182, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 182: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: If a bank prints a large, clearly marked "VOID" poster of a 500-rupee note for a window display, is it a crime?
A: Likely no, because the document must be "so nearly resembling as to be calculated to deceive." A giant, clearly marked poster would not meet the standard of being calculated to deceive. [Source: Section 182, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 182: Making or using documents resembling currency-notes or bank-notes

Q: What is the consequence of treating "prop money" as a minor fine offence compared to the life sentence for actual counterfeiting?
A: The consequence is that the law distinguishes between malicious economic sabotage (counterfeiting) and negligent or low-level deception (making novelty notes), preventing harsh prison sentences for mere irresponsible printing while still allowing police to confiscate deceptive materials. [Source: Section 182, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 183: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

Q: What is the penalty for removing a used revenue stamp from an old document so you can reuse it on a new document?
A: Fraudulently removing a used government revenue stamp from a document, or erasing writing around it so the stamp can be reused, is punishable by up to three years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 183, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 183: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

Q: How does Section 183 of BNS 2023 penalize the fraudulent reuse of government stamps?
A: Section 183 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment, or a fine, or both, on anyone who fraudulently removes or effaces writing from a stamped substance, or removes a used stamp from a document, in order to reuse the stamp for a different document. [Source: Section 183, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 183: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

Q: A clerk carefully steams off an expensive revenue stamp from a cancelled contract and glues it onto a brand-new contract to avoid paying the government stamp duty. What is the clerk charged with?
A: Because the clerk removed a stamp which had been used for a document in order to use it for a different document with intent to cause loss to the Government, the clerk is punishable under Section 183 with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 183, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 183: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

Q: What specific intent is required to make the removal of a stamp or effacement of writing a criminal offence under this section?
A: The act must be done "fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to the Government" in order that the stamp may be "used for a different writing or document." [Source: Section 183, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 183: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

Q: An archivist carefully removes a rare 19th-century revenue stamp from a decaying document strictly to preserve the stamp in a museum display case. Is this a crime?
A: No, because the archivist did not act "fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to the Government" and did not intend for the stamp to be "used for a different writing or document," this is not an offence under Section 183. [Source: Section 183, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 183: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

Q: What is the legal consequence of criminalizing the physical manipulation of stamped documents?
A: The consequence is that the State protects its revenue streams (stamp duties) from petty fraud by making the physical act of tampering with stamps a serious felony carrying up to 3 years in prison, deterring systemic tax evasion in legal and administrative paperwork. [Source: Section 183, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Effacing writing from substance bearing Government stamp, or removing from document a stamp used for it, with intent to cause loss to Government

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 184: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

Q: What is the penalty for actually using a revenue stamp that you know has already been used?
A: Fraudulently using a government revenue stamp for any purpose, knowing it has already been used before, is punishable by up to two years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 184, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 184: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

Q: How does Section 184 of BNS 2023 punish the fraudulent use of old stamps?
A: Section 184 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 2 years imprisonment, or a fine, or both, for anyone who fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to the Government uses a revenue stamp which they know has been used before. [Source: Section 184, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 184: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

Q: A lawyer buys "discounted" revenue stamps from a sketchy vendor, notices they clearly have old ink marks indicating they were peeled off previous legal filings, but attaches them to a new lawsuit anyway to save money. What is the lawyer's crime?
A: Because the lawyer fraudulently used a stamp which he knew to have been before used, he is punishable under Section 184 with imprisonment up to two years. [Source: Section 184, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 184: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

Q: How does the actus reus in Section 184 differ from Section 183?
A: Section 183 penalizes the preparatory physical act of *removing* the stamp or *effacing* the writing, whereas Section 184 penalizes the actual *use* of the recycled stamp. [Source: Section 184, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 184: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

Q: A citizen buys a fresh stamp from the post office. Unknown to the citizen, the postal worker illegally sold them a recycled stamp. The citizen uses it. Is the citizen guilty?
A: No, the statute requires the person to act "fraudulently" and to use a stamp "which he knows to have been before used." An innocent purchaser lacks this knowledge and intent. [Source: Section 184, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 184: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

Q: What is the consequence of having separate sections for "removing" (Sec 183) and "using" (Sec 184) recycled stamps?
A: The consequence is that the law can target both ends of the fraud: the "scavenger" who prepares the fake stamps (punished more harshly with 3 years) and the "customer" who actually uses them on documents (punished with 2 years). [Source: Section 184, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using Government stamp known to have been before used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 185: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

Q: What is the penalty for washing or erasing the cancellation mark off a used stamp so it looks brand new?
A: Erasing a cancellation mark from a used government stamp, or possessing/selling such an altered stamp, with intent to cause loss to the government, is punishable by up to three years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 185, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 185: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

Q: How does Section 185 of BNS 2023 criminalize the alteration of used stamps?
A: Section 185 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment, or a fine, or both, on anyone who fraudulently erases a usage mark from a government stamp, or knowingly possesses, sells, or disposes of a stamp with an erased mark or a known used stamp. [Source: Section 185, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 185: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

Q: A fraudster uses chemical solvents to wash the black cancellation ink off used revenue stamps, making them look mint, and then sells them online as new. What is the maximum sentence?
A: Because he fraudulently erased a mark denoting the stamp had been used, and sold stamps knowing they had been used, he is punishable under Section 185 with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 185, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 185: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

Q: What three specific distinct activities involving marked stamps are criminalized under this single section?
A: The three activities are: 1) erasing or removing the usage mark, 2) knowingly possessing, selling, or disposing of a stamp with an erased mark, and 3) selling or disposing of any stamp known to have been used. [Source: Section 185, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 185: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

Q: If a stamp collector uses a gentle solvent to clean a dirty (but unused) 100-year-old stamp to improve its appearance for their private album, is this a crime?
A: No, because the collector did not erase a "mark... denoting that the same has been used" and did not act "fraudulently or with intent to cause loss to Government," this preservation act is not an offence. [Source: Section 185, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 185: Erasure of mark denoting that stamp has been used

Q: What is the consequence of making it a 3-year felony just to *possess* a stamp with an erased cancellation mark?
A: The consequence is that it severely disrupts the black market for recycled stamps, allowing police to arrest counterfeiters and middlemen simply for holding the tampered inventory, even if they are never caught in the act of erasing the marks or selling them. [Source: Section 185, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 186: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

Q: What is the penalty for making or mailing a fake postage stamp?
A: Making, possessing, or using fictitious stamps for postal purposes is punishable by a fine of up to 200 rupees, and the fake stamps/materials will be seized. [Source: Section 186, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 186: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

Q: How does Section 186 of BNS 2023 penalize the use of fictitious postal stamps?
A: Section 186 of BNS 2023 imposes a fine up to 200 rupees on anyone who makes, knowingly uses for postal purposes, possesses, or creates a die/instrument for making fictitious stamps. [Source: Section 186, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 186: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

Q: A hobbyist creates highly realistic international postage stamps using a high-end printer, but just keeps them in a drawer without ever mailing a letter. Can they be fined?
A: Yes, under sub-section (1)(c), anyone who "has in his possession, without lawful excuse, any fictitious stamp" is punishable by a fine of up to two hundred rupees. [Source: Section 186, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 186: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

Q: What happens to the fake stamps or printing equipment found in a person's possession upon conviction under this section?
A: Sub-section (2) mandates that any such stamp, die, plate, instrument or materials in the possession of any person for making any fictitious stamp "shall be seized and, if seized shall be forfeited." [Source: Section 186, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 186: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

Q: Does the definition of "fictitious stamp" apply to fake stamps of foreign nations, or only Indian stamps?
A: It applies to both; under sub-section (3), "fictitious stamp" means any stamp falsely purporting to be a postage stamp used by the Government of India or by "the Government of any foreign country." [Source: Section 186, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Prohibition of fictitious stamps

content:

Q: What is the consequence of treating the counterfeiting of *postage* stamps as a minor fine offence (200 rupees), while counterfeiting *revenue* stamps carries up to 10 years in prison (Section 181)?
A: The consequence is that the law distinguishes between minor postal fraud (stealing a few rupees of mail delivery service) and serious revenue fraud (evading massive taxes or legal fees on documents), punishing the latter much more severely. [Source: Section 186, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 187: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

Q: What is the penalty for a government mint employee who secretly shorts the amount of silver going into new coins?
A: A mint employee who intentionally alters the legal weight or composition of coins being issued is punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 187, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 187: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

Q: How does Section 187 of BNS 2023 penalize insider tampering at government mints?
A: Section 187 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 7 years imprisonment and a fine on any employee of a lawfully established mint in India who intentionally acts or omits an act to cause a coin to have a different weight or composition than fixed by law. [Source: Section 187, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 187: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

Q: A quality-control inspector at a government mint notices a machine is producing coins with 10% less copper than required. To help the factory manager meet quotas and save money, the inspector intentionally approves the batch. What is the inspector's crime?
A: Because he omitted what he was legally bound to do with the intention of causing coins issued from the mint to be of a different composition, he is punishable under Section 187 with imprisonment up to seven years. [Source: Section 187, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 187: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

Q: What specific employment status is required for an offender to be charged under this section?
A: The offender must be a "Person employed in mint lawfully established in India." [Source: Section 187, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 187: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

Q: A maintenance worker accidentally bumps a dial on a smelting machine, causing the next batch of coins to be slightly overweight. Is the worker guilty under Section 187?
A: No, the offence requires the person to act or omit an act "with the intention of causing any coin... to be of a different weight or composition." Accidental errors lack this intent. [Source: Section 187, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 187: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

Q: What is the legal consequence of creating a specialized offence for mint employees?
A: The consequence is that the law recognizes the unique systemic threat posed by insider corruption at a mint, where even slight, intentional alterations to alloy mixtures can massively devalue the national currency and erode public trust. [Source: Section 187, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Person employed in mint causing coin to be of different weight or composition from that fixed by law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 188: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

Q: Is it a crime for a mint worker to take a coin-stamping tool home?
A: Yes, unlawfully taking a coining tool or instrument out of a lawfully established mint is punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 188, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 188: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

Q: How does Section 188 of BNS 2023 penalize the theft of mint equipment?
A: Section 188 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 7 years imprisonment and a fine for anyone who, without lawful authority, takes any coining tool or instrument out of a lawfully established mint in India. [Source: Section 188, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 188: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

Q: A security guard at a government mint finds an old, retired coin die in the trash. He takes it home to keep as a souvenir. What offence has he committed?
A: Because he took a coining instrument out of the mint without lawful authority, he is punishable under Section 188 with imprisonment up to seven years. [Source: Section 188, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 188: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

Q: Does the prosecution need to prove the person intended to use the stolen instrument to make fake coins?
A: No, the statute only requires proving that the person "without lawful authority, takes out of any mint... any coining tool or instrument." The mere unauthorized removal completes the offence. [Source: Section 188, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 188: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

Q: If the Mint Director signs an authorization form for an engineer to take a broken coining press to an external repair shop, is the engineer guilty of taking an instrument from the mint?
A: No, because the engineer removed the instrument with "lawful authority," the act does not violate Section 188. [Source: Section 188, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 188: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

Q: What is the systemic consequence of harshly punishing the unauthorized removal of mint tools, regardless of intent?
A: The consequence is that the State severely restricts access to the highly specialized tools needed for perfect counterfeiting, ensuring that genuine mint equipment cannot easily fall into the hands of criminal organizations. [Source: Section 188, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawfully taking coining instrument from mint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 189: Unlawful assembly

Q: How many people does it take to form a legally "unlawful assembly," and what must they be doing?
A: An unlawful assembly requires five or more people who share a common criminal object, such as using force against the government, resisting the law, committing mischief, or forcing someone to do something illegally. [Source: Section 189, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 189: Unlawful assembly

Q: How does Section 189 of BNS 2023 define and penalize an unlawful assembly?
A: Section 189 of BNS 2023 defines an unlawful assembly as 5 or more persons with a common object to overawe the government, resist law, commit offences, or use criminal force to take property or compel actions, punishing members with up to 6 months imprisonment (or 2 years if armed or refusing to disperse). [Source: Section 189, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 189: Unlawful assembly

Q: A mob of six people surrounds a farmer, threatening to beat him up unless he signs over the deed to his land. What specific legal definition covers this mob?
A: Because they are an assembly of five or more persons with the common object of using criminal force to compel a person to do what he is not legally bound to do (sign the deed), they constitute an "unlawful assembly" under sub-section (1)(e). [Source: Section 189, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 189: Unlawful assembly

Q: If an assembly starts peacefully to protest a law, but later the crowd decides to start burning police cars, does it become an unlawful assembly?
A: Yes, under the Explanation to sub-section (1), "An assembly which was not unlawful when it assembled, may subsequently become an unlawful assembly." [Source: Section 189, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 189: Unlawful assembly

Q: If four people gather with the common object of committing a criminal trespass, are they an "unlawful assembly"?
A: No, sub-section (1) explicitly states that an assembly must consist of "five or more persons" to be designated an unlawful assembly. They would just be co-conspirators. [Source: Section 189, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 189: Unlawful assembly

Q: What is the legal consequence of sub-section (6) regarding people who hire others to join a riot?
A: The consequence is that the financiers and organizers who hire goons to form an unlawful assembly are punished exactly as if they were physically present in the mob themselves, and are liable for any crimes the hired goons commit. [Source: Section 189, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Unlawful assembly

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 190: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

Q: If I am part of a riot and someone else in the crowd throws a brick that hurts a police officer, can I be charged for the injury?
A: Yes, every member of an unlawful assembly is guilty of any offence committed by another member if the act is done to achieve the group's common object or was known to be a likely outcome. [Source: Section 190, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 190: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

Q: How does Section 190 of BNS 2023 establish collective liability for unlawful assemblies?
A: Section 190 of BNS 2023 states that if an offence is committed by any member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object, or is known to be likely committed, every person who is a member of the assembly at that time is guilty of that offence. [Source: Section 190, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 190: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

Q: Fifty people form an unlawful assembly to violently burn down a government building. One member of the crowd throws a firebomb, committing arson. Can a person standing in the back of the crowd who threw nothing be charged with arson?
A: Yes, because the arson was committed in prosecution of the common object (burning the building), every person who was a member of the assembly at the time is guilty of that offence under Section 190. [Source: Section 190, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 190: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

Q: What are the two alternate conditions under which collective liability attaches to an offence committed by a single member?
A: The offence must either be 1) committed "in prosecution of the common object" or 2) "such as the members of that assembly knew to be likely to be committed in prosecution of that object." [Source: Section 190, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 190: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

Q: If a group forms an unlawful assembly to peacefully but illegally block a road, and suddenly one member pulls out a gun and shoots his personal rival who happened to be driving by, is the rest of the crowd guilty of murder?
A: Unlikely. The murder was a personal vendetta, not done "in prosecution of the common object" (blocking the road), nor was it "likely to be committed" in the course of a sit-in. Therefore, the rest of the assembly is not collectively liable. [Source: Section 190, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 190: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

Q: What is the systemic consequence of this strict collective liability principle in riot situations?
A: The consequence is that it severely deters individuals from participating in violent mobs, as the law holds "bystander" rioters legally responsible for the most extreme crimes committed by the most violent members of their group. [Source: Section 190, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence committed in prosecution of common object

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 191: Rioting

Q: How does the law define a "riot"?
A: A riot occurs when an unlawful assembly, or any member of it, uses force or violence in prosecution of their common object. [Source: Section 191, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rioting

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 191: Rioting

Q: How does Section 191 of BNS 2023 define and punish rioting?
A: Section 191 of BNS 2023 states that whenever force or violence is used by an unlawful assembly in prosecution of its common object, every member is guilty of rioting, punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment (or 5 years if armed with a deadly weapon), or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 191, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rioting

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 191: Rioting

Q: During an unlawful assembly to illegally block a factory, a few members at the front start smashing the factory windows with rocks while the rest just chant. Who is guilty of rioting?
A: Under sub-section (1), because violence was used by a member of the unlawful assembly in prosecution of the common object, *every* member of the assembly is guilty of the offence of rioting. [Source: Section 191, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rioting

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 191: Rioting

Q: What specific aggravating factor increases the maximum punishment for rioting from two years to five years under this section?
A: The maximum punishment increases to five years if the person is "armed with a deadly weapon or with anything which, used as a weapon of offence, is likely to cause death." [Source: Section 191, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rioting

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 191: Rioting

Q: If a group of four people get into a violent fistfight outside a bar to settle a personal score, is it legally a "riot"?
A: No, because a riot requires the use of force by an "unlawful assembly" (which requires five or more people with a specific common object), four people fighting is an affray or assault, not a riot. [Source: Section 191, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rioting

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 191: Rioting

Q: What is the legal consequence of distinguishing "unlawful assembly" (Section 189) from "rioting" (Section 191)?
A: The consequence is that the law can punish the mere formation of a dangerous mob (unlawful assembly) before any harm is done, but escalates the penalty significantly (rioting) the moment the mob crosses the line into actual physical force or violence. [Source: Section 191, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rioting

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 192: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

Q: What is the penalty for intentionally provoking a crowd to start a riot?
A: Malignantly or wantonly doing an illegal act to provoke a riot is punishable by up to one year in prison if a riot actually occurs, and up to six months if it doesn't. [Source: Section 192, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 192: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

Q: How does Section 192 of BNS 2023 punish the act of provoking a riot?
A: Section 192 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 year imprisonment if a riot is committed, or up to 6 months if not committed, on anyone who malignantly or wantonly does an illegal act intending or knowing it will provoke a riot. [Source: Section 192, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 192: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

Q: An agitator stands on a car and illegally burns a religious text, shouting insults to intentionally provoke the gathered crowd into a violent riot. The police arrest him before the crowd reacts. What is his penalty?
A: Because he wantonly did an illegal act intending to provoke a riot, but the offence of rioting was *not* committed, he is punishable under Section 192 with imprisonment up to six months, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 192, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 192: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

Q: Under this section, does the provocative act itself have to be illegal, or can it be a perfectly legal but offensive act?
A: The section specifically requires the person to give provocation "by doing anything which is illegal." A legal (even if highly offensive) act does not satisfy the elements. [Source: Section 192, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 192: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

Q: If a comedian tells an offensive joke on stage (which is not illegal) and the audience gets so angry they start a riot, is the comedian guilty under Section 192?
A: No, because telling the joke was not "doing anything which is illegal," the comedian cannot be charged under Section 192 for provoking the riot. [Source: Section 192, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 192: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

Q: What is the consequence of penalizing the provocateur even if the riot does *not* happen?
A: The consequence is that law enforcement can intervene and arrest agitators who are actively trying to spark mass violence (like throwing a rock at a peaceful protest) before their reckless actions successfully ignite a deadly riot. [Source: Section 192, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wantonly giving provocation with intent to cause riot-if rioting be committed; if not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 193: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

Q: If a riot happens on your property, can you be fined if you don't call the police?
A: Yes, a landowner or occupier can be fined up to 1,000 rupees if they know a riot or unlawful assembly is happening on their land and fail to notify the police or try to stop it. [Source: Section 193, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 193: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

Q: How does Section 193 of BNS 2023 impose duties on landowners regarding riots?
A: Section 193 of BNS 2023 penalizes landowners, occupiers, and their agents with a fine (up to 1,000 rupees in some cases) if they fail to notify police, prevent, or suppress an unlawful assembly or riot taking place on their land or for their benefit. [Source: Section 193, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 193: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

Q: A factory owner realizes his hired security guards have formed an unlawful assembly on his property to violently evict squatters. He sits back and watches without calling the police. Can he be penalized?
A: Yes, under sub-section (2), because the riot was committed for his benefit on his land, and he failed to use lawful means to prevent or suppress it, he is punishable with a fine. [Source: Section 193, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 193: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

Q: Under sub-section (1), what two specific actions must an owner/occupier take to avoid a fine when they know a riot is occurring on their land?
A: They must 1) give the "earliest notice thereof in his or their power to the officer in charge at the nearest police station" and 2) "use all lawful means in his or their power to disperse or suppress the riot." [Source: Section 193, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 193: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

Q: A landlord lives in another country and has no agent on site. A riot spontaneously breaks out on his vacant lot in India. He finds out a week later. Can he be fined?
A: No, the statute requires the owner or their agent to act while "knowing that such offence is being or has been committed, or having reason to believe it is likely to be committed." Without real-time knowledge, he cannot be fined for failing to act. [Source: Section 193, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 193: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

Q: What is the legal consequence of making landowners criminally liable for the riots of others on their property?
A: The consequence is that it prevents feudal landlords, corporate owners, or community leaders from feigning ignorance while "looking the other way" as mobs commit violence on their behalf or on their territory. [Source: Section 193, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Liability of owner, occupier, etc., of land on which an unlawful assembly or riot takes

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 194: Affray

Q: What is the crime of "affray"?
A: An affray is when two or more people disturb the public peace by fighting in a public place. [Source: Section 194, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Affray

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 194: Affray

Q: How does Section 194 of BNS 2023 define and punish an affray?
A: Section 194 of BNS 2023 defines an affray as two or more persons fighting in a public place and disturbing the public peace, which is punishable by up to 1 month imprisonment, or a fine up to 1,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 194, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Affray

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 194: Affray

Q: Two men get into a loud, violent fistfight in the middle of a busy street market, causing bystanders to flee in panic. What specific offence have they committed?
A: Because they are two persons fighting in a public place and disturbing the public peace, they have committed an "affray" under sub-section (1), punishable under sub-section (2). [Source: Section 194, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Affray

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 194: Affray

Q: What is the critical locational element required for a fight to be considered an "affray"?
A: The fighting must take place "in a public place." [Source: Section 194, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Affray

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 194: Affray

Q: Two brothers get into a loud, violent fistfight inside their private, soundproofed basement. Are they guilty of an affray?
A: No, because the fight did not occur "in a public place" and did not "disturb the public peace," it is not an affray (though it could be assault or battery). [Source: Section 194, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Affray

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 194: Affray

Q: What is the consequence of defining "affray" as a distinct crime from assault?
A: The consequence is that the law protects the general public's right to peace and safety in shared spaces; police can arrest brawlers for terrorizing bystanders, even if neither fighter wants to press assault charges against the other. [Source: Section 194, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Affray
