Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 195: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

Q: What is the penalty for attacking a police officer who is trying to break up a riot?
A: Assaulting, obstructing, or using criminal force against a public servant trying to disperse a riot is punishable by up to three years in prison, or a fine of at least 25,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 195, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 195: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

Q: How does Section 195 of BNS 2023 penalize violence against public servants during a riot?
A: Section 195 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 3 years imprisonment, or a minimum fine of 25,000 rupees, or both, for assaulting or obstructing a public servant suppressing a riot; merely threatening or attempting to do so carries up to 1 year imprisonment or a fine. [Source: Section 195, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 195: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

Q: A police officer is trying to disperse an unlawful assembly. A rioter throws a brick at the officer, hitting his shield. What is the penalty for the rioter under this specific section?
A: Because the rioter used criminal force on a public servant endeavouring to disperse an unlawful assembly, he is punishable under sub-section (1) with imprisonment up to three years, or a minimum fine of 25,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 195, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 195: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

Q: Under sub-section (1), what is the unique statutory requirement regarding the fine if the judge chooses to impose one?
A: The fine "shall not be less than twenty-five thousand rupees." [Source: Section 195, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 195: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

Q: A police officer is off-duty, out of uniform, and grocery shopping when he gets into a personal argument with a cashier. The cashier pushes him. Is the cashier guilty under Section 195?
A: No, because the officer was not acting "in the discharge of his duty... in endeavouring to disperse an unlawful assembly, or to suppress a riot or affray," Section 195 does not apply. [Source: Section 195, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 195: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

Q: What is the consequence of making the *threat* or *attempt* to obstruct an officer during a riot a separate, punishable offence (up to 1 year) under sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is that police can immediately arrest and neutralize aggressive individuals who are posturing, shouting threats, or trying to block their path, without having to wait for the individual to actually strike a blow. [Source: Section 195, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Assaulting or obstructing public servant when suppressing riot, etc

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 196: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

Q: What is the penalty for spreading hatred between different religious or racial communities?
A: Promoting enmity, hatred, or ill-will between different groups based on religion, race, language, or caste is punishable by up to three years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 196, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 196: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

Q: How does Section 196 of BNS 2023 punish the promotion of communal disharmony?
A: Section 196 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment (or 5 years if committed in a place of worship) and a fine for promoting enmity between groups on grounds of religion, race, etc., or organizing training with criminal force against such groups. [Source: Section 196, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 196: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

Q: A politician gives a fiery speech urging their regional linguistic group to violently expel all people from a neighboring state who speak a different language, leading to public panic. What is the penalty?
A: Because the politician by spoken words promoted feelings of enmity between different language and regional groups, they are punishable under sub-section (1)(a) with imprisonment up to three years, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 196, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 196: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

Q: Under sub-section (2), what specific locations trigger the enhanced five-year maximum sentence for promoting enmity?
A: The enhanced sentence is triggered if the offence is committed "in any place of worship or in any assembly engaged in the performance of religious worship or religious ceremonies." [Source: Section 196, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 196: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

Q: If a sociologist publishes an academic, data-driven paper objectively detailing historical conflicts between two castes, without any attempt or intent to promote hatred, is it a crime?
A: No, because the act must "promote or attempt to promote... disharmony or feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will." Objective academic research lacking this intent or effect does not violate Section 196. [Source: Section 196, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 196: Promoting enmity between different groups on grounds of religion, race, place of birth, residence, language, etc., and doing acts prejudicial to maintenance of harmony

Q: What is the systemic consequence of sub-section (1)(c) penalizing the organization of "drills" or "training" against a specific community?
A: The consequence is that the law can dismantle communal militias, extremist training camps, and paramilitary hate groups before they execute a coordinated attack, treating the very act of preparing violence against a community as a serious offence. [Source: Section 196, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 197: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

Q: Is it a crime to publicly claim that people of a certain religion cannot be loyal citizens of India?
A: Yes, publishing imputations that a specific religious, racial, or linguistic group cannot bear allegiance to the Constitution or uphold India's sovereignty is punishable by up to three years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 197, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 197: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

Q: How does Section 197 of BNS 2023 penalize speech that harms national integration?
A: Section 197 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 3 years imprisonment (or 5 years in a place of worship) for making assertions that a specific group cannot bear allegiance to India, should be denied citizenship rights, or by spreading false information jeopardizing India's sovereignty. [Source: Section 197, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 197: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

Q: A radical blogger publishes an article stating that members of Caste X inherently hate India and should immediately be stripped of their voting rights. What offence has the blogger committed?
A: Because the blogger asserted that a class of persons shall, by reason of their caste, be deprived of their rights as citizens of India, the blogger is punishable under sub-section (1)(b) with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 197, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 197: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

Q: Under clause (d) of sub-section (1), what must be the potential impact of the false or misleading information to qualify as an offence?
A: The false or misleading information must be "jeopardising the sovereignty, unity and integrity or security of India." [Source: Section 197, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 197: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

Q: A lawyer argues in court that a specific law (not a community) violates the Constitution and asks for it to be struck down. Does this violate Section 197?
A: No, criticizing a law is not the same as making an imputation against a "class of persons" regarding their allegiance to India, so it does not fall under Section 197. [Source: Section 197, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 197: Imputations, assertions prejudicial to national integration

Q: What is the consequence of elevating these specific types of hate speech to crimes against "national integration"?
A: The consequence is that the State treats rhetoric that fundamentally questions the citizenship, loyalty, or basic rights of minority communities not just as personal defamation, but as a direct threat to the survival and unity of the secular republic itself. [Source: Section 197, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 198: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

Q: What is the penalty if a government official intentionally ignores a legal rule just to hurt someone's case?
A: A public servant who knowingly disobeys a direction of the law with the intent to cause injury to any person is punishable by up to one year of simple imprisonment, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 198, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 198: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

Q: How does Section 198 of BNS 2023 punish malicious disobedience by public servants?
A: Section 198 of BNS 2023 imposes simple imprisonment up to 1 year, or a fine, or both, on any public servant who knowingly disobeys a legal direction regarding their conduct, intending or knowing it will likely cause injury to a person. [Source: Section 198, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 198: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

Q: A tax officer is legally directed to release a businessman's frozen bank account within 24 hours of a court order. The officer personally hates the businessman and intentionally delays it for a month, causing the business to default on loans. What is the officer's crime?
A: Because the officer knowingly disobeyed a direction of law regarding his conduct, intending to cause injury to the businessman, he is punishable under Section 198 with simple imprisonment up to one year or a fine. [Source: Section 198, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 198: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

Q: What specific type of imprisonment is prescribed under this section?
A: The section exclusively prescribes "simple imprisonment" (up to one year). [Source: Section 198, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 198: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

Q: A clerk misreads a newly updated legal circular and accidentally files a citizen's application in the wrong folder, delaying their pension by a month. Is the clerk guilty under Section 198?
A: No, the disobedience was an honest mistake. The statute requires the public servant to act "knowingly" and with the intent or knowledge that it will "cause injury to any person." [Source: Section 198, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 198: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

Q: What is the consequence of limiting the punishment for this offence to "simple imprisonment" of one year?
A: The consequence is that while the law provides a remedy against malicious bureaucratic sabotage, it keeps the penalty relatively mild to prevent paralyzing government operations with the constant threat of severe, rigorous prison sentences for administrative disputes. [Source: Section 198, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying law, with intent to cause injury to any person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 199: Public servant disobeying direction under law

Q: What happens if a police officer refuses to record a victim's complaint about a serious crime like rape?
A: A public servant who fails to record information related to specific serious offences (like rape or sexual assault) is punishable by rigorous imprisonment for between six months and two years, plus a fine. [Source: Section 199, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying direction under law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 199: Public servant disobeying direction under law

Q: How does Section 199 of BNS 2023 penalize a public servant's failure to follow investigative directions?
A: Section 199 of BNS 2023 prescribes rigorous imprisonment from 6 months up to 2 years, and a fine, for a public servant who knowingly disobeys laws regulating investigations, improperly requires a person's attendance, or fails to record complaints for specified serious offences (e.g., Section 64, 65). [Source: Section 199, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying direction under law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 199: Public servant disobeying direction under law

Q: A police inspector refuses to write down an FIR from a woman reporting an acid attack (covered under Section 124), telling her to "go settle it privately." What is the mandatory minimum penalty for the inspector?
A: Because he failed to record information relating to a cognizable offence punishable under Section 124, he is punishable under clause (c) with rigorous imprisonment for a term "which shall not be less than six months." [Source: Section 199, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying direction under law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 199: Public servant disobeying direction under law

Q: Under clause (a), what specific illegal demand made by an investigating officer is criminalized?
A: It criminalizes knowingly disobeying any direction of law "which prohibits him from requiring the attendance at any place of any person for the purpose of investigation." [Source: Section 199, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying direction under law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 199: Public servant disobeying direction under law

Q: If a police officer fails to record a complaint about a stolen bicycle (a minor theft), does it trigger the strict penalties of clause (c) in Section 199?
A: No, clause (c) specifically lists the serious offences (like Sections 64, 65, 70, 124, etc., primarily relating to sexual offences and grievous harm) for which failing to record information is a crime under this section. [Source: Section 199, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying direction under law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 199: Public servant disobeying direction under law

Q: What is the systemic consequence of establishing a mandatory minimum of 6 months rigorous imprisonment for police officers who refuse to record rape cases?
A: The consequence is that it combats the entrenched systemic issue of "burking" (police refusing to register serious crimes against vulnerable victims), ensuring victims of sexual violence have legal recourse against officers who deny them access to the justice system. [Source: Section 199, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 200: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

Q: What is the penalty if a hospital turns away a rape or acid attack victim and refuses to give them free first aid?
A: A person in charge of a hospital who fails to provide free, immediate medical treatment to victims of certain serious offences, as required by law, is punishable by up to one year in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 200, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 200: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

Q: How does Section 200 of BNS 2023 punish the denial of medical treatment to victims?
A: Section 200 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 year imprisonment, or a fine, or both, on anyone in charge of a public or private hospital who contravenes Section 397 of the BNSS, 2023 (which mandates free immediate treatment for victims of specific crimes). [Source: Section 200, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 200: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

Q: The head administrator of a private luxury hospital orders staff to refuse entry to an acid attack victim because she has no health insurance, violating Section 397 of the BNSS. What is the administrator's penalty?
A: Because he is in charge of a private hospital and contravened the provisions of Section 397 of the BNSS, 2023, he is punishable under Section 200 with imprisonment up to one year, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 200, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 200: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

Q: Does this section only apply to government-run public hospitals?
A: No, the statute explicitly applies to anyone in charge of a hospital, "public or private, whether run by the Central Government, the State Government, local bodies or any other person." [Source: Section 200, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 200: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

Q: A victim is brought to a small community clinic, but the clinic lacks the surgical equipment needed to treat the massive trauma, so the doctor stabilizes the victim and immediately transfers them to a major hospital. Is the doctor guilty of "non-treatment"?
A: No, providing stabilizing first aid and an immediate medical transfer out of sheer necessity (because the facility lacks capacity) is medically appropriate and does not constitute a malicious contravention of the legal duty to treat. [Source: Section 200, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 200: Punishment for non-treatment of victim

Q: What is the legal consequence of making hospital administrators criminally liable for refusing to treat victims of severe crimes?
A: The consequence is that it legally prioritizes the right to life and bodily integrity over hospital profit margins or administrative bureaucracy, ensuring that victims of extreme violence receive immediate, life-saving care regardless of their financial status. [Source: Section 200, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 201: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

Q: What is the penalty for a public servant who intentionally falsifies an official record to harm someone?
A: A public servant who prepares or translates a document incorrectly, intending to cause injury to any person, is punishable by up to three years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 201, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 201: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

Q: How does Section 201 of BNS 2023 penalize the falsification of official documents by public servants?
A: Section 201 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 3 years imprisonment, or a fine, or both, for any public servant who frames, prepares, or translates a document/electronic record incorrectly, intending or knowing it will likely cause injury to someone. [Source: Section 201, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 201: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

Q: A court clerk is ordered to translate a witness statement. The clerk personally dislikes the defendant, so he intentionally alters the translation to make the defendant look guilty. What is the clerk's crime?
A: Because he is a public servant charged with translation and framed an incorrect document intending to cause injury to the defendant, he is punishable under Section 201 with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 201, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 201: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

Q: Does this section apply to a public servant who alters a private document that they found on the street?
A: No, the statute explicitly requires the public servant to be "charged with the preparation or translation of any document or electronic record" in their capacity "as such public servant." [Source: Section 201, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 201: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

Q: A government surveyor makes a massive mathematical error on a property map, causing a citizen to lose half their land. Is the surveyor guilty under Section 201?
A: No, because the surveyor did not frame the document in a manner "which he knows or believes to be incorrect." Honest mistakes, even devastating ones, lack the requisite criminal intent. [Source: Section 201, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 201: Public servant framing an incorrect document with intent to cause injury

Q: What is the consequence of establishing a specific offence for public servants falsifying documents (up to 3 years) instead of just using general forgery laws?
A: The consequence is that it addresses the unique breach of public trust when an official misuses their state-granted authority to create "official" falsehoods, ensuring strict accountability for the integrity of government records. [Source: Section 201, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 202: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

Q: Can a government employee run a side business if their contract forbids it?
A: No, a public servant who engages in trade while legally bound not to do so is punishable by up to one year of simple imprisonment, a fine, both, or community service. [Source: Section 202, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 202: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

Q: How does Section 202 of BNS 2023 punish public servants for engaging in forbidden commercial activities?
A: Section 202 of BNS 2023 imposes simple imprisonment up to 1 year, a fine, both, or community service on any public servant who engages in trade when legally bound not to do so. [Source: Section 202, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 202: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

Q: An active-duty police inspector, who is strictly forbidden by law from commercial enterprise, secretly opens a restaurant in his wife's name but personally manages the finances and operations. What offence has he committed?
A: Because he is a public servant legally bound not to engage in trade and engaged in trade, he is punishable under Section 202 with simple imprisonment up to one year, a fine, or community service. [Source: Section 202, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 202: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

Q: What non-custodial alternative sentence is explicitly listed in this section alongside simple imprisonment and fines?
A: The section explicitly lists "community service" as an alternative punishment. [Source: Section 202, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 202: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

Q: A low-level municipal sweeper sells homemade crafts on the weekend. The municipal bylaws have no rule preventing sweeping staff from having outside businesses. Is the sweeper guilty?
A: No, because the sweeper is not "legally bound as such public servant not to engage in trade," their side business does not violate Section 202. [Source: Section 202, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant unlawfully engaging in trade

Q: What is the systemic consequence of criminalizing unauthorized trading by public servants?
A: The consequence is that it prevents conflicts of interest, corruption, and the misuse of official power to gain an unfair advantage in private business, ensuring officials remain fully dedicated to public service. [Source: Section 202, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 203: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

Q: What happens if a government auctioneer secretly bids on the seized property they are supposed to be selling?
A: A public servant who unlawfully purchases or bids for property they are legally barred from buying is punishable by up to two years of simple imprisonment, a fine, or both, and the property will be confiscated. [Source: Section 203, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 203: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

Q: How does Section 203 of BNS 2023 penalize public servants for illicit property purchases?
A: Section 203 of BNS 2023 prescribes simple imprisonment up to 2 years, or a fine, or both, and confiscation of the purchased property, for a public servant who purchases or bids on property they are legally bound not to buy. [Source: Section 203, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 203: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

Q: A tax recovery officer organizes the auction of a defaulter's seized mansion. The officer gives his brother cash to secretly bid on and buy the mansion on the officer's behalf. What is the penalty?
A: Because the officer purchased property he was legally bound not to purchase, in the name of another, he is punishable under Section 203 with imprisonment up to two years, and the mansion shall be confiscated. [Source: Section 203, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 203: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

Q: What specific legal mechanism does the statute include to prevent the public servant from keeping the illicitly acquired asset?
A: The statute mandates that "the property, if purchased, shall be confiscated." [Source: Section 203, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 203: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

A: No, unless the officer was "legally bound as such public servant, not to purchase or bid for [that] certain property" (e.g., if it was a seized vehicle he was investigating). General purchases are not criminalized. [Source: Section 203, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 203: Public servant unlawfully buying or bidding for property

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 204: Personating a public servant

Q: What is the penalty for pretending to be a police officer or government official?
A: Falsely pretending to hold a public office, and attempting to do any act under the color of that office, is punishable by imprisonment between six months and three years, plus a fine. [Source: Section 204, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personating a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 204: Personating a public servant

Q: How does Section 204 of BNS 2023 punish the impersonation of public servants?
A: Section 204 of BNS 2023 imposes a mandatory minimum of 6 months, and up to 3 years imprisonment, plus a fine, on anyone who falsely personates a public servant and does or attempts to do an act under the colour of such office. [Source: Section 204, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personating a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 204: Personating a public servant

Q: A con artist buys a fake ID badge, claims to be a health inspector, and enters a restaurant demanding a 5,000 rupee "fine" for a fake health code violation. What is the minimum sentence?
A: Because he personated a public servant and attempted an act under the colour of that office, he is punishable under Section 204 with imprisonment "which shall not be less than six months." [Source: Section 204, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personating a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 204: Personating a public servant

Q: Under Section 204, is it enough just to tell someone you are a public servant to commit the offence?
A: No, the statute requires that the person not only pretends to hold the office, but also "in such assumed character does or attempts to do any act under colour of such office." [Source: Section 204, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personating a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 204: Personating a public servant

Q: An actor plays the role of a judge in a stage play, wearing a robe and banging a gavel in front of an audience. Is the actor guilty of impersonating a public servant?
A: No, because the actor is not doing an act "under colour of such office" with the intent or effect of acting as a real public servant; it is clearly theatrical and not a false pretense of holding actual office. [Source: Section 204, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personating a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 204: Personating a public servant

Q: What is the consequence of instituting a strict mandatory minimum sentence of 6 months for impersonating a public servant?
A: The consequence is that the State severely deters fraudsters who undermine public trust in government authority by using fake official status to extort, intimidate, or scam ordinary citizens. [Source: Section 204, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personating a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 205: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

Q: What is the penalty for wearing a fake police uniform just to trick people into thinking you are a cop?
A: Wearing the uniform or carrying the token of a public servant, intending to make people believe you belong to that class of servants, is punishable by up to three months in prison, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 205, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 205: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

Q: How does Section 205 of BNS 2023 regulate the unauthorized use of official uniforms?
A: Section 205 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 3 months imprisonment, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, for anyone who wears the garb or carries the token of a public servant class they don't belong to, intending or knowing it will deceive people. [Source: Section 205, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 205: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

Q: A teenager buys a realistic-looking traffic police uniform and stands at an intersection, doing nothing but enjoying the fact that drivers are slowing down and saluting him. Can he be arrested?
A: Yes, because he wore garb resembling a public servant's uniform with the intention that it be believed he belongs to that class, he is punishable under Section 205 with imprisonment up to three months or a fine. [Source: Section 205, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 205: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

Q: How does the *actus reus* of Section 205 (Wearing garb) differ from Section 204 (Personating)?
A: Section 205 only requires the passive act of *wearing* the uniform or carrying the token with intent to deceive, whereas Section 204 requires actively *doing or attempting to do an act* under the color of the office. [Source: Section 205, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 205: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

Q: If a person attends a private Halloween costume party dressed as a generic postal worker, with no intent for anyone to believe they are a real on-duty mail carrier, is it an offence?
A: No, the statute requires the "intention that it may be believed, or with the knowledge that it is likely to be believed, that he belongs to that class of public servants." A costume party lacks this deceptive intent. [Source: Section 205, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 205: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

Q: What is the legal consequence of criminalizing the mere wearing of an official uniform (Section 205) even if the person doesn't extort anyone?
A: The consequence is that law enforcement can preemptively arrest impersonators who are loitering or "patrolling" before they actually commit a substantive fraud or extortion (which would trigger the harsher Section 204). [Source: Section 205, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Wearing garb or carrying token used by public servant with fraudulent intent

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 206: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

Q: What is the penalty for going into hiding to avoid being served with a legal summons?
A: Absconding to avoid a summons from a public servant is punishable by up to one month in prison or a 5,000 rupee fine; if the summons is for a court appearance, it increases to six months or a 10,000 rupee fine. [Source: Section 206, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 206: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

Q: How does Section 206 of BNS 2023 punish absconding to evade legal service?
A: Section 206 of BNS 2023 prescribes simple imprisonment up to 1 month or a 5,000 rupee fine for absconding to avoid general summons, escalating to 6 months imprisonment or a 10,000 rupee fine if the summons requires attending Court. [Source: Section 206, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 206: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

Q: A businessman knows he is being sued. When he sees the court process server pull into his driveway with a court summons to produce financial documents, he jumps out the back window and hides in the woods. What is the maximum penalty?
A: Because he absconded to avoid a summons to produce a document in a Court, he is punishable under clause (b) with simple imprisonment up to six months, or a fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both. [Source: Section 206, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 206: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

Q: Under clause (b), what specific destination of the summons triggers the harsher 6-month penalty?
A: The harsher penalty applies if the summons or order is "to attend in person or by agent, or to produce a document or an electronic record in a Court." [Source: Section 206, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 206: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

Q: A man goes on a month-long backpacking trip without internet. During that time, a public servant tries to serve him a notice. He wasn't hiding; he just wasn't home. Is he guilty under Section 206?
A: No, the statute requires that the person absconds "in order to avoid being served." A coincidental absence lacks the specific intent to evade service. [Source: Section 206, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 206: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

Q: What is the consequence of having two different tiers of punishment in this section?
A: The consequence is that while avoiding administrative notices from generic public servants is a minor offence, evading the formal judicial process (a Court) is treated as a significantly more serious contempt of lawful authority. [Source: Section 206, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Absconding to avoid service of summons or other proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 207: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

Q: Can you be punished for tearing down a legal notice that an official taped to your door?
A: Yes, intentionally preventing the service or lawful affixing of a legal notice, or removing it once affixed, is punishable by up to one month in prison, or six months if it relates to a court proceeding. [Source: Section 207, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 207: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

Q: How does Section 207 of BNS 2023 penalize interference with the service of legal documents?
A: Section 207 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 month imprisonment or a 5,000 rupee fine for intentionally preventing service, affixing, or proclamation of a notice, increasing to 6 months or 10,000 rupees if it pertains to a Court appearance or document production. [Source: Section 207, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 207: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

Q: A process server legally staples a court summons to a suspect's front door requiring him to attend a hearing. The suspect's roommate immediately rips it off and throws it away so the suspect won't see it. What is the roommate's crime?
A: Because the roommate intentionally removed a summons to attend a Court from a place to which it was lawfully affixed, he is punishable under clause (b) with simple imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to ten thousand rupees. [Source: Section 207, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 207: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

Q: What specific method of public announcement, aside from physical documents, is protected from interference under this section?
A: The section specifically protects the "lawful making of any proclamation" from being intentionally prevented. [Source: Section 207, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 207: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

Q: A heavy rainstorm washes away a loosely taped public notice from a bulletin board. The property owner sweeps it into the trash. Is the owner guilty under Section 207?
A: No, the owner did not intentionally remove it from the place to which it was "lawfully affixed" to prevent its publication; nature removed it, and the owner just cleaned up the litter. [Source: Section 207, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 207: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

Q: What is the systemic consequence of criminalizing the prevention of service?
A: The consequence is that it guarantees the integrity of procedural due process; defendants cannot delay justice indefinitely by physically blocking process servers, tearing up paperwork, or shouting down public criers. [Source: Section 207, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Preventing service of summons or other proceeding, or preventing publication thereof

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 208: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

Q: What happens if you just ignore a subpoena and don't show up to a meeting ordered by a public servant?
A: Intentionally omitting to attend at the specified time and place, or leaving early without permission, is punishable by up to one month in prison, or six months if the order was to appear in Court. [Source: Section 208, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 208: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

Q: How does Section 208 of BNS 2023 penalize the failure to attend legally mandated proceedings?
A: Section 208 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 month imprisonment or a 5,000 rupee fine for intentionally failing to attend a meeting ordered by a public servant, escalating to 6 months or 10,000 rupees if the order was to attend a Court. [Source: Section 208, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 208: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

Q: A witness is legally summoned to testify before a District Judge at 10:00 AM. He arrives, but gets bored and leaves the courthouse at 10:15 AM before the judge calls him. What offence has he committed?
A: Because he departed from the place where he was bound to attend before the time it was lawful for him to depart, in obedience to a Court summons, he is punishable under clause (b) with simple imprisonment up to six months. [Source: Section 208, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 208: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

Q: What is the necessary *mens rea* (mental state) for a person to be guilty of non-attendance under this section?
A: The person must "intentionally" omit to attend or depart early. Accidental non-attendance (e.g., getting in a car crash) is not an offence. [Source: Section 208, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 208: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

Q: A citizen is summoned to the municipal office by a clerk who actually has no legal authority to issue such summons. The citizen ignores it. Is the citizen guilty?
A: No, the statute requires the summons to proceed "from any public servant legally competent, as such public servant, to issue the same." If the clerk lacked competence, ignoring the void summons is not a crime. [Source: Section 208, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 208: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

Q: What is the consequence of explicitly criminalizing early departure alongside non-attendance?
A: The consequence is that individuals cannot exploit a loophole by technically showing up for one minute and then fleeing; they remain under the lawful authority of the public servant until officially dismissed. [Source: Section 208, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 209: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

Q: What is the penalty for ignoring a formal proclamation demanding you surrender to authorities?
A: Failing to appear in response to a Section 84 proclamation is punishable by up to three years in prison; if the person is formally declared a "proclaimed offender," the penalty jumps to seven years. [Source: Section 209, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 209: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

Q: How does Section 209 of BNS 2023 punish non-appearance by a proclaimed individual?
A: Section 209 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment (or community service) for failing to appear in response to a BNSS Section 84 proclamation, and up to 7 years imprisonment plus a fine if formally declared a proclaimed offender. [Source: Section 209, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 209: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

Q: A murder suspect flees the state. The court issues a proclamation under BNSS Section 84 requiring him to appear, and then makes a declaration pronouncing him a "proclaimed offender." He still refuses to appear. What is the maximum prison sentence for this specific non-appearance?
A: Because a declaration was made pronouncing him a proclaimed offender, he is punishable under Section 209 with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, plus a fine. [Source: Section 209, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 209: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

Q: Under this section, what non-custodial alternative sentence is available for a person who fails to appear *before* they are officially declared a "proclaimed offender"?
A: The statute lists "community service" as a potential alternative punishment for the baseline 3-year offence (but not for the enhanced 7-year offence). [Source: Section 209, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 209: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

Q: If the court's original proclamation failed to specify a "place" and a "time" for the person to appear, and the person doesn't show up, can they be convicted under Section 209?
A: No, the statute strictly requires failure to appear "at the specified place and the specified time." A procedurally defective proclamation that lacks these details cannot trigger this criminal penalty. [Source: Section 209, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 209: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

Q: What is the consequence of treating the evasion of a Section 84 proclamation as a standalone crime with up to 7 years imprisonment?
A: The consequence is that it heavily incentivizes fugitives to surrender, as remaining on the run transforms from mere evasion into a severe independent felony, adding massive prison time even if they beat the underlying charges. [Source: Section 209, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Non-appearance in response to a proclamation under section 84 of Bharatiya Nagarik

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 210: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

Q: What happens if a person intentionally refuses to hand over a document when legally ordered by a public servant?
A: Refusing to produce a requested document is punishable by up to one month in prison, or up to six months if the document was ordered to be produced in a Court. [Source: Section 210, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 210: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

Q: How does Section 210 of BNS 2023 penalize the withholding of documents from authorities?
A: Section 210 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 1 month simple imprisonment or a 5,000 rupee fine for intentionally omitting to produce a document to a public servant, escalating to 6 months or 10,000 rupees if the document must be produced to a Court. [Source: Section 210, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 210: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

Q: A bank manager is legally ordered by a District Court to produce a suspect's electronic transaction records. The manager intentionally ignores the order to protect the bank's wealthy client. What offence has the manager committed?
A: Because he intentionally omitted to produce an electronic record to a Court when legally bound to do so, he is punishable under clause (b) with simple imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to ten thousand rupees. [Source: Section 210, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 210: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

Q: What modern form of record-keeping is explicitly included alongside traditional "documents" in this section?
A: The section explicitly includes an "electronic record." [Source: Section 210, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 210: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

Q: A citizen is ordered to produce a 20-year-old tax receipt. They sincerely search their entire house but realize the document was destroyed in a flood years ago. Are they guilty of an omission?
A: No, the statute requires the person to "intentionally" omit to produce the document. Inability to produce a destroyed document is not an intentional omission. [Source: Section 210, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 210: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

Q: What is the legal consequence of differentiating between public servants and Courts in this section?
A: The consequence is that while failing to provide paperwork to an administrative agency is a minor infraction, obstructing a formal judicial proceeding by hiding evidence is treated as a more severe offence requiring harsher penalties. [Source: Section 210, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to produce document or electronic record to public servant by person legally

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 211: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

Q: What is the penalty if you are legally required to report something to the police but you intentionally stay silent?
A: Intentionally failing to give required information to a public servant is punishable by up to one month in prison; if the information was about a crime, the penalty increases to six months. [Source: Section 211, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 211: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

Q: How does Section 211 of BNS 2023 penalize the omission to furnish legally required information?
A: Section 211 of BNS 2023 imposes simple imprisonment up to 1 month or a 5,000 rupee fine for intentionally omitting to give legally required information, escalating to 6 months or 10,000 rupees if the information respects the commission of an offence or is required to apprehend an offender. [Source: Section 211, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 211: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

Q: A doctor treats a patient for a gunshot wound. By law, the doctor is bound to report gunshot wounds to the police immediately. The doctor intentionally omits to do so to protect the patient. What is the doctor's penalty?
A: Because the information required to be given respects the commission of an offence, the doctor is punishable under clause (b) with simple imprisonment up to six months, or a fine up to ten thousand rupees, or both. [Source: Section 211, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 211: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

Q: Under clause (c), what specific section of the BNSS triggers a specialized 6-month penalty for failing to provide information?
A: The penalty under clause (c) is triggered if the information is required by an order passed under "section 394 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023." [Source: Section 211, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 211: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

Q: A citizen witnesses a petty theft but doesn't report it. Are they guilty under Section 211?
A: It depends on whether they were "legally bound" to give notice. If the law does not specifically bind a random civilian to report that specific minor crime, the omission is not an offence under Section 211. [Source: Section 211, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 211: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

Q: What is the consequence of escalating the punishment in clause (b) for omissions relating to offences?
A: The consequence is that it severely penalizes covering up crimes; while ignoring administrative reporting requirements is a minor infraction, actively withholding evidence of a crime obstructs justice and allows offenders to escape. [Source: Section 211, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to give notice or information to public servant by person legally bound to give

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 212: Furnishing false information

Q: What happens if you are legally required to report a crime, but you lie to the police about what happened?
A: Furnishing false information to a public servant when legally bound to tell the truth is punishable by up to six months in prison; if the information relates to a crime, the penalty is up to two years. [Source: Section 212, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Furnishing false information

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 212: Furnishing false information

Q: How does Section 212 of BNS 2023 penalize furnishing false information to public servants?
A: Section 212 of BNS 2023 prescribes simple imprisonment up to 6 months for furnishing false information when legally bound to provide it, which increases to 2 years imprisonment of either description if the false information pertains to the commission of an offence or apprehending an offender. [Source: Section 212, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Furnishing false information

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 212: Furnishing false information

Q: A village watchman knows a gang of robbers passed through his village heading North. When the police ask, the watchman (who is legally bound to report this) lies and says they went South. What is his crime?
A: Because he furnished false information respecting the commission of an offence or apprehension of offenders, he is punishable under clause (b) with imprisonment of either description up to two years. [Source: Section 212, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Furnishing false information

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 212: Furnishing false information

Q: According to the Explanation in this section, does the word "offence" include crimes committed outside of India?
A: Yes, the Explanation states that "offence" includes acts committed outside India which, if committed in India, would be punishable under specific listed sections (like murder, dacoity, etc.). [Source: Section 212, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Furnishing false information

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 212: Furnishing false information

Q: A witness to a hit-and-run is legally bound to describe the car. In the dark, they mistakenly thought it was a blue sedan, when it was actually a black SUV. They tell police it was a blue sedan. Are they guilty of furnishing false information?
A: No, because they did not furnish information "which he knows or has reason to believe to be false." An honest mistake in perception lacks the requisite criminal knowledge. [Source: Section 212, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Furnishing false information

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 212: Furnishing false information

Q: What is the legal consequence of distinguishing "omission to give information" (Section 211) from "furnishing false information" (Section 212)?
A: The consequence is that actively lying to mislead authorities (Section 212, up to 2 years) is treated as a much more severe obstruction of justice than merely staying silent (Section 211, up to 6 months). [Source: Section 212, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Furnishing false information

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 213: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

Q: Is it a crime to refuse to swear an oath when a judge or official asks you to?
A: Yes, refusing to bind yourself by an oath or affirmation to tell the truth, when legally required by a competent public servant, is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 213, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 213: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

Q: How does Section 213 of BNS 2023 penalize the refusal to take an oath?
A: Section 213 of BNS 2023 imposes simple imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on anyone who refuses to bind himself by an oath or affirmation when required by a legally competent public servant. [Source: Section 213, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 213: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

Q: A witness takes the stand in a civil trial. Before testifying, the judge asks him to swear an oath or make an affirmation to tell the truth. The witness flatly refuses, stating he doesn't believe in oaths. What is the penalty?
A: Because he refused to bind himself by an oath or affirmation when required by a legally competent public servant (the judge), he is punishable under Section 213 with simple imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 213, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 213: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

Q: Does this section only apply to religious "oaths"?
A: No, the statute explicitly includes refusing to bind oneself by an oath "or affirmation," accommodating individuals who object to religious oaths. [Source: Section 213, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 213: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

Q: A police officer stops a speeding driver on the highway and demands the driver "swear to God" they weren't drinking. The driver refuses. Is the driver guilty under Section 213?
A: No, because a traffic cop on the side of the road is generally not "legally competent to require that he shall so bind himself" by an oath in that specific context. [Source: Section 213, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 213: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing the refusal to take an oath or affirmation?
A: The consequence is that it compels individuals to submit to the formal legal framework of perjury; without an oath, witnesses cannot be easily prosecuted for lying, so refusing the oath is penalized to prevent them from testifying without accountability. [Source: Section 213, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing oath or affirmation when duly required by public servant to make it

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 214: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

Q: Can you be jailed for refusing to answer a police officer's questions?
A: If you are legally bound to state the truth on a subject, refusing to answer a legally authorized question from a public servant is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 214, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 214: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

Q: How does Section 214 of BNS 2023 punish the refusal to answer a public servant's questions?
A: Section 214 of BNS 2023 prescribes simple imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, for anyone legally bound to state the truth who refuses to answer an authorized question from a public servant. [Source: Section 214, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 214: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

Q: A person is summoned as a witness in a corruption probe and is legally bound to state the truth. When the investigator asks who authorized the payment, the witness crosses their arms and refuses to speak. What is the penalty?
A: Because the witness was legally bound to state the truth and refused to answer a question demanded by a public servant in the exercise of legal powers, the witness is punishable under Section 214 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 214, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 214: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

Q: What is the crucial prerequisite regarding the individual's legal duty before they can be charged under Section 214?
A: The individual must be "legally bound to state the truth on any subject" before their refusal to answer becomes a criminal offence. [Source: Section 214, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 214: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

Q: A suspect is arrested for theft. During interrogation, the police ask where he hid the stolen goods. He invokes his constitutional right against self-incrimination and refuses to answer. Is he guilty under Section 214?
A: No, because the constitutional right against self-incrimination supersedes statutory duties; a suspect is not "legally bound to state the truth" if it incriminates them, so refusing to answer is not an offence here. [Source: Section 214, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 214: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

Q: What is the systemic consequence of this section?
A: The consequence is that it arms investigators and courts with a coercive tool (the threat of 6 months in jail) to break the silence of uncooperative witnesses who possess critical information but refuse to testify. [Source: Section 214, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to answer public servant authorised to question

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 215: Refusing to sign statement

Q: What is the penalty for refusing to sign a statement you just gave to a public official?
A: Refusing to sign a statement you made, when legally required to do so by a competent public servant, is punishable by up to three months in prison or a 3,000 rupee fine. [Source: Section 215, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to sign statement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 215: Refusing to sign statement

Q: How does Section 215 of BNS 2023 penalize the refusal to sign a statement?
A: Section 215 of BNS 2023 imposes simple imprisonment up to 3 months, or a fine up to 3,000 rupees, or both, on anyone who refuses to sign a statement made by them when legally required to do so by a competent public servant. [Source: Section 215, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to sign statement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 215: Refusing to sign statement

Q: A witness gives a detailed deposition in court. After the clerk types it up, the judge orders the witness to sign the document to verify it. The witness gets cold feet and refuses to sign. What offence has the witness committed?
A: Because the witness refused to sign a statement made by him when required by a legally competent public servant, he is punishable under Section 215 with imprisonment up to three months or a fine. [Source: Section 215, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to sign statement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 215: Refusing to sign statement

Q: Does this section penalize a person for refusing to sign a statement drafted entirely by the police that the person did not actually make?
A: No, the statute explicitly specifies refusing to sign "any statement made by him." It does not compel a person to sign a fabricated or inaccurate statement they did not make. [Source: Section 215, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to sign statement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 215: Refusing to sign statement

Q: A police officer takes down a witness's statement during a preliminary street investigation and demands the witness sign the notepad. The criminal procedure code specifically says statements to police during investigation need not be signed. Is the witness guilty if they refuse?
A: No, because the police officer is not "legally competent to require that he shall sign that statement" in that specific procedural context, the refusal is not an offence. [Source: Section 215, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to sign statement

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 215: Refusing to sign statement

Q: What is the legal consequence of enforcing the signing of statements with a criminal penalty?
A: The consequence is that it prevents witnesses from giving crucial testimony and then later trying to invalidate it or claim they never said it by withholding their formal signature. [Source: Section 215, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Refusing to sign statement

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 216: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

Q: What is the penalty for lying while under oath to a government official?
A: Making a false statement to a public servant while legally bound by an oath or affirmation is punishable by up to three years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 216, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 216: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

Q: How does Section 216 of BNS 2023 penalize false statements made under oath?
A: Section 216 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment of either description up to 3 years, plus a fine, for anyone who, while legally bound by an oath/affirmation to state the truth to an authorized person, makes a statement they know or believe to be false. [Source: Section 216, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 216: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

Q: During a sworn deposition, a witness is asked if he saw the defendant at the bar. He did see him, but swears under oath that he didn't. What is the witness's crime?
A: Because he made a statement under oath to a public servant which he knew to be false, he is punishable under Section 216 with imprisonment up to three years and a fine. [Source: Section 216, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 216: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

Q: What are the two distinct mental states regarding the falsity of the statement that can trigger liability under this section?
A: The person must either make a statement which he "knows or believes to be false" OR one which he "does not believe to be true." [Source: Section 216, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 216: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

Q: A person takes an oath and testifies that a car was speeding at 80 mph. They genuinely believed it was, but radar data later proves it was only going 50 mph. Are they guilty of a false statement on oath?
A: No, because the person did not know or believe their statement to be false, and they did believe it to be true at the time. Honest mistakes under oath are not criminalized under this section. [Source: Section 216, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 216: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to

Q: What is the legal consequence of penalizing false statements made under oath specifically?
A: The consequence is that it protects the integrity of formal fact-finding processes, treating deliberate perjury as a serious corruption of the legal system rather than just a simple lie. [Source: Section 216, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement on oath or affirmation to public servant or person authorised to
