Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 217: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

Q: What happens if you file a fake police report just to get someone's house searched and annoy them?
A: Giving false information to a public servant with the intent to cause them to use their lawful power to injure or annoy another person is punishable by up to one year in prison, or a 10,000 rupee fine, or both. [Source: Section 217, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 217: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

Q: How does Section 217 of BNS 2023 punish the malicious use of false information to trigger official action?
A: Section 217 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 year imprisonment or a 10,000 rupee fine for giving false information to a public servant, intending to cause them to do something they wouldn't normally do, or to use their power to injure/annoy someone. [Source: Section 217, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 217: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

Q: A man hates his neighbor. He calls the police and falsely reports that the neighbor is hiding illegal weapons, hoping the police will raid the house and traumatize the neighbor's family. What is the man's crime?
A: Because he gave false information intending to cause a public servant to use their lawful power to the injury or annoyance of another person, he is punishable under Section 217 with imprisonment up to one year or a fine. [Source: Section 217, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 217: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

Q: Under clause (a), what specific effect must the false information be intended to have on the public servant's actions?
A: It must be intended to cause the public servant "to do or omit anything which such public servant ought not to do or omit if the true state of facts... were known by him." [Source: Section 217, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 217: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

Q: A citizen genuinely believes they saw a neighbor dealing drugs and reports it to the police. The police search the neighbor's house (annoying them) but find nothing. Is the citizen guilty under Section 217?
A: No, the statute requires the person to give information "which he knows or believes to be false." A good-faith, albeit incorrect, report is not a crime. [Source: Section 217, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 217: False information, with intent to cause public servant to use his lawful power to injury of

Q: What is the systemic consequence of this section?
A: The consequence is that it deters malicious individuals from "weaponizing" the police or government agencies to carry out personal vendettas or harass innocent citizens through fake tips and frivolous complaints. [Source: Section 217, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 218: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

Q: What is the penalty for physically stopping a tax officer from seizing your property?
A: Offering resistance to the lawful taking of property by a public servant is punishable by up to six months in prison, or a fine up to 10,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 218, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 218: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

Q: How does Section 218 of BNS 2023 penalize resisting property seizure?
A: Section 218 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 10,000 rupees, or both, for anyone who resists the taking of property by the lawful authority of a public servant they know to be such. [Source: Section 218, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 218: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

Q: Bailiffs arrive with a valid court order to repossess a man's car. The man blocks the driveway, pushes the bailiffs, and refuses to hand over the keys. What is his offence?
A: Because he offered resistance to the taking of property by the lawful authority of a public servant, he is punishable under Section 218 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 218, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 218: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

Q: What must the offender "know or have reason to believe" about the person taking the property for this section to apply?
A: They must know or have reason to believe "that he is such public servant." [Source: Section 218, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 218: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

Q: A man in plain clothes tries to tow away someone's car, claiming to be an undercover tax official but showing no ID. The owner physically stops him. Is the owner guilty under Section 218?
A: Unlikely, if the owner did not know or have "reason to believe that he is such public servant," they were lawfully defending their property from an apparent theft, not resisting lawful authority. [Source: Section 218, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 218: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

Q: What is the consequence of specifically criminalizing resistance to property seizure?
A: The consequence is that it ensures court judgments, tax levies, and asset forfeitures can be safely and effectively executed without officials having to fight property owners in the streets. [Source: Section 218, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance to taking of property by lawful authority of a public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 219: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: What happens if you intentionally disrupt a government auction?
A: Intentionally obstructing the sale of property offered by the lawful authority of a public servant is punishable by up to one month in prison, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 219, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 219: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: How does Section 219 of BNS 2023 punish interference with official sales?
A: Section 219 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 1 month, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on anyone who intentionally obstructs the sale of property offered by the lawful authority of a public servant. [Source: Section 219, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 219: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: A bank is auctioning a foreclosed home under a court order. The former homeowner shows up with an airhorn and blasts it every time the auctioneer tries to speak, preventing any bids from being heard. What is his crime?
A: Because he intentionally obstructed the sale of property offered for sale by the lawful authority of a public servant, he is punishable under Section 219 with imprisonment up to one month or a fine. [Source: Section 219, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 219: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: What is the specific intent required to commit an offence under this section?
A: The obstruction of the sale must be done "intentionally." [Source: Section 219, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 219: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: A loud construction crew happens to start jackhammering the street right outside a government auction, making it impossible to hear the bids, forcing the auction to be postponed. Are the construction workers guilty?
A: No, because their obstruction was a byproduct of their work and not done "intentionally" to obstruct the sale of the property. [Source: Section 219, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 219: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing the obstruction of government sales?
A: The consequence is that it prevents disgruntled individuals, such as foreclosed homeowners or tax defaulters, from sabotaging the State's ability to liquidate seized assets and recover debts. [Source: Section 219, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing sale of property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 220: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: Is it a crime to bid at a government auction if you have no intention or money to actually pay for the item?
A: Yes, bidding on property at a public servant's sale without intending to perform the obligations of the bid is punishable by up to one month in prison, or a fine up to 200 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 220, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 220: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: How does Section 220 of BNS 2023 penalize fraudulent or illegal bidding at official sales?
A: Section 220 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 1 month imprisonment or a 200 rupee fine for purchasing/bidding on property at an official sale on behalf of someone legally incapacitated to buy it, or bidding without the intention to fulfill the bidding obligations. [Source: Section 220, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 220: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: A man's property is being auctioned off by the court to pay his debts. He has his friend attend the auction and place massively high bids to scare off real buyers, knowing the friend has no money and won't actually pay. What is the friend's penalty?
A: Because the friend bid for property "not intending to perform the obligations under which he lays himself by such bidding," he is punishable under Section 220 with imprisonment up to one month or a fine. [Source: Section 220, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 220: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: Aside from fake bids, what other type of bidding is criminalized by this section?
A: Bidding on account of any person (including oneself) "whom he knows to be under a legal incapacity to purchase that property at that sale." [Source: Section 220, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 220: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: A man bids on a seized car at an auction, fully intending to buy it. The next day, he unexpectedly loses his job and can no longer secure the loan to pay for the car. Is he guilty under Section 220?
A: No, because at the time he bid, he was "intending to perform the obligations." A subsequent inability to pay is a breach of contract, not a criminal fake bid. [Source: Section 220, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 220: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Q: What is the systemic consequence of penalizing fake bids at government auctions?
A: The consequence is that it prevents "shill bidding" and bad-faith disruption tactics meant to artificially inflate prices, delay the transfer of property, or ruin the integrity of the public auction process. [Source: Section 220, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Illegal purchase or bid for property offered for sale by authority of public servant

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 221: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

Q: What is the penalty for physically getting in the way of a public servant trying to do their job?
A: Voluntarily obstructing a public servant in the discharge of their public functions is punishable by up to three months in prison, or a fine up to 2,500 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 221, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 221: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

Q: How does Section 221 of BNS 2023 penalize the obstruction of public servants?
A: Section 221 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment of either description up to 3 months, or a fine up to 2,500 rupees, or both, for anyone who voluntarily obstructs a public servant in the discharge of their public functions. [Source: Section 221, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 221: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

Q: A health inspector is trying to enter a restaurant kitchen for a legally mandated surprise inspection. The owner stands in the doorway and refuses to move, physically blocking the inspector. What is the owner's offence?
A: Because the owner voluntarily obstructed a public servant in the discharge of his public functions, he is punishable under Section 221 with imprisonment up to three months or a fine. [Source: Section 221, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 221: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

Q: What is the required mental state regarding the act of obstruction?
A: The obstruction must be done "voluntarily." [Source: Section 221, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 221: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

Q: A man suffers a sudden seizure on the sidewalk, accidentally collapsing in front of a police officer who is chasing a suspect, causing the officer to trip. Is the man guilty of obstruction?
A: No, because the obstruction was an involuntary medical event, not done "voluntarily" as required by the statute. [Source: Section 221, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 221: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

Q: What is the legal consequence of having a general "obstruction" statute?
A: The consequence is that it provides a broad catch-all mechanism to protect the day-to-day operations of the government from physical or logistical interference, even if the interference doesn't rise to the level of assault or threat. [Source: Section 221, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obstructing public servant in discharge of public functions

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 222: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

Q: If a police officer legally orders you to help them catch a fleeing suspect, and you refuse, can you be punished?
A: Yes, intentionally omitting to assist a public servant when legally bound to do so is punishable by up to one month in prison, or up to six months if the assistance was demanded for preventing a crime or apprehending an offender. [Source: Section 222, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 222: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

Q: How does Section 222 of BNS 2023 penalize the failure to assist public servants?
A: Section 222 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 month simple imprisonment or a 2,500 rupee fine for intentionally omitting legally required assistance, escalating to 6 months or 5,000 rupees if demanded to prevent a crime, suppress a riot, or apprehend an offender. [Source: Section 222, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 222: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

Q: A police officer is struggling to arrest a violent bank robber and orders a nearby security guard (who is bound by law to assist) to help hold the suspect. The guard intentionally walks away. What is the guard's penalty?
A: Because the assistance was demanded to apprehend a person charged with an offence, the guard's intentional omission is punishable under clause (b) with simple imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to five thousand rupees. [Source: Section 222, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 222: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

Q: Under clause (b), what kind of public disturbance explicitly triggers the harsher 6-month penalty if a person refuses to help suppress it?
A: The harsher penalty is triggered if the assistance is demanded for suppressing a "riot, or affray." [Source: Section 222, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 222: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

Q: A police officer demands an elderly man in a wheelchair help him chase down a fleeing marathon runner. The elderly man obviously cannot do it. Is he guilty of omission?
A: While the statute says "intentionally omits," courts generally read in a requirement of capability. If it is physically impossible to render assistance, the omission is not a criminal defiance of the law. [Source: Section 222, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 222: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

Q: What is the consequence of escalating the punishment in clause (b)?
A: The consequence is that the law treats refusing to help during acute public safety emergencies (riots, violent arrests) as a much more serious dereliction of civic duty than failing to assist in routine administrative tasks. [Source: Section 222, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to assist public servant when bound by law to give assistance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 223: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

Q: What is the penalty for ignoring a government order, like a curfew or a ban on public gatherings?
A: Disobeying a duly promulgated order is punishable by up to six months in prison if it causes obstruction or annoyance, and up to one year if it causes danger to human life or a riot. [Source: Section 223, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 223: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

Q: How does Section 223 of BNS 2023 penalize disobedience to official public orders?
A: Section 223 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 6 months simple imprisonment for knowingly disobeying a lawful order if it causes/risks obstruction or annoyance, escalating to 1 year imprisonment of either description if it risks human life, health, safety, or causes a riot. [Source: Section 223, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 223: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

Q: The district magistrate legally promulgates an order forbidding religious processions on a specific street to prevent communal violence. A group leader knowingly leads a procession down that street anyway, sparking a riot. What is the penalty?
A: Because the disobedience caused or tended to cause a riot, the leader is punishable under clause (b) with imprisonment of either description up to one year or a fine up to five thousand rupees. [Source: Section 223, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 223: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

Q: Does the offender need to actually *intend* for their disobedience to cause harm or a riot for this section to apply?
A: No, the Explanation explicitly states: "It is not necessary that the offender should intend to produce harm... It is sufficient that he knows of the order which he disobeys, and that his disobedience produces, or is likely to produce, harm." [Source: Section 223, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 223: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

Q: A citizen violates a curfew order, but they had literally been trapped in a cave for three days and had no possible way of "knowing" the order was promulgated. Are they guilty?
A: No, the statute strictly requires that the person disobeys "knowing that, by an order promulgated... he is directed to abstain." Ignorance of the order is a defense here. [Source: Section 223, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 223: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

Q: What is the consequence of the two-tiered punishment system based on the *result* of the disobedience?
A: The consequence is that the law heavily penalizes disobedience that actively threatens public safety (e.g., ignoring quarantine laws during a plague, leading to health risks), while treating mere procedural nuisance as a lesser offence. [Source: Section 223, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 224: Threat of injury to public servant

Q: What is the penalty for threatening a government worker to make them do something for you?
A: Holding out a threat of injury to a public servant (or someone they care about) to induce them to act or delay an act related to their public functions is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 224, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 224: Threat of injury to public servant

Q: How does Section 224 of BNS 2023 punish threatening a public servant?
A: Section 224 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment of either description up to 2 years, or a fine, or both, for threatening a public servant or a person they are interested in, to induce the servant to do or delay an act connected to their public functions. [Source: Section 224, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 224: Threat of injury to public servant

Q: A building contractor's permits are being delayed by a city zoning official. The contractor calls the official and threatens to break his legs if the permits aren't approved by Friday. What offence is committed?
A: Because he held out a threat of injury to a public servant to induce him to do an act connected with the exercise of his public functions, the contractor is punishable under Section 224 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 224, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 224: Threat of injury to public servant

Q: Can a person be charged under this section if they don't threaten the public servant directly, but instead threaten the public servant's child?
A: Yes, the statute covers threats to "any person in whom he believes that public servant to be interested." [Source: Section 224, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 224: Threat of injury to public servant

Q: Two men get into a bar fight over a spilled drink. One threatens to punch the other. It turns out the other man is an off-duty postal worker. Is the first man guilty of threatening a public servant under Section 224?
A: No, because the threat was not made "for the purpose of inducing that public servant to do any act... connected with the exercise of the public functions of such public servant." It was a personal dispute. [Source: Section 224, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 224: Threat of injury to public servant

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing threats meant to influence public functions?
A: The consequence is that it protects the impartiality of the state; officials can execute their duties according to the law without fear of personal reprisal or extortion from disgruntled citizens. [Source: Section 224, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to public servant

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 225: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

Q: What happens if you threaten a victim to stop them from going to the police?
A: Threatening someone to stop them from making a legal application for protection to a public servant is punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 225, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 225: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

Q: How does Section 225 of BNS 2023 penalize witness or victim intimidation?
A: Section 225 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment of either description up to 1 year, or a fine, or both, for threatening a person to induce them to refrain from applying for protection to a legally empowered public servant. [Source: Section 225, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 225: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

Q: An abusive husband beats his wife and tells her, "If you go to the police for a restraining order, I will kill you." What specific offence against public authority has he committed?
A: Because he held out a threat of injury to induce her to refrain from making a legal application for protection to a public servant, he is punishable under Section 225 with imprisonment up to one year or a fine. [Source: Section 225, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 225: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

Q: What specific type of action must the offender be trying to prevent the victim from taking under this section?
A: The offender must be trying to induce the person to refrain from "making a legal application for protection against any injury to any public servant legally empowered... to give such protection." [Source: Section 225, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 225: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

Q: A shopkeeper tells a loiterer, "If you don't leave my store, I'm calling the police to have you trespassed." Is the shopkeeper guilty of threatening the loiterer under Section 225?
A: No, the shopkeeper is applying for protection *themselves*; they are not threatening the loiterer to prevent the *loiterer* from applying for protection. [Source: Section 225, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 225: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

Q: What is the legal consequence of this statute regarding the justice system?
A: The consequence is that it attacks the root of witness intimidation, ensuring that citizens have unimpeded access to police and courts to seek protection without being terrified into silence by their abusers. [Source: Section 225, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threat of injury to induce person to refrain from applying for protection to public

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 226: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

Q: What is the penalty for threatening or attempting suicide to force a government official to do what you want?
A: Attempting to commit suicide to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging official duty is punishable by up to one year of simple imprisonment, a fine, or community service. [Source: Section 226, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 226: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

Q: How does Section 226 of BNS 2023 penalize suicide attempts used as a form of coercion against officials?
A: Section 226 of BNS 2023 imposes simple imprisonment up to 1 year, or a fine, or both, or community service, for attempting to commit suicide with the intent to compel or restrain a public servant from discharging their official duty. [Source: Section 226, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 226: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

Q: A man pours gasoline on himself outside the mayor's office and threatens to light a match unless the mayor signs an order reversing his property tax assessment. What offence has he committed?
A: Because he attempted to commit suicide with the intent to compel a public servant to discharge his official duty in a certain way, he is punishable under Section 226 with simple imprisonment up to one year, a fine, or community service. [Source: Section 226, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 226: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

Q: What non-custodial and non-financial punishment is explicitly listed as an alternative penalty in this section?
A: The section explicitly lists "community service" as an alternative penalty. [Source: Section 226, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 226: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

Q: A severely depressed teenager attempts suicide at home due to bullying. There is no political or coercive motive. Is this an offence under Section 226?
A: No, the statute strictly requires the specific intent "to compel or restrain any public servant from discharging his official duty." A standard suicide attempt lacks this coercive intent against the state. [Source: Section 226, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 226: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

Q: What is the consequence of having a specific section for coercive suicide attempts?
A: The consequence is that it distinguishes between victims of mental health crises (who generally shouldn't be criminalized) and individuals who weaponize self-harm as a tactic of political protest or extortion against the government. [Source: Section 226, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 227: Giving false evidence

Q: What constitutes "giving false evidence" under the law?
A: Giving false evidence occurs when a person legally bound by oath or law to state the truth makes a false statement that they know or believe to be false, or do not believe to be true. [Source: Section 227, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 227: Giving false evidence

Q: How does Section 227 of BNS 2023 define the offence of giving false evidence?
A: Section 227 of BNS 2023 defines it as a person, legally bound by oath or law to state the truth or make a declaration, making a statement they know/believe to be false or do not believe to be true. [Source: Section 227, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 227: Giving false evidence

Q: A translator in a court case is bound by oath to translate a witness's testimony accurately. The witness says, "I saw the man." The translator intentionally tells the court the witness said, "I did not see the man." What has the translator done?
A: Because the translator gave as a true interpretation that which was not true and which he did not believe to be true while bound by oath, he has given false evidence under Section 227. [Source: Section 227, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 227: Giving false evidence

Q: Can a statement regarding a person's "belief" constitute false evidence under this section?
A: Yes, Explanation 2 states that a person may be guilty by stating they believe a thing which they actually do not believe. [Source: Section 227, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 227: Giving false evidence

Q: A witness swears under oath that a signature belongs to the defendant because they genuinely believe it looks like his handwriting, though it turns out to be a forgery. Has the witness given false evidence?
A: No, because the witness stated their belief in good faith and the statement was true as to their actual belief; therefore, they did not make a statement they knew to be false or didn't believe to be true. [Source: Section 227, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 227: Giving false evidence

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing statements made when a person "does not believe them to be true" (even if they don't definitively *know* they are false)?
A: The consequence is that it penalizes reckless perjury; witnesses cannot make wild, unfounded assertions under oath while claiming ignorance, as stating something as a fact without believing it to be true is still perjury. [Source: Section 227, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 228: Fabricating false evidence

Q: What does it mean to "fabricate false evidence"?
A: Fabricating false evidence involves creating a fake circumstance, document, or electronic record with the intent that it be used in a judicial or official proceeding to cause someone to form an erroneous opinion on a material point. [Source: Section 228, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fabricating false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 228: Fabricating false evidence

Q: How does Section 228 of BNS 2023 define fabricating false evidence?
A: Section 228 of BNS 2023 defines it as causing a circumstance to exist or making a false entry/document/electronic record, intending it to appear in an official or judicial proceeding to mislead the decision-maker on a material point. [Source: Section 228, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fabricating false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 228: Fabricating false evidence

Q: A man wants to frame his rival for theft. He sneaks into his rival's house and hides stolen jewels in the rival's closet, hoping the police will find them and arrest the rival. What has the man done?
A: Because he caused a circumstance to exist intending that it may appear in evidence and cause an erroneous opinion touching a material point (the rival's guilt), he has fabricated false evidence under Section 228. [Source: Section 228, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fabricating false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 228: Fabricating false evidence

Q: What type of modern records are explicitly mentioned in this section alongside physical books and documents?
A: The section explicitly includes making a false entry in an "electronic record." [Source: Section 228, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fabricating false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 228: Fabricating false evidence

Q: A teenager uses photoshop to create a fake, humorous award certificate for their friend and posts it online as a joke. Is this fabricating false evidence?
A: No, because there was no intention for the document to "appear in evidence in a judicial proceeding, or in a proceeding taken by law before a public servant," which is a mandatory element of the offence. [Source: Section 228, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fabricating false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 228: Fabricating false evidence

Q: What is the consequence of this definition covering both documentary forgery and physical "circumstances"?
A: The consequence is that planting physical evidence (like a weapon or drugs) is treated under the same severe framework of perjury as forging a signature or doctoring a ledger for a trial. [Source: Section 228, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fabricating false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 229: Punishment for false evidence

Q: What is the punishment for lying in court or fabricating evidence for a trial?
A: Giving or fabricating false evidence for a judicial proceeding is punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. For non-judicial proceedings, it is up to three years. [Source: Section 229, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 229: Punishment for false evidence

Q: How does Section 229 of BNS 2023 prescribe punishments for false evidence?
A: Section 229 of BNS 2023 mandates imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine for false evidence in a judicial proceeding (sub-section 1), and imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine for false evidence in any other case (sub-section 2). [Source: Section 229, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 229: Punishment for false evidence

Q: A man lies under oath during a preliminary police investigation directed by a Magistrate to ascertain whether a suspect should be committed for trial. What is the maximum penalty?
A: Because a preliminary investigation directed by law is a stage of a judicial proceeding, he is punishable under sub-section (1) with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 229, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 229: Punishment for false evidence

Q: According to the Explanations, does a proceeding have to take place physically *inside a courtroom* to be considered a "judicial proceeding" under this section?
A: No, investigations directed by law preliminary to a court proceeding, or directed by a court and conducted under its authority (like a field inquiry), are considered stages of a judicial proceeding. [Source: Section 229, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 229: Punishment for false evidence

Q: A person lies on a standard administrative application for a parking permit. Is this punishable by 7 years in prison under sub-section (1)?
A: No, because a parking permit application is not a "judicial proceeding." It would fall under sub-section (2) (any other case), punishable by up to three years. [Source: Section 229, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 229: Punishment for false evidence

Q: What is the consequence of distinguishing between judicial and non-judicial proceedings in this section?
A: The consequence is that it reflects the higher stakes of the judicial system; perverting the course of justice in a trial where liberty or property is at stake warrants a much harsher 7-year penalty than lying to a generic bureaucrat. [Source: Section 229, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 230: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

Q: What is the penalty if you frame someone for murder to get them sentenced to death?
A: Fabricating or giving false evidence to procure a conviction for a capital offence is punishable by life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years. If the innocent person is actually executed, the perjurer can be sentenced to death. [Source: Section 230, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 230: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

Q: How does Section 230 of BNS 2023 penalize false evidence intended to secure a death penalty conviction?
A: Section 230 of BNS 2023 imposes life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years for giving/fabricating false evidence intending to cause a capital conviction, and if an innocent person is executed as a result, the offender may be punished with death. [Source: Section 230, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 230: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

Q: A man wants to inherit his brother's estate, so he fabricates DNA evidence framing his brother for a horrific capital murder. The brother is convicted and sentenced to death, but the forgery is discovered before the execution. What is the forger's penalty?
A: Because he fabricated false evidence intending to procure a conviction of a capital offence, but the execution did not occur, he is punishable under sub-section (1) with life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years, and a fine. [Source: Section 230, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 230: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

Q: Under sub-section (2), what extreme consequence must occur to trigger the death penalty for the perjurer?
A: An innocent person must be "convicted and executed in consequence of false evidence." [Source: Section 230, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 230: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

Q: A witness genuinely but mistakenly identifies a suspect in a capital murder trial. The suspect is convicted and executed. Later, the real killer confesses. Is the witness sentenced to death under Section 230?
A: No, because Section 230 only applies to one who "gives or fabricates false evidence" (which implies knowing it is false under Sec 227). An honest mistake is not giving "false evidence" in the criminal sense. [Source: Section 230, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 230: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

Q: What is the legal and moral consequence of sub-section (2)?
A: The consequence is the ultimate application of retributive justice; by using the legal system to effectively murder an innocent person, the perjurer forfeits their own life to the same system. [Source: Section 230, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of capital offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 231: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

Q: What is the penalty for giving false evidence to get someone convicted of a serious crime like dacoity or kidnapping?
A: Fabricating or giving false evidence intending to cause a conviction for an offence punishable by life imprisonment or imprisonment of 7 years or more is punished with the same punishment prescribed for that specific offence. [Source: Section 231, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 231: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

Q: How does Section 231 of BNS 2023 penalize false evidence meant to procure convictions for serious, non-capital crimes?
A: Section 231 of BNS 2023 dictates that giving/fabricating false evidence intended to secure a conviction for an offence punishable with life imprisonment or a term of 7 years or upwards makes the offender liable to the same punishment prescribed for that offence. [Source: Section 231, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 231: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

Q: A man hates his neighbor and fabricates evidence to frame him for a robbery, a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison. The neighbor is acquitted, but the fabrication is discovered. What is the fabricator's penalty?
A: Because he fabricated false evidence intending to cause a conviction for an offence punishable by imprisonment of 7 years or upwards, he is punishable as a person convicted of that robbery would be liable to be punished (up to 10 years). [Source: Section 231, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 231: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

Q: What is the minimum potential sentence of the underlying framed offence required to trigger the "mirror punishment" rule under this section?
A: The underlying framed offence must be punishable with "imprisonment for a term of seven years or upwards" (or life imprisonment). [Source: Section 231, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 231: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

Q: A person frames another for petty theft, an offence punishable by up to 3 years in prison. Does Section 231 apply, making the framer liable for 3 years?
A: No, Section 231 only applies to offences punishable by 7 years or upwards. Framing someone for petty theft would fall under the general punishment for false evidence in Section 229(1) (up to 7 years), not the mirror punishment of Section 231. [Source: Section 231, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 231: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

Q: What is the consequence of linking the perjurer's punishment to the punishment of the crime they are framing someone for?
A: The consequence is proportionality; it ensures that the penalty for attempting to destroy someone's life through the courts scales directly with the severity of the false charges being leveled against them. [Source: Section 231, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving or fabricating false evidence with intent to procure conviction of offence punishable

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 232: Threatening any person to give false evidence

Q: What happens if you threaten a witness to force them to lie under oath?
A: Threatening a person with injury to force them to give false evidence is punishable by up to seven years in prison or a fine. If an innocent person is convicted and executed or sentenced to over 7 years because of the coerced lie, the person who made the threat receives the same sentence. [Source: Section 232, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threatening any person to give false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 232: Threatening any person to give false evidence

Q: How does Section 232 of BNS 2023 punish the intimidation of witnesses to produce false evidence?
A: Section 232 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 7 years imprisonment or a fine for threatening a person to compel false evidence. If this causes an innocent person to be convicted and sentenced to death or imprisonment over 7 years, the threatener receives the identical punishment. [Source: Section 232, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threatening any person to give false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 232: Threatening any person to give false evidence

Q: A mafia boss threatens to kill a bystander's family unless the bystander testifies that the boss wasn't at the murder scene. The bystander complies, the boss is acquitted, and an innocent man is convicted and sentenced to death based on that testimony. What is the boss's penalty?
A: Because the innocent person was convicted and sentenced to death in consequence of the coerced false evidence, the boss who threatened the witness shall be punished with death, in the same manner and extent as the innocent person. [Source: Section 232, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threatening any person to give false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 232: Threatening any person to give false evidence

Q: Under sub-section (1), what three categories of "injury" can form the basis of the threat used to coerce false evidence?
A: The threat can be of injury to a person's "person, reputation or property" (or to someone they are interested in). [Source: Section 232, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threatening any person to give false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 232: Threatening any person to give false evidence

Q: A lawyer tells a witness, "If you lie on the stand, I will aggressively cross-examine you and destroy your credibility." Is this a criminal threat under Section 232?
A: No, the lawyer is threatening to expose a lie, not threatening injury "with intent to cause that person to give false evidence." Legal cross-examination is not an illegal "injury." [Source: Section 232, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threatening any person to give false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 232: Threatening any person to give false evidence

Q: What is the consequence of the "mirror punishment" in sub-section (2) for the person making the threat?
A: The consequence is that the mastermind who orchestrates perjury through violent extortion cannot escape severe punishment by blaming the terrified witness; the mastermind bears full criminal liability for the unjust sentence inflicted on the innocent party. [Source: Section 232, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Threatening any person to give false evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 233: Using evidence known to be false

Q: Can you be punished for presenting a forged document in court even if you didn't forge it yourself?
A: Yes, corruptly using evidence that you know is false or fabricated is punished in the exact same manner as if you had given or fabricated the false evidence yourself. [Source: Section 233, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using evidence known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 233: Using evidence known to be false

Q: How does Section 233 of BNS 2023 penalize the usage of false evidence?
A: Section 233 of BNS 2023 dictates that anyone who corruptly uses or attempts to use evidence as true/genuine, knowing it to be false or fabricated, shall be punished in the same manner as if they personally gave or fabricated it. [Source: Section 233, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using evidence known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 233: Using evidence known to be false

Q: A lawyer is handed a forged contract by his client. The lawyer knows it is a forgery but submits it to the judge anyway as genuine evidence to win the civil case. What is the lawyer's offence?
A: Because the lawyer corruptly used evidence he knew to be false as true/genuine, he is punishable under Section 233 in the same manner as if he fabricated the false evidence himself (which, under Section 229, is up to 7 years). [Source: Section 233, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using evidence known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 233: Using evidence known to be false

Q: What is the specific mental requirement regarding the use of the false evidence?
A: The person must use or attempt to use the evidence "corruptly" and "knows" it to be false or fabricated. [Source: Section 233, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using evidence known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 233: Using evidence known to be false

Q: A prosecutor uses a witness's testimony in court, genuinely believing the witness is telling the truth. It is later revealed the witness was lying. Is the prosecutor guilty under Section 233?
A: No, because the prosecutor did not know the evidence to be false. The statute strictly requires knowing use. [Source: Section 233, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using evidence known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 233: Using evidence known to be false

Q: What is the legal consequence of equating the *use* of false evidence with the *fabrication* of it?
A: The consequence is that it closes a loophole where individuals could hire third parties to forge documents and then introduce them in court claiming immunity because they didn't personally create the forgery. [Source: Section 233, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using evidence known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 234: Issuing or signing false certificate

Q: What happens if an official issues a certificate they know contains a lie?
A: Issuing or signing a legally required or admissible certificate, knowing it to be false in any material point, is punished in the same manner as giving false evidence. [Source: Section 234, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issuing or signing false certificate

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 234: Issuing or signing false certificate

Q: How does Section 234 of BNS 2023 penalize the issuance of false certificates?
A: Section 234 of BNS 2023 punishes anyone who issues or signs a legally required or admissible certificate, knowing or believing it to be false in a material point, in the same manner as if they gave false evidence. [Source: Section 234, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issuing or signing false certificate

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 234: Issuing or signing false certificate

Q: A doctor is authorized by law to issue medical fitness certificates for pilots. A perfectly healthy pilot pays the doctor a bribe, and the doctor signs a certificate falsely stating the pilot is legally blind and unfit to fly. What is the doctor's crime?
A: Because he signed a certificate relating to a fact of which the certificate is admissible in evidence, knowing it to be false in a material point, he is punishable under Section 234 in the same manner as if he gave false evidence. [Source: Section 234, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issuing or signing false certificate

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 234: Issuing or signing false certificate

Q: Does this section apply to a minor, irrelevant typo in a certificate?
A: No, the certificate must be known or believed to be false in a "material point." [Source: Section 234, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issuing or signing false certificate

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 234: Issuing or signing false certificate

Q: A university clerk signs a legally required transcript, accidentally typing a "B" instead of an "A" for a student's grade due to a keystroke error. Is the clerk guilty?
A: No, because the clerk did not know or believe the certificate to be false; it was an unintentional clerical error, lacking the necessary *mens rea*. [Source: Section 234, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issuing or signing false certificate

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 234: Issuing or signing false certificate

Q: What is the systemic consequence of this section regarding administrative trust?
A: The consequence is that it heavily protects the evidentiary value of official certificates (like birth, death, medical, and property certificates), ensuring that those who abuse their power to issue fraudulent credentials face severe perjury charges. [Source: Section 234, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Issuing or signing false certificate

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 235: Using as true a certificate known to be false

Q: What is the penalty for using a fake or fraudulent official certificate?
A: Corruptly using a certificate as true, while knowing it is false in a material point, is punished in the same manner as giving false evidence. [Source: Section 235, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true a certificate known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 235: Using as true a certificate known to be false

Q: How does Section 235 of BNS 2023 penalize the usage of false certificates?
A: Section 235 of BNS 2023 dictates that whoever corruptly uses or attempts to use a legally required/admissible certificate as true, knowing it is false in a material point, shall be punished in the same manner as giving false evidence. [Source: Section 235, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true a certificate known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 235: Using as true a certificate known to be false

Q: An immigrant buys a forged birth certificate from a black market dealer. He knows it is completely fake, but he submits it to the passport office to obtain citizenship. What is his offence?
A: Because he corruptly used the certificate as true, knowing it to be false in a material point, he is punishable under Section 235 in the same manner as if he gave false evidence. [Source: Section 235, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true a certificate known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 235: Using as true a certificate known to be false

Q: What specific qualifier describes the manner in which the certificate must be used to trigger this section?
A: The certificate must be used "corruptly." [Source: Section 235, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true a certificate known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 235: Using as true a certificate known to be false

Q: A historian finds an old, forged land grant in an archive and publishes it in a book as an example of 19th-century forgery. Is the historian guilty under Section 235?
A: No, because the historian is not corruptly using it "as a true certificate" to gain a legal advantage; they are presenting it explicitly as a forgery for academic purposes. [Source: Section 235, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true a certificate known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 235: Using as true a certificate known to be false

Q: What is the consequence of treating the use of a false certificate identically to giving false evidence?
A: The consequence is that individuals cannot circumvent perjury laws by relying on written lies created by corrupt officials or forgers; submitting the false paper is treated as legally identical to speaking the lie under oath. [Source: Section 235, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true a certificate known to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 236: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

Q: What is the penalty for lying on a legal declaration form?
A: Making a false statement in a declaration that is legally receivable as evidence is punished in the same manner as giving false evidence. [Source: Section 236, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 236: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

Q: How does Section 236 of BNS 2023 treat false statements in legal declarations?
A: Section 236 of BNS 2023 states that whoever makes a statement they know/believe to be false (or do not believe to be true) in a declaration legally receivable as evidence, touching a material point, shall be punished in the same manner as giving false evidence. [Source: Section 236, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 236: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

Q: A citizen submits a sworn affidavit for a government housing scheme, falsely declaring they own no other property. The housing authority is legally bound to receive this affidavit as evidence. What is the offence?
A: Because the citizen made a false statement touching a material point in a declaration authorized by law to be received as evidence, they are punishable under Section 236 in the same manner as if they gave false evidence. [Source: Section 236, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 236: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

Q: What characteristic must the false statement have regarding the purpose of the declaration for it to be actionable under this section?
A: The false statement must be "touching any point material to the object for which the declaration is made or used." [Source: Section 236, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 236: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

Q: A person fills out a voluntary feedback card at a public hospital and falsely writes their age as 25 instead of 30. Is this punishable under Section 236?
A: No, because a voluntary feedback card is not a declaration that a court or public servant "is bound or authorised by law to receive as evidence of any fact." [Source: Section 236, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 236: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

Q: What is the legal consequence of expanding perjury laws to include written declarations outside of courtrooms?
A: The consequence is that it ensures the integrity of administrative and bureaucratic processes that rely on sworn affidavits or statutory declarations, treating lying on these forms as seriously as lying on the witness stand. [Source: Section 236, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False statement made in declaration which is by law receivable as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 237: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

Q: Can you be punished for using someone else's false affidavit as evidence?
A: Yes, corruptly using a legal declaration as true while knowing it contains a material falsehood is punished in the same manner as giving false evidence. [Source: Section 237, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 237: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

Q: How does Section 237 of BNS 2023 penalize the usage of false declarations?
A: Section 237 of BNS 2023 punishes anyone who corruptly uses or attempts to use a declaration as true, knowing it to be false in a material point, in the same manner as if they gave false evidence. [Source: Section 237, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 237: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

Q: A lawyer submits an affidavit from a witness to the court, fully knowing the witness lied about their whereabouts in the document. What is the lawyer's offence?
A: Because the lawyer corruptly used the declaration as true while knowing it to be false in a material point, the lawyer is punishable under Section 237 in the same manner as giving false evidence. [Source: Section 237, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 237: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

Q: Does a false declaration escape the penalties of this section if it has a minor formatting error making it technically inadmissible?
A: No, the Explanation clarifies that a declaration which is inadmissible "merely upon the ground of some informality" is still a declaration within the meaning of this section. [Source: Section 237, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 237: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

A: No, because the clerk did not "know" the declaration to be false and was not using it "corruptly." [Source: Section 237, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 237: Using as true such declaration knowing it to be false

Q: What is the consequence of the Explanation regarding "informality"?
A: The consequence is that offenders cannot use technical loopholes (like a missing notary stamp or incorrect margin size) as a defense against charges of submitting a substantively false and fraudulent affidavit. [Source: Section 237, BNS 2023]
