content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 238: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

Q: What is the penalty for helping a criminal by hiding the murder weapon or destroying evidence?
A: Causing evidence of a crime to disappear or giving false information to screen the offender is punishable by up to seven years in prison if the underlying crime was a capital offence. The punishment scales down for less severe underlying crimes. [Source: Section 238, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 238: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

Q: How does Section 238 of BNS 2023 punish the destruction of evidence to protect offenders?
A: Section 238 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 7 years imprisonment if the screened offence is capital, up to 3 years if punishable by life or 10 years, and up to one-fourth of the maximum term for lesser offences, for causing evidence to disappear or giving false information to screen an offender. [Source: Section 238, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 238: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

Q: A woman knows her husband murdered their neighbor. To protect him, she thoroughly scrubs the blood from the floor and burns the bloody clothes. What is her penalty?
A: Because she caused evidence of a capital offence to disappear with the intention of screening the offender from legal punishment, she is punishable under clause (a) with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 238, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 238: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

Q: What specific intention is required when a person causes evidence to disappear under this section?
A: The act must be done "with the intention of screening the offender from legal punishment." [Source: Section 238, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 238: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

Q: A janitor cleans a hotel room, inadvertently wiping away fingerprints and washing away blood stains left by a murderer, believing them to be spilled wine. Is the janitor guilty?
A: No, because the janitor did not know an offence had been committed and lacked the specific intention to "screen the offender from legal punishment." [Source: Section 238, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 238: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

Q: What is the consequence of tying the evidence-tampering penalty directly to the severity of the screened offence?
A: The consequence is a proportionate justice system; protecting a shoplifter by hiding stolen goods carries a minor penalty, while protecting a murderer by hiding a body carries a severe 7-year prison sentence. [Source: Section 238, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Causing disappearance of evidence of offence, or giving false information to screen

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 239: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

Q: Can you be punished for knowing about a crime but failing to report it?
A: Yes, if you are legally bound to give information about a crime and you intentionally omit to do so, you can be punished by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 239, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 239: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

Q: How does Section 239 of BNS 2023 penalize the failure to report crimes?
A: Section 239 of BNS 2023 dictates that a person legally bound to give information about an offence who intentionally omits to do so, knowing/believing it was committed, shall be punished with imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both. [Source: Section 239, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 239: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

Q: A village watchman is legally bound under local regulations to report any unnatural deaths to the nearest police station. He finds a murdered body but decides to say nothing because he doesn't want to get involved. What is his penalty?
A: Because he intentionally omitted to give information respecting an offence which he was legally bound to give, he is punishable under Section 239 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 239, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 239: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

Q: Does this section apply to an ordinary citizen who witnesses a minor theft but decides not to call the police?
A: Generally no, unless the citizen is specifically "legally bound to give" information about that particular offence (e.g., under specific statutory duties like reporting child abuse or terrorism). [Source: Section 239, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 239: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

Q: A bank manager suspects a client of fraud and is legally bound to file a Suspicious Activity Report. Before she can file it, she suffers a severe stroke and is hospitalized. Is she guilty of an intentional omission?
A: No, her omission was caused by a medical emergency, not "intentionally" as required by the statute. [Source: Section 239, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 239: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

Q: What is the consequence of limiting this offence to persons "legally bound to inform"?
A: The consequence is that it avoids criminalizing innocent bystanders for mere inaction or fear of getting involved, focusing instead on penalizing professionals, officials, or specific individuals who have a statutory duty to alert authorities. [Source: Section 239, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to give information of offence by person bound to inform

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 240: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

Q: What is the penalty for calling the police and giving them fake details about a crime that occurred?
A: Giving false information about a committed crime, knowing it to be false, is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 240, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 240: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

Q: How does Section 240 of BNS 2023 penalize providing false information about offences?
A: Section 240 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment of either description up to 2 years, or a fine, or both, for anyone who knows an offence was committed and gives information respecting it which they know or believe to be false. [Source: Section 240, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 240: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

Q: A man witnesses a robbery committed by his friend. When the police interview him, he deliberately gives them a false description of the robber, pointing them toward a rival gang member instead. What is his offence?
A: Because he gave information respecting a committed offence which he knew to be false, he is punishable under Section 240 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 240, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 240: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

Q: According to the Explanation, does this section apply if the underlying "offence" being lied about was committed outside of India?
A: Yes, if the act committed outside India would be punishable under certain specified sections (like murder, dacoity, etc.) if committed in India. [Source: Section 240, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 240: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

Q: A witness to a hit-and-run genuinely believes the fleeing car was a red sedan and tells the police this. Camera footage later proves it was a maroon SUV. Is the witness guilty under Section 240?
A: No, because the witness did not give information which they "knows or believes to be false"; it was an honest misidentification. [Source: Section 240, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 240: Giving false information respecting an offence committed

Q: What is the legal consequence of penalizing false information about crimes?
A: The consequence is that it protects police resources from being wasted on deliberate wild goose chases and prevents malicious individuals from using police investigations to frame innocent third parties. [Source: Section 240, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 241: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

Q: What is the punishment for destroying a document or electronic file so it can't be used in court?
A: Destroying, hiding, or rendering illegible a document or electronic record to prevent its use as evidence in a lawful proceeding is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 241, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 241: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

Q: How does Section 241 of BNS 2023 treat the destruction of evidence?
A: Section 241 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 3 years, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, for secreting, destroying, or obliterating a document/electronic record to prevent it from being produced as evidence in a court or before a public servant. [Source: Section 241, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 241: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

Q: A corporate executive receives a subpoena for financial ledgers. Before handing them over, she runs the ledgers through a paper shredder. What is her penalty?
A: Because she destroyed a document after being lawfully summoned to produce it as evidence, she is punishable under Section 241 with imprisonment up to three years or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 241, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 241: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

Q: Can someone be punished under this section even if they haven't been formally summoned yet, but they anticipate the document will be needed in court?
A: Yes, the section covers destroying documents they "may be lawfully compelled to produce" with the intention of preventing its use as evidence, as well as destruction "after he shall have been lawfully summoned." [Source: Section 241, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 241: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

Q: A man routinely deletes old emails to save server space, accidentally deleting an email that a court later realizes it needs for a civil dispute. Is he guilty under Section 241?
A: No, because he deleted the emails as routine maintenance without the specific "intention of preventing the same from being produced or used as evidence." [Source: Section 241, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 241: Destruction of document or electronic record to prevent its production as evidence

Q: What is the consequence of this law on digital forensics?
A: The consequence is that individuals who wipe hard drives, encrypt files maliciously, or physically destroy servers to hide digital evidence face severe criminal spoliation charges, preserving the integrity of court fact-finding. [Source: Section 241, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 242: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

Q: What is the penalty for pretending to be someone else in a court proceeding or to post bail?
A: Falsely personating another person to make an admission, confess judgment, or act as bail or security in a suit or criminal prosecution is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 242, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 242: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

Q: How does Section 242 of BNS 2023 penalize false personation in legal proceedings?
A: Section 242 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment of either description up to 3 years, or a fine, or both, for falsely personating another and in that assumed character doing acts like making admissions or becoming bail in a legal suit or prosecution. [Source: Section 242, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 242: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

Q: A man's brother is arrested. Because the brother has a long criminal record, the man shows up to court claiming to be the brother, hoping the judge will be lenient on him as a "first-time offender." What is the man's offence?
A: Because he falsely personated another to do an act in a criminal prosecution, he is punishable under Section 242 with imprisonment up to three years or a fine. [Source: Section 242, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 242: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

Q: Does the personation have to occur during an active trial to fall under this section?
A: No, it includes actions like causing any process to be issued or becoming "bail or security," which often occur before a trial formally begins. [Source: Section 242, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 242: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

Q: A lawyer legally represents a client in court and says, "On behalf of my client, we admit to the breach of contract." Is the lawyer falsely personating the client under Section 242?
A: No, the lawyer is acting as a legal representative, not "falsely personating" (pretending to actually *be*) the client. [Source: Section 242, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 242: False personation for purpose of act or proceeding in suit or prosecution

Q: What is the legal consequence of criminalizing false personation in court?
A: The consequence is that it protects the fundamental integrity of the judicial system; courts must be able to trust that judgments, bail bonds, and admissions are binding on the actual parties involved, not imposters. [Source: Section 242, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 243: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

Q: What happens if you hide your assets so the court can't seize them to pay a fine or debt?
A: Fraudulently removing, concealing, or transferring property to prevent it from being seized for forfeiture, a fine, or a civil decree is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 243, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 243: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

Q: How does Section 243 of BNS 2023 penalize hiding property from court execution?
A: Section 243 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment or a 5,000 rupee fine for fraudulently removing or transferring property to prevent its seizure for forfeiture, fine, or execution of a decree pronounced or likely to be pronounced. [Source: Section 243, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 243: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

Q: A man loses a massive civil lawsuit and knows the court is about to order his sports car seized to pay the plaintiff. He quickly sells the car to his brother for $1 and tells his brother to hide it. What is his penalty?
A: Because he fraudulently transferred and concealed property intending to prevent it from being taken in execution of a decree he knew was likely to be made, he is punishable under Section 243 with imprisonment up to three years or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 243, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 243: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

Q: Does the court order (decree) have to already be issued for this section to apply?
A: No, the statute covers preventing seizure under a sentence or decree "which has been pronounced, or which he knows to be likely to be pronounced." [Source: Section 243, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 243: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

Q: A debtor legitimately sells his car at fair market value to a stranger in order to use the cash to pay off his court-ordered fine. Is he guilty of fraudulent removal?
A: No, the transfer was not done "fraudulently... intending thereby to prevent that property... from being taken in satisfaction of a fine." He sold it precisely *to* satisfy the fine. [Source: Section 243, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in

content:

Q: What is the consequence of this section regarding civil litigation?
A: The consequence is that it deters judgment-proof tactics; plaintiffs have legal recourse if a defendant tries to maliciously drain their own assets to avoid paying a rightful court-ordered debt. [Source: Section 243, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the penalty for faking ownership of someone else's property so the government can't seize it from them?
A: Fraudulently claiming property you have no right to, in order to prevent it from being seized for someone else's fine, forfeiture, or civil decree, is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 244, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 244: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

Q: How does Section 244 of BNS 2023 penalize fraudulent claims against seized property?
A: Section 244 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment up to 2 years or a fine for anyone who fraudulently accepts or claims property they have no right to, intending to prevent it from being seized for forfeiture, a fine, or a civil decree. [Source: Section 244, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 244: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

Q: A corrupt politician is convicted and ordered to forfeit his mansion. His cousin suddenly produces a fake, backdated deed and claims he has owned the mansion for ten years, hoping to block the forfeiture. What is the cousin's offence?
A: Because the cousin fraudulently claimed an interest in the property, knowing he had no right to it, intending to prevent its forfeiture under a court sentence, he is punishable under Section 244 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 244, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 244: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

Q: How does the target of Section 244 differ from Section 243?
A: While Section 243 targets the person *giving away or hiding* the property (the debtor/convict), Section 244 targets the accomplice who fraudulently *receives or claims* the property to shield it from seizure. [Source: Section 244, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 244: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

Q: A bank forecloses on a house because the owner defaulted on the mortgage, right before the government tries to seize the same house for the owner's unpaid fines. Is the bank guilty under Section 244?
A: No, because the bank is enforcing a legitimate, pre-existing lien. They are not claiming the property "knowing that he has no right or rightful claim." [Source: Section 244, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 244: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing fraudulent claims by third parties?
A: The consequence is that it breaks down rings of complicity; friends, relatives, and shell companies cannot safely act as "straw owners" to protect a criminal's ill-gotten wealth from state seizure. [Source: Section 244, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent claim to property to prevent its seizure as forfeited or in execution

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 245: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

Q: What happens if you deliberately lose a fake lawsuit to protect your money from real creditors?
A: Fraudulently suffering a decree or judgment against yourself for a sum you do not owe, or allowing an already satisfied decree to be executed against you, is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 245, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 245: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

Q: How does Section 245 of BNS 2023 penalize fraudulent civil decrees?
A: Section 245 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 2 years imprisonment or a fine for fraudulently causing or suffering a decree to be passed against oneself for a sum not due, or suffering a decree to be executed after it has already been satisfied. [Source: Section 245, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 245: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

Q: A man is about to go bankrupt. He has his best friend sue him for a massive fake debt. The man deliberately doesn't defend himself and lets the judge order him to pay the friend, so his real creditors get nothing. What is his penalty?
A: Because he fraudulently suffered a judgment to pass against him for a sum not due to protect his assets from rightful creditors, he is punishable under Section 245 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 245, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 245: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

Q: Does this section apply if a person allows a court to execute an order to seize their property for a debt they already paid off in private?
A: Yes, it covers fraudulently suffering a decree to be executed "after it has been satisfied." [Source: Section 245, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 245: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

Q: A woman is sued for a debt she legitimately does not owe, but she simply cannot afford a lawyer and misses her court date, resulting in a default judgment against her. Is she guilty of fraudulently suffering a decree?
A: No, because she did not suffer the decree "fraudulently"; she suffered it due to poverty or negligence, lacking the specific corrupt intent to abuse the legal process. [Source: Section 245, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 245: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

Q: What is the consequence of this law on collusive lawsuits?
A: The consequence is that it prevents the civil court system from being weaponized by debtors who collude with fake creditors to legally launder their assets away from legitimate claimants. [Source: Section 245, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently suffering decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 246: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

Q: What is the penalty for filing a fake lawsuit or making a false claim in court?
A: Making a claim in court that you know to be false, done fraudulently, dishonestly, or with intent to injure/annoy, is punishable by up to two years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 246, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 246: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

Q: How does Section 246 of BNS 2023 penalize making false claims in court?
A: Section 246 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 2 years and a fine on whoever fraudulently, dishonestly, or with intent to injure/annoy any person, makes a claim in Court which they know to be false. [Source: Section 246, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 246: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

Q: A tenant is evicted legally. Out of spite, he files a lawsuit against the landlord claiming the landlord stole his furniture, fully knowing this is a lie. What is his offence?
A: Because he made a claim in Court which he knew to be false, with the intent to injure or annoy the landlord, he is punishable under Section 246 with imprisonment up to two years and a fine. [Source: Section 246, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 246: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

Q: What specific intent is required to convict someone under Section 246 for making a false claim?
A: The claim must be made "fraudulently or dishonestly, or with intent to injure or annoy any person." [Source: Section 246, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 246: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

Q: A woman genuinely believes her neighbor owes her money based on a misunderstood verbal agreement and sues him. The judge rules she is wrong. Is she guilty under Section 246?
A: No, because she did not make a claim "which he knows to be false"; she made an honest mistake of fact or law. [Source: Section 246, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 246: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

Q: What is the systemic consequence of this section on civil litigation?
A: The consequence is that it provides a criminal deterrent against frivolous, malicious, and vexatious litigation designed purely to harass individuals or clog the court system. [Source: Section 246, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly making false claim in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 247: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

Q: What is the punishment for tricking a court into ordering someone to pay you money they don't owe?
A: Fraudulently obtaining a court decree for a sum not due, or executing a decree after it has already been paid off, is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 247, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 247: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

Q: How does Section 247 of BNS 2023 treat fraudulently obtained court decrees?
A: Section 247 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 2 years imprisonment, or a fine, or both, for fraudulently obtaining a decree against any person for a sum not due, or executing a decree after it has been satisfied. [Source: Section 247, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 247: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

Q: A creditor wins a lawsuit against a debtor for 10,000 rupees. The debtor pays the creditor in cash. The creditor then fraudulently goes to court and demands the court execute the original decree to seize the debtor's assets, claiming he was never paid. What is the offence?
A: Because he fraudulently caused a decree to be executed against a person after it had been satisfied, he is punishable under Section 247 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 247, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 247: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

Q: Does this section apply if someone fraudulently allows another person to obtain a false decree in their name?
A: Yes, it covers whoever "fraudulently suffers or permits any such act to be done in his name." [Source: Section 247, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 247: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

Q: A landlord obtains an eviction decree against a tenant. The tenant pays the overdue rent, but the landlord still legally executes the eviction decree because the lease was terminated. Is the landlord guilty under Section 247?
A: No, because the decree was for eviction based on lease termination, not merely for a "sum not due" that was satisfied, and it was executed legally, not "fraudulently." [Source: Section 247, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 247: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing the execution of satisfied decrees?
A: The consequence is that it protects judgment debtors from double jeopardy in civil execution, ensuring creditors cannot abuse the coercive power of the state to double-dip on payments. [Source: Section 247, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulently obtaining decree for sum not due

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 248: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

Q: What happens if you frame someone for a crime or file a completely false police report to hurt them?
A: Instituting criminal proceedings or falsely charging someone with a crime to injure them, knowing there is no just ground, is punishable by up to 5 years in prison (or up to 10 years if the falsely charged crime was a capital/life offence). [Source: Section 248, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 248: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

Q: How does Section 248 of BNS 2023 punish making a false charge of an offence?
A: Section 248 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 5 years imprisonment and a 2 lakh rupee fine for falsely charging someone to cause injury; under clause (b), if the false charge is for an offence punishable with death/life/10+ years, the penalty increases to 10 years imprisonment and a fine. [Source: Section 248, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 248: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

Q: To get revenge on a business rival, a man falsely reports to the police that the rival committed murder (a capital offence), planting fake evidence. What is his penalty?
A: Because he instituted a criminal proceeding on a false charge of an offence punishable with death, knowing there was no just ground and intending to injure, he is punishable under clause (b) with imprisonment up to ten years and a fine. [Source: Section 248, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 248: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

Q: What two mental states are required for a conviction under Section 248 regarding a false charge?
A: The person must act "with intent to cause injury to any person" and must act "knowing that there is no just or lawful ground for such proceeding or charge." [Source: Section 248, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 248: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

Q: A woman truly believes she saw her neighbor stealing her car and reports him to the police. The police later catch the real thief, proving the neighbor innocent. Is the woman guilty?
A: No, because she did not know there was "no just or lawful ground"; she made a genuine mistake, lacking the intent to injure through a deliberately false charge. [Source: Section 248, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 248: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

Q: What is the consequence of scaling the punishment based on the severity of the false charge?
A: The consequence is that the law recognizes the varying degrees of trauma and legal jeopardy inflicted on victims of false accusations; falsely accusing someone of murder is treated much more severely than falsely accusing them of petty theft. [Source: Section 248, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: False charge of offence made with intent to injure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 249: Harbouring offender

Q: What is the penalty for hiding a criminal from the police?
A: Harbouring or concealing someone who you know committed a crime, to protect them from legal punishment, is punishable by up to 5 years in prison if their crime was capital, or up to 3 years if their crime was punishable by life. [Source: Section 249, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 249: Harbouring offender

Q: How does Section 249 of BNS 2023 penalize harbouring an offender?
A: Section 249 of BNS 2023 dictates that harbouring an offender to screen them from punishment yields up to 5 years imprisonment if the offence is capital, up to 3 years if punishable by life/10 years, and up to one-fourth the maximum term for lesser offences. [Source: Section 249, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 249: Harbouring offender

Q: A man knows his friend just committed an armed robbery (punishable by life imprisonment). He lets his friend hide in his basement for a week to avoid the police manhunt. What is the man's penalty?
A: Because he harboured a person he knew to be an offender liable to life imprisonment, with the intention of screening him, he is punishable under clause (b) with imprisonment up to three years and a fine. [Source: Section 249, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 249: Harbouring offender

Q: According to the Exception, who is immune from prosecution under Section 249 for harbouring an offender?
A: The section "shall not extend to any case in which the harbour or concealment is by the spouse of the offender." [Source: Section 249, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 249: Harbouring offender

Q: A hotel owner rents a room to a polite stranger. The stranger turns out to be a wanted serial killer. Is the hotel owner guilty of harbouring an offender?
A: No, because the hotel owner did not know or have reason to believe the person was an offender, and thus lacked the intention of screening him from legal punishment. [Source: Section 249, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 249: Harbouring offender

Q: What is the consequence of the spousal exception in this section?
A: The consequence is that the law acknowledges the powerful bonds of marriage, opting not to criminalize husbands or wives who succumb to the natural human instinct to shelter their spouses from state prosecution. [Source: Section 249, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 250: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

Q: What is the penalty for accepting a bribe to cover up a crime or not report a criminal?
A: Accepting a gift or property in exchange for concealing a crime or protecting an offender from legal punishment is punishable by up to seven years in prison if the crime was a capital offence. [Source: Section 250, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 250: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

Q: How does Section 250 of BNS 2023 penalize accepting gratification to screen an offender?
A: Section 250 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 7 years imprisonment (for capital offences), 3 years (for life/10-year offences), or one-fourth the maximum term (for lesser offences) on anyone who accepts gratification in consideration of concealing an offence or screening an offender. [Source: Section 250, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 250: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

Q: A witness sees a man commit a murder. The murderer offers the witness 10 lakh rupees to "forget what you saw" and never tell the police. The witness accepts the money. What is the witness's offence?
A: Because the witness accepted gratification in consideration of his not proceeding against a person for a capital offence, he is punishable under clause (a) with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 250, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 250: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

Q: Does this section require the person accepting the bribe to actually succeed in screening the offender from punishment?
A: No, the offence is complete upon accepting, attempting to obtain, or agreeing to accept the gratification "in consideration of" screening the offender, regardless of the ultimate success of the cover-up. [Source: Section 250, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 250: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

Q: A victim's family accepts a formal, court-approved financial settlement from the perpetrator in a compoundable offence case, thereby ending the criminal proceedings. Are they guilty under Section 250?
A: No, this is legal because Section 251 contains an Exception stating that Sections 250 and 251 do not extend to any case in which the offence may "lawfully be compounded." [Source: Section 250, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 250: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing the acceptance of hush money?
A: The consequence is that it severely punishes the commodification of justice, ensuring that criminals cannot simply buy the silence of witnesses or victims to escape state prosecution for serious crimes. [Source: Section 250, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift, etc., to screen an offender from punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 251: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

Q: What is the penalty for offering someone a bribe to hide a crime or protect a criminal?
A: Offering a gift or restoring property in exchange for concealing an offence or screening an offender from legal punishment is punishable by up to seven years in prison if the screened offence was capital. [Source: Section 251, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 251: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

Q: How does Section 251 of BNS 2023 treat offering gratification to screen an offender?
A: Section 251 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 7 years (for capital offences), 3 years (for life/10-year offences), or one-fourth the maximum term (for lesser offences) on whoever gives or offers gratification to screen an offender or conceal an offence. [Source: Section 251, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 251: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

Q: A hit-and-run driver offers a pedestrian 50,000 rupees not to tell the police what they saw. The pedestrian agrees. What is the driver's offence regarding the bribe?
A: Because the driver offered gratification in consideration of the pedestrian not proceeding against him to bring him to legal punishment, the driver is punishable under Section 251 based on the severity of the hit-and-run offence. [Source: Section 251, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 251: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

Q: Does this section only apply to offering money as a bribe?
A: No, it broadly covers whoever "gives or causes, or offers or agrees to give or cause, any gratification" or "restores or causes the restoration of any property." [Source: Section 251, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 251: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

Q: A shoplifter is caught by the store owner. The owner says, "Return the stolen watch, pay for it, and I won't call the police." The shoplifter agrees. Is the shoplifter guilty of offering a bribe to screen an offence?
A: Generally no, under the Exception, the provisions do not extend to any case in which the offence may "lawfully be compounded" (and minor theft is often compoundable with the owner's consent). [Source: Section 251, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 251: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing the offer of hush money?
A: The consequence is that it punishes the corruptor as severely as the corrupted, preventing wealthy criminals from using their financial power to buy immunity from victims or witnesses. [Source: Section 251, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Offering gift or restoration of property in consideration of screening offender

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 252: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

Q: What is the penalty for taking money to help find stolen goods without trying to catch the thief?
A: Taking a reward under the pretense of helping to recover stolen property is punishable by up to two years in prison unless you use all your power to ensure the thief is apprehended and convicted. [Source: Section 252, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 252: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

Q: How does Section 252 of BNS 2023 penalize taking a gift to recover stolen property?
A: Section 252 of BNS 2023 punishes anyone who takes gratification on account of helping recover stolen movable property with up to 2 years imprisonment, or a fine, unless they use all means in their power to cause the offender to be apprehended. [Source: Section 252, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 252: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

Q: A man's car is stolen. A local gang leader tells the man, "Give me 20,000 rupees and I'll get your car back." The gang leader takes the money, returns the car, but refuses to tell the police who stole it. What is his penalty?
A: Because he took gratification to recover stolen property but did not use all means in his power to cause the offender to be apprehended, he is punishable under Section 252 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 252, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 252: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

Q: What condition allows someone to legally take a reward for recovering stolen property?
A: They must use "all means in his power to cause the offender to be apprehended and convicted of the offence." [Source: Section 252, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 252: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

Q: A private investigator is hired to find stolen jewelry. The PI finds the jewels, identifies the thief, reports everything to the police, testifies in court, and then accepts their agreed-upon fee. Is the PI guilty?
A: No, because the PI used all means in their power to cause the offender to be apprehended and convicted, fulfilling the conditional requirement of the statute. [Source: Section 252, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 252: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

Q: What is the consequence of tying the recovery reward to the apprehension of the thief?
A: The consequence is that it prevents the creation of a lucrative "recovery extortion" black market where criminals steal property specifically to charge the owners a fee to get it back. [Source: Section 252, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Taking gift to help to recover stolen property, etc

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 253: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

Q: What is the penalty for hiding someone who broke out of jail or has an active arrest warrant?
A: Harbouring a person who has escaped lawful custody or has an active apprehension order is punishable by up to 7 years in prison if their underlying offence was capital. [Source: Section 253, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 253: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

Q: How does Section 253 of BNS 2023 penalize harbouring an escaped offender?
A: Section 253 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 7 years imprisonment (for capital offences), 3 years (for life/10-year offences), or one-fourth the maximum term (for lesser offences) for harbouring an escaped convict or a person ordered to be apprehended, intending to prevent their apprehension. [Source: Section 253, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 253: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

Q: A convicted murderer escapes from a high-security prison. His friend hears about the escape on the news and lets the murderer hide in his attic to evade the police. What is the friend's offence?
A: Because he harboured a person who escaped from lawful custody for a capital offence, intending to prevent his apprehension, he is punishable under clause (a) with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 253, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 253: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

Q: According to the Explanation, does this section apply if the escaped person committed their crime outside of India but is liable to be detained in India under extradition laws?
A: Yes, the term "offence" includes acts committed outside India if they would be punishable in India and the person is liable to be apprehended under extradition laws. [Source: Section 253, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 253: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

Q: A woman's husband escapes from jail and shows up at her doorstep. She lets him in and hides him from the police. Is she guilty under Section 253?
A: No, because the Exception explicitly states that the provisions do not extend to the case in which the harbour or concealment is "by the spouse of the person to be apprehended." [Source: Section 253, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 253: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

Q: What is the legal consequence of distinguishing between harboring a regular suspect (Section 249) and a known escapee (Section 253)?
A: The consequence is a comprehensive framework that specifically addresses the heightened defiance of the justice system involved in actively hiding someone who has already been formally ordered arrested or has physically broken out of state custody. [Source: Section 253, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Harbouring offender who has escaped from custody or whose apprehension has been

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 254: Penalty for harbouring robbers or dacoits

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 255: Public servant disobeying direction of law with intent to save person from punishment or

Q: What happens if a police officer or judge deliberately breaks the rules to let a criminal go free?
A: A public servant who knowingly disobeys a legal direction regarding their conduct, intending to save someone from punishment or protect property from forfeiture, is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 255, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying direction of law with intent to save person from punishment or

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 255: Public servant disobeying direction of law with intent to save person from punishment or

Q: How does Section 255 of BNS 2023 penalize corrupt public servants who protect offenders?
A: Section 255 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 2 years imprisonment or a fine for a public servant who knowingly disobeys any direction of the law as to how they should conduct themselves, intending to save a person from legal punishment or property from forfeiture. [Source: Section 255, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying direction of law with intent to save person from punishment or

content:

Q: A police inspector arrests a wealthy businessman's son for a hit-and-run. The inspector deliberately fails to file the First Information Report (FIR) as legally required, knowing this will result in the son avoiding trial. What is the inspector's offence?
A: Because he is a public servant who knowingly disobeyed a direction of law regarding his conduct, intending to save a person from legal punishment, he is punishable under Section 255 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 255, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant disobeying direction of law with intent to save person from punishment or

A: No, the offence is complete if the public servant disobeys the law "intending thereby to save, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby save" the person, regardless of the final outcome of the case. [Source: Section 255, BNS 2023]

A: No, because the clerk did not "knowingly" disobey the law with the "intent to save" the person from punishment; it was an honest mistake. [Source: Section 255, BNS 2023]

A: A public servant who prepares an official record incorrectly with the intent to save someone from punishment or protect property from forfeiture is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 256, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 257: Public servant in judicial proceeding corruptly making report, etc., contrary to law

Q: What is the penalty for a judge or magistrate who intentionally gives an illegal verdict?
A: A public servant in a judicial proceeding who corruptly or maliciously makes a report, verdict, or decision they know is contrary to law is punishable by up to seven years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 257, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant in judicial proceeding corruptly making report, etc., contrary to law

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 257: Public servant in judicial proceeding corruptly making report, etc., contrary to law

Q: How does Section 257 of BNS 2023 penalize corrupt judicial decisions?
A: Section 257 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment up to 7 years, or a fine, or both, for a public servant who corruptly or maliciously makes a report, order, or verdict in a judicial proceeding knowing it to be contrary to law. [Source: Section 257, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public servant in judicial proceeding corruptly making report, etc., contrary to law

A: Because the magistrate corruptly made a decision in a judicial proceeding which he knew to be contrary to law, he is punishable under Section 257 with imprisonment up to seven years or a fine. [Source: Section 257, BNS 2023]

content:

A: Generally no, it applies to public servants who have the authority to "make or pronounce... any report, order, verdict, or decision" in a judicial proceeding. [Source: Section 257, BNS 2023]

A: No, because the judge did not issue the verdict "corruptly or maliciously," nor did they "know" it was contrary to law at the time; judicial error is not the same as corrupt judicial misconduct. [Source: Section 257, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 259: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

Q: What happens if a police officer deliberately lets a criminal escape arrest?
A: A public servant legally bound to arrest someone who intentionally fails to do so, or intentionally lets them escape, is punishable by up to 7 years in prison if the criminal was facing capital charges. [Source: Section 259, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 259: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

Q: How does Section 259 of BNS 2023 penalize officials who let suspects escape?
A: Section 259 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 7 years imprisonment (if the suspect faced a capital offence), 3 years (for life/10-year offences), or 2 years (for lesser offences) for a public servant bound to apprehend someone who intentionally omits to do so or aids their escape. [Source: Section 259, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 259: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

Q: A police officer is sent to arrest a bank robber (an offence punishable by more than 10 years). The officer recognizes the robber as an old classmate and intentionally lets him slip out the back door. What is the officer's offence?
A: Because the officer intentionally omitted to apprehend a person liable to be apprehended for an offence punishable by ten years imprisonment, he is punishable under clause (b) with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 259, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 259: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

Q: What is the core characteristic of the public servant required to trigger Section 259?
A: The public servant must be "legally bound as such public servant to apprehend or to keep in confinement" the person. [Source: Section 259, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 259: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

Q: A lone, unarmed constable encounters five heavily armed terrorists. Outnumbered and outgunned, the constable retreats and the terrorists escape. Is the constable guilty of an intentional omission?
A: No, the constable's failure to apprehend was due to a lack of physical capability and self-preservation against overwhelming force, not an "intentional omission" to let them escape out of corrupt or malicious intent. [Source: Section 259, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 259: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

Q: What is the consequence of tying the public servant's punishment to the severity of the escapee's crime?
A: The consequence is that the justice system treats the dereliction of duty proportionally; letting a petty thief escape is a serious breach, but letting a murderer escape is treated as a major crisis warranting up to 7 years in prison. [Source: Section 259, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 260: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

Q: What is the penalty for a prison guard who deliberately lets a convicted criminal escape?
A: A public servant legally bound to keep a convicted person in confinement who intentionally lets them escape is punishable by up to 14 years in prison or life imprisonment if the escapee was on death row. [Source: Section 260, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 260: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

Q: How does Section 260 of BNS 2023 differ from Section 259 regarding escaped persons?
A: While Section 259 deals with suspects *charged* with offences, Section 260 deals with persons already *under sentence of a Court* or lawfully committed. It imposes harsher penalties: up to life imprisonment (if the escapee was under a death sentence), 7 years (for life/10-year sentences), or 3 years (for lesser sentences). [Source: Section 260, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 260: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

Q: A prison guard accepts a massive bribe to look the other way while a convicted serial killer (sentenced to death) climbs over the prison wall. What is the guard's penalty?
A: Because the guard intentionally suffered a person under sentence of death to escape from confinement, the guard is punishable under clause (a) with imprisonment for life or up to fourteen years. [Source: Section 260, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 260: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

Q: Does this section apply if the escapee was simply awaiting trial?
A: It applies if they are "under sentence of a Court" OR "lawfully committed to custody" (which covers pretrial detention), falling under clause (c) if no sentence has yet been passed. [Source: Section 260, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 260: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

Q: A violent riot breaks out in a prison. In the chaos, several inmates overwhelm the guards, break down the doors, and escape. Are the guards guilty under Section 260?
A: No, because the guards did not "intentionally" suffer the inmates to escape or aid them; the escape was forced upon them against their will. [Source: Section 260, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 260: Intentional omission to apprehend on part of public servant bound to apprehend person

Q: What is the consequence of the extreme penalties (up to life imprisonment) in clause (a)?
A: The consequence is that the state places the highest possible premium on executing its most severe sentences; a guard who releases a death-row inmate commits an act considered almost as severe as murder itself. [Source: Section 260, BNS 2023]
