content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 262: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

Q: What is the penalty for resisting arrest or trying to run away from the police?
A: Intentionally resisting your own lawful arrest or escaping from lawful custody is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine, in addition to the punishment for the original crime. [Source: Section 262, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 262: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

Q: How does Section 262 of BNS 2023 treat resisting one's own arrest?
A: Section 262 of BNS 2023 penalizes anyone who intentionally offers resistance/obstruction to their own lawful apprehension, or escapes custody, with imprisonment up to 2 years or a fine, in addition to the penalty for their original offence. [Source: Section 262, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 262: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

Q: A shoplifter is stopped by a police officer. When the officer tries to put handcuffs on him, the shoplifter shoves the officer and runs away. What new offence has he committed?
A: Because he intentionally offered resistance to his lawful apprehension and attempted to escape, he is punishable under Section 262 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 262, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 262: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

Q: Does the punishment for resisting arrest replace the punishment for the original crime?
A: No, the Explanation clarifies that "The punishment in this section is in addition to the punishment for which the person... was liable for the offence with which he was charged." [Source: Section 262, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 262: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

Q: A man is attacked by thugs pretending to be police officers. Believing they are kidnappers, he fights back and runs away. The "officers" were actually plainclothes cops with no ID. Is he guilty under Section 262?
A: No, because he did not "intentionally" resist a "lawful apprehension"; he lacked the mens rea as he reasonably believed he was defending himself against an unlawful attack. [Source: Section 262, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 262: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

Q: What is the consequence of explicitly adding this punishment to the original crime's sentence?
A: The consequence is a strong deterrent against fleeing or fighting the police; criminals know that resisting arrest will only objectively worsen their final prison sentence regardless of the underlying charge. [Source: Section 262, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction by a person to his lawful apprehension

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 263: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

Q: What happens if you try to stop the police from arresting someone else or help them escape?
A: Resisting the lawful arrest of another person or rescuing them from custody is punishable by 2 to 7 years in prison, or even life imprisonment if the person being rescued was on death row. [Source: Section 263, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 263: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

Q: How does Section 263 of BNS 2023 penalize resisting the arrest of another?
A: Section 263 of BNS 2023 imposes tiered punishments for resisting another's apprehension or rescuing them: up to 2 years for minor offences, 3 years for 10-year offences, 7 years for capital/life offences, and up to life imprisonment if rescuing a death-row inmate. [Source: Section 263, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 263: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

Q: Police are arresting a suspected terrorist (a capital offence). A sympathizer drives a truck into the police barricade to rescue the suspect, allowing him to flee. What is the sympathizer's penalty?
A: Because he rescued a person liable to be apprehended for an offence punishable with death, he is punishable under clause (c) with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 263, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 263: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

Q: How does the punishment scale under Section 263?
A: The punishment scales directly with the severity of the offence committed by the person being rescued (from 2 years for minor offences up to life imprisonment for rescuing someone sentenced to death). [Source: Section 263, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 263: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

Q: A crowd witnesses plainclothes officers dragging a woman into an unmarked van without identifying themselves. The crowd, genuinely believing it is a kidnapping, physically stops the van. Are they guilty?
A: No, because they did not know it was a "lawful apprehension"; lacking that knowledge, they did not have the specific intent to illegally obstruct justice. [Source: Section 263, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 263: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

Q: What is the legal consequence of distinguishing the rescue of another from resisting one's own arrest?
A: The consequence is that the state treats third-party interference as a distinct and highly dangerous assault on public order, severely punishing accomplices and mobs who try to physically override the justice system. [Source: Section 263, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension of another person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 264: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

Q: What is the penalty for a public servant letting someone escape in situations not covered by other specific laws?
A: A public servant legally bound to apprehend someone who lets them escape, in cases not covered by sections 259-261, faces up to three years in prison if done intentionally, or two years if done negligently. [Source: Section 264, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 264: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

Q: How does Section 264 of BNS 2023 act as a catch-all for public servants permitting escape?
A: Section 264 of BNS 2023 covers cases not provided for in Sections 259-261, punishing public servants who omit to apprehend or suffer escape with up to 3 years imprisonment (if intentional) or up to 2 years simple imprisonment (if negligent). [Source: Section 264, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 264: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

Q: A bailiff is ordered by a family court judge to briefly detain a man for contempt of court (a civil/minor matter not explicitly covered under the major criminal escape sections). The bailiff accepts a bribe and intentionally lets the man walk out. What is the penalty?
A: Because he is a public servant legally bound to keep a person in confinement and intentionally suffered him to escape in a case not otherwise provided for, he is punishable under clause (a) with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 264, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 264: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

Q: What distinguishes the punishment under clause (a) and clause (b) in this section?
A: Clause (a) covers "intentionally" suffering escape (punishable by up to 3 years of either description), while clause (b) covers "negligently" doing so (punishable by up to 2 years of simple imprisonment). [Source: Section 264, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 264: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

Q: A health inspector is legally authorized to quarantine individuals but one individual sneaks out of the facility at night despite reasonable security measures. Is the inspector guilty?
A: No, if the inspector exercised reasonable care, they did not act "negligently" or "intentionally," so they are not criminally liable under Section 264. [Source: Section 264, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 264: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

Q: What is the consequence of having this "catch-all" provision?
A: The consequence is that it closes legal loopholes, ensuring that public servants cannot escape liability for dereliction of duty simply because the specific type of confinement or apprehension order doesn't perfectly match the major criminal statutes. [Source: Section 264, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Omission to apprehend, or sufferance of escape, on part of public servant, in cases not

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 265: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

Q: What is the penalty for resisting arrest or escaping in minor situations not covered by the main escape laws?
A: Resisting lawful apprehension, escaping, or rescuing someone in cases not specifically covered by other laws is a minor offence punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 265, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 265: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

Q: How does Section 265 of BNS 2023 function regarding resistance to apprehension?
A: Section 265 of BNS 2023 serves as a residuary clause for cases not provided for in Sections 262/263, prescribing up to 6 months imprisonment or a fine for intentionally resisting apprehension, escaping, or rescuing another person from lawful custody. [Source: Section 265, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 265: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

Q: A person is lawfully detained by a magistrate under a special local regulation (not a standard criminal charge). While the paperwork is being processed, the person shoves the guard and runs out of the building. What is the penalty?
A: Because he escaped from custody in a case not provided for in section 262 or 263, he is punishable under the catch-all Section 265 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 265, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 265: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

Q: How does the scope of Section 265 compare to Sections 262 and 263?
A: Sections 262 and 263 deal with resistance and escape regarding criminal "offences," whereas Section 265 broadly covers "any case not provided for," encompassing civil detainments, preventive custody, or other lawful non-criminal apprehensions. [Source: Section 265, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 265: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

Q: A person is illegally detained by a private security guard without any lawful authority. The person forcibly breaks free. Are they guilty under Section 265?
A: No, because the custody was not "lawful," and the right to private defense allows resisting unlawful detention. [Source: Section 265, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 265: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

Q: What is the consequence of limiting the punishment to six months in this residuary section?
A: The consequence is a proportionate legal response; because the underlying detentions covered here are generally civil or minor regulatory matters rather than serious crimes, the penalty for escaping them is correspondingly light. [Source: Section 265, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Resistance or obstruction to lawful apprehension or escape or rescue in cases not otherwise

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 266: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

Q: What happens if a prisoner violates the conditions of their early release or parole?
A: If someone knowingly violates a condition of their remitted punishment, they must serve the remainder of their original sentence. [Source: Section 266, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 266: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

Q: How does Section 266 of BNS 2023 treat the violation of remission conditions?
A: Section 266 of BNS 2023 dictates that whoever knowingly violates any condition of their conditionally remitted punishment shall be punished with the original sentence, or whatever portion of it they have not yet suffered. [Source: Section 266, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 266: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

Q: A convict is granted early release on the condition that he does not leave the state. Two months later, he knowingly moves to a neighboring state. What is the penalty?
A: Because he knowingly violated the condition on which remission was granted, he is punishable under Section 266 by having to serve the remaining portion of his original sentence. [Source: Section 266, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 266: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

Q: Does this section impose any new prison time beyond the original sentence?
A: No, the punishment is strictly limited to "the punishment to which he was originally sentenced" or "so much of that punishment as he has not already suffered." [Source: Section 266, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 266: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

Q: A parolee is ordered not to associate with known felons. While taking the bus to work, a known felon sits next to him and starts talking. Is the parolee guilty of violating remission?
A: No, because he did not "knowingly" or voluntarily violate the condition; the interaction was forced upon him without intent. [Source: Section 266, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 266: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

Q: What is the consequence of tying the penalty directly to the unserved portion of the original sentence?
A: The consequence is that early release is treated as a conditional privilege, not an absolute right; breaking trust immediately reactivates the original legal debt owed to society without requiring a whole new trial. [Source: Section 266, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Violation of condition of remission of punishment

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 267: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

Q: What is the penalty for insulting a judge or causing a scene in a courtroom?
A: Intentionally insulting a public servant or interrupting them while they are conducting a judicial proceeding is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 267, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 267: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

Q: How does Section 267 of BNS 2023 penalize contemptuous behavior in court?
A: Section 267 of BNS 2023 imposes simple imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on anyone who intentionally insults or interrupts a public servant sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding. [Source: Section 267, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 267: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

Q: During a heated trial, a spectator starts screaming obscenities at the judge because they disagree with a ruling, forcing the trial to pause. What is the spectator's offence?
A: Because the spectator intentionally offered an insult and caused interruption to a public servant sitting in a judicial proceeding, he is punishable under Section 267 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 267, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 267: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

Q: Does the public servant have to be a formal judge in a traditional courtroom for this section to apply?
A: No, the section broadly covers any "public servant" while they are "sitting in any stage of a judicial proceeding." [Source: Section 267, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 267: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

Q: A witness has a severe coughing fit during testimony, forcing the judge to pause the proceedings for ten minutes. Is the witness guilty of an interruption?
A: No, because the interruption was not caused "intentionally"; it was an involuntary physical reaction. [Source: Section 267, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 267: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

Q: What is the systemic consequence of this section regarding courtroom decorum?
A: The consequence is that it arms judges and magistrates with direct statutory power to immediately penalize disruptive behavior, ensuring that the dignity and orderly function of the courts are preserved. [Source: Section 267, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult or interruption to public servant sitting in judicial proceeding

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 268: Personation of assessor

Q: What happens if you pretend to be someone else to serve on a jury or as a legal assessor?
A: Intentionally pretending to be someone else to be empaneled as an assessor, or serving as one when you know you are legally ineligible, is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 268, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation of assessor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 268: Personation of assessor

Q: How does Section 268 of BNS 2023 penalize the personation of an assessor?
A: Section 268 of BNS 2023 prescribes imprisonment up to 2 years, or a fine, or both, for anyone who by personation intentionally causes themselves to be empaneled/sworn as an assessor, or serves knowing they are legally disqualified. [Source: Section 268, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation of assessor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 268: Personation of assessor

Q: A man receives a summons for his brother to serve as an assessor in a trial. The man decides to go in his brother's place and swears the oath under his brother's name. What is his offence?
A: Because he intentionally caused himself to be empaneled and sworn as an assessor by personation, knowing he was not entitled to be returned, he is punishable under Section 268 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 268, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation of assessor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 268: Personation of assessor

Q: Can someone be convicted under this section without pretending to be someone else?
A: Yes, if they do not impersonate anyone but still "voluntarily serve as such assessor" "knowing himself to have been so returned, empanelled or sworn contrary to law." [Source: Section 268, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation of assessor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 268: Personation of assessor

Q: A citizen is empaneled as an assessor. They are legally disqualified due to a minor, obscure property-ownership clause they genuinely did not know about. Are they guilty under Section 268?
A: No, because they did not serve "knowing" that they were returned or sworn contrary to law; it was an innocent mistake of legal eligibility. [Source: Section 268, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation of assessor

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 268: Personation of assessor

Q: What is the consequence of strictly punishing the fraudulent empanelment of assessors?
A: The consequence is that it protects the fundamental fairness of the trial process, preventing compromised or unauthorized individuals from infiltrating the bodies that help determine guilt or innocence. [Source: Section 268, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Personation of assessor

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 269: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

Q: What is the penalty for jumping bail or failing to show up to court?
A: Failing to appear in court after being released on a bail bond, without a sufficient excuse, is a separate crime punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine, in addition to forfeiting the bond. [Source: Section 269, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 269: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

Q: How does Section 269 of BNS 2023 penalize the failure to appear on bail?
A: Section 269 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 1 year, or a fine, or both, on anyone released on bail who fails to appear in Court without sufficient cause (the burden of proof lying on the accused). [Source: Section 269, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 269: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

Q: A defendant is released on bail while awaiting trial for theft. On the day of the trial, he decides to go to the beach instead of showing up to court. What is his new penalty?
A: Because he failed to appear in Court in accordance with his bail bond without sufficient cause, he is punishable under Section 269 with imprisonment up to one year or a fine. [Source: Section 269, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 269: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

Q: In a prosecution under Section 269, who has the burden of proving why the accused missed their court date?
A: The burden of proving "sufficient cause" lies strictly upon the accused person who failed to appear. [Source: Section 269, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 269: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

Q: A defendant is released on bail. On the morning of his trial, he is involved in a severe car crash and is rushed to the hospital in a coma. Is he guilty of jumping bail?
A: No, because the severe accident and hospitalization constitute "sufficient cause" for failing to appear, overcoming the burden of proof. [Source: Section 269, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 269: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

Q: What is the legal consequence of making "jumping bail" an independent criminal offence?
A: The consequence is that it allows the state to punish absconders directly, ensuring that defendants face actual jail time for defying court orders, rather than just losing their financial bail deposit. [Source: Section 269, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Failure by person released on bail bond or bond to appear in Court

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 270: Public nuisance

Q: What constitutes a "public nuisance" under the law?
A: A public nuisance is an act or illegal omission that causes common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public or neighbors, or obstructs people using public rights, and it is not excused just because it provides some convenience. [Source: Section 270, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 270: Public nuisance

Q: How does Section 270 of BNS 2023 define a public nuisance?
A: Section 270 of BNS 2023 defines a public nuisance as an act/illegal omission causing common injury, danger, or annoyance to the public, neighborhood dwellers, or persons exercising a public right. [Source: Section 270, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 270: Public nuisance

Q: A factory owner decides to dump toxic, foul-smelling chemical waste directly into a public street drainage ditch every night. The fumes make the entire neighborhood sick and prevent people from walking on the street. What is this act defined as?
A: Because the act causes common injury, danger, and annoyance to the public and neighborhood dwellers, the factory owner is guilty of a public nuisance under Section 270. [Source: Section 270, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 270: Public nuisance

Q: If a factory creates a terrible stench that ruins a neighborhood's air quality, but the factory owner argues that it employs 500 locals and is good for the economy, is the nuisance excused?
A: No, the section explicitly states that "a common nuisance is not excused on the ground that it causes some convenience or advantage." [Source: Section 270, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 270: Public nuisance

Q: A homeowner plays their stereo loudly at 2:00 PM for ten minutes while cleaning their house. Their direct next-door neighbor finds it slightly annoying, but no one else hears it. Is this a public nuisance?
A: No, this is likely a private nuisance; it does not cause "common" annoyance to the "public or to the people in general who dwell or occupy property in the vicinity." [Source: Section 270, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public nuisance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 270: Public nuisance

Q: What is the legal consequence of codifying the definition of a public nuisance?
A: The consequence is that it provides a broad, flexible tool for law enforcement to protect the general welfare, safety, and comfort of communities against antisocial behavior, pollution, or hazardous activities that affect the public at large. [Source: Section 270, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Public nuisance

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 271: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: What is the penalty for carelessly spreading a deadly disease?
A: Negligently or unlawfully doing an act that you know or have reason to believe will likely spread a life-threatening disease is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 271, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 271: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: How does Section 271 of BNS 2023 penalize the negligent spread of disease?
A: Section 271 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine, or both, on whoever unlawfully or negligently does an act they know/believe is likely to spread the infection of a disease dangerous to life. [Source: Section 271, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 271: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: During an outbreak of a deadly virus, a man who knows he is infected sneezes openly on public transport without wearing a mask, negligently disregarding health guidelines. What is his penalty?
A: Because he negligently did an act which he knew was likely to spread the infection of a disease dangerous to life, he is punishable under Section 271 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 271, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 271: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: What level of intent or knowledge is required for a conviction under Section 271?
A: The person must act "unlawfully or negligently" and must "know or have reason to believe" that the act is likely to spread the disease. [Source: Section 271, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 271: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: A nurse unknowingly contracts a deadly disease and, feeling perfectly healthy, goes to work and accidentally infects patients. Is the nurse guilty under Section 271?
A: No, because the nurse did not "know or have reason to believe" they were infected and likely to spread the disease, meaning the act was not done with the requisite negligent state of mind. [Source: Section 271, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 271: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: What is the systemic consequence of this public health section?
A: The consequence is that it imposes a basic civic duty of care regarding infectious diseases, criminalizing reckless behavior during public health crises to protect the broader population. [Source: Section 271, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 272: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: What is the penalty for deliberately trying to infect people with a deadly disease?
A: Malignantly doing an act that you know is likely to spread a life-threatening disease is a severe offence punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 272, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 272: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: How does Section 272 of BNS 2023 differ from Section 271 regarding the spread of disease?
A: While Section 271 covers "negligent" acts (punishable by up to 6 months), Section 272 covers acts done "malignantly" (with evil intent), increasing the punishment to up to 2 years imprisonment, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 272, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 272: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: A person diagnosed with a deadly, highly contagious virus becomes bitter. He deliberately goes to crowded events and coughs on people's food to make them suffer like he is. What is his offence?
A: Because he malignantly did an act which he knew was likely to spread a disease dangerous to life, he is punishable under Section 272 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 272, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 272: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: What specific mental state elevates an act under this section compared to Section 271?
A: The act must be done "malignantly," meaning with a deliberate, wicked intent to cause harm by spreading the infection. [Source: Section 272, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 272: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: A doctor performing a high-risk surgery on an infected patient accidentally drops a scalpel, which slightly exposes a colleague. The doctor did not act malignantly. Is the doctor guilty under Section 272?
A: No, because there was no malignant intent; at worst it was negligence, and if it was a pure unavoidable accident, no offence was committed at all. [Source: Section 272, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 272: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

Q: What is the consequence of establishing a higher tier of punishment for malignant transmission?
A: The consequence is that the law distinguishes between mere foolishness (negligence) and biological malice (weaponizing one's own infection), allowing prosecutors to seek harsher penalties for those who intentionally endanger public health. [Source: Section 272, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Malignant act likely to spread infection of disease dangerous to life

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 273: Disobedience to quarantine rule

Q: What is the penalty for breaking government quarantine rules during an outbreak?
A: Knowingly disobeying a government rule regarding quarantine (such as for ships, planes, or infected places) is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 273, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to quarantine rule

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 273: Disobedience to quarantine rule

Q: How does Section 273 of BNS 2023 enforce quarantine rules?
A: Section 273 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine, or both, on whoever knowingly disobeys government rules for putting transport into quarantine or regulating intercourse between infected and uninfected places. [Source: Section 273, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to quarantine rule

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 273: Disobedience to quarantine rule

Q: The government issues a mandatory quarantine for all trains arriving from a city with an outbreak. A passenger on the train knowingly sneaks out of the quarantined train station to go home. What is his offence?
A: Because he knowingly disobeyed a government rule for regulating intercourse with a transport in a state of quarantine, he is punishable under Section 273 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 273, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to quarantine rule

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 273: Disobedience to quarantine rule

Q: What specific condition must the rule meet to be enforceable under this section?
A: It must be a rule "made by the Government" regarding the quarantine of transport or regulating intercourse involving places where an infectious disease prevails. [Source: Section 273, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to quarantine rule

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 273: Disobedience to quarantine rule

Q: A sailor disembarks from a ship at a port before the government issues the official quarantine order for that vessel. Is the sailor guilty of breaking quarantine?
A: No, because the rule must exist and be "knowingly" disobeyed at the time of the act; he cannot disobey a rule that hasn't been made yet. [Source: Section 273, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to quarantine rule

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 273: Disobedience to quarantine rule

Q: What is the consequence of this section on state public health powers?
A: The consequence is that it gives teeth to government emergency orders, ensuring that the state has the legal authority to physically isolate infections and criminally prosecute those who breach those isolation zones. [Source: Section 273, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Disobedience to quarantine rule

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 274: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

Q: What happens if a person tampers with food or drinks to make them harmful before selling them?
A: Adulterating food or drink to make it noxious, with the intent to sell it, is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 274, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 274: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

Q: How does Section 274 of BNS 2023 penalize the adulteration of food?
A: Section 274 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever adulterates food/drink to make it noxious, intending or knowing it is likely to be sold. [Source: Section 274, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 274: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

Q: A dairy farmer mixes contaminated river water into his milk supply to increase the volume, making the milk likely to cause food poisoning, and ships it to a local market to be sold. What is his offence?
A: Because he adulterated an article of drink to make it noxious, intending to sell it, he is punishable under Section 274 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 274, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 274: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

Q: Does this section require the adulterated food to actually be sold to secure a conviction?
A: No, the offence is complete upon the act of adulteration itself, provided there is an "intent to sell" or knowledge that it is "likely... to be sold." [Source: Section 274, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 274: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

Q: A chef accidentally undercooks chicken at a private dinner party, causing the guests to get sick. The food was not for sale. Is the chef guilty under Section 274?
A: No, because the chef did not deliberately "adulterate" the food to make it noxious, and there was no "intent to sell" it, as it was a private gathering. [Source: Section 274, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 274: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

Q: What is the public consequence of this specific adulteration law?
A: The consequence is that it protects consumer safety at the source of production, deterring greedy manufacturers from cutting corners with harmful additives before the products ever reach store shelves. [Source: Section 274, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of food or drink intended for sale

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 275: Sale of noxious food or drink

Q: What is the penalty for knowingly selling rotten or harmful food to the public?
A: Selling or offering to sell food or drinks that you know are noxious or unfit for consumption is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 275, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of noxious food or drink

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 275: Sale of noxious food or drink

Q: How does Section 275 of BNS 2023 deal with the sale of noxious food?
A: Section 275 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on anyone who sells or offers for sale food/drink knowing or having reason to believe it is noxious or unfit. [Source: Section 275, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of noxious food or drink

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 275: Sale of noxious food or drink

Q: A butcher's refrigerator breaks, and his meat spoils. Instead of throwing it away, he knowingly sprays it with a chemical to hide the smell and puts it in the display case for customers to buy. What is his offence?
A: Because he exposed for sale an article of food knowing it was in a state unfit for food, he is punishable under Section 275 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 275, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of noxious food or drink

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 275: Sale of noxious food or drink

Q: Is actual sale required, or is merely displaying the bad food enough for an offence?
A: Displaying it is enough; the section covers whoever "sells, or offers or exposes for sale" the noxious item. [Source: Section 275, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of noxious food or drink

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 275: Sale of noxious food or drink

Q: A grocery store clerk sells canned goods that are secretly contaminated with botulism from the factory. The cans look perfectly normal and are unexpired. Is the clerk guilty?
A: No, because the clerk did not "know or have reason to believe" that the food inside the sealed cans was noxious or unfit. [Source: Section 275, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of noxious food or drink

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 275: Sale of noxious food or drink

Q: What is the legal consequence of separating adulteration (Section 274) from sale (Section 275)?
A: The consequence is a comprehensive regulatory net: Section 274 catches the corrupt manufacturer who taints the food, while Section 275 catches the corrupt retailer who knowingly passes that tainted food onto the consumer. [Source: Section 275, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of noxious food or drink

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 276: Adulteration of drugs

Q: What is the penalty for tampering with medicine to make it less effective or harmful?
A: Adulterating a drug or medical preparation to lessen its efficacy, change how it works, or make it noxious, with the intent to sell it as unadulterated, is punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 276, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 276: Adulteration of drugs

Q: How does Section 276 of BNS 2023 penalize the adulteration of drugs?
A: Section 276 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 1 year, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever adulterates a drug to lessen its efficacy/make it noxious, intending/knowing it will likely be sold or used as if it were unadulterated. [Source: Section 276, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 276: Adulteration of drugs

Q: A pharmaceutical manufacturer secretly dilutes a life-saving antibiotic with chalk powder to double his profits, knowing it will be sold to hospitals as the full-strength drug. What is his offence?
A: Because he adulterated a medical preparation to lessen its efficacy, intending it to be sold for medicinal purposes as if it had not undergone adulteration, he is punishable under Section 276 with imprisonment up to one year or a fine. [Source: Section 276, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 276: Adulteration of drugs

Q: What specific effects must the adulteration have on the drug to trigger this section?
A: The adulteration must be done in a manner that lessens the efficacy, changes the operation, or makes the drug or medical preparation noxious. [Source: Section 276, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 276: Adulteration of drugs

Q: A pharmacist accidentally spills a tiny amount of sterile water into a jar of ointment, which technically adulterates it but has zero effect on its medical efficacy or safety. Is the pharmacist guilty under Section 276?
A: No, because the adulteration did not "lessen the efficacy or change the operation" of the drug, nor make it noxious, and lacked criminal intent. [Source: Section 276, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 276: Adulteration of drugs

Q: What is the consequence of focusing specifically on the "efficacy" of drugs?
A: The consequence is that the law recognizes that making a medicine weaker (even if not overtly toxic) is a severe threat to public health, as patients relying on the drug will not receive the necessary treatment. [Source: Section 276, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Adulteration of drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 277: Sale of adulterated drugs

Q: What happens if a person knowingly sells tampered or weakened medicine?
A: Selling, offering for sale, or issuing tampered drugs from a dispensary, knowing they have been adulterated to lessen their efficacy or make them harmful, is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 277, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of adulterated drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 277: Sale of adulterated drugs

Q: How does Section 277 of BNS 2023 deal with the sale of adulterated medical preparations?
A: Section 277 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on anyone who knowingly sells, exposes for sale, or issues for medicinal use an adulterated drug as if it were unadulterated. [Source: Section 277, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of adulterated drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 277: Sale of adulterated drugs

Q: A hospital pharmacist discovers that a batch of painkillers has been severely diluted by the supplier. Instead of reporting it, he knowingly dispenses them to patients as full-strength painkillers to avoid losing money. What is his offence?
A: Because he issued a drug from a dispensary for medicinal purposes as unadulterated, knowing its efficacy had been lessened, he is punishable under Section 277 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 277, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of adulterated drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 277: Sale of adulterated drugs

Q: Can a person be convicted under Section 277 if they didn't sell the drug, but just administered it?
A: Yes, the section covers whoever "causes it to be used for medicinal purposes by any person not knowing of the adulteration." [Source: Section 277, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of adulterated drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 277: Sale of adulterated drugs

Q: A cashier at a pharmacy sells a box of cough syrup. Unbeknownst to her, the manufacturer had diluted the syrup before shipping it. Is the cashier guilty?
A: No, because she did not "know" the drug had been adulterated; lacking knowledge, she lacks the mens rea for the offence. [Source: Section 277, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of adulterated drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 277: Sale of adulterated drugs

Q: What is the legal consequence of distinguishing between adulterating drugs and selling them?
A: The consequence is that the legal system can separately prosecute the corrupt manufacturers who taint the drugs (Section 276) and the corrupt distributors/medical professionals who knowingly administer them to vulnerable patients (Section 277). [Source: Section 277, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of adulterated drugs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 278: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

Q: What is the penalty for selling one medicine by pretending it is a completely different medicine?
A: Knowingly selling or dispensing a drug or medical preparation under the guise of it being a different drug is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 278, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 278: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

Q: How does Section 278 of BNS 2023 penalize the misrepresentation of drugs?
A: Section 278 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever knowingly sells, exposes for sale, or issues from a dispensary any drug as a different drug or medical preparation. [Source: Section 278, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 278: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

Q: A pharmacy runs out of an expensive heart medication. To keep making money, the pharmacist knowingly puts cheap vitamin pills into the heart medication bottles and sells them to patients. What is his offence?
A: Because he knowingly sold a medical preparation as a different drug, he is punishable under Section 278 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 278, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 278: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

Q: Does the substituted drug have to be harmful for a conviction under this section?
A: No, the offence is simply selling or issuing a drug "as a different drug." The danger lies in the deception and the patient not receiving the actual medication they need, regardless of whether the substitute itself is directly toxic. [Source: Section 278, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 278: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

Q: A doctor prescribes generic Ibuprofen. The pharmacist legally fills the prescription with generic Ibuprofen, but the patient thought they were getting a specific brand name. Is the pharmacist guilty under Section 278?
A: No, as long as the generic drug is pharmacologically the same preparation prescribed and legally substituted, the pharmacist did not knowingly sell a "different drug" in the deceptive sense intended by this section. [Source: Section 278, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 278: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

Q: What is the public health consequence of enforcing this section?
A: The consequence is that it ensures strict integrity in the medical supply chain, preventing quackery and deadly substitutions where patients are tricked into taking the wrong pharmacological substances. [Source: Section 278, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale of drug as a different drug or preparation

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 279: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

Q: What is the penalty for polluting a public water source?
A: Voluntarily corrupting or fouling the water of a public spring or reservoir so that it becomes less fit for its ordinary use is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 279, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 279: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

Q: How does Section 279 of BNS 2023 protect public water sources?
A: Section 279 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever voluntarily fouls the water of any public spring/reservoir, rendering it less fit for its ordinary purpose. [Source: Section 279, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 279: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

Q: A local business owner decides to save on waste disposal costs by secretly dumping his chemical run-off into the town's primary drinking water reservoir, making the water unsafe to drink. What is his offence?
A: Because he voluntarily corrupted the water of a public reservoir, rendering it less fit for its ordinary purpose, he is punishable under Section 279 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 279, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 279: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

Q: Under Section 279, does the water have to become completely toxic or lethal to trigger the offence?
A: No, it only needs to be rendered "less fit for the purpose for which it is ordinarily used." [Source: Section 279, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 279: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

Q: A hiker is walking near a public spring. He trips, falls in the mud, and accidentally knocks a small clump of dirt into the spring. Is he guilty of fouling the water?
A: No, because he did not "voluntarily" corrupt or foul the water; it was an accident. [Source: Section 279, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 279: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

Q: What is the legal consequence of applying this specific standard to public water?
A: The consequence is that the state aggressively protects communal water security, ensuring that any deliberate degradation of a shared vital resource is treated as a criminal act against the public welfare. [Source: Section 279, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fouling water of public spring or reservoir

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 280: Making atmosphere noxious to health

Q: What is the penalty for polluting the air and making it harmful to breathe?
A: Voluntarily polluting the atmosphere in a way that makes it noxious to the health of people living or doing business nearby, or passing on a public road, is punishable by a fine up to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 280, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making atmosphere noxious to health

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 280: Making atmosphere noxious to health

Q: How does Section 280 of BNS 2023 address air pollution?
A: Section 280 of BNS 2023 penalizes whoever voluntarily vitiates the atmosphere, making it noxious to the health of persons in the neighborhood or on a public way, with a fine that may extend to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 280, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making atmosphere noxious to health

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 280: Making atmosphere noxious to health

Q: A man decides to burn a massive pile of old tires and plastic in his backyard right next to a busy public street. The toxic black smoke billows over the road and into his neighbors' windows, making people cough and choke. What is his offence?
A: Because he voluntarily vitiated the atmosphere, making it noxious to the health of persons dwelling in the neighborhood and passing along a public way, he is punishable under Section 280 with a fine up to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 280, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making atmosphere noxious to health

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 280: Making atmosphere noxious to health

Q: What is the maximum statutory penalty for this offence under Section 280?
A: The maximum penalty is strictly a fine which may extend to one thousand rupees (there is no provision for imprisonment in this specific section). [Source: Section 280, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making atmosphere noxious to health

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 280: Making atmosphere noxious to health

Q: A municipality is conducting controlled, legally permitted burning of agricultural waste miles away from the city. A sudden, unexpected freak wind blows some smoke toward a highway for a few minutes. Are they guilty under Section 280?
A: No, because the pollution of that specific public way was not done "voluntarily"; the act was legally permitted and the wind shift was an act of nature. [Source: Section 280, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making atmosphere noxious to health

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 280: Making atmosphere noxious to health

Q: What is the consequence of having a relatively low penalty (a fine) for this specific air pollution offence?
A: The consequence is that while this section serves as a basic deterrent against localized, acute nuisances (like burning trash), major industrial or systemic environmental crimes are generally prosecuted under dedicated, more severe modern environmental protection statutes rather than this general penal code provision. [Source: Section 280, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making atmosphere noxious to health

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 281: Rash driving or riding on a public way

Q: What is the penalty for reckless driving on a public road?
A: Driving or riding any vehicle on a public way in a rash or negligent manner that endangers human life or is likely to cause injury is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 281, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash driving or riding on a public way

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 281: Rash driving or riding on a public way

Q: How does Section 281 of BNS 2023 penalize rash driving?
A: Section 281 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 1,000 rupees, or both, on whoever drives/rides on a public way in a rash or negligent manner that endangers human life or is likely to cause hurt/injury. [Source: Section 281, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash driving or riding on a public way

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 281: Rash driving or riding on a public way

Q: A teenager is speeding at 100 mph down a crowded residential street just for the thrill of it, swerving between pedestrians. Fortunately, no one is hit. What is his offence?
A: Because he drove a vehicle on a public way in a manner so rash as to endanger human life, even though no one was actually hurt, he is punishable under Section 281 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 281, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash driving or riding on a public way

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 281: Rash driving or riding on a public way

Q: Does this section require an actual accident or injury to occur for a conviction?
A: No, the offence is complete if the driving is so rash or negligent as "to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury"; actual harm is not required. [Source: Section 281, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash driving or riding on a public way

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 281: Rash driving or riding on a public way

Q: A man suffers a sudden, unprecedented heart attack while driving at the speed limit, causing his car to swerve wildly onto the sidewalk. Is he guilty of rash driving?
A: No, because the swerving was not caused by a "rash or negligent" voluntary act; it was an unforeseeable medical emergency. [Source: Section 281, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash driving or riding on a public way

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 281: Rash driving or riding on a public way

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing the "likelihood" of causing hurt in this section?
A: The consequence is a proactive legal tool for police to stop and penalize dangerous drivers before they actually kill or maim someone, establishing a baseline standard of care for operating vehicles on public roads. [Source: Section 281, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash driving or riding on a public way

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 282: Rash navigation of vessel

Q: What is the penalty for driving a boat recklessly?
A: Navigating any vessel in a rash or negligent manner that endangers human life or is likely to cause injury is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 10,000 rupees. [Source: Section 282, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash navigation of vessel

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 282: Rash navigation of vessel

Q: How does Section 282 of BNS 2023 apply the concept of rash driving to waterways?
A: Section 282 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 10,000 rupees, or both, on whoever navigates a vessel in a rash/negligent manner endangering human life or likely causing hurt/injury. [Source: Section 282, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash navigation of vessel

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 282: Rash navigation of vessel

Q: A man is driving a speedboat at top speed through a marked swimming zone near a public beach, forcing swimmers to dive out of the way. What is his penalty?
A: Because he navigated a vessel in a manner so rash as to endanger human life and likely cause injury, he is punishable under Section 282 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to 10,000 rupees. [Source: Section 282, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash navigation of vessel

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 282: Rash navigation of vessel

Q: How does the maximum fine for rash navigation compare to rash driving under Section 281?
A: The maximum fine for rash navigation (Section 282) is 10,000 rupees, which is ten times higher than the 1,000 rupee maximum fine for rash driving (Section 281). [Source: Section 282, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash navigation of vessel

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 282: Rash navigation of vessel

Q: A ferry captain is navigating carefully when a massive, unmapped underwater debris field suddenly tears the hull, endangering passengers. Is the captain guilty?
A: No, if the captain was navigating carefully, the incident was not caused by a "rash or negligent" manner of navigation. [Source: Section 282, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash navigation of vessel

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 282: Rash navigation of vessel

Q: What is the consequence of imposing a significantly higher fine for maritime negligence compared to road negligence?
A: The consequence reflects the potentially catastrophic nature of maritime accidents (like sinking a passenger ferry or massive property damage) and the often higher commercial stakes involved in vessel navigation compared to standard road traffic. [Source: Section 282, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Rash navigation of vessel

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 283: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

Q: What is the penalty for deliberately misleading a ship using false signals or buoys?
A: Exhibiting a false light, mark, or buoy intending to mislead a navigator is a serious offence punishable by up to seven years in prison and a mandatory fine of at least 10,000 rupees. [Source: Section 283, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 283: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

Q: How does Section 283 of BNS 2023 penalize maritime sabotage via false signals?
A: Section 283 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 7 years and a mandatory minimum fine of 10,000 rupees on whoever exhibits a false light, mark, or buoy intending or knowing it is likely to mislead any navigator. [Source: Section 283, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 283: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

Q: A group of thieves sets up a fake lighthouse beam on a rocky shore during a storm, hoping a cargo ship will follow the light, crash on the rocks, and spill its cargo for them to loot. What is their offence?
A: Because they exhibited a false light intending to mislead a navigator, they are punishable under Section 283 with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine of not less than 10,000 rupees. [Source: Section 283, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 283: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

Q: What is unique about the fine structure in Section 283?
A: Unlike most sections which specify a maximum fine, Section 283 specifies a minimum mandatory fine ("shall not be less than ten thousand rupees") in addition to imprisonment. [Source: Section 283, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 283: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

Q: A child playing on the beach shines a powerful flashlight out to sea for a few seconds. A passing ship sees it. Is the child guilty of an offence under Section 283?
A: No, because the child lacked the requisite mens rea; they did not "intend" or "know it to be likely" that the light would mislead a navigator. [Source: Section 283, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 283: Exhibition of false light, mark or buoy

Q: What is the consequence of the severe penalties (7 years and a mandatory minimum fine) for this specific act?
A: The consequence is a strong deterrent against a historic and highly dangerous form of maritime sabotage (wrecking), recognizing that deceiving a navigator can easily result in mass casualties and massive economic destruction. [Source: Section 283, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the penalty for a ferry operator who overloads their boat and puts passengers at risk?
A: Knowingly or negligently conveying people for hire in a vessel that is unsafe or overloaded enough to endanger their lives is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 284, BNS 2023]

A: Section 284 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever knowingly/negligently conveys persons by water for hire in a vessel so unsafe or overloaded that it endangers their lives. [Source: Section 284, BNS 2023]

A: Because he knowingly conveyed persons by water for hire in a vessel so loaded as to endanger their lives, he is punishable under Section 284 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 284, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 285: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation

Q: What is the penalty for blocking a public road or river and causing a hazard?
A: Causing danger, obstruction, or injury on a public road or waterway by doing an act, or failing to maintain property in your charge, is a public nuisance punishable by a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 285, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 285: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation

Q: How does Section 285 of BNS 2023 address physical obstructions to public ways?
A: Section 285 of BNS 2023 imposes a fine up to 5,000 rupees on whoever causes danger, obstruction, or injury to any person in a public way or line of navigation by doing an act or omitting to take order with property in their charge. [Source: Section 285, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 285: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation

Q: A construction company is building a house and leaves a massive pile of bricks right in the middle of the public road overnight without any warning lights, causing a car to crash into it. What is the penalty?
A: Because they caused danger and obstruction in a public way by omitting to take proper order with property in their charge, they are punishable under Section 285 with a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 285, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 285: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation

Q: Can a person be punished under this section simply for failing to act?
A: Yes, the offence can be committed "by omitting to take order with any property in his possession or under his charge." [Source: Section 285, BNS 2023]

content:

A: No, because the tree was not property "in his possession or under his charge," nor did he do any act to cause the obstruction. [Source: Section 285, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Danger or obstruction in public way or line of navigation

Q: What is the consequence of imposing only a fine for this offence?
A: The consequence is that while creating a static physical hazard is illegal and punishable, it is treated as a severe civic violation (nuisance) rather than an act requiring imprisonment, focusing instead on financial deterrence to ensure property owners maintain safe boundaries. [Source: Section 285, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 286: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

Q: What happens if a person is careless with poisonous chemicals and endangers others?
A: Handling a poisonous substance rashly, or failing to secure it properly, in a way that endangers human life is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 286, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 286: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

Q: How does Section 286 of BNS 2023 penalize negligence regarding poisons?
A: Section 286 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on anyone who rashly/negligently handles a poisonous substance, or omits to safely guard it, endangering human life. [Source: Section 286, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 286: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

Q: A farmer buys highly toxic pesticide and leaves the unsealed bucket sitting on the sidewalk outside a busy school while he goes to buy lunch. What is his offence?
A: Because he negligently omitted to take such order with a poisonous substance in his possession as is sufficient to guard against probable danger to human life, he is punishable under Section 286 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 286, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 286: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

Q: Can a person be convicted under Section 286 if they didn't actively do anything with the poison, but just left it out?
A: Yes, the section explicitly covers whoever "knowingly or negligently omits to take such order" with the poisonous substance to guard against probable danger. [Source: Section 286, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 286: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

Q: A chemist stores cyanide in a heavily locked, reinforced safe, following all regulations. A highly skilled team of thieves blows up the safe and steals it. Is the chemist guilty of negligence?
A: No, because the chemist did not negligently omit to take sufficient order to guard against probable danger; the theft was an unforeseeable criminal act by third parties. [Source: Section 286, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 286: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

Q: What is the consequence of holding possessors of poison criminally liable for mere omission of care?
A: The consequence is that it places a strict, affirmative legal duty on anyone possessing toxic substances to proactively secure them, recognizing that poisons are inherently dangerous to the public if left unguarded. [Source: Section 286, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to poisonous substance

Q: What is the penalty for being careless with fire or flammable materials?
A: Rashly or negligently handling fire or combustible matter, or failing to secure it, in a way that endangers human life is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 2,000 rupees. [Source: Section 287, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to fire or combustible matter

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 287: Negligent conduct with respect to fire or combustible matter

A: Section 287 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 2,000 rupees, or both, on whoever acts rashly with fire/combustible matter, or negligently omits to guard against probable danger to human life from it. [Source: Section 287, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to fire or combustible matter

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 287: Negligent conduct with respect to fire or combustible matter

A: Because he negligently omitted to take sufficient order with combustible matter in his possession to guard against probable danger to human life, he is punishable under Section 287 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 287, BNS 2023]

content:

A: No, because lighting a candle in a home is a standard act, and the fire was caused by an unforeseeable act of nature, not by a "rash or negligent" act. [Source: Section 287, BNS 2023]
