Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 288: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

Q: What is the penalty for handling explosives carelessly?
A: Handling explosives rashly or negligently, or failing to safely store explosives in your possession, endangering human life, is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 288, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 288: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

Q: How does Section 288 of BNS 2023 deal with negligence regarding explosives?
A: Section 288 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever rashly/negligently handles an explosive substance, or negligently fails to guard against probable danger from it. [Source: Section 288, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 288: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

Q: A construction worker leaves a box of dynamite unattended on a busy public sidewalk while he goes to take a phone call. What is his offence?
A: Because he negligently omitted to take sufficient order with an explosive substance in his possession to guard against probable danger to human life, he is punishable under Section 288 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 288, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 288: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

Q: Must an actual explosion occur for a person to be convicted under this section?
A: No, the offence is complete upon the rash act or negligent omission that "endangers human life" or creates a "probable danger" from the explosive, even if it does not detonate. [Source: Section 288, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 288: Negligent conduct with respect to explosive substance

A: No, because the company took sufficient order to guard against "probable" danger by clearing the area and using barricades; they were not negligent regarding the unforeseeable trespasser. [Source: Section 288, BNS 2023]

A: The consequence is that it enforces strict operational discipline on industries (like mining or demolition) and individuals dealing with explosives, recognizing that a single oversight can cause immediate, mass casualties. [Source: Section 288, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 289: Negligent conduct with respect to machinery

Q: What happens if a person is careless with dangerous machinery and puts people at risk?
A: Operating machinery rashly, or negligently failing to secure and guard machinery under your care, endangering human life, is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 289, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to machinery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 289: Negligent conduct with respect to machinery

Q: How does Section 289 of BNS 2023 penalize negligence regarding machinery?
A: Section 289 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever rashly operates machinery, or negligently omits to guard against probable danger to human life from machinery in their care. [Source: Section 289, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to machinery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 289: Negligent conduct with respect to machinery

Q: A factory manager refuses to install safety guards on heavy industrial presses to speed up production. A worker gets their arm pulled into the exposed gears. What is the manager's offence?
A: Because he knowingly omitted to take sufficient order with machinery under his care to guard against probable danger to human life, he is punishable under Section 289 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 289, BNS 2023]

content:

Q: What is the penalty for failing to secure a construction or demolition site?
A: Negligently failing to take sufficient safety measures when demolishing, repairing, or constructing a building to prevent danger from falling debris is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 290, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to pulling down, repairing or constructing buildings, etc.

A: Section 290 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever negligently omits to take sufficient measures to guard against danger to human life from a falling building during demolition, repair, or construction. [Source: Section 290, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to pulling down, repairing or constructing buildings, etc.

content:

A: Because he negligently omitted to take sufficient measures to guard against probable danger to human life from the fall of the building, he is punishable under Section 290 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 290, BNS 2023]

A: Negligently failing to take sufficient measures to control an animal in your possession, creating a probable danger to human life or risk of grievous hurt, is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 291, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Negligent conduct with respect to animal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 291: Negligent conduct with respect to animal

A: Section 291 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever knowingly/negligently omits to guard against probable danger to human life or grievous hurt from an animal in their possession. [Source: Section 291, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 291: Negligent conduct with respect to animal

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 292: Punishment for public nuisance in cases not otherwise provided for

Q: What is the penalty for causing a public nuisance if there isn't a specific law for that exact type of nuisance?
A: Committing a public nuisance in a situation not explicitly covered by other sections of the penal code is a residuary offence punishable by a fine up to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 292, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for public nuisance in cases not otherwise provided for

A: Section 292 of BNS 2023 serves as a residuary penal clause, stating that whoever commits a public nuisance in any case not otherwise punishable by the Sanhita shall be punished with a fine extending to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 292, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for public nuisance in cases not otherwise provided for

content:

A: Because it causes a common danger/annoyance to the public not specifically covered elsewhere in the code, he commits a public nuisance punishable under the residuary Section 292 with a fine up to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 292, BNS 2023]

content:

content:

A: The consequence is that law enforcement has a flexible, low-level tool to penalize new or highly unusual forms of antisocial behavior that disrupt public order, without having to wait for the legislature to draft a specific law for every possible scenario. [Source: Section 292, BNS 2023]

Q: What happens if you are officially ordered to stop causing a public nuisance but you keep doing it anyway?
A: Repeating or continuing a public nuisance after a public servant with lawful authority has legally ordered you to stop is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 293, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Continuance of nuisance after injunction to discontinue

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 293: Continuance of nuisance after injunction to discontinue

Q: How does Section 293 of BNS 2023 escalate the punishment for persistent public nuisances?
A: Section 293 of BNS 2023 imposes simple imprisonment up to 6 months, or a fine up to 5,000 rupees, or both, on whoever continues/repeats a public nuisance after being enjoined to stop by a lawfully authorized public servant. [Source: Section 293, BNS 2023]

A: Because they repeated a public nuisance after having been enjoined by a public servant with lawful authority not to do so, they are punishable under the escalated Section 293 with imprisonment up to six months or a fine. [Source: Section 293, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 293: Continuance of nuisance after injunction to discontinue

A: No, because the injunction must be issued by a "public servant who has lawful authority to issue such injunction," not just a private citizen. [Source: Section 293, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 294: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

Q: What makes a book, picture, or electronic file "obscene" under the law?
A: A material is legally obscene if it is lascivious, appeals to prurient interest, or tends to deprave and corrupt the people likely to read or see it. [Source: Section 294, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 294: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

Q: How does Section 294 of BNS 2023 define and penalize obscenity?
A: Section 294 of BNS 2023 defines obscenity (lascivious/prurient effect) and penalizes the sale, distribution, import, or advertisement of obscene objects/electronic content with up to 2 years imprisonment (5 years for repeat offences) and fines. [Source: Section 294, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 294: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

Q: A publisher knowingly prints and sells highly explicit pornographic magazines at a local newsstand, which tend to corrupt the public. What is his penalty on his first conviction?
A: Because he sells and publicly exhibits an obscene book/paper, he is punishable on first conviction under Section 294(2) with imprisonment up to two years and a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 294, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 294: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

Q: Are scientific or religious texts depicting nudity considered obscene under this law?
A: No, the Exception clause exempts materials where publication is "justified as being for the public good" (like science, literature, art) or kept bona fide for religious purposes, including ancient monuments and temples. [Source: Section 294, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

A: No, because the publication falls under the Exception, being justified for the public good in the interest of science and learning, rather than appealing to prurient interests. [Source: Section 294, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the consequence of escalating the punishment for repeat obscenity offenders?
A: The consequence is a structural crackdown on commercial pornography networks; the jump from 2 years to 5 years for a second conviction is designed to put organized distributors out of business permanently. [Source: Section 294, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Sale, etc., of obscene books, etc.

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 295: Sale, etc., of obscene objects to child

Q: Is the penalty different if obscene materials are sold or given to a child instead of an adult?
A: Yes, selling, distributing, or exhibiting obscene objects to a child carries a harsher penalty: up to three years in prison on the first conviction, and up to seven years for repeat convictions. [Source: Section 295, BNS 2023]

A: Section 295 of BNS 2023 specifically targets whoever sells, distributes, or exhibits obscene objects (as defined in Section 294) to a child, increasing the penalty to 3 years imprisonment on first conviction, and up to 7 years on subsequent convictions. [Source: Section 295, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 296: Obscene acts and songs

Q: What is the penalty for singing an obscene song or doing an obscene act in public?
A: Doing an obscene act in a public place, or singing/reciting obscene songs or words near a public place to the annoyance of others, is punishable by up to three months in prison or a fine up to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 296, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obscene acts and songs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 296: Obscene acts and songs

Q: How does Section 296 of BNS 2023 penalize public obscenity?
A: Section 296 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 3 months, or a fine up to 1,000 rupees, or both, on whoever does an obscene act in a public place, or sings/utters obscene songs/words in or near a public place, to the annoyance of others. [Source: Section 296, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obscene acts and songs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 296: Obscene acts and songs

A: Because he uttered obscene words in a public place to the annoyance of others, he is punishable under Section 296 with imprisonment up to three months or a fine up to 1,000 rupees. [Source: Section 296, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Obscene acts and songs

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 296: Obscene acts and songs

A: No, because the act must be done "in or near any public place" and "to the annoyance of others," neither of which apply to a secluded, private space where no one else is annoyed. [Source: Section 296, BNS 2023]

A: Yes, keeping an office or place to draw an unauthorized private lottery is punishable by up to six months in prison or a fine. Additionally, publishing proposals related to such a lottery carries a fine up to 5,000 rupees. [Source: Section 297, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 297: Keeping lottery office

A: Section 297 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 6 months imprisonment or a fine for keeping an office to draw an unauthorized lottery, and a fine up to 5,000 rupees for publishing any proposal or scheme tied to the drawing of such a lottery. [Source: Section 297, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 298: Injuring or defiling place of worship with intent to insult religion of any class

Q: What is the penalty for vandalizing a temple, mosque, or church to insult a religion?
A: Destroying, damaging, or defiling a place of worship or a sacred object, with the intent to insult a religion or knowing it will be seen as an insult, is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 298, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injuring or defiling place of worship with intent to insult religion of any class

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 298: Injuring or defiling place of worship with intent to insult religion of any class

Q: How does Section 298 of BNS 2023 protect places of worship from religious hate crimes?
A: Section 298 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 2 years, or a fine, or both, on whoever destroys, damages, or defiles a place of worship/sacred object with intent to insult, or knowing it is likely to insult, the religion of any class. [Source: Section 298, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injuring or defiling place of worship with intent to insult religion of any class

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 298: Injuring or defiling place of worship with intent to insult religion of any class

A: Because they destroyed and defiled a place of worship and sacred objects with the intention of insulting the religion of that class of persons, they are punishable under Section 298 with imprisonment up to two years or a fine. [Source: Section 298, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Injuring or defiling place of worship with intent to insult religion of any class

A: Yes, the offence requires either "the intention of thereby insulting the religion" or "the knowledge that any class of persons is likely to consider such destruction, damage or defilement as an insult to their religion." [Source: Section 298, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the penalty for committing hate speech meant to outrage a specific religious group?
A: Deliberately and maliciously insulting the religion or religious beliefs of any class of citizens, via spoken/written words, signs, or electronic means, to outrage their religious feelings, is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 299, BNS 2023]

[Source: Section 299, BNS 2023]

A: Because they used written and electronic means with deliberate and malicious intention of outraging the religious feelings of a class of citizens by insulting their beliefs, they are punishable under Section 299 with imprisonment up to three years or a fine. [Source: Section 299, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 303: Theft

Q: How does Indian law define the crime of stealing?
A: Theft is defined as intending to dishonestly take movable property out of someone's possession without their consent, and moving that property in order to take it. The punishment is up to three years in prison or a fine, with community service possible for first-time offenders stealing less than 5,000 rupees who return the property. [Source: Section 303, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 303: Theft

Q: What does Section 303 of BNS 2023 state about theft?
A: Section 303 of BNS 2023 defines theft as dishonestly moving movable property out of a person's possession without consent. It prescribes up to 3 years imprisonment or fine, with repeat offenders facing 1 to 5 years rigorous imprisonment, and specific community service provisions for minor first-time thefts. [Source: Section 303, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 303: Theft

Q: A man visits his friend's house. While the friend is out of the room, he sees a gold watch on the table, puts it in his pocket intending to sell it later, and leaves. What is his offence?
A: Because he intended to dishonestly take movable property out of his friend's possession without consent, and moved the watch by putting it in his pocket, he has committed theft under Section 303. [Source: Section 303, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 303: Theft

Q: Can a tree growing in the ground be the subject of theft?
A: A thing attached to the earth is not movable property and cannot be the subject of theft; however, it becomes capable of being the subject of theft as soon as it is severed from the earth. [Source: Section 303, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 303: Theft

Q: A person owes money to a watch repairman. The repairman lawfully retains the watch as security for the debt. The person sneaks into the shop and takes his own watch back without paying, to deprive the repairman of his security. Has he committed theft?
A: Yes, even though it is his own watch, taking it out of the repairman's lawful possession without consent, intending to deprive him of the security, is done dishonestly, constituting theft. [Source: Section 303, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 303: Theft

Q: What is the consequence for a first-time offender who steals property valued at 2,000 rupees?
A: Under the proviso to Section 303, if it is a first offence, the value is less than five thousand rupees, and the offender returns the value or restores the stolen property, they shall be punished with community service instead of imprisonment. [Source: Section 303, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 304: Snatching

Q: What is the legal definition of grabbing someone's phone out of their hand and running away?
A: This is defined as "snatching," a specific form of theft where the offender suddenly, quickly, or forcibly seizes, grabs, or takes away movable property from a person or their possession. It is punishable by up to three years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 304, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Snatching

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 304: Snatching

Q: How does Section 304 of BNS 2023 define and penalize snatching?
A: Section 304 of BNS 2023 defines snatching as theft where the offender suddenly, quickly, or forcibly seizes or grabs movable property from a person or their possession. It imposes imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine. [Source: Section 304, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Snatching

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 304: Snatching

Q: A woman is walking down the street carrying a purse. A thief runs up behind her, violently yanks the purse off her shoulder, and sprints away. What specific offence has he committed?
A: Because he committed theft by suddenly and forcibly seizing movable property from her person, he has committed snatching, punishable under Section 304 with imprisonment up to three years and a fine. [Source: Section 304, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Snatching

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 304: Snatching

Q: How does snatching differ from regular theft under this section?
A: Snatching requires the specific element that the offender "suddenly or quickly or forcibly seizes or secures or grabs" the property from a person or their possession, elevating the physical confrontation compared to stealthy theft. [Source: Section 304, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Snatching

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 304: Snatching

Q: A pickpocket carefully and unnoticed slips a wallet out of a man's pocket on a crowded train without any sudden, quick, or forcible grabbing motion. Is this snatching?
A: No, while it is theft, it lacks the sudden, quick, or forcible grabbing required to be classified specifically as snatching under Section 304. [Source: Section 304, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Snatching

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 304: Snatching

Q: What is the consequence of creating a distinct offence for "snatching"?
A: The consequence is that law enforcement can specifically target and appropriately penalize aggressive street crimes (like chain-snatching or phone-grabbing) that involve physical shock and a higher risk of injury to the victim than ordinary stealth theft. [Source: Section 304, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Snatching

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 305: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

Q: What is the penalty for stealing from inside someone's home, a car, or a temple?
A: Stealing from a human dwelling, a vehicle used for transport, a place of worship (such as an idol), or stealing government/local authority property is an aggravated form of theft punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 305, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 305: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

Q: How does Section 305 of BNS 2023 penalize theft in specific protected locations?
A: Section 305 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine for theft committed in a dwelling, tent, or vessel; of/from any means of transport; of an idol in a place of worship; or of government/local authority property. [Source: Section 305, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 305: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

Q: A burglar breaks into a family's house at night while they are sleeping and steals their laptop and jewelry from the living room. What is his penalty?
A: Because he committed theft in a building used as a human dwelling, he is punishable under Section 305 with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 305, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 305: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

Q: Does this section apply if someone steals a bicycle parked on the street?
A: Yes, it covers theft "of any means of transport used for the transport of goods or passengers," which would include stealing a bicycle. [Source: Section 305, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 305: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

Q: A person steals a park bench belonging to the local municipal corporation from a public park. Does this fall under Section 305 even if it's not a house or vehicle?
A: Yes, because clause (e) specifically covers the theft "of any property of the Government or of a local authority," bringing it under the harsher penalties of Section 305. [Source: Section 305, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 305: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

Q: What is the consequence of classifying these specific types of theft together under a higher seven-year penalty?
A: The consequence is that the law provides enhanced deterrence against thefts that violate the sanctity of the home, disrupt vital public transportation, desecrate religious sites, or strip public assets, treating them as far more severe than ordinary theft. [Source: Section 305, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 306: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

Q: What is the penalty for an employee who steals from their employer?
A: A clerk or servant who commits theft of property in the possession of their master or employer is punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 306, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 306: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

Q: How does Section 306 of BNS 2023 penalize workplace theft?
A: Section 306 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine on whoever, being employed as a clerk or servant, commits theft of property in the possession of their master or employer. [Source: Section 306, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 306: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

Q: A shop assistant is entrusted with managing the cash register during his shift. Before leaving for the day, he pockets a wad of cash from the drawer and goes home. What is his penalty?
A: Because he committed theft as a servant of property in the possession of his employer, he is punishable under Section 306 with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 306, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 306: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

Q: Does Section 306 apply to an independent contractor stealing from a client?
A: No, the section specifically requires the offender to be "a clerk or servant, or being employed in the capacity of a clerk or servant" stealing from their "master or employer." [Source: Section 306, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 306: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

Q: A company director, who legally shares possession and control of the company assets with other directors, misappropriates company funds. Is he guilty under Section 306?
A: No, because a director is generally not considered a mere "clerk or servant," and the offence would likely fall under criminal breach of trust rather than this specific theft provision. [Source: Section 306, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 306: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

Q: What is the consequence of prescribing a harsher seven-year penalty for employee theft compared to ordinary theft?
A: The consequence is that the law heavily deters the violation of the special trust inherent in the employer-employee relationship, where servants have easier, authorized access to property and are expected to safeguard it. [Source: Section 306, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft by clerk or servant of property in possession of master

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 307: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

Q: What happens if a thief breaks into a house carrying a loaded gun, just in case they need to use it, but never actually fires it?
A: Committing theft while having made preparation to cause death, hurt, or restraint—even if the weapon is not used—is a severely aggravated offence punishable by up to ten years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine. [Source: Section 307, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 307: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

Q: How does Section 307 of BNS 2023 penalize prepared, armed theft?
A: Section 307 of BNS 2023 imposes rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years and a fine on whoever commits theft having made preparation to cause death, hurt, or restraint to any person in order to commit the theft, escape, or retain the property. [Source: Section 307, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 307: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

Q: A pickpocket plans to steal a wealthy man's wallet at a train station. He places three muscular friends nearby with instructions to tackle and restrain the victim if the victim notices and fights back. He steals the wallet successfully without the friends needing to intervene. What is his offence?
A: Because he committed theft having made preparation for causing restraint to the victim in order to effect his escape or retain the property, he is punishable under Section 307. [Source: Section 307, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 307: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

Q: What specific type of imprisonment is mandated under Section 307?
A: The section explicitly mandates "rigorous imprisonment" for a term which may extend to ten years. [Source: Section 307, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 307: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

Q: A hungry teenager steals an apple from a fruit stall without carrying any weapons, planning any violence, or bringing accomplices to restrain anyone. He is caught. Does Section 307 apply?
A: No, because he did not make "preparation for causing death, or hurt, or restraint"; this would be ordinary theft, not the aggravated offence under Section 307. [Source: Section 307, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 307: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

Q: What is the consequence of penalizing the "preparation" for violence during a theft?
A: The consequence is that the law proactively targets the high potential danger posed by armed or organized thieves, punishing their violent readiness even if the victim wisely chooses not to resist and avoids actual injury. [Source: Section 307, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Theft after preparation made for causing death, hurt or restraint in order to committing

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 308: Extortion

Q: How does Indian law define blackmail or forcing someone to hand over money through threats?
A: Extortion is defined as intentionally putting a person in fear of any injury to themselves or another, and thereby dishonestly inducing them to deliver property or valuable security. It is punishable by up to seven years in prison, with harsher penalties for severe threats. [Source: Section 308, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Extortion

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 308: Extortion

Q: What are the provisions for extortion under Section 308 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 308 of BNS 2023 defines extortion (inducing delivery of property via fear of injury) and penalizes it with up to 7 years imprisonment. Threats of death/grievous hurt carry up to 10 years, and merely attempting to induce fear carries up to 2 years. [Source: Section 308, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Extortion

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 308: Extortion

Q: A hacker sends a message to a business owner: "Send me one lakh rupees in crypto, or I will leak your customer database and destroy your company's reputation." The owner pays out of fear. What is the offence?
A: Because the hacker intentionally put the owner in fear of injury (to reputation/property) and thereby dishonestly induced the delivery of money, he has committed extortion under Section 308. [Source: Section 308, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Extortion

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 308: Extortion

Q: Can a blank piece of paper be the subject of extortion?
A: Yes, if a person is dishonestly induced by fear to sign or affix their seal to a blank paper that "may be converted into a valuable security," it constitutes extortion. [Source: Section 308, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Extortion

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 308: Extortion

Q: A creditor tells his debtor, "If you don't pay me the money you legally owe me by tomorrow, I will file a civil lawsuit against you." The debtor pays. Is the creditor guilty of extortion?
A: No, because threatening to take lawful legal action is not threatening an illegal "injury," and demanding the return of a lawful debt is not a "dishonest" inducement. [Source: Section 308, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Extortion

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 308: Extortion

Q: What is the consequence of prescribing up to ten years imprisonment for extortion by threat of accusation of a capital offence?
A: The consequence is that the law heavily penalizes severe blackmail—such as threatening to frame someone for murder or rape—recognizing that such extreme psychological terror can completely ruin a victim's life and compel them to surrender all their assets. [Source: Section 308, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Extortion

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 309: Robbery

Q: When does a simple theft or extortion become the more serious crime of robbery?
A: Theft becomes robbery if the offender voluntarily causes or threatens instant death, hurt, or wrongful restraint to commit the theft or escape. Extortion becomes robbery if the offender is physically present and induces the victim to hand over property through fear of instant death, hurt, or restraint. [Source: Section 309, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 309: Robbery

Q: How does Section 309 of BNS 2023 classify and penalize robbery?
A: Section 309 of BNS 2023 defines robbery as aggravated theft or extortion involving the causing or threat of instant death, hurt, or wrongful restraint. It is punishable by rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years (14 years on a highway at night), and causing hurt during robbery carries up to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 309, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 309: Robbery

Q: A man approaches a pedestrian on the street, pulls out a knife, and demands his wallet, threatening to stab him right then and there if he refuses. The pedestrian hands it over. What is the offence?
A: Because he extorted the wallet by putting the victim in fear of instant hurt while in his presence, the extortion is elevated to robbery under Section 309. [Source: Section 309, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 309: Robbery

Q: Under Section 309, what defines an offender as being "present" during an extortion?
A: The explanation states that an offender is present if he is "sufficiently near to put the other person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint." [Source: Section 309, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 309: Robbery

Q: A kidnapper calls a father on the phone and says, "Leave 10,000 rupees at the park tomorrow, or I will kill your child who is currently locked in my basement." Is this robbery?
A: No, because the kidnapper is not in the physical presence of the victim putting him in fear of "instant" death or hurt. It is extortion, but it does not meet the specific immediacy and presence requirements to be classified as robbery. [Source: Section 309, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 309: Robbery

Q: What is the consequence of the provision allowing up to 14 years imprisonment for highway robbery at night?
A: The consequence is that the state provides maximum deterrence to protect vulnerable travelers on desolate roads in the dark, recognizing that highway banditry poses a massive threat to public safety and interstate commerce. [Source: Section 309, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 310: Dacoity

Q: What is the legal term and penalty for a gang of five or more people committing a robbery together?
A: When five or more persons conjointly commit or attempt to commit robbery, it is called "dacoity." It is punishable by life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years, and a fine. [Source: Section 310, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dacoity

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 310: Dacoity

Q: How does Section 310 of BNS 2023 define and punish dacoity?
A: Section 310 of BNS 2023 defines dacoity as robbery committed conjointly by 5 or more persons. It imposes life imprisonment or up to 10 years rigorous imprisonment. If murder is committed during dacoity, all members face death or life imprisonment. [Source: Section 310, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dacoity

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 310: Dacoity

Q: A highly organized gang of six armed men storms a bank. Three hold the tellers at gunpoint, two guard the doors, and one waits in the getaway car outside. They steal cash and flee. What is their specific offence?
A: Because five or more persons conjointly committed a robbery (including those present and aiding), every person involved is said to commit dacoity, punishable under Section 310. [Source: Section 310, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dacoity

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 310: Dacoity

Q: Do all five people have to be actively stealing to be guilty of dacoity?
A: No, the total count includes those "conjointly committing or attempting to commit a robbery, and persons present and aiding such commission or attempt." [Source: Section 310, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dacoity

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 310: Dacoity

Q: Four men plan to rob a jewelry store. They execute the robbery perfectly and escape with the goods. There are strictly no other accomplices involved. Can they be charged with dacoity?
A: No, because dacoity strictly requires "five or more persons." Since there were only four, they can be charged with robbery, but the legal threshold for dacoity has not been met. [Source: Section 310, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dacoity

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 310: Dacoity

Q: What is the consequence of making every gang member liable for murder committed by any one of them during a dacoity?
A: The consequence is a strict doctrine of collective responsibility; it deters violent gangs by ensuring that if a robbery turns fatal, the getaway driver or lookout will face the death penalty or life in prison right alongside the actual shooter. [Source: Section 310, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dacoity

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 311: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

Q: What is the minimum penalty for using a deadly weapon during a robbery?
A: If an offender uses a deadly weapon, causes grievous hurt, or attempts to cause death or grievous hurt while committing robbery or dacoity, they must be punished with a minimum of seven years in prison. [Source: Section 311, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 311: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

Q: How does Section 311 of BNS 2023 enhance the punishment for violent robbery?
A: Section 311 of BNS 2023 sets a mandatory minimum sentence of not less than 7 years imprisonment if the offender uses a deadly weapon, causes grievous hurt, or attempts to cause death/grievous hurt during a robbery or dacoity. [Source: Section 311, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 311: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

Q: During a bank robbery, a dacoit fires a shotgun at a security guard, intending to kill him, but misses completely. What is the minimum prison term the dacoit faces for this specific act?
A: Because he attempted to cause death at the time of committing dacoity (and used a deadly weapon), he is punishable under Section 311 with imprisonment that shall not be less than seven years. [Source: Section 311, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 311: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

Q: Is the seven-year term under Section 311 a maximum limit or a minimum baseline?
A: It is a minimum baseline; the section explicitly states the imprisonment "shall not be less than seven years." [Source: Section 311, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 311: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

Q: A robber verbally threatens to punch a victim, causing them to hand over their money. No weapon is shown, and no physical contact occurs. Does the seven-year minimum of Section 311 apply?
A: No, because the robber did not use a "deadly weapon," did not cause "grievous hurt," and did not attempt to cause "death or grievous hurt," so the mandatory minimum of Section 311 is not triggered. [Source: Section 311, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 311: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

Q: What is the consequence of prescribing a mandatory minimum sentence for armed robbery?
A: The consequence is that judges have less discretion to give lenient sentences to violent, armed criminals, ensuring that anyone who brings lethal force into a robbery faces severe, guaranteed incarceration. [Source: Section 311, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Robbery, or dacoity, with attempt to cause death or grievous hurt

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 312: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

Q: What is the penalty for trying to commit a robbery while carrying a deadly weapon, even if the robbery fails?
A: Attempting to commit robbery or dacoity while armed with a deadly weapon is punishable by a mandatory minimum of seven years in prison. [Source: Section 312, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 312: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

Q: What does Section 312 of BNS 2023 say about armed attempts?
A: Section 312 of BNS 2023 states that if an offender is armed with any deadly weapon at the time of merely attempting to commit robbery or dacoity, their imprisonment shall not be less than seven years. [Source: Section 312, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 312: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

Q: A man walks into a convenience store holding a machete and demands the cash register be opened. Before anything is handed over, the police burst in and arrest him. What is his minimum penalty?
A: Because he attempted to commit robbery while armed with a deadly weapon, he is punishable under Section 312 with imprisonment that shall not be less than seven years. [Source: Section 312, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 312: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

Q: What is the difference between Section 311 and Section 312?
A: Section 311 applies when the offender actually "commits" the robbery/dacoity and "uses" a weapon or causes/attempts violence, while Section 312 applies when they merely "attempt" the robbery/dacoity while simply being "armed" with a deadly weapon. [Source: Section 312, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 312: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

Q: A man attempts to rob a pedestrian by aggressively demanding money with his fists raised. He is completely unarmed. Does Section 312 apply?
A: No, because Section 312 strictly requires the offender to be "armed with any deadly weapon" at the time of the attempt. [Source: Section 312, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 312: Attempt to commit robbery or dacoity when armed with deadly weapon

Q: What is the consequence of giving the same seven-year minimum for an armed attempt (Section 312) as for armed completion (Section 311)?
A: The consequence is that the law treats the decision to bring a deadly weapon into a criminal encounter as the primary danger to society, punishing the violent readiness equally whether the crime succeeds or fails. [Source: Section 312, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 313: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

Q: Is it a crime just to be a member of a gang of thieves?
A: Yes, belonging to a gang associated for the purpose of habitually committing theft or robbery (other than dacoits) is punishable by up to seven years of rigorous imprisonment and a fine. [Source: Section 313, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 313: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

Q: How does Section 313 of BNS 2023 target organized thievery?
A: Section 313 of BNS 2023 imposes rigorous imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine on whoever belongs to a gang associated in habitually committing theft or robbery, provided they are not a gang of dacoits. [Source: Section 313, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 313: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

Q: The police uncover a syndicate of pickpockets who live together and exclusively make their living by stealing wallets on trains every single day. Even if a specific member wasn't caught stealing today, what offence are they guilty of?
A: Because they belong to a gang of persons associated in habitually committing theft, they are punishable under Section 313 with rigorous imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 313, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 313: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

Q: Does this section apply to a gang that habitually commits dacoity?
A: No, the section explicitly excludes "a gang of dacoits," because belonging to a gang of dacoits is a far more serious offence covered separately (under Section 310) which carries up to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 313, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 313: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

Q: A man occasionally buys stolen goods from a local gang of thieves but does not participate in their thefts or belong to their association. Is he guilty under Section 313?
A: No, because he does not "belong to" the gang associated for habitually committing theft; his crime would be receiving stolen property, not gang membership under this section. [Source: Section 313, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 313: Punishment for belonging to gang of robbers, etc.

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing gang membership itself rather than just specific acts of theft?
A: The consequence is that law enforcement can dismantle the infrastructure of organized crime networks, prosecuting career criminals for their systemic association without needing to catch them in the act of a specific robbery. [Source: Section 313, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 314: Dishonest misappropriation of property

Q: What happens if you find someone's lost wallet on the street and decide to keep the money instead of returning it?
A: If you dishonestly misappropriate or convert movable property to your own use—like keeping a found wallet when you could easily identify the owner—you are punishable by six months to two years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 314, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 314: Dishonest misappropriation of property

Q: How does Section 314 of BNS 2023 define and punish dishonest misappropriation?
A: Section 314 of BNS 2023 defines dishonest misappropriation as dishonestly converting any movable property to one's own use. It prescribes a minimum of 6 months and up to 2 years imprisonment, plus a fine. [Source: Section 314, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 314: Dishonest misappropriation of property

Q: A man borrows a book from his friend's library with the genuine intent to return it. A week later, he realizes the book is rare, decides to keep it, and sells it to a dealer. What is his offence?
A: Because he came into possession of the property lawfully but later dishonestly appropriated it to his own use, he has committed dishonest misappropriation under Section 314. [Source: Section 314, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 314: Dishonest misappropriation of property

Q: Is misappropriating property for just a temporary period considered an offence?
A: Yes, Explanation 1 clearly states that a "dishonest misappropriation for a time only is a misappropriation within the meaning of this section." [Source: Section 314, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 314: Dishonest misappropriation of property

Q: A person finds a gold coin on a public road, has no way of knowing who dropped it, and keeps it. Is this misappropriation?
A: No, if the finder does not know or have the means to discover the owner, taking the property and keeping it without believing the owner can be found is not a dishonest misappropriation under this section. [Source: Section 314, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 314: Dishonest misappropriation of property

Q: What is the legal consequence of distinguishing misappropriation from theft?
A: The consequence is that the law covers scenarios where the initial taking was innocent, lawful, or involved found property (lacking the immediate trespass required for theft), but where a subsequent dishonest intent to keep it makes the act criminal. [Source: Section 314, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 315: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

Q: What is the penalty for stealing a dead person's belongings before their legal heirs can claim them?
A: Dishonestly misappropriating property known to have been in the possession of a deceased person at the time of death is punishable by up to three years in prison, which increases to seven years if the offender was the deceased's employee. [Source: Section 315, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 315: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

Q: How does Section 315 of BNS 2023 penalize misappropriating a deceased person's property?
A: Section 315 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 3 years and a fine on whoever dishonestly misappropriates property knowing it belonged to a deceased person and hasn't reached a legal heir. If the offender was a clerk/servant of the deceased, it extends to 7 years. [Source: Section 315, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 315: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

Q: A wealthy man dies in his home. Before the police or relatives arrive, his hired nurse takes several expensive watches from his bedside table and hides them in her bag to sell later. What is her penalty?
A: Because she dishonestly misappropriated a deceased person's property, and was employed as a servant to the deceased, she is punishable under Section 315 with imprisonment up to seven years and a fine. [Source: Section 315, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 315: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

Q: Under Section 315, does it matter if the property had already been legally transferred to the deceased's son before it was taken?
A: Yes, the section specifically targets property that "has not since been in the possession of any person legally entitled to such possession." If the son already had lawful possession, taking it would be standard theft from the son, not misappropriation from the deceased. [Source: Section 315, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 315: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

Q: An estranged relative discovers their uncle died. They move his car into their own garage purely to protect it from vandals until the will is read, without any intention of keeping it permanently. Are they guilty?
A: No, because they did not "dishonestly" misappropriate or convert the property to their own use; acting to preserve the estate for the rightful heirs lacks criminal intent. [Source: Section 315, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 315: Dishonest misappropriation of property possessed by deceased person at the time of his death

Q: What is the consequence of providing a harsher penalty for employees under this section?
A: The consequence is that the law strictly deters opportunistic looting by caretakers, domestic staff, or nurses who have intimate access to a person's home and assets during the highly vulnerable period immediately following their death. [Source: Section 315, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 316: Criminal breach of trust

Q: What is the penalty for misusing money or property that was entrusted to you?
A: Criminal breach of trust—dishonestly misappropriating or disposing of property entrusted to you in violation of a legal direction or contract—is punishable by up to five years in prison. The penalty increases up to ten years or life imprisonment depending on the offender's role (e.g., public servant, banker, or employee). [Source: Section 316, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal breach of trust

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 316: Criminal breach of trust

Q: What are the provisions for criminal breach of trust under Section 316 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 316 of BNS 2023 penalizes dishonestly misappropriating entrusted property. The base punishment is up to 5 years imprisonment. It increases for carriers/warehouse-keepers (up to 7 years), clerks/servants (up to 7 years), and public servants/bankers/agents (up to 10 years or life). [Source: Section 316, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal breach of trust

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 316: Criminal breach of trust

Q: An executor of a will dishonestly disobeys the law directing him to divide the estate among the heirs, and instead transfers all the funds into his personal bank account. What is his offence?
A: Because he was entrusted with dominion over property and dishonestly used it in violation of the legal direction prescribing how the trust is to be discharged, he has committed criminal breach of trust under Section 316. [Source: Section 316, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal breach of trust

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 316: Criminal breach of trust

Q: If an employer deducts provident fund contributions from employees' wages but fails to deposit them into the fund, is this criminal breach of trust?
A: Yes, Explanations 1 and 2 explicitly state that an employer who deducts such contributions is deemed "entrusted" with them, and defaulting on payment to the fund violates the law, constituting criminal breach of trust. [Source: Section 316, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal breach of trust

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 316: Criminal breach of trust

Q: A financial agent is instructed to invest his client's money in government bonds. Believing in good faith it would be more profitable, he buys private bank shares instead. The shares crash, causing a loss. Is this criminal breach of trust?
A: No, because he acted in good faith, not "dishonestly." While he is liable for a civil breach of contract due to the loss, he has not committed the criminal offence under this section. [Source: Section 316, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal breach of trust

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 316: Criminal breach of trust

Q: What is the consequence of prescribing life imprisonment for breach of trust by bankers, agents, or public servants?
A: The consequence is that the law maximally deters corruption and systemic fraud by those who hold immense economic power and public trust, recognizing that their betrayals can wipe out the life savings of thousands or severely damage state infrastructure. [Source: Section 316, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal breach of trust

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 317: Stolen property

Q: What qualifies as "stolen property" under Indian law, and what is the penalty for receiving it?
A: Stolen property includes property obtained via theft, extortion, robbery, cheating, misappropriation, or criminal breach of trust. Dishonestly receiving it carries up to three years in prison, which increases to ten years or life if received from dacoits or by habitual dealers. [Source: Section 317, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stolen property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 317: Stolen property

Q: How does Section 317 of BNS 2023 define and penalize dealing in stolen property?
A: Section 317 of BNS 2023 defines stolen property broadly (including proceeds of cheating/misappropriation). Receiving it carries up to 3 years imprisonment. Receiving property from dacoity or habitually dealing in stolen goods carries up to 10 years or life imprisonment. [Source: Section 317, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stolen property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 317: Stolen property

Q: A pawnshop owner routinely buys stolen laptops at a massive discount from a local gang, fully knowing they are stolen, and resells them for a high profit. What is his penalty?
A: Because he habitually receives or deals in property which he knows or has reason to believe to be stolen, he is punishable under Section 317 with imprisonment for life, or up to ten years, and a fine. [Source: Section 317, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stolen property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 317: Stolen property

Q: Does property obtained through cheating or criminal breach of trust count as "stolen property"?
A: Yes, Section 317 explicitly includes property where possession was transferred by cheating, or which has been criminally misappropriated, or subject to criminal breach of trust. [Source: Section 317, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stolen property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 317: Stolen property

Q: A thief steals a watch and sells it to an innocent buyer. The police recover the watch and return it to the rightful owner. The owner then legally sells it to a second buyer. Is the watch still considered "stolen property" when the second buyer gets it?
A: No, because the section states that if stolen property "subsequently comes into the possession of a person legally entitled to the possession thereof, it then ceases to be stolen property." [Source: Section 317, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stolen property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 317: Stolen property

Q: What is the consequence of harshly penalizing the receivers of stolen property?
A: The consequence is that the law chokes the economic incentive for theft; by targeting the black market dealers who convert stolen goods into cash, it eliminates the profit motive that drives primary offenders to steal in the first place. [Source: Section 317, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Stolen property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 318: Cheating

Q: How does the law define fraud or conning someone out of their money or property?
A: Cheating involves deceiving a person to fraudulently or dishonestly induce them to deliver property, consent to retain property, or do/omit an act that causes them harm. The baseline penalty is up to three years in prison, increasing up to seven years if valuable securities are involved. [Source: Section 318, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 318: Cheating

Q: What does Section 318 of BNS 2023 encompass regarding cheating?
A: Section 318 of BNS 2023 defines cheating as deceiving someone to fraudulently/dishonestly induce delivery of property or actions causing harm. Punishments range from 3 years (base) up to 7 years (if inducing delivery of property or valuable security), and 5 years if bound to protect the victim. [Source: Section 318, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 318: Cheating

Q: A man exhibits a fake diamond to a jeweler, intentionally deceiving the jeweler into believing it is real, and dishonestly induces him to buy it for a large sum. What is his offence?
A: Because he intentionally deceived the victim by exhibiting a fake sample and dishonestly induced the payment of money, he has committed cheating, punishable under Section 318. [Source: Section 318, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 318: Cheating

Q: Can concealing facts amount to cheating under this section?
A: Yes, the Explanation to Section 318 states that "A dishonest concealment of facts is a deception within the meaning of this section." [Source: Section 318, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 318: Cheating

Q: A contractor signs an agreement to supply building materials, fully intending to fulfill it. However, his supplier goes bankrupt, and he fails to deliver the materials. Has he committed cheating?
A: No, because at the time of obtaining the contract/money, he had a genuine intention to deliver. He only broke the contract afterwards. He is liable for civil breach of contract, not criminal cheating. [Source: Section 318, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 318: Cheating

Q: What is the legal consequence of penalizing cheating under Section 318?
A: The consequence is that the law protects the integrity of commercial transactions and personal trust, providing a criminal remedy against scams, counterfeiting, and false pretenses that undermine the economy and cause financial ruin. [Source: Section 318, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 319: Cheating by personation

Q: What is the penalty for pretending to be someone else to cheat a victim?
A: Cheating by personation—pretending to be another person, whether real or imaginary, living or deceased—is a specific form of cheating punishable by up to five years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 319, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating by personation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 319: Cheating by personation

Q: How does Section 319 of BNS 2023 define and punish cheating by personation?
A: Section 319 of BNS 2023 defines cheating by personation as cheating by pretending to be someone else, substituting one person for another, or misrepresenting identity. It is punishable by imprisonment up to 5 years and a fine. [Source: Section 319, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating by personation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 319: Cheating by personation

Q: A scammer calls an elderly woman, pretending to be her grandson who is currently traveling abroad, and begs her to wire him money for an emergency hospital bill. She wires the money. What specific offence has the scammer committed?
A: Because the scammer cheated by pretending to be some other person (the grandson), he has committed cheating by personation under Section 319. [Source: Section 319, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating by personation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 319: Cheating by personation

Q: If a person cheats by pretending to be a highly successful businessman who does not actually exist, is it still personation?
A: Yes, the Explanation clarifies that "The offence is committed whether the individual personated is a real or imaginary person." [Source: Section 319, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating by personation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 319: Cheating by personation

Q: An actor performs on stage portraying a famous historical figure, and people buy tickets to watch the play. Is this cheating by personation?
A: No, because there is no "cheating" involved; the audience is not deceived into delivering property under fraudulent pretenses, as they know they are watching a theatrical performance. [Source: Section 319, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating by personation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 319: Cheating by personation

Q: What is the consequence of creating a distinct, elevated penalty for personation compared to basic cheating?
A: The consequence is that the law provides stricter deterrence against identity theft and impersonation fraud (like phishing or fake officials), recognizing that these crimes exploit the victim's pre-existing trust in the person being impersonated. [Source: Section 319, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Cheating by personation
