Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 320: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

Q: What is the penalty for hiding your assets so that your creditors cannot seize them to pay off your debts?
A: Dishonestly or fraudulently concealing, removing, or transferring property without adequate consideration to prevent it from being distributed to creditors is punishable by six months to two years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 320, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 320: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

Q: How does Section 320 of BNS 2023 penalize fraudulent concealment from creditors?
A: Section 320 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment between 6 months and 2 years, or a fine, on whoever dishonestly removes, conceals, or transfers property without adequate consideration, intending to prevent its lawful distribution among creditors. [Source: Section 320, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 320: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

Q: A businessman owes millions to his suppliers and knows they are about to file for his bankruptcy. To save his assets, he secretly transfers the titles of his luxury cars and real estate to his brother-in-law for zero rupees. What is his penalty?
A: Because he fraudulently transferred property without adequate consideration, intending to prevent its distribution among his creditors, he is punishable under Section 320 with imprisonment of six months to two years. [Source: Section 320, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 320: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

Q: Does this section only apply if you are hiding your own property from your own creditors?
A: No, it also applies if you prevent the distribution of property "among his creditors or the creditors of any other person," covering accomplices who help hide assets. [Source: Section 320, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 320: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

Q: A man legitimately sells his car to a stranger at fair market value to raise cash to pay his medical bills, even though he also has outstanding credit card debt. Is he guilty under Section 320?
A: No, because the transfer was made with "adequate consideration" and was not done "dishonestly or fraudulently" to defraud creditors, but rather to meet an immediate lawful need. [Source: Section 320, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 320: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

Q: What is the legal consequence of enforcing Section 320?
A: The consequence is that it protects the integrity of the bankruptcy and debt-recovery systems, ensuring that debtors cannot use sham transactions to cheat legitimate creditors out of their rightful claims. [Source: Section 320, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property to prevent distribution among creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 321: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

Q: What is the penalty for preventing your creditors from collecting what you owe them by hiding a debt owed to you?
A: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing any debt or demand due to yourself or another from being legally available to pay off creditors is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 321, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 321: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

Q: How does Section 321 of BNS 2023 address the hiding of receivables?
A: Section 321 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 2 years, or a fine, or both, on whoever dishonestly or fraudulently prevents any debt or demand due to themselves (or another) from being made available according to law for the payment of their creditors. [Source: Section 321, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 321: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

Q: A man is facing severe debt and his creditors are about to garnish his income. He has a large uncollected invoice owed to him by a client, but he secretly tells the client to hold the money indefinitely so the creditors can't touch it. What is his offence?
A: Because he dishonestly prevented a debt due to himself from being made available according to law for the payment of his debts, he is punishable under Section 321 with imprisonment up to two years. [Source: Section 321, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 321: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

Q: Does this section apply if a person fraudulently prevents a debt due to a friend from being used to pay that friend's creditors?
A: Yes, the section covers preventing a debt due "to himself or to any other person" from being made available for the payment of his debts "or the debts of such other person." [Source: Section 321, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 321: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

Q: A creditor tries to collect a debt from a man, but the man genuinely believes the debt is legally invalid and disputes it in court, preventing its collection. Is he guilty under Section 321?
A: No, because legitimately disputing a debt in a legal forum is not acting "dishonestly or fraudulently." [Source: Section 321, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 321: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing the obstruction of debt collection under this section?
A: The consequence is that the law closes a loophole where a debtor might appear bankrupt while secretly hoarding receivables, ensuring that all liquid assets are fairly distributed to legitimate creditors. [Source: Section 321, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly or fraudulently preventing debt being available for creditors

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 322: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

Q: What happens if you sign a property deed that falsely states how much money was paid, in order to commit fraud?
A: Dishonestly executing or signing a property transfer deed that contains a false statement about the consideration (price paid) or the true beneficiary is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 322, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 322: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

Q: What does Section 322 of BNS 2023 say about fraudulent property deeds?
A: Section 322 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment or a fine on anyone who dishonestly/fraudulently executes or becomes a party to a deed transferring property, if it contains false statements about the consideration or the true beneficiary. [Source: Section 322, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 322: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

Q: Two men execute a deed selling a piece of land. They secretly agree the actual price is 50 lakh rupees, but to evade taxes and defraud the government, they falsely state in the deed that the consideration is only 10 lakh rupees. What is their offence?
A: Because they dishonestly became parties to a deed of transfer containing a false statement relating to the consideration, they are punishable under Section 322 with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 322, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 322: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

Q: What specific falsehoods in a deed trigger this section?
A: The section specifically targets false statements "relating to the consideration for such transfer or charge" or "relating to the person or persons for whose use or benefit it is really intended to operate" (such as a benami transaction). [Source: Section 322, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 322: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

Q: A clerk at the registry office inadvertently types the wrong purchase price on a deed due to a typo, and the parties sign it without noticing. Are they guilty under Section 322?
A: No, because the false statement was not included "dishonestly or fraudulently," but merely by accident, lacking the required criminal intent. [Source: Section 322, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 322: Dishonest or fraudulent execution of deed of transfer containing false statement of consideration

Q: What is the legal consequence of enforcing Section 322?
A: The consequence is that the state protects public records, tax revenues, and third-party rights by ensuring that legal instruments of transfer accurately reflect the true financial reality and identity of the parties involved. [Source: Section 322, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 323: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

Q: What is the penalty for simply hiding your own property to commit a fraud?
A: Dishonestly or fraudulently concealing or removing any property—whether yours or someone else's—or fraudulently releasing a claim you are entitled to, is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 323, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 323: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

Q: How does Section 323 of BNS 2023 penalize fraudulent property concealment?
A: Section 323 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 3 years imprisonment or a fine for whoever dishonestly or fraudulently conceals or removes any property (of themselves or another), or dishonestly releases any claim they are entitled to. [Source: Section 323, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 323: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

Q: A man is facing a massive civil lawsuit for damages. Anticipating he will lose, he systematically moves his valuable artwork and gold out of his house and hides them in a remote storage locker under a fake name to prevent seizure. What is his offence?
A: Because he dishonestly concealed and removed his own property to defraud potential judgment creditors, he is punishable under Section 323 with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 323, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 323: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

Q: Does Section 323 apply to forgiving a debt?
A: Yes, if a person "dishonestly releases any demand or claim to which he is entitled" (like forgiving a debt just so creditors cannot seize the receivable), it constitutes an offence under this section. [Source: Section 323, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 323: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

Q: A person moves their expensive jewelry into a hidden safe in their basement purely to protect it from local burglars. Are they guilty under Section 323?
A: No, because concealing property to protect it from theft is a lawful act of security; it is not done "dishonestly or fraudulently." [Source: Section 323, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 323: Dishonest or fraudulent removal or concealment of property

Q: What is the consequence of this broad provision against property concealment?
A: The consequence is that it provides a versatile legal tool to prosecute various forms of asset-hiding and sham transactions that don't neatly fit into standard theft or bankruptcy fraud, ensuring debtors cannot manipulate their apparent net worth. [Source: Section 323, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 324: Mischief

Q: How does the law define "mischief" or vandalism against someone else's property?
A: Mischief involves causing the destruction of property, or changing its situation to destroy or diminish its value or utility, with the intent (or knowledge) of causing wrongful loss or damage. Punishments scale from six months for minor damage to five years for damage over one lakh rupees or if preparation for violence was made. [Source: Section 324, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 324: Mischief

Q: What are the elements and penalties of Mischief under Section 324 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 324 of BNS 2023 defines mischief as destroying or diminishing the value of property to cause wrongful loss. Penalties depend on damage value: up to 6 months (base), up to 1 year (government property), up to 2 years (20,000–1,00,000 rupees), up to 5 years (over 1 lakh rupees, or if prepared for violence). [Source: Section 324, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 324: Mischief

Q: Out of spite, a man sneaks onto his neighbor's farm and deliberately cuts down several expensive fruit-bearing trees, causing 50,000 rupees in damage. What is his offence?
A: Because he caused a change in the property that diminished its value, intending to cause wrongful loss, he has committed mischief. Since the damage is between twenty thousand and one lakh rupees, he faces up to two years imprisonment under Section 324. [Source: Section 324, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 324: Mischief

Q: Can a person commit mischief by destroying their own property?
A: Yes, Explanation 2 and Illustration (d) clarify that mischief can be committed by an act affecting property belonging to the offender themselves, such as destroying their own assets to prevent a creditor from seizing them. [Source: Section 324, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 324: Mischief

Q: A person accidentally backs their car into a neighbor's fence, causing severe damage. Have they committed mischief?
A: No, because mischief requires the specific "intent to cause, or knowing that he is likely to cause, wrongful loss or damage." Pure accidents lack this mental element. [Source: Section 324, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 324: Mischief

Q: What is the consequence of scaling the punishment for mischief based on the monetary value of the damage?
A: The consequence is a proportionate justice system where petty vandalism (like breaking a window) receives minor penalties, while catastrophic sabotage (like destroying highly valuable industrial equipment) is treated as a severe felony. [Source: Section 324, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 325: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

Q: What is the penalty for intentionally killing or severely injuring an animal to cause damage?
A: Committing mischief by killing, poisoning, maiming, or rendering useless any animal is punishable by up to five years in prison, or a fine, or both. [Source: Section 325, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 325: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

Q: How does Section 325 of BNS 2023 address violence against animals as mischief?
A: Section 325 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment of up to 5 years, or a fine, or both, on whoever commits mischief by killing, poisoning, maiming, or rendering useless any animal. [Source: Section 325, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 325: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

Q: A farmer is angry at a rival and deliberately throws poisoned meat over the fence, which the rival's expensive guard dog eats and dies from. What specific offence has the farmer committed?
A: Because he committed mischief (intending wrongful loss) by poisoning and killing an animal, he is punishable under Section 325 with imprisonment up to five years. [Source: Section 325, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 325: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

Q: Does Section 325 apply only to highly valuable or specific types of animals like cattle or elephants?
A: No, the language of the section is broad and applies to "any animal," regardless of its specific monetary value or species, as long as the act constitutes mischief. [Source: Section 325, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 325: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

Q: A veterinarian legally euthanizes an incurably sick horse to end its suffering, at the owner's request. Is the vet guilty under Section 325?
A: No, because the act was done lawfully, with consent, and without the intent to cause "wrongful loss or damage," meaning it does not fulfill the foundational definition of mischief required for this section. [Source: Section 325, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 325: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

Q: What is the consequence of imposing a harsh five-year penalty for this specific type of mischief?
A: The consequence is that the law recognizes the unique cruelty of harming living creatures as a form of vandalism, providing strong deterrence against inflicting suffering on animals merely to spite their human owners. [Source: Section 325, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by killing or maiming animal

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 326: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

Q: What are the penalties for large-scale vandalism like destroying public infrastructure, water supplies, or committing arson?
A: Section 326 addresses severe forms of mischief. Damaging water supplies, public roads, or causing inundations carries up to five years in prison. Tampering with navigation signals or committing arson carries up to seven years. Arson involving a place of worship or human dwelling is punishable by up to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 326, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 326: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

Q: How does Section 326 of BNS 2023 classify aggravated mischief regarding infrastructure and fire?
A: Section 326 of BNS 2023 scales penalties for severe mischief: 5 years for affecting water supplies, roads, or causing inundations; 7 years for damaging navigation signals or using fire/explosives to damage property; and life imprisonment or 10 years for arson against a dwelling or place of worship. [Source: Section 326, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 326: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

Q: During a protest, a rioter throws a crude firebomb into an occupied residential apartment block, intending to burn it down. The fire is quickly extinguished. What is the maximum penalty the rioter faces?
A: Because he committed mischief using an explosive substance intending to cause the destruction of a building used as a human dwelling, he is punishable under Section 326 with imprisonment for life, or up to ten years, and a fine. [Source: Section 326, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 326: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

Q: Does tampering with a lighthouse signal fall under this section?
A: Yes, clause (d) explicitly covers "destroying or moving any sign or signal used for navigation... or other thing placed as a guide for navigators," punishable by up to seven years. [Source: Section 326, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 326: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

Q: A farmer accidentally leaves a tractor parked on a public dirt road, temporarily making it impassable for a few hours. Is he guilty of mischief under Section 326(b)?
A: No, because mischief requires the specific criminal intent or knowledge to cause wrongful loss/damage. Merely accidental or negligent obstruction is not "mischief" under this section. [Source: Section 326, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 326: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

Q: What is the consequence of prescribing life imprisonment for arson involving human dwellings?
A: The consequence is that the state treats the intentional burning of homes as a near-capital offence, recognizing that it not only destroys property but poses a catastrophic and uncontrollable risk to human life. [Source: Section 326, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief by injury, inundation, fire or explosive substance, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 327: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

Q: What happens if someone tries to derail a train, sabotage an airplane, or sink a large ship?
A: Committing mischief with the intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, or large vessel (over 20 tons) is punishable by up to ten years in prison. If the sabotage involves fire or explosives, the penalty increases to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 327, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 327: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

Q: What are the penalties for sabotaging major transport under Section 327 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 327 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 10 years imprisonment and a fine for mischief intending to destroy or render unsafe any rail, aircraft, or vessel over 20 tons. If fire or explosives are used in the attempt, it is punishable by life imprisonment or up to 10 years. [Source: Section 327, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 327: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

Q: A terrorist sneaks onto an airport tarmac and plants a small explosive charge on the landing gear of a commercial aircraft, intending to cause a crash upon takeoff. What is his specific offence?
A: Because he attempted to commit mischief by an explosive substance to destroy or render unsafe an aircraft, he is punishable under Section 327 with imprisonment for life, or up to ten years. [Source: Section 327, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 327: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

Q: Does Section 327 apply if someone sabotages a small, 5-ton recreational rowboat without a deck?
A: No, the section specifically applies to a "decked vessel or any vessel of a burden of twenty tons or upwards," so a small, undecked 5-ton boat would fall under general mischief, not this aggravated section. [Source: Section 327, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 327: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

Q: A railway maintenance worker negligently fails to tighten a bolt on a rail track, making it unsafe for trains. Is he guilty under Section 327?
A: No, because the section requires "intending to destroy or render unsafe, or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby destroy or render unsafe." Negligence without intent or active knowledge of likelihood does not constitute mischief. [Source: Section 327, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 327: Mischief with intent to destroy or make unsafe a rail, aircraft, decked vessel or one of twenty tons burden

Q: What is the consequence of imposing life imprisonment for explosive sabotage against major transport?
A: The consequence is maximum deterrence against mass-casualty terrorism; the law recognizes that fire or explosives on trains, planes, or large ships inevitably endanger dozens or hundreds of lives simultaneously. [Source: Section 327, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 328: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

Q: What is the penalty for intentionally crashing a ship so that you can steal its cargo?
A: Intentionally running a vessel aground or ashore with the intent to commit theft or misappropriate the property on board is a serious offence punishable by up to ten years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 328, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 328: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

Q: How does Section 328 of BNS 2023 address maritime theft?
A: Section 328 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 10 years and a fine on whoever intentionally runs any vessel aground or ashore, intending to commit theft or dishonest misappropriation of the property contained therein. [Source: Section 328, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 328: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

Q: A cargo ship captain is bribed by a local pirate gang. He deliberately steers his ship onto a reef near the coast so that the pirates can board the stranded vessel and steal the shipping containers. What is his penalty?
A: Because he intentionally ran the vessel aground with the intent that theft of the property contained therein may be committed, he is punishable under Section 328 with imprisonment up to ten years. [Source: Section 328, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 328: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

Q: Is the actual theft required to be completed for an offender to be guilty under Section 328?
A: No, the offence is complete when the vessel is intentionally run aground "intending to commit theft" or "with intent that such theft... may be committed," even if the thieves are caught before taking anything. [Source: Section 328, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 328: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

Q: A captain intentionally beaches his sinking ship on a sandy shore to prevent it from going down in deep water and to save the lives of the crew and the cargo. Is he guilty?
A: No, because his intent was to save lives and preserve property, not to "commit theft" or "dishonestly misappropriate" the cargo. [Source: Section 328, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 328: Punishment for intentionally running vessel aground or ashore with intent to commit theft, etc.

Q: What is the legal consequence of establishing a specific offence for running a vessel aground for theft?
A: The consequence is that the law specifically combats organized maritime crimes like "wrecking" or insider piracy, where the navigational control of the ship itself is weaponized to facilitate massive cargo theft. [Source: Section 328, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 329: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

Q: What is the legal definition of trespassing on someone else's property or breaking into their home?
A: Criminal trespass is entering or remaining on someone's property to commit an offence, intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor. If this trespass occurs in a building, tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling or for worship/custody of property, it is called "house-trespass," carrying a higher penalty. [Source: Section 329, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 329: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

Q: How does Section 329 of BNS 2023 define and punish trespass?
A: Section 329 of BNS 2023 defines criminal trespass (entering/remaining on property to commit an offence, intimidate, or annoy) and house-trespass (trespassing in a human dwelling, place of worship, or property custody). Criminal trespass carries up to 3 months imprisonment, while house-trespass carries up to 1 year. [Source: Section 329, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 329: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

Q: A disgruntled former employee storms into his old boss's private office, refusing to leave, and continuously shouts insults and threats at the boss to annoy and intimidate him. What is his offence?
A: Because he entered property in the possession of another with the intent to intimidate, insult, or annoy the person in possession, he has committed criminal trespass under Section 329. [Source: Section 329, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 329: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

Q: Does a person have to walk entirely inside a house to be guilty of house-trespass?
A: No, the Explanation to Section 329 clearly states that "The introduction of any part of the criminal trespasser’s body is entering sufficient to constitute house-trespass." [Source: Section 329, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 329: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

Q: A lost hiker wanders onto a farmer's large, unmarked private field seeking directions. He means no harm and leaves when asked. Is he guilty of criminal trespass?
A: No, because he did not enter with the "intent to commit an offence or to intimidate, insult or annoy any person." He merely made an innocent mistake. [Source: Section 329, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 329: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

Q: What is the consequence of distinguishing "house-trespass" from general "criminal trespass"?
A: The consequence is that the law affords a much higher degree of protection and a stricter penalty (up to one year instead of three months) for violations of the sanctity, privacy, and security of a person's home or place of worship. [Source: Section 329, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal trespass and house-trespass

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 330: House-trespass and house-breaking

Q: What is the difference between simply trespassing in a house and the more serious crime of house-breaking?
A: House-breaking occurs when a trespasser forces entry or exit using specific methods, such as making a hole in a wall, scaling a wall, picking a lock, using criminal force, or entering through a passage not meant for human entrance. [Source: Section 330, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass and house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 330: House-trespass and house-breaking

Q: What constitutes house-breaking under Section 330 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 330 of BNS 2023 defines house-breaking as committing house-trespass by entering or quitting through six specific means: a self-made passage, scaling a wall, opening a closed passage, opening a lock, using criminal force/assault, or unfastening a secured entrance. [Source: Section 330, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass and house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 330: House-trespass and house-breaking

Q: A thief wants to steal from a house. He finds that the front door is securely locked, so he uses a crowbar to pry the lock off, opens the door, and steps inside. What specific legal offence is this?
A: Because he committed house-trespass and effected his entrance by opening a lock in order to commit the trespass, he has committed house-breaking under Section 330. [Source: Section 330, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass and house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 330: House-trespass and house-breaking

Q: If a trespasser enters a house lawfully through an open door, but then steals something and leaves by breaking open a locked back window, is that house-breaking?
A: Yes, Section 330 states that a person commits house-breaking if, having committed an offence therein, "he quits the house or any part of it" by opening a lock or unfastening a fastened passage. [Source: Section 330, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass and house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 330: House-trespass and house-breaking

Q: A man walks through an open front door into his neighbor's house uninvited to angrily yell at him. He enters and leaves through the open door without touching any locks, walls, or forcing past anyone. Has he committed house-breaking?
A: No, he has committed house-trespass, but because he did not use any of the six specific forced or unnatural methods of entry/exit listed in Section 330, it does not escalate to house-breaking. [Source: Section 330, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass and house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 330: House-trespass and house-breaking

Q: What is the consequence of strictly defining the six methods of house-breaking?
A: The consequence is that the law distinguishes between mere unlawful presence (trespass) and the aggressive, calculated circumvention of a homeowner's physical security measures, allowing for appropriately harsher penalties for burglars who defeat locks or break walls. [Source: Section 330, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass and house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 331: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

Q: What are the general penalties for breaking into someone's house, and how do they change if the crime happens at night?
A: House-breaking is punishable by up to two years in prison. However, if committed after sunset and before sunrise, the penalty increases to three years. If the intent is to commit theft, it extends to ten years (or fourteen years if at night). [Source: Section 331, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 331: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

Q: How does Section 331 of BNS 2023 scale punishments for house-trespass and house-breaking?
A: Section 331 of BNS 2023 scales penalties based on timing and intent: Base penalty is up to 2 years; night-time is 3 years. Intent to commit theft carries up to 10 years (14 years at night). Preparation for violence carries up to 10 years (14 at night), and causing grievous hurt carries up to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 331, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 331: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

Q: A burglar breaks into a house at 2:00 AM with the specific intention of stealing a safe. He is caught before taking anything. What is the maximum penalty he faces?
A: Because he committed house-breaking after sunset and before sunrise in order to commit theft, he is punishable under Section 331(4) with imprisonment of up to fourteen years. [Source: Section 331, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 331: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

Q: If a group of three burglars break into a house at night, and one of them unexpectedly stabs the homeowner, are the other two liable for the violence?
A: Yes, sub-section (8) states that if any person jointly concerned in committing night-time house-breaking causes grievous hurt or death, every person jointly concerned shall be punished with life imprisonment or up to ten years. [Source: Section 331, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 331: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

Q: A man breaks into his ex-girlfriend's apartment during the day to secretly retrieve a sweater he believes belongs to him, but she catches him and he runs away peacefully. Can he be charged with the maximum 14-year penalty?
A: No, the 14-year penalty applies only to night-time house-breaking with intent to commit theft, or with preparation for hurt. A daytime break-in without violence or major theft intent carries a lower base penalty under this section. [Source: Section 331, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 331: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

Q: What is the consequence of imposing severe night-time ("after sunset and before sunrise") enhancements for burglary?
A: The consequence is that the law provides maximum deterrence against nocturnal home invasions, recognizing that nighttime break-ins cause profound psychological terror and drastically increase the likelihood of violent, fatal confrontations in the dark. [Source: Section 331, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Punishment for house-trespass or house-breaking

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 332: House-trespass in order to commit offence

Q: What is the penalty for trespassing into a house with the intent to commit a very serious crime, like murder or rape?
A: If house-trespass is committed with the intent to commit an offence punishable by death, the trespass itself is punishable by life imprisonment or up to ten years. If the intended offence is punishable by life imprisonment, the trespass carries up to ten years. [Source: Section 332, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass in order to commit offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 332: House-trespass in order to commit offence

Q: How does Section 332 of BNS 2023 penalize house-trespass based on the severity of the intended offence?
A: Section 332 of BNS 2023 links the trespass penalty to the intended crime: intent to commit a capital offence carries life or up to 10 years; intent for a life-imprisonment offence carries up to 10 years; intent for an imprisonment offence carries up to 2 years (or 7 years if the intent is theft). [Source: Section 332, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass in order to commit offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 332: House-trespass in order to commit offence

Q: An assassin walks through an unlocked door into a victim's house, intending to murder him, but the victim is not home and the police arrest the assassin waiting inside. What is the penalty for the trespass?
A: Because he committed house-trespass in order to commit an offence punishable with death (murder), he is punishable under Section 332 with imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to ten years. [Source: Section 332, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass in order to commit offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 332: House-trespass in order to commit offence

Q: If someone trespasses to commit a minor offence punishable only by a fine, does Section 332 apply?
A: No, Section 332 explicitly categorizes the intended offences as those "punishable with death," "punishable with imprisonment for life," or "punishable with imprisonment." It does not provide an enhanced tier for fine-only offences. [Source: Section 332, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass in order to commit offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 332: House-trespass in order to commit offence

Q: A man trespasses into a house intending to commit theft, but changes his mind and leaves without taking anything. Is he immune from punishment under Section 332?
A: No, the offence is complete upon the trespass "in order to the committing" of the offence. The specific intent to commit theft allows for the imprisonment to be extended to seven years, even if the theft was aborted. [Source: Section 332, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass in order to commit offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 332: House-trespass in order to commit offence

Q: What is the consequence of linking the penalty of the trespass to the intended crime?
A: The consequence is a preventive justice framework where the law severely punishes the dangerous preliminary step (the home invasion) based on the catastrophic harm the offender intended to inflict, allowing intervention before the primary crime occurs. [Source: Section 332, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass in order to commit offence

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 333: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

Q: What happens if someone trespasses into your house carrying weapons or tools meant to tie you up or hurt you?
A: Committing house-trespass after making preparations to cause hurt, assault, or wrongfully restrain anyone inside is punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 333, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 333: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

Q: What is the provision for armed or prepared house-trespass under Section 333 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 333 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine on whoever commits house-trespass having made preparation for causing hurt, assault, wrongful restraint, or putting someone in fear of such acts. [Source: Section 333, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 333: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

Q: An angry ex-business partner trespasses into a man's home carrying handcuffs and a baton, intending to hold the man hostage to extort money. He is stopped in the hallway. What is his specific offence?
A: Because he committed house-trespass having made preparation for wrongfully restraining and assaulting a person, he is punishable under Section 333 with imprisonment up to seven years. [Source: Section 333, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 333: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

Q: Does the trespasser actually have to hurt someone for this section to apply?
A: No, the section penalizes the trespass committed "having made preparation" for hurt or restraint. The actual infliction of violence is not required to trigger this seven-year penalty. [Source: Section 333, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 333: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

Q: A man trespasses into a house completely unarmed and without any means to restrain anyone, simply intending to sleep on the couch. Can he be charged under Section 333?
A: No, because he did not make "preparation for causing hurt... or for wrongfully restraining any person." He would face lower penalties for simple house-trespass instead. [Source: Section 333, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 333: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

Q: What is the consequence of specifically criminalizing the "preparation" for violence during a home invasion?
A: The consequence is that it empowers law enforcement to neutralize highly dangerous, premeditated threats (like armed home invaders) with severe penalties the moment they cross the threshold, rather than waiting for them to actually attack the occupants. [Source: Section 333, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: House-trespass after preparation for hurt, assault or wrongful restraint

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 334: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

Q: What is the penalty for breaking open a locked box, safe, or container to steal or damage what's inside?
A: Dishonestly breaking open or unfastening any closed receptacle (like a safe or locked box) believed to contain property is punishable by up to two years in prison. If the person was entrusted with the receptacle, the penalty increases to three years. [Source: Section 334, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 334: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

Q: How does Section 334 of BNS 2023 penalize breaking open property receptacles?
A: Section 334 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 2 years imprisonment for dishonestly breaking open a closed receptacle believed to contain property. The punishment increases to 3 years if the offender was entrusted with the receptacle but lacked authority to open it. [Source: Section 334, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 334: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

Q: A courier is hired to deliver a locked briefcase to a bank. Curious and greedy, he uses a screwdriver to force open the locks during transit to see if there is cash inside, though he finds only documents. What is his penalty?
A: Because he was entrusted with a closed receptacle and dishonestly broke it open without authority, he is punishable under Section 334(2) with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 334, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 334: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

Q: Does the receptacle actually have to contain valuable property for the offence to be committed?
A: No, the section applies if the receptacle contains "or which he believes to contain property." The offender's belief that there is property inside is sufficient. [Source: Section 334, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 334: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

Q: A homeowner loses the key to his own safe and uses a crowbar to break it open to retrieve his passport. Is he guilty under Section 334?
A: No, because breaking open his own safe is done lawfully and with authority; it is not done "dishonestly or with intent to commit mischief." [Source: Section 334, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 334: Dishonestly breaking open receptacle containing property

Q: What is the legal consequence of creating a specific offence for breaking receptacles?
A: The consequence is that it provides a direct legal remedy against the violation of physical security measures (like tampering with safes, lockers, or sealed cargo), independent of whether a theft is actually completed or whether the container held anything valuable. [Source: Section 334, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 335: Making a false document

Q: What constitutes "forgery" or making a fake legal document or electronic record?
A: Making a false document (forgery) involves dishonestly creating, signing, or altering a document or electronic record with the intent to make people believe it was authorized by someone who didn't actually authorize it, or secretly altering a document after it was signed. [Source: Section 335, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false document

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 335: Making a false document

Q: What are the elements of making a false document under Section 335 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 335 of BNS 2023 defines making a false document/electronic record as: (A) dishonestly executing/signing it to falsely appear authorized; (B) unlawfully altering a material part after execution; or (C) causing an intoxicated, unsound, or deceived person to sign/alter it without knowing the contents. [Source: Section 335, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false document

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 335: Making a false document

Q: An accountant is given a pre-signed blank cheque by his boss to pay a vendor 5,000 rupees. The accountant secretly fills in "50,000 rupees" and cashes it himself. Has he committed forgery?
A: Yes, by filling up the cheque without authority for a fraudulent amount, he has unlawfully altered a document in a material part, thus making a false document under Section 335. [Source: Section 335, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false document

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 335: Making a false document

Q: Can a person commit forgery by signing their own real name?
A: Yes, Explanation 1 clarifies that "A man’s signature of his own name may amount to forgery," such as signing a bill of exchange intending people to believe it was signed by a different person who happens to share the exact same name. [Source: Section 335, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false document

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 335: Making a false document

Q: A secretary notices a minor spelling error in a client's name on a contract and corrects the typo in pen before filing it, without any intent to defraud anyone. Is this forgery?
A: No, because the alteration was not done "dishonestly or fraudulently," and a minor spelling correction may not constitute a "material part" alteration intended to deceive. [Source: Section 335, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false document

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 335: Making a false document

Q: What is the consequence of explicitly including electronic records and signatures in the definition of a false document?
A: The consequence is that the law modernizes fraud prosecution, ensuring that cybercrimes involving digital contracts, emails, and cryptographic signatures are punished just as severely as traditional paper forgery. [Source: Section 335, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false document

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 336: Forgery

Q: What are the base penalties for committing forgery, such as faking a signature to claim property?
A: Forgery is generally punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. However, if the forgery is done with the intent to cheat, the penalty increases to up to seven years. If it is done to harm someone's reputation, it is punishable by up to three years. [Source: Section 336, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 336: Forgery

Q: What is the punishment scheme for forgery outlined in Section 336 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 336 of BNS 2023 prescribes up to 2 years imprisonment for basic forgery. If intended for cheating, the punishment extends to 7 years. If intended to harm someone's reputation, it extends to 3 years. [Source: Section 336, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 336: Forgery

Q: A student fakes a university degree certificate and submits it to a company during a job interview, intending to cheat the employer into hiring him. What is his specific penalty?
A: Because he committed forgery intending that the forged document be used for the purpose of cheating, he is punishable under Section 336(3) with imprisonment up to seven years. [Source: Section 336, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 336: Forgery

Q: If a person forges a scandalous letter in their rival's name purely to ruin their rival's political career, what subsection of forgery applies?
A: Sub-section (4) applies, because the forgery was committed intending that the document shall harm the reputation of a party, making it punishable by up to three years in prison. [Source: Section 336, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 336: Forgery

Q: A man writes a joke contract promising to give his friend the moon, signing it as the President, purely for a comedy sketch. Everyone knows it is fake. Has he committed forgery?
A: No, because he did not make the document "with intent to cause damage or injury... or to support any claim or title... or with intent to commit fraud." Lacking fraudulent intent, it is not forgery. [Source: Section 336, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 336: Forgery

Q: What is the consequence of having different penalty tiers for forgery in Section 336?
A: The consequence is that the law scales the punishment based on the specific harm intended: financial fraud (cheating) is punished most severely, reputation harm is moderate, and general or minor forgery receives the baseline penalty. [Source: Section 336, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 337: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

Q: What is the penalty for forging government documents, like an Aadhaar card, a court order, or a marriage certificate?
A: Forging a court record, government identity document (like Aadhaar or voter ID), public register (birth, marriage), or a document made by a public servant is a serious offence punishable by up to seven years in prison and a fine. [Source: Section 337, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 337: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

Q: How does Section 337 of BNS 2023 penalize the forgery of public records?
A: Section 337 of BNS 2023 imposes imprisonment up to 7 years and a fine on whoever forges court records, government identity documents (Aadhaar/Voter ID), public registers (birth/marriage), or official public servant certificates. [Source: Section 337, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 337: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

Q: A man wants to hide his criminal past to get a visa, so he uses photo-editing software to forge a clean police clearance certificate, making it look like it was issued by the local police commissioner. What is his offence?
A: Because he forged a document purporting to be a certificate made by a public servant in his official capacity, he is punishable under Section 337 with imprisonment up to seven years. [Source: Section 337, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 337: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

Q: Does this section cover digital databases, like altering a government database to add a fake birth entry?
A: Yes, the Explanation clarifies that "register" includes any "list, data or record of any entries maintained in the electronic form," so forging an electronic public register falls under this section. [Source: Section 337, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 337: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

Q: A student makes a clearly fake, oversized Aadhaar card out of cardboard for a school play. Is he guilty under Section 337?
A: No, because it lacks the fraudulent intent required for forgery; it is not "purporting to be" a real identity document intended to deceive anyone into accepting it as genuine. [Source: Section 337, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 337: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

Q: What is the consequence of strictly penalizing the forgery of public registers and IDs?
A: The consequence is that it protects the foundation of the state's administrative and judicial systems, ensuring that citizens and institutions can trust the authenticity of court orders, identities, and vital statistics. [Source: Section 337, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of record of Court or of public register, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 338: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

Q: What is the penalty for forging high-value financial documents like a will or a property deed?
A: Forging a valuable security, a will, an authority to adopt, or receipts acknowledging the payment of money or delivery of property is heavily punished, carrying life imprisonment or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 338, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 338: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

Q: How does Section 338 of BNS 2023 address the forgery of wills and valuable securities?
A: Section 338 of BNS 2023 imposes life imprisonment or up to 10 years imprisonment on whoever forges a valuable security, a will, an authority to transfer property/money, or receipts acknowledging payment/delivery of property. [Source: Section 338, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 338: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

Q: A greedy nephew finds his wealthy aunt's valid will, which leaves everything to charity. He perfectly forges a new will, dating it later than the real one, leaving her entire estate to himself. What is his penalty?
A: Because he forged a document which purports to be a will, he is punishable under Section 338 with imprisonment for life, or up to ten years in prison. [Source: Section 338, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 338: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

Q: Does forging a fake rent receipt to claim a tax deduction fall under Section 338?
A: Yes, because it is a "document purporting to be an acquittance or receipt acknowledging the payment of money," making its forgery punishable under this severe section. [Source: Section 338, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 338: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

Q: A lawyer drafts a template will for a client but leaves it unsigned. Is this draft a forged will?
A: No, because drafting a document with authorization without any false signatures or fraudulent alterations does not constitute "making a false document" or forgery. [Source: Section 338, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 338: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

Q: What is the consequence of treating the forgery of wills and securities so harshly?
A: The consequence is maximum deterrence against sophisticated financial crimes that can instantly transfer massive amounts of wealth or irrevocably alter inheritance rights, causing devastating economic harm to the rightful owners. [Source: Section 338, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 339: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

Q: What is the penalty if you haven't forged a document yourself, but you possess a fake Aadhaar card or forged will intending to use it?
A: Possessing a forged public document (like an ID or court record) with the intent to use it fraudulently is punishable by up to seven years in prison. If you possess a forged valuable security or will, the penalty increases to life imprisonment or up to seven years. [Source: Section 339, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 339: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

Q: How does Section 339 of BNS 2023 penalize the possession of specific forged documents?
A: Section 339 of BNS 2023 penalizes possessing a forged document knowing it is forged and intending to use it. Possession of forged public records (Section 337) carries up to 7 years. Possession of forged wills/valuable securities (Section 338) carries life imprisonment or up to 7 years. [Source: Section 339, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 339: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

Q: Police raid a fraudster's house and find a stack of forged property deeds (valuable securities) in his safe. He hadn't used them yet, but he planned to sell them to unsuspecting buyers. What is his offence?
A: Because he had possession of documents described in Section 338 knowing they were forged and intending to use them fraudulently as genuine, he is punishable under Section 339 with life imprisonment or up to seven years. [Source: Section 339, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 339: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

Q: If a person possesses a forged birth certificate but does not know it is fake, can they be punished under Section 339?
A: No, the section strictly requires that the person has possession "knowing the same to be forged and intending that the same shall fraudulently or dishonestly be used." Innocent possession is not a crime. [Source: Section 339, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 339: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

Q: A police detective seizes a forged voter ID card as evidence in a case and keeps it in his desk to present in court. Is the detective guilty?
A: No, because while he knows it is forged, he does not have the intent "that the same shall fraudulently or dishonestly be used as genuine." He is holding it lawfully. [Source: Section 339, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 339: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing the mere possession of these specific forged documents?
A: The consequence is that law enforcement can prosecute counterfeiters, document traffickers, and fraudsters before they successfully execute their scams, intervening while they are holding the tools of their intended fraud. [Source: Section 339, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Having possession of document described in section 337 or section 338, knowing it to be forged and intending to use it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 340: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

Q: What is the penalty for actually using a forged document to trick someone?
A: A document made wholly or partly by forgery is a "forged document." Anyone who fraudulently or dishonestly uses a document they know is forged as if it were genuine is punished exactly as if they had committed the forgery themselves. [Source: Section 340, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 340: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

Q: How does Section 340 of BNS 2023 treat the usage of forged documents?
A: Section 340 of BNS 2023 defines a "forged document" and states that whoever fraudulently/dishonestly uses as genuine a document they know (or have reason to believe) is forged, shall be punished in the same manner as if they had forged it themselves. [Source: Section 340, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 340: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

Q: A man buys a fake university degree from a counterfeiter. He then submits it to a government agency to secure a high-paying job. He didn't make the fake degree, but what is his penalty?
A: Because he fraudulently used as genuine a document he knew was forged, he is punishable under Section 340 in the exact same manner as if he had forged the document himself (which, depending on the document type and intent, dictates the penalty). [Source: Section 340, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 340: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

Q: If a person uses a partially altered electronic record, does this count as using a forged document?
A: Yes, sub-section (1) clarifies that "A false document or electronic record made wholly or in part by forgery is designated a forged document or electronic record." [Source: Section 340, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 340: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

Q: A bank teller receives a forged cheque from a customer. Unaware that it is fake, the teller processes it and hands over the cash. Is the teller guilty under Section 340?
A: No, because the teller did not know or have "reason to believe to be a forged document." The fraudulent use requires knowledge or reasonable belief of the forgery. [Source: Section 340, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 340: Forged document or electronic record and using it as genuine

Q: What is the consequence of punishing the user of a forged document the same as the forger?
A: The consequence is that it eliminates the loophole where a person who commissions a forgery but does not physically make it could escape harsh punishment, treating the execution of the fraud as equally culpable as its preparation. [Source: Section 340, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 341: Making or possessing counterfeit seal, etc., with intent to commit forgery punishable under section 338

Q: What is the penalty for making or owning fake seals or plates used to forge documents?
A: Making or possessing counterfeit seals, plates, or instruments intending to use them for forgery is punishable by up to seven years in prison. If the intended forgery involves valuable securities or wills (Section 338), the penalty can escalate to life imprisonment. Merely possessing them knowingly without specific intent carries up to three years. [Source: Section 341, BNS 2023]

A: Section 341 of BNS 2023 penalizes making/possessing counterfeit seals or plates intended for forgery. Forging valuable securities/wills (Section 338) carries life or up to 7 years. Forging other documents carries up to 7 years. Mere knowing possession without specific intent carries up to 3 years. Fraudulent use is punished identically to making them. [Source: Section 341, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the penalty for faking watermarks or authentication devices on paper or other materials?
A: Counterfeiting any device or mark (like a watermark) used to authenticate documents on any material, or possessing material with such fake marks, is punishable by up to seven years in prison. If the mark is meant for valuable securities or wills, the penalty can extend to life imprisonment. [Source: Section 342, BNS 2023]

A: Section 342 of BNS 2023 penalizes counterfeiting marks/devices used for authentication on any material, or possessing such material. Marks for valuable securities/wills (Section 338) carry life or up to 7 years imprisonment. Marks for other documents carry up to 7 years. [Source: Section 342, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 343: Fraudulent cancellation, destruction, etc., of will, authority to adopt, or valuable security

Q: What happens if you intentionally destroy or hide someone else's will or financial documents to cause them financial harm?
A: Fraudulently destroying, canceling, defacing, or hiding a will, an authority to adopt, or a valuable security to cause damage or injury is a severe crime punishable by life imprisonment or up to seven years in prison. [Source: Section 343, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent cancellation, destruction, etc., of will, authority to adopt, or valuable security

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 343: Fraudulent cancellation, destruction, etc., of will, authority to adopt, or valuable security

Q: What are the provisions for destroying valuable documents under Section 343 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 343 of BNS 2023 imposes life imprisonment or up to 7 years imprisonment on whoever fraudulently/dishonestly destroys, cancels, defaces, secretes, or commits mischief regarding a will, authority to adopt, or valuable security, intending to cause damage. [Source: Section 343, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent cancellation, destruction, etc., of will, authority to adopt, or valuable security

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 343: Fraudulent cancellation, destruction, etc., of will, authority to adopt, or valuable security

Q: A greedy sibling discovers their parent's latest will, which leaves the family home to a younger brother. The sibling sneaks into the study, shreds the document, and burns the pieces to ensure the property is divided equally under intestate law. What is their penalty?
A: Because the sibling fraudulently destroyed a document purporting to be a will with intent to cause damage to the younger brother, they are punishable under Section 343 with imprisonment for life, or up to seven years. [Source: Section 343, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Fraudulent cancellation, destruction, etc., of will, authority to adopt, or valuable security

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 343: Fraudulent cancellation, destruction, etc., of will, authority to adopt, or valuable security

Q: If someone merely hides a property deed behind a bookshelf so the owner can't find it to sell the property, does this count?
A: Yes, the section covers anyone who "secretes or attempts to secrete" any valuable security with intent to cause damage or injury, making the act of hiding it punishable. [Source: Section 343, BNS 2023]

Q: A person mistakenly believes an old, canceled property deed is scrap paper and throws it into the recycling bin. Are they guilty under Section 343?
A: No, because the act was done mistakenly, not "fraudulently or dishonestly, or with intent to cause damage or injury." It lacks the requisite criminal mens rea. [Source: Section 343, BNS 2023]

Q: What is the consequence of imposing life imprisonment for the destruction of a will or security?
A: The consequence is that the law treats the malicious destruction of these documents as functionally equivalent to extreme forgery or major theft, because destroying a will completely obliterates the legal and financial rights of the intended heirs. [Source: Section 343, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 344: Falsification of accounts

Q: What is the penalty for an employee who cooks the books or alters company accounting records to hide fraud?
A: If a clerk, officer, or servant willfully and with intent to defraud falsifies, destroys, alters, or makes false entries in their employer's books, accounts, or electronic records, they can be punished by up to seven years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 344, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Falsification of accounts

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 344: Falsification of accounts

Q: How does Section 344 of BNS 2023 address the falsification of accounts by employees?
A: Section 344 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 7 years imprisonment or a fine on any clerk/servant/officer who willfully and with intent to defraud destroys, alters, falsifies, or makes false entries in their employer's books, electronic records, or accounts. [Source: Section 344, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Falsification of accounts

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 344: Falsification of accounts

Q: An accountant at a mid-sized company is embezzling cash. To hide the missing money, she logs into the corporate accounting software and deliberately deletes several large transaction records and alters others to balance the ledger. What is her offence?
A: Because she, acting in the capacity of a clerk, willfully and with intent to defraud falsified and altered an electronic record belonging to her employer, she is punishable under Section 344 with imprisonment up to seven years. [Source: Section 344, BNS 2023]

A: No, the Explanation states that it is sufficient to allege a "general intent to defraud without naming any particular person intended to be defrauded or specifying any particular sum of money... or any particular day." [Source: Section 344, BNS 2023]
