A: No, because the section strictly requires that the alteration or false entry be made "wilfully, and with intent to defraud." A genuine clerical error lacks criminal intent. [Source: Section 344, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 345: Property mark

Q: What is a "property mark" and what is the penalty for using a fake one to mislead people about who owns an item?
A: A property mark is a mark used to denote that movable property belongs to a specific person. Using a false property mark on goods or packages to make people believe they belong to someone else is punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine, unless proven it was without intent to defraud. [Source: Section 345, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 345: Property mark

Q: How does Section 345 of BNS 2023 define and penalize false property marks?
A: Section 345 of BNS 2023 defines a property mark as a mark denoting ownership of movable property. Using a false property mark to deceptively indicate belonging to another person is punishable by up to 1 year imprisonment or a fine, unless the accused proves no intent to defraud. [Source: Section 345, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 345: Property mark

Q: A local manufacturer makes low-quality leather bags and stamps them with the distinct, registered logo of a famous luxury designer to trick customers into thinking the bags are genuine items from that designer. What is his offence?
A: Because he marked movable property in a manner reasonably calculated to cause it to be believed that the goods belonged to a person to whom they did not belong, he used a false property mark and is punishable under Section 345 with up to one year in prison. [Source: Section 345, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 345: Property mark

Q: Who bears the burden of proof regarding the "intent to defraud" under this section?
A: The section shifts the burden slightly to the accused, stating that whoever uses a false property mark shall be punished "unless he proves that he acted without intent to defraud." [Source: Section 345, BNS 2023]

A: No, because if they can prove that they "acted without intent to defraud" and it was merely an administrative accident, they are exempt from punishment under this section. [Source: Section 345, BNS 2023]

A: Removing, destroying, defacing, or adding to a property mark with the intent or knowledge that it will likely cause injury to any person is punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 346, BNS 2023]

A: Section 346 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 year imprisonment or a fine on whoever removes, destroys, defaces, or adds to a property mark, intending or knowing it is likely to cause injury to any person. [Source: Section 346, BNS 2023]

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 347: Counterfeiting a property mark

Q: What is the penalty for directly counterfeiting another person's or the government's property mark?
A: Counterfeiting a property mark used by another person is punishable by up to two years in prison. If the counterfeited mark is one used by a public servant to denote quality, origin, or exemption, the penalty increases to up to three years. [Source: Section 347, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Counterfeiting a property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 347: Counterfeiting a property mark

Q: How does Section 347 of BNS 2023 address the counterfeiting of property marks?
A: Section 347 of BNS 2023 penalizes counterfeiting a property mark used by another person with up to 2 years imprisonment. Counterfeiting a mark used by a public servant (e.g., to denote quality or origin), or using such a fake mark, carries up to 3 years imprisonment. [Source: Section 347, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Counterfeiting a property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 347: Counterfeiting a property mark

Q: A farmer makes a fake stamp identical to the official government agricultural inspector's stamp. He stamps his own sub-standard wheat bags to make buyers think they passed the government quality check. What is his offence?
A: Because he counterfeited a mark used by a public servant to denote that property is of a particular quality, he is punishable under Section 347(2) with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 347, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Counterfeiting a property mark

A: Yes, sub-section (2) explicitly penalizes anyone who "uses as genuine any such mark knowing the same to be counterfeit," making the knowing use just as punishable (up to 3 years) as the creation. [Source: Section 347, BNS 2023]

A: The consequence is that the law provides extra protection to government certifications (like safety, quality, or tax-exempt stamps), recognizing that faking public seals undermines state authority and endangers public welfare more broadly than private trademark infringement. A: Making or possessing any die, plate, or instrument intended to counterfeit a property mark, or possessing a fake property mark to falsely claim ownership of goods, is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 348, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or possession of any instrument for counterfeiting a property mark

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 348: Making or possession of any instrument for counterfeiting a property mark

A: Section 348 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment or a fine on whoever makes or possesses any die/plate/instrument for counterfeiting a property mark, or possesses a property mark to falsely denote ownership of goods. [Source: Section 348, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making or possession of any instrument for counterfeiting a property mark

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 348: Making or possession of any instrument for counterfeiting a property mark

A: Because he had in his possession a die and instrument for the purpose of counterfeiting a property mark, he is punishable under Section 348 with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 348, BNS 2023]

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 349: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

Q: What is the penalty for selling or stocking goods that have fake property marks or brand logos?
A: Selling, exposing, or possessing for sale goods with a counterfeit property mark is punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine, unless the seller can prove they took precautions, had no reason to suspect the fake, and cooperated with authorities. [Source: Section 349, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 349: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

Q: How does Section 349 of BNS 2023 penalize selling goods with counterfeit marks?
A: Section 349 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 year imprisonment or a fine on whoever sells or possesses for sale goods with counterfeit property marks, unless the accused proves they took reasonable precautions, had no reason to suspect the forgery, and provided all information about their supplier. [Source: Section 349, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 349: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

Q: A street vendor is caught selling cheap plastic sunglasses bearing the counterfeit logo of an expensive designer brand. He refuses to tell the police where he bought them. What is his penalty?
A: Because he sold goods with a counterfeit property mark and failed to give all information in his power regarding his supplier (failing the defense under clause b), he is punishable under Section 349 with imprisonment up to one year. [Source: Section 349, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 349: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

Q: Can a shop owner avoid punishment if they genuinely didn't know the goods were counterfeit?
A: Yes, but the burden of proof is on them. They must prove that they took reasonable precautions, had no reason to suspect the mark was fake at the time, and that they gave prosecutors all information about where they got the goods. [Source: Section 349, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 349: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

Q: A consumer buys a counterfeit designer purse from a market, knowing it's fake, and keeps it in her closet for personal use. Is she guilty under Section 349?
A: No, the section specifically targets whoever "sells, or exposes, or has in possession for sale" counterfeit goods. Mere possession for personal use does not trigger this offence. [Source: Section 349, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 349: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

Q: What is the consequence of placing the burden on the seller to prove their innocence regarding the supplier?
A: The consequence is that it heavily disincentivizes retailers from turning a blind eye to shady suppliers. To legally protect themselves, vendors are forced to maintain supply chain transparency and cooperate with law enforcement in tracking down the actual counterfeit manufacturers. [Source: Section 349, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Selling goods marked with a counterfeit property mark

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 350: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

Q: What is the penalty for putting a false label on a package to lie about what's inside or its quality?
A: Making a false mark on a package or receptacle to trick people into believing it contains goods it doesn't, or that the goods are of a different nature or quality, is punishable by up to three years in prison or a fine, unless done without intent to defraud. [Source: Section 350, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 350: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

Q: How does Section 350 of BNS 2023 address false marks on receptacles?
A: Section 350 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 years imprisonment or a fine on whoever makes or uses a false mark on a package/receptacle to deceptively indicate its contents, nature, or quality, unless they prove they acted without intent to defraud. [Source: Section 350, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 350: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

Q: A company packages cheap synthetic oil into metal drums and stamps the drums with the industry-standard mark for "100% Pure Organic Olive Oil," intending to sell them at a premium. What is their offence?
A: Because they made a false mark upon a receptacle containing goods to make people believe the goods are of a nature/quality different from the real nature, they are punishable under Section 350(1) with imprisonment up to three years. [Source: Section 350, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 350: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

Q: If a person simply uses a deceptively marked box that someone else created, without making the mark themselves, are they liable?
A: Yes, sub-section (2) states that whoever "makes use of any false mark in any manner prohibited under sub-section (1)" shall be punished exactly as if they had made the mark themselves. [Source: Section 350, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 350: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

Q: A family reuses an old "Premium Coffee" tin to store sewing supplies in their home, and a guest mistakenly opens it expecting coffee. Did the family violate Section 350?
A: No, because reusing a container for personal storage at home is done "without intent to defraud" anyone. [Source: Section 350, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 350: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing false marks on receptacles regarding the nature or quality of goods?
A: The consequence is that it protects consumers and public servants (like customs or tax inspectors) from widespread packaging fraud, ensuring that labels accurately reflect the contents and safety of sealed commercial goods. [Source: Section 350, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Making a false mark upon any receptacle containing goods

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 351: Criminal intimidation

Q: What is criminal intimidation, and what happens if someone threatens to kill you or burn your house down?
A: Criminal intimidation is threatening someone with injury to their person, reputation, or property to cause alarm or force them to do something. It is punishable by up to two years in prison. If the threat involves death, grievous hurt, arson, or imputing unchastity to a woman, the penalty increases to up to seven years. [Source: Section 351, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal intimidation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 351: Criminal intimidation

Q: How does Section 351 of BNS 2023 define and penalize criminal intimidation?
A: Section 351 of BNS 2023 defines criminal intimidation as threatening injury to person, property, or reputation to cause alarm or coerce action, punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment. Aggravated threats (e.g., death, arson, unchastity) carry up to 7 years. Anonymous threats carry an additional 2 years. [Source: Section 351, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal intimidation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 351: Criminal intimidation

Q: A man sends an anonymous letter to a local politician threatening to publish a fabricated scandal about the politician's deceased father unless the politician drops out of the election. What is his specific penalty?
A: Because he committed criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication, he is punishable under Section 351(4) with up to two additional years on top of the base penalty, and the threat to a deceased relative's reputation is explicitly covered by the Explanation. [Source: Section 351, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal intimidation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 351: Criminal intimidation

Q: If someone threatens to ruin the reputation of your deceased grandmother, does that count as a threat to "you"?
A: Yes, the Explanation clarifies that "A threat to injure the reputation of any deceased person in whom the person threatened is interested, is within this section." [Source: Section 351, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal intimidation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 351: Criminal intimidation

Q: A creditor tells a debtor, "If you don't pay me back by Friday, I will file a perfectly legal civil lawsuit against you." Is the creditor guilty of criminal intimidation?
A: No, because threatening to take lawful legal action is not threatening an illegal "injury," nor is it forcing the person to do an act "which he is not legally bound to do" (since he is legally bound to pay his debts). [Source: Section 351, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal intimidation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 351: Criminal intimidation

Q: What is the consequence of imposing an additional penalty for anonymous threats?
A: The consequence is that it deters cowards and cyberbullies from leveraging the terror of the unknown to harass victims, recognizing that an untraceable threat causes significantly more psychological distress and alarm. [Source: Section 351, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Criminal intimidation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 352: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

Q: What is the penalty for deliberately insulting someone to start a fight or riot?
A: Intentionally insulting someone to provoke them, knowing it is likely to cause them to break the public peace or commit an offence, is punishable by up to two years in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 352, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 352: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

Q: How does Section 352 of BNS 2023 penalize intentional insults?
A: Section 352 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 2 years imprisonment or a fine on whoever intentionally insults someone, giving them provocation while intending or knowing it is likely to cause them to break the public peace or commit an offence. [Source: Section 352, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 352: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

Q: A protestor intentionally hurls deeply offensive slurs at a rival group's leader during a tense street rally, specifically hoping the leader will throw a punch and start a riot. Even if the leader ignores him, what is the protestor's offence?
A: Because he intentionally insulted the leader intending to give provocation that he knew was likely to cause a breach of the public peace, he is punishable under Section 352 with imprisonment up to two years. [Source: Section 352, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 352: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

Q: Does a fight actually have to break out for the person hurling insults to be punished?
A: No, the offence is complete upon intentionally giving the insult and provocation, "intending or knowing it to be likely" that it will cause a breach of peace, regardless of whether the victim actually snaps and commits violence. [Source: Section 352, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 352: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

Q: A comedian roasts a willing participant during a private comedy club show. The participant finds a joke tasteless but doesn't get violent. Is the comedian guilty under Section 352?
A: No, because in the context of a consensual comedy roast, the comedian does not intend or know it to be likely that the insult will provoke the participant to "break the public peace, or to commit any other offence." [Source: Section 352, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 352: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

Q: What is the legal consequence of criminalizing "fighting words" and intentional provocation?
A: The consequence is that the law intervenes to prevent street violence and riots at the verbal stage, punishing the agitator who sparks the conflict rather than only punishing the person who physically reacts to extreme provocation. [Source: Section 352, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 353: Statements conducing to public mischief

Q: What is the penalty for spreading fake news or rumors designed to cause riots, mutiny, or hatred between communities?
A: Making or circulating false statements, rumors, or alarming news (including online) intending to cause military mutiny, public panic, or incite hatred between different religious, racial, or linguistic groups is punishable by up to three years in prison. If done in a place of worship, the penalty increases to up to five years. [Source: Section 353, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements conducing to public mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 353: Statements conducing to public mischief

Q: How does Section 353 of BNS 2023 regulate statements causing public mischief?
A: Section 353 of BNS 2023 penalizes making/circulating false statements/rumors intended to cause military mutiny, public alarm, or inter-community hatred with up to 3 years imprisonment. If committed in a place of worship, the punishment extends to 5 years. A good-faith belief in the truth of the statement is an exception. [Source: Section 353, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements conducing to public mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 353: Statements conducing to public mischief

Q: A provocateur creates a fake video claiming a specific linguistic community is planning a terror attack, and he broadcasts it inside a crowded temple during a festival to incite immediate violence against that community. What is his penalty?
A: Because he circulated false information to promote feelings of hatred between linguistic groups, and did so in a place of worship, he is punishable under Section 353(3) with imprisonment up to five years and a fine. [Source: Section 353, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements conducing to public mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 353: Statements conducing to public mischief

Q: If a journalist publishes an alarming report about a potential riot, but genuinely believes her reliable sources, is she guilty?
A: No, the Exception explicitly states that it is not an offence if the person has "reasonable grounds for believing that such statement... is true and makes, publishes or circulates it in good faith and without any such intent as aforesaid." [Source: Section 353, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements conducing to public mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 353: Statements conducing to public mischief

Q: A citizen posts a true, verified news article about a tragic event that naturally causes some public alarm, but adds no false information or inciteful commentary. Are they guilty under Section 353?
A: No, the section specifically targets any "statement, false information, rumour, or report" circulated with the malicious intent to cause mutiny, panic, or incite hatred, not the good-faith sharing of verified facts. [Source: Section 353, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements conducing to public mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 353: Statements conducing to public mischief

Q: What is the consequence of explicitly including "electronic means" in this section?
A: The consequence is that it empowers authorities to swiftly combat the viral spread of weaponized disinformation and hate speech on social media platforms, which can instantly trigger mass panics or communal riots across the country. [Source: Section 353, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Statements conducing to public mischief

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 354: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

Q: What is the penalty for forcing someone to do something by threatening them with curses or "Divine displeasure"?
A: Forcing or trying to force someone to do something (or stop doing something) by making them believe they will become the target of Divine displeasure (like a curse or religious condemnation) if they don't comply is punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine. [Source: Section 354, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 354: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

Q: What does Section 354 of BNS 2023 prohibit regarding Divine displeasure?
A: Section 354 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 1 year imprisonment or a fine on whoever voluntarily induces someone to act or omit an act by threatening that refusal will render them an object of Divine displeasure through some act of the offender (e.g., sitting dharna, threatening self-harm). [Source: Section 354, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 354: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

Q: A cult leader tells a follower that unless the follower signs over the deed to his house, the leader will perform a ritual suicide on the follower's doorstep, bringing a generational curse upon the follower's family. What is the leader's offence?
A: Because he attempted to cause a person to do an act he is not legally bound to do by inducing him to believe he would be rendered an object of Divine displeasure, he is punishable under Section 354 with imprisonment up to one year. [Source: Section 354, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 354: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

Q: Does this section cover a priest simply telling a congregation that skipping prayers is a sin?
A: No, it specifically targets inducing a person by threatening that they will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure "by some act of the offender" (like sitting dharna or self-harm) to coerce them into doing something they aren't legally bound to do. [Source: Section 354, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 354: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

Q: A person warns their friend that smoking is bad for their health and might anger God, hoping the friend will quit. Is this a crime?
A: No, because giving general religious or moral advice without threatening a coercive "act of the offender" to bring down Divine wrath does not constitute the specific criminal intimidation outlined in this section. [Source: Section 354, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 354: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

Q: What is the consequence of criminalizing threats of Divine displeasure?
A: The consequence is that it protects vulnerable individuals from extreme psychological extortion and religious blackmail, recognizing that threats of spiritual ruin or curses can be just as coercive as threats of physical violence in highly religious societies. [Source: Section 354, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Act caused by inducing person to believe that he will be rendered an object of Divine displeasure

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 355: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

Q: What is the penalty for being drunk and disorderly in public?
A: Appearing in a public place (or trespassing) while intoxicated and causing annoyance to others is punishable by simple imprisonment up to twenty-four hours, a fine up to one thousand rupees, or community service. [Source: Section 355, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 355: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

Q: How does Section 355 of BNS 2023 handle public misconduct by intoxicated persons?
A: Section 355 of BNS 2023 states that whoever, in a state of intoxication, appears in public or trespasses and conducts themselves in a manner causing annoyance to any person, shall be punished with simple imprisonment up to 24 hours, a fine up to 1,000 rupees, or community service. [Source: Section 355, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 355: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

Q: A man gets heavily intoxicated at a bar, stumbles out onto a busy public sidewalk, and starts loudly singing off-key, blocking pedestrian traffic and severely annoying passing families. What is his penalty?
A: Because he appeared in a public place in a state of intoxication and caused annoyance to others, he is punishable under Section 355 with simple imprisonment up to 24 hours, a fine up to 1,000 rupees, or community service. [Source: Section 355, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 355: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

Q: If a person gets drunk inside their own soundproof private home and goes to sleep without bothering anyone, are they breaking this law?
A: No, the offence specifically requires appearing "in any public place, or in any place which it is a trespass in him to enter," and conducting himself to "cause annoyance to any person." Private, non-disruptive intoxication is not covered. [Source: Section 355, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 355: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

Q: A person taking medically prescribed sedatives becomes unexpectedly disoriented and rests quietly on a public park bench without annoying anyone. Are they guilty under Section 355?
A: No, because even if they are in a state of intoxication in public, they did not conduct themselves "in such a manner as to cause annoyance to any person." [Source: Section 355, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 355: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

Q: What is the consequence of adding "community service" as a punishment option for public intoxication?
A: The consequence is that the justice system can focus on rehabilitation and restitution for minor nuisance offences, keeping jails free from non-violent intoxicated individuals while still imposing a meaningful penalty that benefits society. [Source: Section 355, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Misconduct in public by a drunken person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 356: Defamation

Q: What is defamation, and what is the penalty for it?
A: Defamation is making or publishing false statements, signs, or representations intending to harm someone's reputation. It is punishable by simple imprisonment up to two years, a fine, or community service. [Source: Section 356, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 356: Defamation

Q: How does Section 356 of BNS 2023 define and penalize defamation?
A: Section 356 of BNS 2023 defines defamation as making/publishing imputations (via words, signs, representations) intending to harm a person's reputation. It penalizes defamation, as well as printing or selling defamatory matter, with simple imprisonment up to 2 years, a fine, or community service. It includes 10 exceptions for truthful public-good statements, good-faith opinions, and authorized censures. [Source: Section 356, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 356: Defamation

Q: A newspaper editor knowingly publishes a fabricated story claiming a local doctor deliberately poisoned patients, intending to ruin the doctor's practice. What is his offence?
A: Because he made and published an imputation intending to harm the doctor's reputation, and it does not fall under any exceptions, he is guilty of defamation and punishable under Section 356(2) with simple imprisonment up to two years. [Source: Section 356, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 356: Defamation

Q: Can a person be charged with defamation for making a statement about someone who is already dead?
A: Yes, Explanation 1 states that imputing anything to a deceased person may amount to defamation if it would have harmed their reputation if alive, and is intended to be hurtful to the feelings of their family or relatives. [Source: Section 356, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 356: Defamation

Q: A witness testifies in open court, accusing the defendant of fraud. Is the witness guilty of defamation?
A: No, Exception 8 protects those who prefer an accusation in good faith to lawful authorities, and Exception 4 protects true reports of court proceedings, ensuring judicial functions are not hindered by defamation claims. [Source: Section 356, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 356: Defamation

Q: What is the consequence of adding "community service" as a punishment option for defamation in BNS 2023?
A: The consequence is that it offers a restorative justice alternative to imprisonment for speech-related offences, allowing offenders to make amends to society rather than burdening the prison system for reputational harms. [Source: Section 356, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Defamation

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 357: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

Q: What happens if a hired caretaker legally abandons an infant or a severely disabled person they were paid to look after?
A: If a person is bound by a lawful contract to care for someone who is helpless (due to youth, mental illness, or disease) and voluntarily fails to do so, they can be punished with up to three months in prison or a fine up to five thousand rupees. [Source: Section 357, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 357: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

Q: How does Section 357 of BNS 2023 address the abandonment of helpless persons by contracted caretakers?
A: Section 357 of BNS 2023 imposes up to 3 months imprisonment or a fine up to 5,000 rupees on whoever, being bound by a lawful contract to attend to a helpless person (due to youth, unsoundness of mind, or disease), voluntarily omits to do so. [Source: Section 357, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 357: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

Q: A live-in nurse signs a contract to provide 24/7 care for a bedridden elderly man with dementia. One night, the nurse simply walks out to attend a party, leaving the man completely alone and unable to feed himself. What is her offence?
A: Because she was bound by a lawful contract to supply the wants of a person who is helpless by reason of disease and bodily weakness, and voluntarily omitted to do so, she is punishable under Section 357 with imprisonment up to three months. [Source: Section 357, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 357: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

Q: Does this section apply to a passerby who sees a lost child crying but doesn't stop to help?
A: No, the section explicitly applies only to whoever is "bound by a lawful contract to attend on or to supply the wants" of the helpless person. A random passerby has no contractual duty of care. [Source: Section 357, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 357: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

Q: A contracted caretaker suffers a sudden, severe heart attack and collapses, leaving their disabled patient unattended for hours. Are they guilty under Section 357?
A: No, because their failure to attend on the patient was due to a medical emergency, not because they "voluntarily omits so to do." [Source: Section 357, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 357: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

Q: What is the legal consequence of criminalizing the breach of a civil contract in this specific context?
A: The consequence is that the law elevates a standard breach of contract into a criminal offence when human life and basic survival are at stake, recognizing that abandoning a helpless person causes immediate, life-threatening harm that civil damages cannot adequately address. [Source: Section 357, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Breach of contract to attend on and supply wants of helpless person

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 358: Repeal and savings

Q: What does the BNS 2023 mean when it says the Indian Penal Code is "repealed"? Does it mean old criminals go free?
A: No, old criminals do not go free. While the Indian Penal Code (IPC) of 1860 is repealed, the "savings" clause ensures that any crimes committed, investigations started, or liabilities incurred under the old IPC are still prosecuted and punished exactly as if the IPC was still in effect. [Source: Section 358, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Repeal and savings

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 358: Repeal and savings

Q: What is the legal function of Section 358 of BNS 2023?
A: Section 358 of BNS 2023 explicitly repeals the Indian Penal Code (1860). However, its savings clauses protect the validity of previous operations, accrued rights/liabilities, and ongoing investigations/proceedings, which continue as if the IPC were not repealed. [Source: Section 358, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Repeal and savings

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 358: Repeal and savings

Q: A man committed a robbery in 2021 when the IPC was in force, but the police only gathered enough evidence to arrest him in 2025 after the BNS took effect. Under which law is he prosecuted?
A: Because the offence was committed before the repeal, sub-section (2)(c) and (e) ensure that the penalty and legal proceedings are instituted and enforced as if the IPC had not been repealed, meaning he is prosecuted under the old IPC. [Source: Section 358, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Repeal and savings

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 358: Repeal and savings

Q: If a new investigation procedure is introduced in the BNS, how are actions taken under the old IPC treated?
A: Sub-section (3) provides that anything done or action taken under the old IPC shall be "deemed to have been done or taken under the corresponding provisions of this Sanhita," ensuring a smooth administrative transition. [Source: Section 358, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Repeal and savings

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 358: Repeal and savings

Q: Does the repeal completely wipe out the IPC from the legal history of India?
A: No, sub-section (4) explicitly maintains the general application of section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which guarantees that the repeal of an act does not revive anything not in force or affect the previous operation of the repealed enactment. [Source: Section 358, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Repeal and savings

content:
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS) - Section 358: Repeal and savings

Q: What is the consequence of having a detailed "Repeal and savings" section at the end of the BNS 2023?
A: The consequence is that it provides a stable legal bridge during the transition from the colonial-era penal code to the new Sanhita, preventing a catastrophic legal vacuum where past offenders could escape justice on a technicality of changing statutes. [Source: Section 358, BNS 2023]

metadata.section_title: Repeal and savings
